INTRODUCTION 
 
I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, 
Tourism and Culture, having been authorized by the Committee to present on its behalf, do 
hereby present this Three Hundred Sixty Third Repor t on the Action Taken by the 
Government on the recommendations/ observations of the Committee contained in its Three 
Hundred Twenty-Fourth Report on the subject “Issues  relating to Untraceable Monuments 
and Protection of Monuments in India”. 
2. The Three Hundred Twenty-Fourth Report  of the Department-related Parliamentary 
Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and Cultur e was presented to the Hon’ble 
Chairman, Rajya Sabha on 15 th  June, 2022 and thereafter was presented to the Par liament on 
the 8th  December, 2022.  
3.  The Action Taken Replies on the recommendations  of the Committee contained in its 
Three Hundred Twenty-Fourth Report were received fr om the Ministry of Culture on 4 th  
October, 2023. 
4. The Committee considered and adopted the Report in its meeting held on the 6 th  
December, 2023.   
 
 
(V. Vijayasai Reddy)

The Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Transport, Tourism and Culture deals with the Actio n Taken by the Ministry of Culture on 
the recommendations/observations as contained in it s Three Hundred Twenty Fourth Report 
on ‘Issues relating to Untraceable Monuments and Pr otection of Monuments in India’ which 
was presented to both the Houses of Parliament on 8th  December, 2022.   
2.        The Action Taken Replies were received fr om the Ministry on 4 th  October, 2023 in 
respect of all the observations/ recommendations co ntained in the Report. The replies have 
been categorized as follows:-

been accepted by the Committee:

Total: 8  
  
Chapter-IV:  
Recommendations/Observations in respect of which th e final replies of the Ministry 
are still awaited: 
Paragraph Nos.: 9, 38, 41, 42, 43.4.3, 43.5.3, 43.6.3, 43.7.3, 43.8.3, 43.9.3, 43.11.3, 
43.11.4, 43.12.3, 43.14.3  
Total: 14  
  
  
  
  
  
  
 REPORT

2 
 
Chapter I  
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY 
THE MINISTRY  
  
Recommendation/Observation  
1. The Committee acknowledges the steps taken by AS I to retrace the monuments that 
were deemed to be missing by CAG in its 2013 Perfor mance Audit but feels that the same 
reflects at the questionable state of protection and preservation of monuments, with ASI being 
unaware of the physical untraceability of several o f the Centrally Protected Monuments 
under its ambit.  The Committee recommends that the  ASI immediately undertake a survey of 
the remaining CPMs which were not inspected in the CAG Audit survey and ascertain 
whether there are any other missing monuments in th e country apart from the 24 monuments 
of the original survey.  The Committee further reco mmends that a physical survey of all the 
Centrally Protected Monuments must mandatorily be c arried out by ASI from time to time as 
per a fixed time schedule. Digital log books may be  maintained which may contain textual 
and photographic/video record of the state of physi cal preservation of the monument, exact 
location coordinates and clearly demarcated prohibited and regulated areas in the vicinity of 
the monument. These digital records may be made eas ily accessible to the general public to 
avoid any ambiguities and details may also be published regarding the date on which the last 
survey was conducted, due date for the next survey and the contact details of the ASI officials 
in-charge of maintaining and protecting the monument.   
(Para 10)  
Reply of the Ministry  
1.1 The monuments and the sites has been frequently  inspected at the circle, Regional and 
headquarter level by the officers of the ASI. The w ork of the survey through the Total station 
and Photogrammetric is under process.   
1.2 For keeping all the data of a monument in one p lace, ASI is in the process of 
preparing a “Heritage App” and “Health Card’. Herit age app would be meant for keeping 
monument's record in one place including its year o f notification, area, ownership, 
archaeological significance, internal and external status of the monument and the scope will 
be of adding inspection record in the App. It also will be accessible to the general public. 
 
Assessment of security requirements at Centrally Protected Monuments 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
2. The Committee is concerned to note that out of t he 3693 Centrally Protected 
Monuments, security guards are posted at only 248 C PMs/sites/museums i.e. less than about 
6.7 percent of the total number of CPMs. The Commit tee notes with dismay that out of the 
total requirement of 7000 personnel for protection of Monuments, the Government could 
provide only 2578 security personnel at 248 locatio ns due to budgetary constraints. The 

3 
 
Committee observes that budgetary constraints shoul d not be an excuse for not providing 
security guards to protect our rich cultural herita ge. It is the bounden duty of the 
Government of the day to protect our cultural herit age sites. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that budget may be provided by the Gover nment to appoint 7000 personnel for 
protection of the Monuments or as per the study con ducted by IIT, Delhi. In view of this 
worrying state of affairs, the Committee is of the strong view that the budgetary allocation 
available with the Ministry/ASI for safeguarding our Centrally Protected Monuments needs a 
serious relook. The Committee recommends that the M inistry/ASI may conduct an urgent 
thorough assessment of the security requirements an d budgetary allocation required for the 
same and a strong case may be made to the Ministry of Finance requesting allocation of 
additional funds for this purpose so as to ensure a  basic state of protection for all Centrally 
Protected Monuments across the country to preserve them for generations to come. The 
Committee also recommends that the local Panchayats  and police may be involved in 
safeguarding the monuments and if necessary, the AM ASR Act may be amended in this 
regard.  
(Para 22)  
Reply of the Ministry  
2.1 In 2022, ASI signed an MoU with the Indian Inst itute of Technology, Delhi on 
collaboration for providing expertise in the field of security and surveillance on monuments, 
sites, museums, and offices. A dedicated team of ex perts from the partnered institution will 
visit centrally protected monuments and will furnis h an analysis report containing short, 
medium and long terms security challenges along with solutions. Thereupon a comprehensive 
security policy to combat various identified issues  faced at the CPMS will be drafted. 
Subsequently, the requirement of the funds may be i dentified and accordingly, the 
requirement will duly be placed. The recommendation s of the committee are duly noted for 
exploring feasibility. 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
3. The Committee takes note of the existing framewo rk and recommends that in the 
upcoming amendment of the AMASR Act being worked up on by the Ministry, strong 
provisions may be incorporated for fixing accountab ility of concerned Government officials 
to ensure that necessary steps are taken timely for  tackling encroachment of Centrally 
Protected Monuments. The concerned officials should  be liable to be prosecuted in case of 
gross negligence of their duties with regard to tac kling encroachment of CPMs. The 
Committee further recommends that the Ministry may examine the powers given to District 
Forest Officers (DFOs) under The Wildlife (Protecti on) Act, 1972 and consider granting 
similar powers to ASI officials in order to effecti vely curb the issue of encroachment of 
Centrally Protected Monuments.  
(Para 25)  
 

4 
 
Reply of the Ministry  
3.1 Amendment in the AMASR Act, 1958 is under consi deration. 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
4. The Committee notes that no proposal exists at p resent with ASI for empowering local 
bodies to provide security guards to the unprotecte d monuments. The Committee feels that 
given their proximity and cultural ties with local monuments, local bodies are best suited to 
look after the protection of historical monuments especially those which are not under the list 
of Centrally Protected Monuments (CPMs). Empowering  local bodies to provide security 
guards at such monuments for their protection can g o a long way in ensuring that these 
monuments are preserved in their present state for generations to come. The Committee, 
therefore, strongly recommends that provisions to e mpower the local bodies for the 
protection of historical monuments and to make them accountable may be incorporated in the 
amendment of the AMASR Act that is being worked upon by the Ministry.  
(Para 33)  
Reply of the Ministry  
4.1 Noted for implementation. 
  
Recommendation/Observation  
5. The Committee feels that there is a scope for us ing satellite imagery to monitor the 
Centrally Protected Monuments (CPMs) across the country for encroachment and any illegal 
construction activities in the prohibited and regul ated areas of the same. Satellite imagery 
should also be used to try and trace the monuments which are untraceable at present and to 
ensure that no existing CPMs become untraceable in the future. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that ASI may approach ISRO and, if feasi ble, sign a Memorandum of 
Understanding with ISRO to utilize ISRO satellite imagery for the above mentioned purposes.  
(Para 35)  
Reply of the Ministry  
5.1 Noted for implementation to monitor the central ly protected monuments for 
encroachment to trace the untraceable monuments. 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
6. The Committee may be apprised of detailed guidel ines, if any, issued by the 
Ministry/ASI under the AMASR Act in this regard.  
(Para 43.2.3)  
 

5 
 
Reply of the Ministry  
6.1 A policy for photographers to operate within th e premises of protected monuments 
has been notified in 2017. 
  
Recommendation/Observation  
7. The Committee is surprised to note the reply fur nished by the Ministry, after 9 years 
have passed since the CAG Report was laid before th e Parliament. The Committee may be 
apprised of the specific action taken by the Ministry in this regard, at the earliest.  
(Para 43.10.3)  
Reply of the Ministry  
7.1 In this context it is stated that Rule 8(d) of the AMASR Rules, 1959 specifies 
requirement of a licence from the ASI to undertake photography of a visitor by charging the 
fee. 
  
Recommendation/Observation  
8. The Committee recommends that fixed timelines sh ould be put in place for carrying 
out effective action on-ground to tackle encroachme nts at the earliest and any delays may 
immediately be taken up at higher levels. Accountab ility may be fixed on both Central/State 
officials for time-bound action for removal of encr oachment at Centrally Protected 
Monuments.  
(Para 43.13.3)  
Reply of the Ministry  
8.1 For the effective implementation of the removal  of the encroachments and authorised 
constructions/activities in and around the monument s, the provision will be included in the 
amendment of the AMASR ACT and Rule.       
  
  
 
 
  
  
  
 
 
  
  
  

6 
 
 Chapter II  
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT 
DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE REPLIES OF THE MINISTRY  
 
Recommendation/Observation  
1. The Committee further notes that out of the 92 m onuments declared “missing” by the 
CAG, 42 monuments have been identified due to effor ts made by the ASI and out of the 
remaining 50 monuments, 14 are affected by rapid ur banisation, 12 are submerged by 
reservoir/dams while the location of the remaining 24 is untraceable.  The Committee feels 
that the distinction made by the Ministry regarding  the monuments lost to 
urbanisation/reservoirs and 24 monuments which are untraceable is an academic distinction 
since monuments lost to urbanisation/reservoirs are  as irrecoverable as the ones which are 
presently untraceable with scant hope of being foun d in future.  Moreover, the fact that the 
ASI had been unable to prevent the loss of the 14 m onuments to urbanisation and 12 to 
reservoirs/dams and only located them after the stu dy by CAG suggests that the ASI had no 
cognisance of these monuments prior to the study. The number of monuments lost from public 
viewing must therefore be held to be 50 taking into  account those lost to urbanisation or 
reservoirs.  The ASI has assured that the remaining  42 of the 92 monuments exist physically 
but the Committee would like to know whether these monuments exist in their entirety and 
undamaged or whether the ASI has only managed to lo cate some remains and ruins of such 
monuments.   
(Para 11)  
Reply of the Ministry  
1.1 To ascertain the conservation status of these m onuments, they shall be again inspected 
through the field offices of ASI. 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
2. The Ministry has stated that there is no term ca lled “Missing Monuments” in the 
AMASR Act and the term only came into existence as it was used by the Audit team on their 
Report. The Committee opines that the AMASR Act pro vides for the preservation and 
protection of ancient historical monuments and it would have been inconsistent to include the 
concept of “Missing Monuments” in the Act.  That th e situation warrants the use of such 
phrases only serves to underline the apathy of the Ministry and ASI regarding the 
preservation of our historical monuments.  The Mini stry has also stated that the exercise of 
removing the untraceable monuments under Section 35  of the AMASR Act has not been 
initiated by the ASI as there are chances that some  of these monuments shall be traced out in 
near future. The Committee observes that Section 35  of the AMASR Act, 1958 has the 
provision to issue notification only for such CPMs which have as per the opinion of the 
Central Government have ceased to be of national im portance. The monuments which have 
become “untraceable” have become so due to official  apathy and may not have ceased to be 

7 
 
of national importance had they been existing.  The  situation of a “Missing Monument” 
cannot be automatically equated with loss of its hi storical importance.  The Committee 
recommends that the Untraceable Monuments may not b e removed from the list of Centrally 
Protected Monuments by taking recourse to Section 3 5 as that Section provides the exclusion 
only of such monuments which have in the opinion of the Central Government ceased to be of 
national importance.  In fact, there is the danger that in case of such removal, there would be 
no imperative to find the untraceable monument and it would be well and truly lost to 
posterity. Since untraceable monuments also cannot continue to be on the Protected list, the 
Committee recommends that the list of Untraceable M onuments may be maintained as such 
and if necessary, the AMASR Act may be amended to include this terminology.   
(Para 12)  
Reply of the Ministry  
2.1 The observation shall be taken into considerati on while amending the AMASR Act. 
  
Recommendation/Observation  
3. The Committee feels that a thorough review of th e AMASR Act in consultation with all 
stakeholders and State Governments is the need of t he hour. The Committee, therefore, 
appreciates the process initiated by the Ministry o f Culture to amend the AMASR Act. The 
Committee agrees with the view that having the same  limits for all monuments for prohibited 
area and regulated area for restricting/regulating construction-related activities near the 
monument, is not a practical approach as the requir ement for such limitations could vary a 
lot depending on various factors specific to each m onument. The Committee, therefore, feels 
that the upcoming amendment which provides for such  monument-specific prohibited and 
regulated areas is much needed and hopes that once the amendment is passed, all necessary 
steps are taken to ensure that the monument-specifi c limits are decided upon for each 
Centrally Protected Monument at the earliest. The C ommittee notes that the ASI would be 
surveying all 3693 monuments while delineating monu ment specific protected and regulated 
limits and desires that a Report of the survey may be submitted to the Committee. However, 
the provisions of the Act may be strictly adhered t o in terms of the prohibited areas around 
the monument and even Government officials violating the provisions should be prosecuted.  
(Para 17)  
Reply of the Ministry  
3.1 For dealing with the NOCs cases in the circles and RD offices, the google and Bhuvan 
maps, wherever possible to delineate, were created for  showing protected, prohibited and 
regulated limit of the monuments. Since ASI is work ing on the amendment of the AMASR 
Act accordingly the marking of prohibited, regulated and prohibited limits on the Survey map 
would be initiated. 
 
 

8 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
4. The Committee reiterates the following recommend ation made in para 39 of its 311 th  
Report on ‘Creation of Regulatory Framework for pro tection of Historical Sites and 
Monuments’:  
The Committee fails to see why a person living in t he Regulated Area of a CPM 
should be required to seek permission from the Comp etent Authority under the 
AMASR Rules for carrying out innocuous maintenance activities such as filling of 
cracks, whitewashing, replacement of windows etc. T he Committee feels that such 
uncalled-for interference makes lives harder for pe ople living nearby the monuments 
and could slowly cause feelings of anguish towards the monument itself. Given the 
large number of monuments across the country and th e limited budgetary resources 
available with the Government, it is pertinent that  people residing near the 
monuments are encouraged to look after the monument s and protect them. Besides, 
placing such unnecessary curbs and implementing the m is a wastage of limited 
Government resources and turns the focus away from where it should be - actually 
protecting and preserving the monument itself. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Ministry may undertake a thorou gh review of the AMASR Act 
and Rules and omit any provisions that provide for seeking permissions for minor 
works where the same is not actually needed and str eamline the process for applying 
for permission in case where the same is actually needed. Steps may urgently be taken 
to make it possible for the entire process for seek ing permission for construction 
activities in prohibited and regulated areas, to be  completed online so as to not cause 
any hassle to bona fide residents living near the monuments.  
(Para 18)  
Reply of the Ministry  
4.1 The Ministry of Culture in consultation with AS I is working on the amendment of the 
AMASR Act, and such issues shall be taken into consideration in the amendment of the act. 
  
Permitting Religious Activities in Religious Historical Monuments  
Recommendation/Observation  
5. The Committee feels that several historical monu ments across the country hold 
immense religious significance to a large number of  people and allowing 
pujas/worship/certain religious activities at such monuments can fulfill legitimate aspirations 
of the people. The Committee, therefore, recommends  that ASI may explore the possibility of 
permitting pujas/worship/certain religious activiti es at historical Centrally Protected 
Monuments of religious significance, subject to the  condition that it can be established that 
such activities would not have any detrimental effe ct on the state of conservation and 
preservation of the monument.  
(Para 40)  

9 
 
Reply of the Ministry  
5.1 Noted for exploring feasibility. In this regard , it is to submit that as per the policy 
decision revival of worship is not allowed where it  was not in vogue at the time of protection 
or abandoned since long. 
  
  
  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

10 
 
Chapter III  
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH REPLIES OF 
THE MINISTRY HAVE NOT BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE COMMITTEE  
  
Recommendation/Observation  
1. The Committee observes that the CAG audit had po inted out that the Ministry through 
the ASI had not conducted a comprehensive survey/re view to identify monuments which were 
of national importance for inclusion in the list of  CPMs.  Similarly, there were no efforts to 
identify those monuments which had lost the stature  of national importance over a period of 
time.  The Committee is dismayed to note that even a decade after the CAG Audit Report,  the 
Ministry and the ASI are yet to conduct a comprehen sive survey to identify monuments which 
are of national importance or of those which had lo st their stature of national importance. 
The Committee urges the Ministry and ASI to conduct  surveys to include monuments of 
national importance and also those which have lost their importance over time.  This would 
ensure that the resources of the Ministry and ASI a re utilised  in a justified manner for 
deserving monuments  and are not diverted to protec ting those which are no longer of 
national importance.  
(Para 13)  
Reply of the Ministry  
1.1 ASI is working on preparing the criteria for th e monuments for declaring them as a 
monument of national importance. On the basis of an cientness, architecture, art, history, 
science, religion, tradition, inscriptional value a nd incident and so on another merit of the 
monument and site, the criteria would be determined. On the basis of which the present list of 
the monument could also be assessed. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation  
1.2 The Committee reiterates its earlier position t hat the Ministry and ASI should 
conduct the survey for identifying monuments on pri ority, in a time-bound manner. 
Further, the details and criteria for classificatio n of monuments may also be furnished 
to the Committee.                                                                                                                        
                                                                                                                                                       
Recommendation/Observation  
2. The Committee further recommends that the Minist ry of Culture and ASI should 
undertake a survey of all the 3693 Centrally Protec ted Monuments to ensure that they are in 
existence and to provide adequate maintenance and protection.  
(Para 14)  
 
 

11 
 
Reply of the Ministry  
2.1 As stated in para 10 that the work of Survey is  in progress and monuments are 
frequently being inspected by the ASI officers. For regular maintenance, ASI is taking care of 
all the monuments and sites. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation  
2.2 The Committee further recommends that the surve y results must be placed in 
public domain and it must include data regarding ex penditure incurred on them and 
the problems in and around the monuments.  
 
Recommendation/Observation  
3. It has also come to the notice of the Committee that various important historical 
monuments and sites such as Rama Temple at Peddathu mbalam village, Adoni Taluka; 
Kethavaram Rock Arts and Belum Caves in Kurnool etc. which, although not under the list of 
Centrally Protected Monuments, are of high historical significance but devoid of any security 
guards and proper road connectivity. The Committee,  therefore, recommends that the 
Ministry may urgently make provisions for posting s ecurity guards at these sites and 
adequate measures may be taken for promotion of tou rism at the same, in coordination with 
the concerned Ministries/Departments. The Ministry of Culture may coordinate with the 
Ministry of Road Transport & Highways and State Pub lic Works Department to ensure 
proper road/highway connectivity to these important historical sites in order to allow tourists 
to reach these sites.  
(Para 23)  
Reply of the Ministry  
3.1 These three monuments/sites are already declare d protected by the State Government. 
Therefore, related actions are well within the juri sdiction of State Government (MoC may 
review the reply) 
  
Further Recommendation/Observation  
3.2 The Committee notes that the said monuments com e under the jurisdiction of 
the State Government. However, it is recommended th at the Ministry/ASI can persuade 
or work in coordination with the concerned State Go vernment to take required action 
in this instant case. Further, it is also suggested  that the Ministry/ASI may consider  
inclusion of these monuments in the list of Centrally Protected Monuments.  Decision  in 
this regard may also be communicated to the Committee.  
 
 
 

12 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
4. The Committee feels that State Level Co-ordinati on Committees are a necessary 
instrument for coordination between the Ministry of  Culture and respective State 
Governments for resolving important issues such as removal of encroachment of monuments. 
The Committee may be apprised of the number of Stat es where such State Level Co-
ordination Committee has not been formed so far and the steps taken by the Ministry in order 
to ensure the formation of these Co-ordination Committees.  
(Para 28)  
Reply of the Ministry  
4.1 So far State Level Co-ordination Committee is f ormed in 11 States (Assam, Bihar, 
Chattisgarh, J&K, Kerala, Meghalaya, Odisha, Puduch erry, Punjab, Rajasthan, Sikkim), 
attempts are being made to constitute the committees in rest of the states. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation  
4.2 The Committee reiterates that the process of fo rmation of the State Level Co-
ordination Committee in the remaining States must b e expedited. The State 
Governments should be persuaded to form this Commit tee without further delay within 
a stipulated period.  
  
Recommendation/Observation  
5. The Committee notes that a mere Rs. 3.33 crore b udgetary allocation has been made 
to ASI for the conservation and preservation of unp rotected monuments during the current 
financial year 2022-23. The Committee strongly feel s that this amount seems to be grossly 
insufficient given the large number of unprotected historical monuments in the country, as 
well as a large number of State Protected Monuments  which often face gross neglect by the 
respective State Governments. The Committee is of t he view that the protection and 
preservation of historical monuments other than tho se already under the protection of 
Central and State Governments, should also be looke d after by the Archaeological Survey of 
India, at least to a basic extent.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry 
may allocate a special budget for protection, prese rvation and restoration, wherever 
necessary, of unprotected/neglected historical monuments across the country.  
(Para 30)

5.1 The Ministry of Culture has allocated special b udget under budget sub-head 22.01.27

restoration of unprotected/neglected historical mon uments across the country and for this Rs. 
2.50 Crore provision is kept for the financial year  2023-24. This Scheme is continued from 
2013 onward.

conservation of the unprotected/neglected historical monuments.  
  
Vacancies in ASI  
Recommendation/Observation  
6. The Committee notes that since Monument Attendan ts are responsible for day to day

shortage as one of the reasons for its apathy in ma intaining monuments, it appears that the 
delay in filling up vacancies is one of the main re asons for the pathetic state of monuments in 
the country. The Committee recommends that vacancies of Monument Attendants and Guards 
should be filled up on a war footing so that none o f the CPMs is left unguarded and 
unmaintained. The Committee desires to be informed about the recruitment status of 
Monument Attendants. The Committee does not find an y reason that vacancies should be

higher levels may also be filled up at the earliest . The Committee recommends that the

appointing ex-servicemen to guard the monuments.

Action taken by the Ministry on certain recommendat ions made in the Report of the

1. The Committee notes that the 324th Report of the  Departmental Standing 
Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture, on "Is sues relating to Untraceable 
Monuments and Protection of Monuments in India", wa s forwarded to the Ministry of 
Culture for necessary action on 15 
th  June 2022.  The Ministry not only failed to send a n 
interim reply within the stipulated period of three  months but also failed to respond to 
the multiple reminders issued by the Secretariat th roughout 2022 and 2023. Further,

total of 35 recommendations as contained in the 324 th  Report, by 4 th  October, 2023, i.e.,

2. The Committee expresses its deep concern and disapp ointment at this apparent 
lack of seriousness, on the part of the Ministry, i n responding to the Committee’s 
recommendations addressing critical issues.  Disreg arding or trivializing the views of 
the Committee undermines the trust, credibility and  seriousness of the Ministry 
towards the development and preservation of the nat ion’s cultural heritage. The

 Recommendation/Observation

this sample of 1655 monuments.  The Committee has p erused the list of 24 untraceable 
monuments submitted by the Ministry and it is pertu rbed to find that the Barakhamba 
Cemetery in the very heart of the Capital city is a mong the untraceable monuments.  If even 
monuments in the Capital city cannot be maintained properly, it does not bode well for 
monuments in remote places in the country. Upon que ry of the Committee, the Ministry has 
informed that no further study of the remaining mon uments has been undertaken for 
ascertaining how many more monuments are missing fr om the total number of 3693 CPMs.  
The Committee is perturbed to note that having foun d out that at least 24 monuments are

(Para 9)

yet inoperative and a general lack of information o n the work of the ASI as well as the built

cultural heritage of India.  The Committee recommen ds that the ASI highlight the CPMs and

deterrent to buyers who may otherwise not know that it is stolen property.  
(Para 43.11.3)  
Recommendation/Observation  
3.12 The Committee notes that the numbers of antiqu ities retrieved are not even the tip of 
the iceberg in comparison to the huge number of ant iques smuggled out from country.  One 
of the reasons for the vulnerability of Indian anti ques for smuggling is the lack of database 
on the antiques in different parts of the country.  This drawback has not been rectified even 
after the CAG pointed it out nearly a decade before . The stolen idols and antiques are 
auctioned at auctions organized by global auction h ouses but again as pointed out by the 
CAG, the ASI never participates or collects informa tion on Indian antiques put on sale in 
global auctions as there is no explicit provision i n the AAT 1972.  The Antiquities Act also 
does not have any penal provisions which could be a  deterrent.  The Committee recommends 
the ASI and Ministry may give wide publicity to the  theft of antiquities as soon as it takes

(Para 43.11.4)

security guards to protect our rich cultural herita ge. It is the bounden duty of the

INTRODUCTION 
 
I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, 
Tourism and Culture, having been authorized by the Committee to present on its behalf, do 
hereby present this  Three Hundred Sixty-Fourth Report on the Action Taken by the 
Government on the recommendations/ observations of the Committee contained in its Three 
Hundred Forty-Third Report on Demands for Grants (2023-24) of Ministry of Tourism. 
2. The Three Hundred Forty-Third Report of the Department -related Parliamentary 
Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture was presented to the Parliament on 
the13th March, 2023. 
3.  The Action Taken Replies on the recommendations of the Committee contained in its 
Three Hundred Forty-Third Report were received from the Ministry of Tourism on 6th 
October, 2023.

selecting 25 tourist sites as pilot project for formation of a separate police unit in the

Recommendation/Observation 
10.      The Committee observes that the Ministry is planning to leverage India’s presidency

Promotion and Publicity scheme has not yet been approved and the Ministry can conduct 
only the crucial and unavoidable activities at this stage. The Committee feels that this would

has stated th at alternative methods of promotion are being used but has not specified the

Ministry should have closed down the overseas offices only after providing al ternate methods

promotional strategy, and a syn ergized campaign in association with the Travel Trade, State 
Governments and Indian Missions. The Government continuously engages with industry 
experts and other relevant stakeholders and take their suggestions and feedback for 
promotion of varied tourism products of India and attract tourist with specific interest and to

Indian Tou rism to the Tourism officers. Tourism officer in Indian Missions prepared a

Surrender of Savings  
Recommendation/Observation 
1.        The Committee observes that in the last three years, the allocation at the Revised 
Estimates stage is half of the Budgetary Estimates and the Actual Expenditure is even less. 
The utiliz ation percentage of the Ministry for the last two years i.e. 2020 -21 & 2021 -22 is 
only 89.85 & 82.89 respectively and for the FY 2022 -23 it is only 34.56% till 31st January 
2023.While expenditure in 2020 may be understandably low due to the pandemic, the s tatus 
in respect of 2021 and 2022 is no better. The utilization percentage of only 34.6% in 2022 -23 
is unacceptable. The Committee does not accept the reply of the Ministry that the change in 
procedure of release of funds was a factor in low utilization  of funds. The change in 
procedure was for all Ministries and other Ministries have managed to utilize  most of their 
funds by December, 2022. 
 (Para 15) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1      During the current financial year 2022 -23, the Ministry projected allocatio n of Rs. 
1543.61 Crores at RE stage against the BE allocation of Rs. 2,400.00 Crores.   Against the 
projection of Rs. 1543.61 crores, the Ministry of Finance allowed an allocation of Rs. 
1343.13 crores.   The projection at RE Stage was reduced by the Ministr y due to less 
expenditure in the first two quarters of the Financial year.   
1.2      The Ministry of Finance revised the procedure for release of funds under Central 
Sector and Centrally Sponsored Schemes.   Implementation of the revised procedure posed 
certain challenges like nominating Central Nodal Agencies (CNAs), Sub Agencies (SAs), 
selection of Banks, mapping of the CNAs Sub Agencies and the Banks on the Public 
Finance Management System portal, etc. which took considerable time for resolution 
resulting in low level of expenditure.   Further, the unspent balances lying with the 
Implementing Agencies were to be fully returned to the CNA's Account by all the 
Implementing Agencies.   Release of funds to the Implementing Agencies in respect of 
Schemes like Swadesh Darshan, PRASHAD, Assistance to Central Agencies and Assistance 
to Institutes of Hotel Management, Food Craft Institutes, etc. was not possible till the 
unspent balance lying with all the Implementing Agencies was returned to the Central Nodal 
Agencies‟ Account.   The implementing agencies took lot of time in returning the unspent 
balance, inspite of vigorous efforts by the Ministry. In the Month of September 2022, the 
Ministry of Finance slightly relaxed the condition of refunding unspent balances by all the 
Implementing Agencies to enable further release of fund under the any Scheme and allowed 

27 
 
release of funds to those implementing agencies which have returned the unspent 
balances.       
1.3      Another reason for lesser expenditure is the fact that  no new projects were sanctioned 
under Swadesh Darshan, which is the flagship Scheme of the Ministry, which consume major 
share of the Ministry‟s budget, as the Scheme was reviewed, and a revamped Scheme of SD 
2.0 was introduced.   Accordingly, the expendit ure under this Scheme was limited to the on -
going projects sanctioned under SD 1.0.   There is delay on the part of some of the State 
Governments in submitting requisite documents like Utilization Certificates, Completion 
Certificates, etc. despite regular interaction with the State Governments.  
  
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
1.4      The Committee notes that the Ministry of Tourism has cited reasons such as 
challenges and delays in implementation of revised procedure for release of funds by 
Ministry of Finance viz. nominating CNAs/SAs, selection of banks, mapping of CNAs/ 
SAs on PFMS, return of unspent balances by implementing agencies etc. which are 
primarily procedural in nature. The Committee is of the opinion that the Ministry 
should sort out the procedural issues which led to delays, so that funds are fully utilized 
in future.   
  
 Recommendation/Observation 
2.        The Committee further finds that the entire budget allocation of Rs. 2400 crores is 
under Revenue Head with nil allocation to Capi tal Head. The Ministry has submitted that a 
major portion of the outlay amounting to Rs.1742 crores is earmarked for development of 
infrastructure for tourism development and Rs. 242.00 crores for promotion and branding 
activities. For tourism infrastructu re Schemes, an amount of Rs, 1412.00 crores is allocated 
for Swadesh Darshan, Rs. 250.00 crores is kept for the Scheme of PRASHAD (Pilgrimage 
Rejuvenation and Spiritual and Heritage Augmentation Drive) and Rs 80 crores is allocated 
for Scheme for Assistance to Central Agencies for Tourism Infrastructure Development. 
(Para 17) 
3.        Much of the budgetary outlay is for development of infrastructure. Swadesh Darshan, 
the flagship scheme of the Ministry is focused on development of theme based infrastructur e. 
Infrastructure for all tourist amenities like creation of tourist information centre, reception 
centre, convention centres, cafeterias, beautification of tourist attractions are covered under 
this scheme. The Committee does not find it rational that tho ugh Capital assets are being 
created under the schemes of the Ministry, the entire expenditure is classified under Revenue. 
Revenue expenditure is short -term, recurring expenditure mostly pertaining to salaries, 
operating expenses, administrative costs etc . Due to its very nature, revenue expenditure 
cannot be reduced as the expenses such as salaries and wages are incurred irrespective of 
the activities carried out. The Committee finds however that for the last five years, the 
budgetary allocation of the Ministry has been halved at the Revised Estimates stage and even 

28 
 
this budget has remained unutilized. The Actual expenditure for the past five years has been 
much less than the budget allocated in Revised Estimates. 
(Para 18) 
4.        The Committee notes the submissions of the Ministry that though at the macro level, 
the budget is under Revenue Head, yet within the Schemes, there would be Object Heads 
pertaining to “Creation of Capital assets.” Under the two Major schemes, Swadesh Darshan 
and PRASHAD, ther e is no recurring expenditure on salary etc. These schemes are mainly 
meant for asset creation and only 5% funds are given for O&M (Operations and 
Maintenance). However, though only assets are being created under these schemes, the outgo 
of funds can be re duced depending on the progress of the projects and receipt of 
Utilization Certificates. 
(Para 19) 
5.        The Committee observes that creation of capital assets leads to value creation and 
generates future cash flows for the economy. Further, the multip lier effect of Capital 
expenditure is much more than that of the Revenue expenditure. In India, the multiplier effect 
of Capital expenditure made by the Central Government is estimated at 2.45 and for State 
Governments, it is around 2 while the multiplier effect of Revenue expenditure is only 0.99 
(RBI Bulletin, December, 2020) . Wrong classification therefore may not give the correct 
picture on total investment in infrastructure and may impact both the Index of Industrial 
Production and the GDP. The Committee notes that the classification as Revenue is arbitrary 
without following any valid criteria in case of various projects of Ministry of Tourism. The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry may take up the matter with the Ministry of Finance 
and submit a detailed explanation to the Committee.

16.1.1. Background  
Women should feel safe and most comfortable while travelling and enjoying tourist

the Committee would lik e to be apprised of the reason for the aforementioned 
discrepancy. 
 Recommendation/Observation 
19.      The Committee observes that the creation of tourism infrastructure by way of roads, 
cruise terminals, railway connectivity, and medical facilities has its multiplier effect in terms 
of overall economic growth and employment generation and acts as a catalyst to economic 
development of the country. The Commit tee desires to be appraised of the progress of work 
on the remaining 15 railway stations. The Committee also observes that the Ministry of 
Tourism during the last Demand for Grants had been pursuing the matter of road 
connectivity of 114 destinations under  MoRTH, respective State Governments and State 
PWDs. The Committee desires to be apprised of the progress in the matter. 
(Para 119) 
Reply of the Ministry 
19.1    Update regarding road connectivity of 114 destinations has not been received from 
MoRTH, State Governments or PWDs. The matter regarding early completion of the projects 
was taken up with Ministry of Railways in various meetings and the Task Force meeting held 
under the chairmanship of Secretary (T). Ministry of Railways has submitted the status of  the 
projects, which is at ANNEXURE I. 
  
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
19.2    The Committee recommends that the Ministry may proactively follow up with 
MoRTH and State Governments/PWDs and obtain the updated information regarding 
road connectivity of 114 destinations. 
  
Global Perspective – Comparison of India With Other Countries 
Recommendation/Observation 
20.      The Committee appreciates the various initiatives taken by the Ministry to promote 
tourism. However the Committee observes that the reimbursement of the SEIS (Service 
Exports from India Scheme) is probably the single largest issue raised most during the 
pandemic by country’s inbound trade as well as others in the tourism industry, like hotels, 
which benefited from the scheme. Under the SEIS Scheme the Government offered domestic 
exports duty credit scrips in the range of 5% to 7% of the net foreign exchange  earned 
depending upon the nature of services. These SEIS scrips could be used to pay import duty or 

43 
 
can be encashed by selling it to any importer. The Committee notes that for FY 2019-20, SEIS 
benefits were capped at Rs. 5 Cr and rates for eligible servic e categories were reduced 
across the board by 2 because of budgetary constraints imposed by the Ministry of Finance 
for implementing the Scheme. Now the SEIS Scheme has not been extended beyond FY 2019 -
20. 
(Para 127) 
Recommendation/Observation 
21.      The Committee observes that in view of the fact that the tourism sector was facing the 
crisis of the century, the Committee had recommended that the Ministry take up the SEIS rate 
reduction issue with the Ministry of Commerce to increase the rate of SEIS bene fits to 10% 
and extend the scheme for a further period of 2-3 years for enabling cost savings. 
(Para 128) 
Recommendation/Observation 
22.      The Committee notes that the tourism industry has not yet gained its pre -pandemic 
levels in India and many busines ses are struggling to recover their losses. The Committee 
observes that SEIS incentives enable Tour Operators to maintain some price parity vis -à-vis 
the competition. The Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation to the Ministry to 
again take up the matter with the Ministry of Commerce. 
(Para 129) 
Reply of the Ministry 
22.1    Hon‟ble Minister of Tourism has taken up the matter with Hon‟ble Finance Minister 
and Hon‟ble Minister of Commerce & Industry but the same has not been approved. 
  
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
22.2    The Committee observes that Service Exports for India Scheme (SEIS) despite 
being a vital scheme, has not been extended beyond FY 2019 -20. Further, the Ministry 
has stated that the matter regarding SEIS was taken up with Hon‟ ble Finance Minister 
and Hon‟ble Minister of Commerce & Industry but the same has not yet been 
approved. The Committee would like to be apprised of the reasons cited by the 
concerned Ministries for discontinuing SEIS. Further, the Committee reiterates its 
recommendation given in the 343 rd and 357 th Report on the SEI scheme in view of the 
fact that the tourism industry has not yet gained its pre -pandemic levels in India and 
many businesses are struggling to recover their losses.  
  
Recommendation/Observation 
23.      The Committee further observes that the Finance Act, 2020 which was announced just 
before the start of COVID -19 crisis, inter alia, had come up with the new insertion of Tax 
Collected at Source (TCS) provisions under Section 206C (1G)(a) of Incom e Tax Act, 1961 

44 
 
pertaining to TCS @ 5% on foreign remittance through Liberalized Remittance Scheme 
(LRS) and under Section 206C (1G)(b) pertaining to TCS@5% on the selling of overseas tour 
packages by tour operators. The Committee had recommended rollback of the provision for 
the reason that Indian Tour Operators are unable to match the prices offered for Outbound 
tours in comparison to Foreign Tour Service Providers due to additional burden of taxes 
which include GST and the newly inserted TCS provision. 
(Para 130) 
24.      The Committee observes that the TCS has now been increased from 5% to 20% which 
would be detrimental to the Outbound Tour businesses of Tour Operators. The Committee 
reiterates its earlier recommendation to roll back the TCS provision. 
(Para 131) 
Reply of the Ministry 
 24.1    Hon‟ble Minister of Tourism has taken up the matter with Hon‟ble Finance Minister 
and Hon‟ble Minister of Commerce & Industry.  
  
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
24.2    The Committee would like to be apprised about the status of the matter taken up 
with Ministry of Finance regarding increasing of TCS from 5% to 20% and would 
reiterate again its recommendation to roll back the TCS provision. 
  
E-Visa Scheme  
Recommendation/Observation 
25.      The Committee appreciates the initiatives taken by the Ministry to facilitate the issue 
of e -Visa. The Committee would also like to be informed about the initiative of “Visa at 
Your Doorstep”. 
(Para 148) 
Reply of the Ministry 
25.1    The matter has been taken up with the Ministry of Home Affairs.  
  
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
25.2    The Committee desires to know about the status of the matter taken up with the 
Ministry of Home Affairs regarding initiative of “Visa at Your Doorstep” scheme.

 Green and Sustainable Tourism 
Recommendation/Observation 
26.      The Committee asked the Ministry whether any roadmap has been formulated for 
promoting green and sustainable tourism and the steps taken so far to incentivize  green and 
sustainable practices in the tourism sector and the key challenges in this regard. The 
Committee also asked for details of the funds allocated and utilized  towards green and 
sustainable tourism in the last 5 years. 
(Para 162) 
Reply of the Ministry 
26.1    To position India as a preferred global destination for sustainable and responsible 
tourism. Ministry of Tourism has formulated National Strategy for Sustainable Tourism. 
Following strategic pillars have been identified for the development of sustainable tourism in 
the strategy document: - 
 Promoting Environmental Sustainability 
 Protecting Biodiversity 
 Promoting Economic Sustainability 
 Promoting Socio-Cultural Sustainability 
 Scheme for Certification of Sustainable Tourism 
 IEC and Capacity Building 
 Governance 
26.2    The Ministry of Tourism organized a National summit for developing Sustainable and 
Responsible Tourism Destination and Responsible Traveller Campaign in association with 
RTSOI and UNEP on 4th June, 2022 at New Delhi on eve of World Environment Day.  
  
26.3    In order to promote sustainable and responsible tourist destinations and promote 
sustainable tourism in the country, Ministry of Tourism in association with IITTM, UNEP 
and RTSOI organized five Regional Workshops covering all States/ UTs of the country. The 
summit and workshops saw participation from representatives from identified central 
Ministries, State Governments/ UT Administration and Industry Stakeholders. An estimated 
expenditure of Rs.56.4 lakh has been incurred on organizing these. 
  
26.4    Ministry of T ourism has now revamped its Swadesh Darshan scheme as Swadesh 
Darshan 2.0 (SD 2.0) with the objective to develop sustainable and responsible destinations 
following a tourist & destination centric approach.

 Further Recommendation/ Observation

about the details of fund allocation and utilization towards green and sustainable

 CHAPTER-II 
  
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT 
DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE REPLIES OF THE MINISTRY 
  
Development of Greenfield and Brownfield Airports and the Challenges thereof 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.        The Committee observes that the Government has granted in-principle approval for 21 
Greenfield Airport projects since 2008, which is a crucial step towards meeting the growing 
air traffic demand in the country. However, more Greenfield airports need to be developed to 
cater to the increasing demand and to achieve the vision laid out in the National Civil 
Aviation Policy, 2016 to enab le 30 crore domestic ticketing by 2022 and 50 crore by 2027. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should encourage more State 
Governments and private airport developers to propose Greenfield airport projects and to 
streamline its approval process to expedite the development of airports. 
 (Para 11) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1      Government of India (GoI) has formulated a Greenfield Airports (GFA) Policy, 2008 
for development of Greenfield airports in the country. As per the policy, if any d eveloper 
including the State Government desires to develop an airport, they are required to identify a 
suitable site and get the Pre-feasibility Study conducted for construction of airport and submit 
a proposal to the Central Government for 'Site Clearance' followed by 'In-Principle' approval.  
1.2      As per the request of Project Proponent(s), Airports Authority of India also assists and 
prepares Pre-feasibility Report, OLS Report, DPR etc. relating to development of Greenfield 
Airport. 
1.3      As on da te, under GFA Policy, 2008, 12 Greenfield airports viz. Durgapur in West 
Bengal, Shirdi and Sindhudurg in Maharashtra, Kannur in Kerala, Pakyong in Sikkim, 
Kalaburagi and Shivamogga in Karnataka, Orvakal (Kurnool) in Andhra Pradesh, Kushinagar 
in Uttar Pra desh, Itanagar in Arunachal Pradesh, Mopa in Goa and Rajkot in Gujarat have 
been operationalized. Further, Six more Greenfield Airports, viz. Noida(Jewar) in Uttar 
Pradesh, Navi Mumbai in Maharashtra, Vijayapura and Hassan in Karnataka, Dholera in 
Gujarat and Bhogapuram in Andhra Pradesh are under various stages of development.  
1.4      Further, Site Clearance for setting up Greenfield Airports at Mandi, Kottayam and Puri 
have recently been accorded. Moreover, applications for setting up Greenfield airport s at 
Doloo(Silchar), Kota and Raichur are under examination. 
  
  
  

10 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
2.        The Committee observes that the list of airports under planning or expansion includes 
several airports that are being developed under PPP mode. PPPs can  bring in private sector 
expertise and investment, which can help in accelerating the airport development process 
and improving operational efficiency. Therefore, the government should encourage more 
PPPs for airport development, especially for Greenfield airports. 
 (Para 14) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1      The Ministry agrees with the recommendations of the Committee and has encouraged 
development of new Airports by State Governments and Private partners. It can be seen that 
out of 21 'in principle'  approval granted by MoCA for setting up of 21 Greenfield airports 
across the country, Projects like Durgapur, Sindhudurg, Kannur, Mopa have been 
operationalized with Private investment or under PPP. Other Greenfield airports under 
development viz., Navi Mumbai, Noida (Jewar), Bhogapuram are also being executed under 
PPP mode. 
  
Recommendation/Observation 
3.        The Committee desires to know the number of airports with throughput above 1.5 
mppa which have an ASQ rating of less than 4.5 and number of airports with throughput less 
than 1.5 mppa which have an ASQ rating of less than 4.0 as on date. The Committee may be 
apprised of the steps being taken by AAI to upgrade the quality of services provided at each 
such airport with low ASQ ratings.  
(Para 17) 
Reply of the Ministry 
3.1      The ASQ survey is conducted exclusively for Major airports. In India, the airports 
Economic Regulatory Authority (AERA) designates major airports based on their passenger 
footfall. Previously, major airports were classified as those with an annual  passenger count of 
1.5 million. However, this threshold has now been raised to 3.5 million passengers annually. 
Consequently, the ASQ survey is carried out for airports with a footfall exceeding 3.5 million 
passengers per annum. Airport Operators are comm itted to provide high -quality services to 
passengers and continuously improving their airport experiences.At present, the ASQ survey 
has been conducted at 13 AAI airports with a throughput of 3.5 million passengers per annum 
or more. All of these airports,  except Srinagar, received ASQ ratings above 4.5. Srinagar 
airport received a rating of 4.3. 
3.2      The primary issue leading to a lower rating at Srinagar airport was the long waiting 
time at the Drop Gate due to limited X -ray machines and check points by CRPF. To address 
this, AAI has taken the following steps:- 
 Installed additional 4 X-BIS machines for security screening. 
 Widened the road at the Drop Gate to reduce check-in times. 

11 
 
 Introduced 14 E -carts for passenger transportation between the Drop Gate  and the 
airport, significantly enhancing convenience.  
3.3      These measures have reduced waiting times and improved passenger comfort at 
Srinagar airport. 
  
Observations of the Committee  
Recommendation/Observation 
4.        The Committee notes that the following issues need wider consultations and deeper 
analysis:- iii) Various issues relating to Greenfield Airports Policy, 2008 and National Civil 
Aviation Policy, 2016 such as review of the said Policies, grant of „ In-Principle Approval‟ 
and „Site Clearance‟ for new Greenfield projects; and iv) Development of Greenfield 
Airports under the Greenfield Airports Policy, 2008, across the country especially in the 
States where there are no Greenfield Airports, presently.  
(Para 18) 
Reply of the Ministry 
4.1      With regards to Review of the GFA Policy, 2008 and NCAP, 2016 suggestion of the 
Committee has been noted.  
4.2      With regards to development of Greenfield airports in the States where there are no 
Greenfield airports it is informed that as per GFA Policy 2008, if any developer including the 
State Government desires to develop an airport, they are required to identify a suitable site 
and get the Pre -feasibility Study conducted for construction of airport and submit  a proposal 
to the Central Government for 'Site Clearance' followed by 'In-Principle' approval.  
4.3      Therefore, the respective State Government/ developer have the freedom to initiate the 
proposal for development of greenfield airport in their State, which is considered by MoCA 
as per GFA Policy. MoCA and its organisations provide requisite support and facilitate the 
project proponents in development of Greenfield Airports.  
  
Need for a comprehensive policy on brownfield airports  
Recommendation/Observation 
5.        The Committee notes that the NCAP, 2016 gives the guiding principles for the 
upgradation and expansion of existing airports. The Committee feels that the Ministry may 
come up with a clear policy as regards the criteria to be followed in te rms of the decision to 
be made regarding the type of airport project to be taken up i.e., the parameters that should 
decide whether the Ministry/ AAI should opt for a greenfield project instead of a brownfield 
or civil enclave project. The Committee feels that this clarity would permit AAI to work 
towards improving air connectivity and result in economic growth.  
 (Para 23) 
  

12 
 
Reply of the Ministry 
5.1      Brownfield airport development projects face many constraints in terms of land 
availability, design li mitations etc. At the same time, Brownfield airport projects are 
necessary to revamp, expand and modernise existing airports. With more tier 2 city airports 
expected to become major airports, the number of brownfield airport development projects is 
likely to grow.  
5.2      Greenfield Airports are developed as per the provisions of  Greenfield Airports Policy 
read with National Civil Aviation Policy (NCAP), 2016. 
5.3      Wherever State Government is able to provide the desired land and there are no air 
space issues with Defence, Greenfield Airports are developed on need basis, such as 
Bhogapuram in Visakhapatnam, Mopa in Goa, Noida (Jewar) in Uttar Pradesh, Navi Mumbai 
in Maharashtra. 
5.4      However, where State Govt. is unable to provide adequate land  for Greenfield airport 
free of cost and encumbrances and if a Defence Airfield is available nearby then AAI can 
take up development of a Civil Enclave can be developed so as to provide additional capacity 
to the already saturated existing airport.

Modernisation of Airfield Infrastructure (MAFI) scheme  
Recommendation/Observation 
16.      The Committee appreciates the timely replacement of RNAs at various Civil Enclaves. 
However, it also observes that due to various operational and administrative rea sons, PDCs 
given earlier could not be adhered to and wherever PDCs have elapsed, IAF has been 
approached to get revised PDC. The Committee notes that unlike Greenfield/ Brownfield 
airports which are managed by a single operator, the Civil Enclave Airports are managed by 
two operators, i.e., the AAI/ State Government/ Private enterprises and the IAF. Hence, the 
Committee feels that there has to be perfect coordination between both the aforesaid 
agencies for smooth functioning of Civil Enclaves. It hopes that  the operational/ 
administrative reasons for lapse of PDCs, if any, may be examined and sorted out with IAF in 
future, so as to avoid delays. The Committee recommends that the proposed installation of 
navigational aids at various Civil Enclaves may be expe dited to facilitate air operations of 
civilian aircrafts, even in poor visibility and adverse weather conditions, enhancing safety of 
air travel.

Reply of the Ministry 
16.1    Replacement of Radio Navigational aids at civil enclaves under MAFI project is sole 
decision of Indian Air Force/Indian Navy. AAI constantly coordinates and extends help in 
early commissioning of the facilities. 
  
Recommendation/Observation

the Civil Enclaves at Defence airports. While the Committee fully understands the 
requirement of these Enclaves for Defence needs, it is however of the opinion that  the 
requirements of the commercial aircraft operations has to be addressed as well. Keeping in 
view the development of the region and increased business and employment potential, 
feasibility of development of full-fledged airport may be considered on a case-to-case basis to 
avoid the tough balance between defence and commercial operations at Civil Enclaves. The 
Committee therefore recommends that issues such as expediting swapping of land under land 
Barter Matrix formula, delinking of working permissions for lease rentals, extension of watch 
hours for civilian/ commercial flights, restrictions/ constraints for round the clock 
operations, expansion of existing airport, and duality of security agencies for providing 
security, are areas which can be jointly ad dressed by the Ministries of Civil Aviation and 

18 
 
Defence. A mechanism beneficial for both commercial and defence operations should be 
evolved therefor.

Reply of the Ministry 
17.1    There are 29 Civil Enclaves being operated by AAI. There is an existing mechanism at 
different levels to resolve the issues between AAI and IAF/MoD related to land requirement, 
air space requirement, operational watch hours for civil flights etc.  
17.2    When a Civil Enclave reaches saturation level or based on the r equirement, new 
Greenfield airport is also planned/ implemented such as Bhogapuram in Vishakhapatnam, 
Mopa in Goa, Doloo in Silchar. 
  
Recommendation/Observation 
18.      The Committee is aware that „Land Barter Matrix‟ formula was used to solve the

whether it is being used to sort out issues at other Civil Enclaves in Defence Airports also.

Reply of the Ministry 
18.1    As per approved Barter Matrix, in addition to Bagdogra, Defence land has been 
handed over to AAI at Darbhanga, Thanjavur, Srinagar and Pune. While at Thoise and

Recommendation/Observation

the feasibility of  reducing the time frame may be considered, keeping in view the cost

Reply of the Ministry 
19.1    The timeframe for execution of work depends upon volume of work to be undertaken

19.2    Even subsequent to the issuance of permission by the Ministry of Defence, the

ii. Execution of MoU. 

19 
 
iii. Creation of assets falling in defence land which sometimes include building of new

 19.3    In view of the above, 2 years‟ time for construction of civil enclave is reasonable.

20.1    The provisions of DGCA CAR are not applicable at Civil Enclaves. In Civil Enclaves,

Recommendation/Observation

savings for the airlines and also a consequent reduction of carbon footprint. The Committee 
is of the opinion that this environment friendly initiative should be fully encouraged as it 
would decrease the impact on the environment and also ensure savings for the Airlines on 
account of fuel. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministries of Civil Aviation 
and Defence should proactively co-ordinate among themselves, to ensure success of the FUA 
policy.

Security at airports  
Recommendation/Observation

total outstanding COD dues. The Committee notes the huge amount of outsta nding dues 

20 
 
which are payable to CISF by the NASFT, especially the dues of the 16 JV airports and

22.1    NASFT central manage Aviation Security Fee and release for COD accordingly.

Increasing airport density and availability in the country  
Recommendation/Observation 
23.      The Committee appreciates the various measures being undertaken by the Ministry to 
improve air connectivity across the country. The Committee notes that to make air travel 
accessible to more people across the country, it is necessary to have opera tional airports in 
more cities. Providing air connectivity to more cities in an aspirational developing country 
like India stimulates economic growth by creation of new opportunities in terms of trade & 
tourism. It also facilitates access to better healthc are, education and other services for 
people across the country. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry may 
ensure that a robust mechanism is in place to achieve the operationalization of the airports/ 
heliports/ water aerodromes targeted during the years 2022-23 and 2023-24.  
 (Para 93) 
Reply of the Ministry 
23.1    Mechanism to achieve the operationalisation of aerodromes under the UDAN scheme, 
is as under:- 
 The Project Evaluation Committee (“PEC”) has been constituted to review the 
progress of the aerodromes and the allocation of funds. The progress of 
development/upgradation of Airports/Heliports/WA is reviewed from time to time.  
 Moreover, MoCA in consultat ion with State Government/Pawan Hans Ltd., Ministry 
of Ports, shipping & Waterways, BCAS, DGCA also review the status to achieve the 
timely operationalization of the airports/ heliports/ water aerodromes. 
  
Recommendation/Observation 
24.      The Committee notes that India's ranking has decreased from 118 in 2009 to 121 in 
2019, in 'Air Connectivity / GDP score' as per IATA's 2020 'Air Connectivity' Report. This 
could indicate that India's air connectivity gains have not been able to keep up with its GDP 

21 
 
growth. The Committee recommends that the Ministry may ensure that effective measures are 
taken to strengthen air connectivity at a rapid pace to further push India on its path of 
economic growth. 
 (Para 94) 
Reply of the Ministry 
24.1    Development of new A irports and augmentation of capacities of existing airports by 
their modernisation/upgradation is happening at a rapid pace throughout the country. Under 
Greenfield Airports Policy, 12 Greenfield airports have been operationalized and 06 
Greenfield airports are under different stages of development.  
24.2    Further, Ministry of Civil Aviation (MoCA) has launched Regional Connectivity 
Scheme (RCS) - UDAN (Ude Desh ka Aam Nagrik) on 21 -10-2016 to enhance regional air 
connectivity from unserved and underserve d airports in the country and making air travel 
affordable to the masses. Till 31.10.2023,75 aerodromes (including airports, heliports and 
water aerodromes) have been operationalised across the country under UDAN  providing

Increasing the number of international airports  
Recommendation/Observation 
25.      The Committee observes that international air connectivity in tier 2 cities can help 
improve trade, increase tourism and attract foreign investment in the region. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the Ministry may actively analyse the pote ntial for international 
traffic at the presently operational non -international airports as well as upcoming greenfield 
airports.  
(Para 101) 
Reply of the Ministry 
25.1    Upgradation of infrastructure at airports is a continuous process and is undertaken b y 
Airports Authority of India (AAI) and other Airport Developers from time to time depending 
on the availability of land, traffic demand etc. Further, declaration of an airport as 
International Airport depends upon traffic potential, demand from airlines f or operation of 
international flights and bilateral Air Services Agreement. It also includes provision of 
Ground Lighting facilities, Instrument Landing System, runway length, Immigration, Health 
and Animal & Plant Quarantine services etc. 

22 
 
25.2    Moreover, in accordance with Air Services Agreements, Indian designated carriers are 
free to mount operations to/from any international airport to foreign destinations as per 
mutually agreed capacity limits. However, start of international flight from any point in  India 
is purely a commercial decision of the airlines on the basis of economic viability of the route 
and other associated factors. 
25.3    The most recent airport to be designated as an international airport is Kushinagar 
Airport, located in a tier III city. Besides, under GFA Policy, 2008 new International 
Greenfield airports at Jewar, Navi Mumbai, Dholera, and Bhogapuram are being developed.  
  
Accommodating future growth  
Recommendation/Observation 
26.      The Committee observes that brownfield airports have a limited scope for expansion 
which results in high costs of land acquisition for expansion and rehabilitation. Civil 
enclaves, on the other hand, face constraints in terms of accessibility of a ir space, land and 
operational watch hours. The Committee feels that greenfield airports, despite the initial 
requirement of huge capital, are best suited to meet the demands of air traffic growth in the 
nearby region for several coming decades. It is ofte n noted that airport infrastructure 
projects run into delays, sometimes for several years. The Committee, therefore, recommends 
that the Ministry/ AAI may consider alternate greenfield options in the vicinity of a 
brownfield/ civil enclave project before g ranting permission for the development/ expansion 
of the same. Extensive cost -benefit analysis may be done on a case - to-case basis in terms of 
long-term costs to the Government and benefits accrued to the public at large over several 
coming decades.  
(Para 111) 
Reply of the Ministry 
26.1    Brownfield airport development projects face many constraints in terms of land 
availability, design limitations etc. At the same time, Brownfield airport projects are 
necessary to revamp, expand and modernise existing a irports. With more tier 2 city airports 
expected to become major airports, the number of brownfield airport development projects is 
likely to grow.  
26.2    Greenfield Airports are developed as per the provisions of  Greenfield Airports Policy 
read with National Civil Aviation Policy (NCAP), 2016. Wherever State Government is able 
to provide the desired land and there are no air space issues with Defence, Greenfield 
Airports are developed on need basis, such as Bhogapuram in Visakhapatnam, Mopa in Goa, 
Noida(Jewar) in Uttar Pradesh, Navi Mumbai in Maharashtra. 
26.3    However, where State Govt. is unable to provide adequate land for Greenfield airport 
free of cost and encumbrances and if a Defence Airfield is available nearby then AAI can 
take up development of a Civil Enclave can be developed so as to provide additional capacity 
to the already saturated existing airport.  

23 
 
Recommendation/Observation

sector in the next 20 years, as per APAO. The Committee agrees with the observation that 
land acquisition delays often cause time and cost overruns. The Committee recommends that 
the Ministry may look into such issues before awarding a project.  
(Para 113) 
Reply of the Ministry 
27.1    Land being a State subject, the respective State Governments have the sole 
responsibility for land acquisition and each State has its own specific policy to deal with the

concerned constantly follow up with the related State / UT Governments for speedy 
acquisition of land. 
  
Recommendation/Observation

window clearance system for all statutory compliances to minimise delays in the execution of 
airport projects.  
(Para 114) 
Reply of the Ministry 
28.1    The Greenfield A irport (GFA) Policy, 2008 outlines a comprehensive framework for 
the development of new airports in the country. Under this policy, the approval process is 
structured in two distinct stages: "Site-Clearance" followed by "In-Principle" approval. 
28.2    The Project Proponent is also required to obtain other statutory approvals from 
agencies concerned. MoCA facilitates them, whenever they face any difficulty in obtaining 
these approvals/clearances.

Recommendation/Observation

in the number of points of call in favour of foreign carriers. The Committee may be apprised

(Para 119) 
Reply of the Ministry 
29.1    The operations of foreign airlines are governed by bilateral Air Services Agreement

Government of India follows a policy of promoting more international operations by Indian 

24 
 
carriers from non -metro points either directly or through their own domestic operatio ns. 
Currently, due to significant imbalance in the number of points of call infavor of foreign 
carriers, the Government of India does not grant any non -metro city as a new point of call to

Recommendation/Observation

global transit hub for international flights. The Committee feels that the Ministry should work

(Para 120) 
Reply of the Ministry 
30.1    The Ministry of Civil Aviation notes the point of the Committee regarding  obtaining

30.2    As far as airports in India are concerned the Airlines of India are free to 
operate international flights from any point in India .They however do so based on 
commercial considerations. As such development of any Airport as a hub is dependent on the

international hub airports in India. 
  
Profitability of airports

Feasibility of creating multiple entry routes to tackle congestion in major airports

28 
 
should ensure that all its airports increase their air cargo capacities in line with the demands

expansion of airports across the country.

Capture Mechanism’ to augment the financial requirements of airport sector in the

further development, maintenance and expansion of airports across the country.

National Civil Aviation Policy 2016, and fiscal policies such as rationalisation of GST, which 
reflect the vision  of the Government to develop India as a global MRO hub. The Committee 
also notes that presently only repairs of noncore activities other than engine repairs etc. are 
being carried out in India. It hopes that the aforesaid policy would enable the India MRO  to 
take up major technical repairs as well. Aircraft manufacturers (OEMs) may be encouraged 
to open MRO facilities in India.  
 (Para 181) 
13.      The Committee also observes that most of the foreign Aircraft Manufacturers & OEMs 
prefer to utilize their own MROs established abroad despite reduced labour, shipping, 
Turnaround Time and finance cost of replacements & inventory in India. The Committee 
recommends that the Ministry may focus on highlighting these aspects to prospec tive MROs 
who want to set up establishments in the country. The Committee is of the view that the 
growth of the MRO sector will also depend on how efficiently it can address and remove the 
key challenges faced by MRO players in India. It hopes that the Min istry will make all out 
efforts to implement the various fiscal measures at the ground level and also ensure proactive 
interaction with MRO industry to remove any bottlenecks that may arise.  
 (Para 182)

portion of overall expenditure of any airlines operator, setting up MRO services in the 
country would reduce the expenditure on MRO services and subsequently reduce the airfares 
in the domestic routes, which will conse quently reduce the cost of air travel and benefit the 
passengers.

Reply of the Ministry 
14.1    There are 150 (Operator + Standalone) AMOs/Maintenance, Repair & Overhaul 
MROs approved in India for Line/Base maintenance. Out of which 49 standal one MROs

46 
 
14.2    Government seeks to facilitate setting up of aircraft MRO services in India through 
various policy, regulatory and ot her incentives and the Government has taken various 
measures to create a conducive environment for the development of Aircraft Maintenance, 
Repair and Overhaul (MRO) services. 
14.3    With a view to incentivise the growth of MROs in the country and also co ntribute to 
the ease of doing business, MoCA has brought out the new MRO Guidelines in Sept. 2021 
with a view to create a congenial atmosphere in the country for the development of the MRO 
industry for aircraft/ helicopter/ drones and their engines and oth er parts. These guidelines 
inter-alia provide for transparency in the allotment of land doing away with levy of any 
royalty or cess of whatsoever nature on MRO operators and at AAI airports through call of 
open tenders. 
14.4    Further on 9th June 2023, AA I has issued Land Management Circular through which 
allotment of land/ space for setting up MROs (for self/3rd party) at AAI Airports to willing 
agencies on card rate basis for a period of 25 years. No royalty/ concession fee shall be 
payable/ applicable for self and 3rd party MRO services. 
14.5    The other key measures taken by the Government to incentivise MROs in the country 
are:- 
i. GST on MRO has been reduced from 18% to 5% with full Input Tax Credit from 1st 
April, 2020. 
ii. Transactions sub -contracted by f oreign original equipment manufacturers (OEMs)/ 
MRO to domestic MRO are treated as 'exports' with zero -rated GST from 1st April, 
2020 
iii. Exempted Customs Duty on tools and tool kits 
iv. Reduced Goods and Services Tax rates on various spare parts, accessories, and  
consumables 
v. Simplified clearance processing of parts 
vi. Relaxed restriction on utilization of duty-free parts from one year to three years 
vii. Extended stay in India of foreign aircraft for entire duration of MRO work or 6 
months, whichever is lesser 
viii. Revised the Notification to enable export of serviceable parts 
ix. 100% Foreign Direct Investment permitted via automatic route for MRO 
x. Liberalized policy for borrowing and lending in Foreign Currency and Rupees on 
competitive terms for MROs 
xi. Modalities prescribed for con cessional temporary imports of spare parts by foreign 
airlines for repair of their aircraft in transit. 
14.6    The taxation issues pertaining to MRO sector have also been taken up with Ministry of 
Finance in the meetings held between M/o Civil Aviation an d M/o Finance, as well as vide 
follow-up letters. Most recently, a meeting was held between Hon'ble Minister of Civil

Aviation and Hon'ble Finance Minister on 26/06/2023 wherein the taxation issues pertaining

been categorized as follows:-
