2.        The Chairman extended greetings to all the Members and informed that in the last 
meeting on 6 th October, 2023, the Committee heard the views of the Secretary, Ministry of 
Ports, Shipping &  Waterways on the subject of Ship Building, Repair and Recycling. Now, 
the Committee has invited the representatives of Gujarat Maritime Board, Ship Recycling 
Industries Association and the Directorate General of Shipping to provide valuable insights 
into the Ship Recycling Industry.  
(After the witnesses took their respective seats) 
3.        The Chairman welcomed the representatives of Gujarat Maritime Board, Ship 
Recycling Industries Association and the Directorate General of Shipping.  He observed that 
the Alang Ship Recycling Yard located in Bhavnagar, Gujarat, is one of the most preferred 
ship recycling destinations around the world and it caters to nearly 98 per cent of the 
recycling capacity in India. The Chairman asked the  Ship Recycling Association  to provide 
information regarding the safety and sanitary conditions of the workers and the welfare 
measures taken to ensure their well -being at the Alang Yard. Citing the ill effects of the 
recycling activity and weak enforcement of environment and labour-related laws in India, the 
Chairman enquired whether the ship yards in Alang are adhering rigorously to the 
regulations prescribed under the Hong Kong Convention (HKC).  He also sought information 
about the details of infrastructure development undertaken  by the Gujarat Maritime Board as 
well as the process of allotment of plots to ship breakers 
The Chairman observed that  India‟s current share in the ship breaking or recycling market is 
about 25 per cent of the global share, having decreased from about 40 % earlier.   The 
Chairman sought information on the present status, challenges faced, possible solutions and 
the scope of improvement in the area of ship recycling.  He observed that the Ministry in its 
earlier meeting had cited the following two reasons for  this decrease and desired to know the 
status of the same : 
 The policy change by the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) due to which the TMT 
(Thermo-Mechanically Treated) steel bars made from recycled steel from ships are no 
longer recognized for reinforcement purposes, leading to significant revenue loss and 
reduction in turnover for the ship-breaking industries at Alang.  A Committee under 
the chairmanship of BIS was examining the issue and was due to give its report 
shortly.   

75 
 
 The second major issue was stated to be non-arrival of ships from EU countries due to 
the Basel Ban Agreement of 2019 which prohibits any hazardous material of OECD 
countries from being taken to non-OECD countries. 
5.        The Chairman asked Directorate General of Shipping (DGS)  about the latest measures 
and initiatives taken to enhance safety standards for shipping and prevent accidents at sea 
and addressing challenges related to piracy and security threats in maritime regions. 
6.       The CEO, Gujarat Maritime Board, informed that  as of 2022, India is at second 
position with 32.28 per cent of the global share in ship recyling, after Bangladesh.   The 
Alang Ship Recycling yard has recycled almost 4.5 million LTD or more than 400 ships a 
year, accounting for 98% of India's total and 3 2% of the global ship volume. Out of 131 
operational plots, 101 are HKC -compliant, while 27 have applied for EU certification for 
ship recycling. He informed that this industry follows a circular economy and all items are 
reused or recycled. There are more  than 200 shops of retailers and wholesaler dealers in 
Alang for items recovered from ships which are sold there.   There are more than 60 -plus 
induction furnaces and 80 -plus re -rolling mills at Bhavnagar which re -rolls the steel 
recovered from the ships to  provide  TMT bars.   There is systematic disposal with TSDF 
(Treatment, Storage and Disposal Facilities), and environmentally and ecologically -
compliant method for ship recycling is being used. 
7.       He informed that the trend in ship recycling is fluct uating not only in India but all 
around the globe.  In 2021, all across the world, approximately 13,000 ships were recycled, 
and, in 2022, the figure came down to almost 6,500 due to reasons like increased transport 
costs and adverse impact of Covid -19. How ever, the following major reasons have been 
identified for substantial decline in Alang: 
 Decline in the business-cycle of the world economy;  
 Shortage of ships and increased freight rates;  
 Strong competition among nations and their need for steel;  
 Non-arrival of ship from EU countries; 
 Non-recognition by BIS standards; and 
 Rise in cost of recycling due to statute, environment and safety-compliance. 
 

76 
 
8.        He apprised the Committee that seven major initiatives that were required to be taken 
for HKC comp liance have been completed, namely, recycling facility management plan, 
ship-specific dismantling plan, oily waste reception facility, paint -chip removal plan, 
asbestos waste handling, hazardous waste management and water treatment plants.   He also 
informed that three conditions required for HKC to come into force have also been 
completed. Thereafter, he explained about the impact and benefits of Hong Kong 
International Convention. 
9.        It was informed that for compliance of EU certification, Medical f acilities at yards are 
also being developed and fifty -six per cent of the work of hospital facilities has been 
completed. For training purposes of workers, an advanced labour safety and training institute 
has been established. Since its inception in 2003, more than 1.5 lakh workers have been 
trained there. Free accommodation has been provided to more than one thousand workers.   
With reference to downstream waste management, it was informed that 99.95 per cent of the 
salvaged materials are dispatched to down stream industries and traders for use. However, 
less than 0.05 per cent is treated as hazardous waste. The facility to treat this waste will be 
upgraded to make it fully complied with EU norms. 
10.      Regarding the issue of non -arrival of ships from EU countries, tt was submitted 
that Ministry of External Affairs has informed that a political agreement, that is the EU's 
Waste Shipment Regulation has been reached between the European Parliament and the 
European Council in November, which signifies that the EU will agree to send their ships to 
Alang yards by next year after the certification. The Committee was also informed that the 
Government of India has taken following steps to support this industry: 
 Customs duty on ship recycling has been reduced from 2.5 per cent to zero, which has 
helped the yard owners. 
  Incentives of Rs.50 lakhs have been given to those yards which are HKC certified. 
 Annual charges have also been relaxed for the yards to the tune of Rs.52 crore in the 
financial year 2020-21, 2021-22 and Rs.28 crore in 2023-24. 
11.     The Committee was also informed about the short -term, medium-term and long -term 
initiatives for the development of the Alang yard.   It was informed that amen dments have 
been made in Ship Recycling Regulations, 2015 as a short -term measure.  As a mid -term 
measure, auctioning the vacant plots have been started and as a long -term measure, a Master 

77 
 
Plan of Alang -Sosiya Ship Recycling Yard to develop new plots and d ouble the capacity of 
the plots has been adopted.   The Committee was also informed that a 10 -kilometre long 
stretch along the coastline is also being developed, which will lead Alang to become the 
highest capacity ship recycling yard in the world. Further,  the plot sizes will also be 
expanded from 40-80 m to 200-300m. 
12.      The Chairman again raised the issue of non recognition of TMT steel bars for 
reinforcement purposes and asked about the difference between Basel Ban Agreement, Hong 
Kong Convention an d EU recognition. The CEO, Gujarat Maritime Board explained that in 
2019, the European Union decided that any hazardous waste, produced in the OECD 
countries, will not be exported to the non -OECD countries. Since the ship -breaking 
industries come under the  hazardous waste category, the ships were stopped from being 
transferred from EU countries to the non-OECD countries for recycling.   
(Shri Dushyant Singh in the Chair) 
13.      A Member enquired about the development of Trauma centre and other facilities like 
library, cultural centres, etc. The CEO informed that fifty -six per cent of the work has been 
completed and the hospital with state -of-the-art technology and equipment will be ready 
within next few months. With reference to community centres, he informed that some centres 
have been built, however, they are not functional yet. He also noted the issue raised by the 
Member regarding provision of green spaces, libraries, etc for the psychological well -being 
of workers and assured that action would be taken on the same. 
14.      Upon a query by a Member about the impact on labour safety after application of rules 
and regulations of HKC, CEO apprised that it has led to increase in labour safety because the 
entire process of recycling is now systematic and more methodological. However, a  problem 
which is now occurring is due to the size of the plots because the size of the ships nowadays 
is quite huge and the yards are smaller.   
15.      Upon the query by the Acting Chairman regarding GST earnings and the nee d for 
development of tertiary industries, CEO informed that the major problem lies with the BIS 
standards as it does not allow recycled steel bars (more than 8 mm) to be used for building or 
other purposes. Earlier, before the enforcement of BIS standards, most of the small industries 

78 
 
were selling the bars made by recycling ship steel in Bhavnagar zone. However, now most of 
these industries have closed and thousand of workers have lost their jobs. The Acting 
Chairman also enquired about the financial struct ure, earning and taxation system. In the 
response, CEO stated that they have conducted research to expand their capacity and will 
submit a report for the information of the Committee. He also informed that in the coming 
ten years, more than 20000 ships wil l be recycled and since Europe has capacity to recycle 
only ten per cent of their ships, rest 90 per cent will be sent to India. 
16.      The Acting Chairman also enquired about the agreements with EU countries to create 
more shipbuilding areas and technol ogy exchange. The CEO, Gujarat Maritime Board 
(GMB) stated that once the Basel Ban hurdle is over, then agreement can be made with the 
countries for ship recycling. It was also informed that these days, the recycling plan of ship is 
made at the time of its  construction. GMB and the Ship Recycling Association have been in 
talks with ship owners to understand their requirements for recycling and accordingly 
enhancing the recycling facilities at Alang as per new technologies and methodologies. 
17.      Thereafter, Secretary, Ship Recycling Industries Association, gave a brief 
presentation. He informed that Ship Recycling in India began in 1912 in Kolkata and 
Mumbai. In 1983, a ship recycling yard was established on the western coast of Gulf of 
Cambay near Alang  Village due to its high intertidal gradient, allowing large ships to reach 
the shore.   He also informed that Alang Shipyard is eco -friendly, cost-efficient and follows 
Green Ship Recycling as it does not use any natural resources like iron ore or coal or  
electricity or water for production of steel. 
18.      With reference to reduction of Custom Duty on recycling to zero, the Acting 
Chairman enquired about the benefits and the beneficiaries. He also asked about the 
expansion of recycling facilities to oth er coastal areas. The representatives of GMB 
submitted that they would send a detailed note on this issue. The Secretary also informed that 
regular medical check -up for all workers in the recycling yards is conducted biannually and 
specific medical check-up is conducted for the workers involved in removal and handling of 
hazardous materials like asbestos, glass wood and hydrocarbons. In this connection, the 
Acting Chairman sought information about the common illness being faced by the workers. 
CEO, GMB informed that trade specific disease are not prevalent there. However, accidents 

79 
 
happen sometimes and a trauma centre is under construction to handle such cases. It was also 
informed that during Covid period only 20 people were found to be Covid positive out o f 
40000 people. There have been no casualty in Alang and workers are properly trained 
through mock drills, emergency preparedness. Workers are also equipped with PPE kits and 
helmets for their safety.  
19.      Secretary, Ship Recyling Association apprised  the Committee that the operation 
procedure is supervised by a certified safety officer, and key facility equipment includes fire 
fighting, water storage, breathing sets, gas meters, Co2, H2S, and oxygen meters for 
confidential work, ensuring safety in all  operations. Central Salt Research Organisation 
regularly conducts environmental impact analysis including monitoring of gas emission, sea 
water and soil water. It has been found till today there has been no instance of oil spilling in 
Alang. It was also i nformed by Chairman, GMB that training is a pre -requisite for any 
worker. There are three training modules free of cost – 12 days‟ comprehensive safety 
training programme, 3 days‟ refresher safety training only for workers who trained earlier 
and then 2 days‟ for gas cutter safety training. There is special training and drills for confined 
space, asbestos removal and evacuation in emergency. 
20.      The Committee was informed about the achievements of Alang yard like mandatory 
issuance coverage to all, AICC  Provident Fund and   other benefits; multispecialty hospital 
started from   March 2019, operated by Red Cross; upgradation to fulfil remaining facility 
i.e., trauma centre; fully equipped operation theatre is in progress; a housing colony, phase I, 
under operation from 2018. There is also a plan to develop housing colony in front of each 
yard equipped with fully operated TSDF site, which is available only in India.   
21.      The Acting Chairman also raised the issue of payment to labour when there is no 
work. However, it was informed that Government supports the plot owners. The Chairman 
further enquired about the fee for a plot. In response, CEO, GMB informed that the plot is 
available on lease basis which costs around  three hundred rupees per square metre.  There are 
different other charges like development charges, housing cess, etc and a subsidy is given 
when there is a recession. In 2021, around Rs. 54 crore worth of different charges was 
subsidized to ease the burden on plot owners. He also assured to se nd a note indicating plot 
fee, labour cost and other different charges. 

80 
 
22.      Upon a query on adherence to HCK norms, Secretary, Ship Recycling Associatio n 
informed that they are spending around Rs.5 crore to Rs.10 crore in each yard for meeting 
international standards.  There is a gap of around 30 to 50 dollars for Pakistan, Bangladesh 
and India. Around 15 dollars have been saved by reducing the duty of 2.5 percent and the 
remaining 15 -20 dollars will be saved once the HKC comes into force. With referenc e to 
expenses, it was informed that it varies from ship to ship. Reefer ships have higher costs as it 
has more hazardous waste and requires more labour and lengthy removal processes. 
Container and bulker ships have lower costs as there is no hazardous mate rial. Handling 
hazardous waste as per HKC certification, costs 15 -20 dollars per ship. Class N.K. ships 
charge 20 lakh rupees per annum for certification maintenance, unlike Pakistan and 
Bangladesh.  
23.     It was also reiterated that the steel in Pakista n is recycled and used in all construction 
works because there is shortage of steel. The cost for the plot owner to sell the steel turns out 
to be much more than what we get in India. However, in case of India, BIS Standard does not 
allow more than a certa in diameter of re -rolled steel for structural work. Before this quality 
control order, the ship recycling industry used 60 per cent of its ship recycling plate for 
manufacturing TMT bars. After implementing of this   quality control order, the industry 
became scrap-based, sending material to a furnace plant for ingot production. The industry is 
working on its ASTM -A131 steel plate, which exceeds BIS standards. The committee had 
already visited the plant and praised the plate's quality. If approved, the plate  will be used in 
a rolling mill for TMT bars. 
24.      Secretary, Ship Recycling Association apprised the Committee that they had a 
meeting with GMB and Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways in October and 
convinced EU to amend their hazardous waste la w, which will give an edge to India and EU 
ships may reach India by next year.    By voluntarily enforcing HKC 2009, Alang yards can 
establish a minimum three to four -year long -term association with selected 
ports/plots/facility. There are approximately 5000 owners in the world and 300 recycling 
yards and 111 HKC complied Indian yards, but only 15 -20 ship owners are sending their 
ships in India. Therefore, support from international community becomes important.  

81 
 
25.      CEO also clarified that, in the European Union, all the countries together have only 10 
per cent capacity to recycle the ships. GMB proved to EU that 90 per cent of the ships were 
going to non -EU compliant yards for recycling purposes and convinced them to certify 
Alang yards  which are complying with the regulations. With reference to flags of 
convenience, Chief surveyor, DGS informed that after the enforcement of HKC or SOLAS 
Convention, the era of flags of convenience will be over.   
26.      Secretary, Ship Recycl ing Association informed the Committee about the steps taken 
by Government of India to boost the ship recycling industry . The MoPSW has passed the 
Ship Recycling Act, 2019, removing 2.5 per cent Customs Duty, amending the Admiralty 
Act for smooth recycling , and providing Rs.50 lakh financial assistance to HKC -compliant 
plots in form of subsidy. He added that the Central Government provided financial assistance 
of Rs.11 crore for construction of labour housing colony, Rs.20 crore for hospital, Rs.49 
crore for obtaining the HKC -compliant plot and Rs.30 crore for providing training. It was 
also informed that GMB and Government of India participated in EUSR Summit to boost 
business.  Also, the MoPSW is supporting the industry by amending the Quality Control 
Order.  .  Ministry of Health is working on the affiliation of GMB multi-specialty hospital, its 
upgradation and work as per the EU requirement.   MoPSW is also working to amend a few 
clauses of Ship Recycling Code, 2013. Government has also resolved the issue pertaining to 
Customs, GPCB, ESIC and also some finance related issues. 
27.      He also gave brief overview of steps taken by GMB for boosting the industry by 
constructing a 25 crores labour housing colony, providing financial relief of 52 crores in 
2023-24 and 26 crores during Covid -19, amending the Ship Recycling Regulation, allotting 
free land, merging plots for larger ships, upgrading the multi -speciality hospital, and locating 
a new landfill site. He also added that the hospital run by GMB is providin g free -of-cost 
facilities not only to the Ship Recycling Yard's labour but also to the twenty surrounding 
villages. Thereafter, he showed some visuals of Alang Ship recycling Yard showcasing the 
work process at the site. He also made a point that GMB is pa ying ESIC for each and every 
labour, however, till today, the ESIC has not spent a single penny on recycling yard. 
 
 

82 
 
 
28.        The stakeholders assured to give the details in writing on the issues which could not 
be answered at that point of time. 
(The witnesses then withdrew)

CHAPTER-I 
  
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY 
THE MINISTRY 
  
Capacity of Major Ports 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.        The Committee observes that of all the Major Ports, only the JNPA has achieved a 
world-class Turn Around time of 24 hours for Containers. The Committee commends the 
JNPA for this seminal achievement and exhorts the other Major Ports to follow the good 
practices of the JNPA to improve their respective Turn Around times. 
 (Para 22) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1      The recommendation of the Committee is well noted. 
  
Recommendation/Observation 
2.        The Committee also notes that the Average Ship Output Per Berth Day, like the TRT, 
shows only a marginal increase for many ports, and some ports have even shown a decline in 
output. Though the Paradip Port has crossed the threshold of 30,000 tones, yet unless all 
Major Ports project discernible increase in their performance parameters, the efforts of 
individual Ports would not help achieve the objectives. The Committee recommends that the 
Ministry takes special efforts towards monitoring the ground situation at ports that impede 
the performance progress.. 
(Para 27) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1      The recommendation of the Committee is well noted. Several mechanization projects 
are currently underway at various stages in t he Ports. The completion of these mechanization 
projects will contribute significantly to the overall improvement of OSBD. These projects are 
monitored at both the port and ministry levels, ensuring effective oversight and successful 
implementation. Additionally, the Ministry is focusing on enhancing the OSBD through an 
increased share of Public -Private Partnership (PPP) berths, which will not only improve 
operational efficiency but also boost OSBD. 
  
Recommendation/Observation 
3.        The Committee observes that mechanization of berths, minimum dwell time, skilled 
labor, and port connectivity for reduction in evacuation time are essential to reduce the 

3 
 
Turnaround time and recommends that the Ministry may make efforts toBring in greater PPP 
partnerships for mechanization of berths. 
 (Para 30) 
Reply of the Ministry 
3.1      Noted. 
 
DRAFTS OF INDIAN PORTS VERSUS FOREIGN PORTS 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
4.        The Committee observes that the world over, the shipping industry is moving towards 
mega-size vessels with ships of 20,000 TEU and above. While a Capesize vessel requires 
upwards of 18m draft, the draft at Indian ports is in the range of 14 -16 metersonly, owing to 
siltation. The Committee observes that the geographical and topogra phical limitations being 
are identical for both the public and private ports inIndia, how but the private ports have 
been able to develop drafts matching with world class ports whereas the public ports have 
lagged behind. The Gujarat Pipavav port has a dra ft of 18.5 metres and plans to extend it to 
20.5 metres. The Committee, while acknowledging the high dredging costs, underscores that 
the ports drafts must be in sync with the growing size of the ships in the interest of 
maximizing the benefits of large ships in cargo handling. 
 (Para 33) 
Reply of the Ministry 
4.1      Most of the Major Ports have achieved a draft depth of 14 meters, while other Major 
Ports i.e. Kamarajar, Paradip, Deendayal, and Cochin, are working towards achieving even 
deeper drafts of up to 18 meters. Furthermore, the development of Vadhavan Port into a 
Mega Port, boasting an impressive draft depth of 20 meters, is a strategic move aimed at 
further bolstering the capabilities and competitiveness of maritime infrastructure. To make 
the major ports more competitive with Global Ports, the Ministry is exploring the possibility 
of treating the channel as a national asset and also examining the feasibility of funding the 
entire dredging cost, after studying the extant practices followed by the  other countries in the 
world. 
  
Recommendation/Observation 
5.        Ports must increase draft according to the respective cargo profile. Indian container 
terminals must target an 18m+ draft. With the evolving ship types andIncreasing port parcel 
sizes, loading and discharge rates must be enhanced. The Committee also emphasizes that 
greater ship sizes and container loads need increased mechanization at Indian ports to 
improve the loading and unloading ecosystem. Dual cycle cranes and Automated Guided 
Vehicles (AGVs) may be introduced in ports to ensure incremental productivity. 

4 
 
 (Para 34) 
Reply of the Ministry 
5.1      The recommendation of the Committee is well noted. 
 
 
 Recommendation/Observation 
6.        The Committee notes the huge pension liabilities of the Mumbai port. However, it feels 
that such liabilities did not emerge in a day and are known from the time it got accumulated. 
Necessary contingency planning should have been effected and due mechanism put in place. 
The Committee appreciates that the  port has now limited induction to technical and 
professional posts but notes that the present sanctioned strength of port employees at 7,462 is 
still much higher than JNPA and private ports of Mundra and JSW Jaigarh. 
 (Para 43) 
Reply of the Ministry 
6.1      The observations of the Committee are well noted. During the fiscal year 2022 -23, the 
port has contributed ₹ 825 crore to bridge the gap. The shortfall in the pension fund 
investments and actuarial valuation as of 31.03.2023 is ₹2108.57 crore which is a reduction 
as compared to previous years. Considering the trend in the coming years the gap is expected 
to reduce further. Furthermore, the port is wholeheartedly committed to addressing this gap. 
The Mumbai Port Authority has formulated a plan, as ev ident in the commitment to 
contribute 90% of the amounts received from land monetization proposals. In the fiscal year 
FY 2023-24, an amount of ₹520 crore has already been contributed (up to 31.08.2023) to the 
Pension Fund as a commitment towards meeting t he pension liabilities. Current working 
strength of employees is 3327. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
7.        The Committee observes that automation being critical to productivity enhancement is 
also necessary to reduce the staff strength of the port. But, the Digitalization process is still 
ongoing in the port with Port Enterprise Business System, GIS -based Estate Operations 
Management System, and Integrated Access Surveillance System. The Committee 
recommends that the Port implements the digitization and a utomation programme in a time 
bound manner without any further delay. 
(Para 44) 
Reply of the Ministry 
7.1      The suggestion is well noted. 
 Recommendation/Observation 
8.The Committee observes that the iron ore in Goa is of low -grade material for which 
beneficiation needs to be done before it is exported. Moreover, a grade of only up to 62.5 per 
cent can be exported. The Committee observes that the Mormugao port relied hea vily on the 

5 
 
revival of iron ore export for its sustenance. As dependence on one commodity is laden with 
risk for any port, the Committee suggests that the port explores the possibility of other 
commodities, like bauxite, gypsum etc. from Goa and other neig hboring States for 
transportation. The Committee observes that the Mormugao Port authorities had informed 
that transportation of iron ore cargo from Karnataka could be a possible alternative in case 
the iron ore mines in Goa were not  revived. The Committee feels that as there are ports like 
Krishnapatnam, Kakinada and Vishakhapatnam which can handle the cargo, it is unlikely 
that interstate cargo would come to Mormugao port unless attractive rates and concessions 
are offered by the Port. The Committee recom mends that the Mormugao Port may put in 
place, proactive strategies to attract cargo from neighboring states. 
 (Para 52) 
Reply of the Ministry 
8.1      Mormugao Port has set up a Business Development Cell which is actively working in 
line with the recommendations of the committee. Further the Port is offering concessions to 
attract cargo on case to case basis. 
  
Recommendation/Observation 
9.        Regarding the development of the cruise terminal, at the meeting in Goa with the 
Mormugao Port Authori ty, the Ministry of Tourism, the State Government of Goa and 
various Tour Operators, the Committee was informed that there are only day cruises 
operating at present. The Committee had enquired about media reports on Goa port being 
dropped from the cruise c ircuit of three top cruise liners. The Committee was informed that 
there had been an incident with one cruise liner due to an altercation with taxi drivers at the 
port gates. As such, the issue had been taken up with the Goa government. There was now 
better coordination with all parties, including the taxi drivers. The Committee observes that 
globally, the cruise industry was dominated by a few companies and such incidents would 
mar the prospects of Goa in the international cruise circuit. The Committee obs erved that the

swift movement of goods to and from ports, reducing transportation bottlenecks and delays.

international trading partners. Additionally, effective connectivity can attract investments, as 
businesses are more likely to invest in regions with streamlined logistics infrastructure.

private sector partner to secure a reasonable return while enabling value addition for public 
resources. This can only be achieved by establishing clear and transparent norms for the 
PPP and by entering into unambiguous and specific contractual relationship. Concession 
Agreements are generally made for 30 years an d with the rapidly changing market scenario, 
every change cannot be anticipated at the bidding stage in contractsspanning three decades. 
In fact private players are now looking for even longer concession periods in the port sector. 
The Adani Ports and Spec ial Economic Zone (APSEZ) has won a bid to build a Greenfield 
port in Tajpur, West Bengal for aConcession period of 99 years. The MCA, 2021 also has 
provisions for 45 years Concession Period for multi -phase investments. The port sector is 
capital intensive and longer Concession periods which would lead to gestation for a larger 
Capital cycle may become the norm in future. It is unimaginable that the conditions 
prevailing at the time of the Agreement would remain the same in the next century.

INITIATIVES FOR LEGAL DISPUTES AND ARBITRATION 
Recommendation/Observation 
50.      The Committee observes that a thorough discussion on all aspects of a proposed 
policy with all stakeholders and taking into consideration the viewpoints of the stakeholders 

49 
 
should be sufficient to make a policy which would address all the concernsof the stakeholders 
to the extent possible. It is understandable that once a policy is in place, the Government 
does not wish to make frequent changes in it. However, the success of the PPP pr ojects is 
essential for the achievement of the Maritime India Vision and the Ministry should make 
every effort to address the stakeholders’ concerns. The Committee recommends that in case 
of contentious issues emerging from the discussions with the stakeho lders, the Ministry may 
again consult the stakeholders and try to resolve their concerns. The Committee also 
recommends that the Ministry may explore the possibility of creating a standing mechanism 
consisting of representatives of the Ministry, concerned Port and the PPP Operators to

Reply of the Ministry 
50.1    Noted. MoPSW has announced the revised Model Concession Agreement (MCA) - 
2021 on 18th November, 2021. Article 19 has the mechanism for dispute resolution. In case 
of a dispute between the parties,  
 a)            The parties shall first meet so as to disc uss and resolve the matter in mutual 
agreement.  
b)            If above fails, the Concessionaire may agree to refer the matter to a conciliation and 
settlement committee established by the Concessioning Authority in line with the Arbitration 
and Conciliation Act, 2015.  
c)            In case both above processes fail, the dispute shall be referred to SAROD – Ports.  
d)            In the event of constitution of a statutory Adjudicatory Board as per provision of 
Major Port Authorities Act, 2021 or such othe r forum with powers to receive and adjudicate 
upon disputes between the Concessionaire and the Concessioning Authority, all disputes not

other forum with mutual consent of the parties in accordance with the applicable laws. 
e)            Both parties can challenge the award in a Court of Law in case they are aggrieved 
with award. Approaching SAROD Ports or CSC depends on mutual agreement between the

Recommendation/Observation

Reply of the Ministry 

50 
 
51.1    The Major Port Authorities Act, 2021 was notified on 18.02.2021 and came into force

Adjudicatory Board Rules 2023 were notified on 17.01.2023.

CAPACITY OF MAJOR PORTS 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.        The Committee observes that while port capacity is considered to be saturated at 70 -
75% of capacity, some of the Major Ports are functioning far below the mark. Mormugao 
operates at only 27% capacity, while Chennai and VoCA operate just at 32%.. 
 (Para 18) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1      The capacity of Major Ports has been re -rated with respect to global bench marks as 
per Berthing Policy 2016. The actual usable capacity of the ports is lower than the re -rated 
capacity. Hence, the utilization percentage against actual usable capa city is higher in these 
ports. However, a number of factors contribute to the low capacity utilization at these ports, 
including restrictions imposed by Goa State Pollution Control Board for handling cargo at 
Mooring Dolphins and other berths, single Railw ay line from Vasco to Tinaighat, challenges 
due to common hinterland and competition from other ports. The ports are taking steps to 
improve their capacity utilization, such as mechanizing berths, converting berths into 
container terminals, and promoting the use of oil jetties. 
1.2 Marmugao Port Authority (MoPA): Mormugao Port operates at 68% of its Usable 
Capacity, and 27% of its Re -rated capacity. The capacity as per CTO at Mooring Dolphins is 
only 4.75 as against re -rated capacity of 18.50 Milliontones. A lso seen from the table the 
rerated capacity of berth no 6, 7 and 8 is 17.40, 13.70 and 5.20 respectively as against usable 
capacity of 6.50, 5.20 and 1.00 Milliontones. Thus due to the restrictions imposed by Goa 
State Pollution Control Board for handling  cargo at Mooring Dolphins and other berths, Port 
is unable to handle cargo beyond the prescribed limit by GSPCB. Due to single Railway line 
from Vasco to Tinaighat, Mormugao Port is unable to evacuate cargo effectively through 
rakes. This affects the disc harge of vessel as it cannot discharge the cargo in stockyard, 
unless the cargo from the yard is evacuated. Details may be seen at Annexure-1. 
 
1.3 VO Chidambarnar Port Authority (VOCPA) 
VOC Port‟s has the rated capacity of 111.46 MMT and Usable Capacity o f81.47 MMT in FY 
2022-23. Against the Usable Capacity of 81.47 MMT, VOC Port has achieved the utilization 
of 46.7% in FY 2022 -23 by handling 38.04 MMT. Further, it is informed that 5 Port viz., 
Cochin, Chennai, Kattupalli, Ennore and Karaikal are competing  with VOC Port for the 
Common Hinterland Cargo Traffic. 

54 
 
 In-depth breakup of the Rated Capacity, Usable Capacity and its utilization are furnished at 
Annexure-2. 
a. Captive Berths are operated by Power plants and are functioning to its requirements and its  
coal needs / availability. 
b. Container terminals are operating at the Capacity of above 75% and to cater to the 
increasing container handling needs, action has been taken to convert the Port operated berth 
into an additional Container Terminal and Conces sion agreement in this regard was signed 
with M/s J M Baxi Ports & Logistics Limited on 03.09.2022. 
c. Tender for mechanization of the North Cargo Berth -III is in process. 
d. Oil jetty is being used for handling the defined cargoes and its promotion to im prove its 
utilization has been taken up. 
e.            One Berth, NCB II which was under PPP is presently non - operational and is under 
NCLT. 
f. Further, Berth Utilization was measured based on the tonnage basis. However, certain 
cargoes like Windmill Blades& Machinery, Iron and Steel, RoRo -Rock Boulders and other 
break bulk cargo have lesser handling rate and higher berth occupancy, which impacts the 
capacity utilization to a certain degree. Hence, based on the nature of cargo being handled at 
the Port, Berth Utilization and its occupancy differ across Ports. 
 
1.4 Chennai Port Authority (ChPA) 
The Capacity Utilization of Chennai Port during the last 3 years ending FY2022 -23 
has been 42%, 47% and 47% respectively at desired (ideal) occupancy level (85% f or 
Containerized Cargo & 70% for Other Cargoes). The national average of Capacity Utilization 
of Major Ports as observed in the report is only 49%. The marginal shortfall is only due to the 
common hinterland being shared by 3 major ports & 2 private ports operating in the state of 
Tamil Nadu and the ports in the adjacent states of Kerala, Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka.  
  
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
1.5      The Committee appreciates the steps being taken by ports to improve their 
capacity utilization, mechanization of berths, promotion of use of oil jetties etc and 
desires to know if any action has been taken to resolve the issue of  the single railway 
line from Vasco to Tinaighat which is hindering the evacuation of cargo and such other 
port specific issues which are contributing to the low capacity utilization of ports.  
  
Recommendation/Observation 
2.        The Committee observes that there is still much untapped potential to be harnessed so 
as to increase the capacity of most of the Maj or Ports. The Committee points out that the 
capacity utilization of the Non -Major Ports in India has remained at 64%, which is much 

55 
 
higher than the average capacity utilization in the Major Ports and recommends that the 
Major Ports may set targets to incre ase the utilization of their existing capabilities to an 
optimum level.  
 (Para 19) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1      Major ports have experienced remarkable traffic growth of approximately 10% during 
the fiscal year 2022 -23. Recognizing the importance of accommodating future demand in 
light of this substantial growth, it has become imperative to ensure spare capacity. To address 
this need, we are focusing on capacity expansion on two fronts: firstly, by introducing new 
berths, and secondly, by optimizing o ur existing infrastructure through the mechanization of 
berths, deepening of channels, and enhancing evacuation capacity. These strategic initiatives 
are vital for not only sustaining our current momentum but also for effectively meeting the 
increasing demands of the future.

(Comparative statement of the provisions of the three MCAs placed at Annexure XIV). The 
first revision came after a decade and brought only minor changes in a few of the provisions. 
The second revision came within 03 years and brought about a major overhaul in existing 
regulations, with the introduction of market based tariff fixation, abolition of the authority of 
TAMP, provisions for change in cargo, etc. It is not surprising that the existing 
Concessionaires find themselves in a disadvantageous position vis -a-vis the new 
Concessionaires under the MCA, 2021.  
 (Para 192) 

62 
 
Reply of the Ministry 
10.1    Noted. The proviso clause to Section 27(1) of the Major Port Authorities Act, 2021, 
provides freedom to the Concessionaire to fix tariff based on the market conditions.  
10.2 The existing PPP concessions would be governed by the respective signed Concession 
Agreement and tariff provisions contained in respective signed Concession Agreement and 
tariff guidelines, if any, stipulated at the time of the Concession agreement. Government of 
India requires the Project sponsors (Major Ports) to award PPP projects through a transparent 
open competitive bidding process, due diligence through DPR, research and analysis for both 
short and long term business continuity during concession period are part of this process. 
This is also to ensure greater transparency and consistency to the bid process and terms of 
contract, level playing field to all players, throughout the project life cycle and market 
discovery of rates.  Hence, saying existing Concessionaires are in a disa dvantageous position 
vis-a-vis the new Concessionaires under the MCA, 2021 does not seem correct in full merit. 
  
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
10.3    The Committee may be informed of the report of the Committee for deliberating 
on the issue.   
  
Recommendation/Observation 
11.      The Committee also observes that the new Agreement was issued with the purpose of 
countering the lukewarm response of the private sector in PPP projects and to provide a 
framework to increase PPP participation to boost p ort performances. The Committee 
observes that in 2019, on the issue of periodic revision of SoR (Schedule of Rates) for land, it 
had been decided not to apply revision of SoR for land every 05 years for PPP projects as it 
may not be in the overall interest  of the Major Ports. TheCommittee feels that the 
retrospective application of the MCA, 2021 should be examined in the same spirit. The 
Concessions given to the private operators generally are passed on to exporters/importers by 
leveraging costs and therefo re the general public can only benefit by these measures. The 
Committee feels that the Ministry may take these concerns into account while examining the 
requests of the existingConcessionaires.  
 (Para 193) 
Reply of the Ministry 
11.1    In MCA 2021, the Concessionaire shall, as consideration for the use, in its capacity as 
a bare licensee of the Project Site and the equipment comprised in the Port‟s Assets, made 
available in accordance with Article 2.4, pay to the Concessioning Authority ₹ 1 (the 
“License Fee”). 
11.2 On the aspect of making enabling provisions to provide option to the existing PPP 
Concessionaires for migration to the market determined tariff regime, as has been done for 
the prospective bidders / concessionaires for new PPP projects, the majority of the  Major 

63 
 
Ports Chairpersons opined that such an arrangement would be desirable as it would provide a 
level playing field to the Concessionaires, presently being governed under different tariff 
norms, operating at a Port. However, considering the procedural c omplexities involved in 
drafting a workable solution within the framework of the existing rules and regulations, a 
detailed comprehensive study of the whole issue, including legal, financial and contractual 
aspects, would be advisable. 
11.3 Based on the vi ews expressed by Chairpersons of the Major Port Authorities during 
the meeting, the Ministry has decided to constitute a Committee of Chairpersons, to study the 
whole issue in a holistic manner. Report of the committee is yet to be received.. 
  
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
11.4   The Committee may be informed of the report of the Committee for deliberating 
on the issue.    
  
Recommendation/Observation 
12.      The Committee notes that the issue is under examination by a Committee consisting of 
the Chairmen of various Major Ports and desires that the Ministry may update the Committee 
on its outcome. 
 (Para 194) 
Reply of the Ministry 
12.1    The Committee has not yet submitted its recommendations. 
  
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
12.2    The Committee may be informed of the report of the Committee for deliberating 
on the issue.

REPORT
 
 
Demand No. 82 pertains to the Ministry of Tourism.  The Ministry of Tourism in their written note has informed that tourism is a major social phenomenon of the modern society with
 enormous economic consequences.  Its importance as an instrument for economic development and employment generation particularly in remote and backward areas has been now
 well recognised the world over. 
The provisions in this demand mainly include allocations for the Secretariat of the Ministry of Tourism, the expenditure on the headquarter establishment of the Directorate General of
 Tourism and the regional and field offices under it, expenditure on production and publicity material for the promotional programmes, both domestic and overseas; provisions for
 creation of infrastructural facilities like Tourist Bungalows, Yatri Niwas, Wayside Amenities etc. and Grants in Aid to the various Tourism Training Institutes of the Ministry of
 Tourism. The Director General of Tourism functions as the nodal agency for the formulation of national policies and programmes and the coordination of activities of various Central
 Government agencies, State Governments and the Private Sector for the development and growth of Tourism in the country. 
Tourism is the world’s largest export industry.  According to the World Tourism Organisation, about 612.8 million tourists travel internationally in 1997 and spent about US$ 444
 billion.  It is estimated that tourism accounts for about 8% of the total world exports and more than 30% of international trade in services.  In 1997-98 travel and tourism was expected
 to provide direct and indirect employment for 212 million people and accounted for 10.7% of the global work force. 
The international tourist traffic to India during 1951 was just 16,829.  Over a period of 46 years, the arrivals increased to 2.37 million in 1997 and registered a compounded annual rate
 of growth of about 3.8%.  The foreign exchange earnings from tourism during 1997-98 was estimated to be about Rs.11,264 crores (US $ 3173 million).  The rate of growth in foreign
 exchange earning from tourism is exceptionally high.  The foreign exchange earnings for 1998-99 is projected to be Rs.12215.19 crores. During the Eighth Five Year Plan period, the
 foreign tourist arrivals including the nationals of Pakistan and Bangladesh recorded an annual growth of 5.6%.  The growth rate in arrivals, exclusive of nationals of Pakistan and
 Bangladesh, was 8.1%.  During the year 1997-98,  tourist arrivals were 23,70,985 inclusive of the nationals of Pakistan and Bangladesh as compared to 23,34,438 during 1996-97.  
The most significant feature of the tourism industry is its capacity to generate large scale employment opportunities particularly in remote and backward areas as it is a labour intensive
 industry.  It offers enormous potential for economically utilising the natural attractions like landscapes, mountains, beaches, rivers, etc. which would otherwise remain either idle or
 underutilised.  It also applies to a multitude of man-made attractions like monuments, palaces, forts and unique rural and city environments.

Institutes of Hotel Management, Catering Technology and Applied Nutrition at different locations in the country
Food Craft Institutes at different locations
Indian Institute of Skiing & Mountaineering
National Institute of Water Sports

 particular year but is being done during the last so many years.  This reduction in the budgetary allocations affected the growth and development of tourism in the country negatively.

 products in India as environmental friendly and sustainable destinations and encouraging the State Government and Private sector to create infrastructure facilities by providing

11.            FACILITIES FOR FOREIGN TOURIST
 
It has been observed by the Committee that Airport is the first place where the tourist comes into contact with the local people and his interaction on arrival start with the various
 agencies viz. Custom, Visa, Immigration, Foreign Exchange, Transport, Shopping at duty free shops etc.  The Committee understands that the foreign tourist encounters lot of
 problems with all these agencies and besides it the airports in the country also lack adequate toilet/drinking water facility and other civic amenities.  The foreign tourist is also targeted
 by touts who fleece him to no end.  The tourists feels cheated and carries the impression that instead of getting welcome from India they are being harassed and neglected.  The
 Committee was of the view that first impression is the last impression and when tourist would not get proper treatment at the Airport itself their entire expectations towards the
 country would get negated and after getting back to their own country it is not known what sort of Indian picture they will depict to their own country men.  The Committee therefore
 recommends that there should be one high ranking Officer at all the Airports for maintaining efficient coordination amongst all the agencies like customs, immigration, visa, security,
 foreign exchange, operating at the Airport.  This power should preferably be vested with the Airport Director. The Ministry of Home Affairs may take necessary steps to provide
 better security to the tourists not only at the airports but within  the country as well.

 Governments should be 50% each.

19.       CIVIC AMENITIES ON NATIONAL HIGHWAYS FOR TOURISTS
 
The Committee noted with concern that there are shortage of toilet/drinking water facility on the national highways.  The Committee was of the view that most of the tourists are of
 adventurous nature and they prefer to perform their journeys by roads, but since the above facilities are not commonly available on national highways they find it inconvenient to
 travel on those roads.  Sometimes the road sides are used for easing out which creates insanitary conditions.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that such facilities may be
 created on the national highways 100% funded by the Central Government and that a condition may be added in the licence/lease granted to the petrol pumps and restaurants on
 national highways to provide drinking water and toilet facility for the tourist and other travelling public.  The maintenance of toilet/drinking water facilities and other civic amenities
 so created under this scheme may be given to private parties/voluntary agencies.

st report recommended for  relaxation in Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ) Restrictions,  keeping in view of the increasing importance and awareness of the

 tourism. The Committee, therefore, reiterates its earlier recommendations contained in its 31st report and desires the Ministry of Environment and Forests should take liberal view and

The Committee understands that although I.T.D.C. has been earning profits but these are declining with each passing year.  The Committee was also informed that
 disinvestment/
restructuring of the I.T.D.C. is also under consideration and due to this they are not able to take any decision with regard to the new investments in various projects. 
 The delay in taking a decision has been effecting the financial performance of I.T.D.C.
The Committee, therefore, recommends that decision with regard to the disinvestment/restructuring of I.T.D.C. should be taken at an early date so that it is able to take its investment
 decision in time to check the decline in its financial performance.

 REPORT  
 
The Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, 
Tourism and Culture deals with the Action Taken by the Ministry of Culture on the 
recommendations/observations as contained in its T hree Hundred Fifty-First Report on  
„Functioning of National Akademis and other Cultural Institutions‟ which was presented to both 
the Houses of Parliament on 24th July, 2023.  
 
2.  The Action Taken Replies were received from the Ministry on 22nd July, 2024 in respect 
of all the observa tions/recommendations contained in the Report. The replies hav e been 
categorized as follows:- 
 
Chapter-I: 
Recommendations/Observations which have been accepted by the Ministry:  
Paragraph Nos.: 6, 12, 13, 19, 70, 86, 118, 128, 129(ix) and 129(x).

of the replies of the Ministry:

62, 63, 64, 68, 69, 71, 77, 78, 79,  85, 87, 88, 89, 102, 103, 108, 117, 127, 129(i), 129(iv), 
129(v), 129(vii), 129(viii), 129(xi), 129(xii) and 129(xiii). 
Total: 45 
 
Chapter-III: 
Recommendations/Observations in respect of which replies of the Ministry have not been 
accepted by the Committee: 
Paragraph Nos.: 17, 18, 32, 37, 38, 55, 67, 82, 92, 93, 94, 95, 121, 129(ii), 129(iii) and 
129(vi).  
Total: 16 
 
Chapter-IV:  
Recommendations/Observations in respect of which the final replies of the Ministry are 
still awaited: 
Paragraph Nos.: Nil  
Total: Nil 
 

 
2 
  
CHAPTER-I 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE 
MINISTRY 
 
Achievements, Programmes and Initiatives of the National Akademis 
Recommendation/Observation 
1. The Committee appreciates the efforts made by the Akademis in organizin g various 
cultural programmes and events to achieve their mandate to preserve and promote the diverse 
cultures and art forms of the country. 
(Para 6) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1 Ministry places high regard to the appreciation given by the august Committee.  
 
Budgetary Allocation and Issues  
Recommendation/Observation 
2. The Committee recommends the Akademis to explore the option of CSR (Corporate 
Social Responsibility) Funds available for "protection of national heritage, art and culture 
including restoration of buildings and sites of historical importance and works of art; setting up 
public libraries; promotion and development of traditional arts and handicrafts;" as provided in 
clause (v) of Schedule VII of the Companies Act, 2013 read with Section 135. The Committee 
recommends that some portion of the CSR Fund may be mandatorily earmarked for the 
development and promotion of Culture and Cultural Institutions. Government can think of 
making such amendments in the legislation related to CSR. 
 (Para 12) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1 The autonomous bodies are encouraged to garner CSR funds, funds from other Ministries 
and also from Non-Government Sources. An SOP is being issued to all in this regard. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
3. In Committee's view a long -term guarantee of sustained funding will go a long way in 
creating a stable environment to implement ambitious plans. Artistic excellence can flourish 
only in good cultural infrastructure. Thus, Committee feels that Private partners can also 
provide financial support t hrough sponsorships, grants, donations, or investments under PPP 
mode. 

 
3 
  
(Para 13) 
Reply of the Ministry 
3.1 The recommendation of the Committee has been communicated to all autonomous 
bodies under Akademi division of Ministry of Culture . Ministry has, other wise also, been 
directing its bodies to increase their sustainable internal revenue through sponsorships,  
collaborations and investments under PPP.  A comprehensive SOP is being issued in this regard. 
 
Election and Tenure of Heads of the National Akademis and Cultural Institutions 
Recommendation/Observation 
4. Committee, further, suggests that one Member of Parliament should be included on the 
Governing Board of each of the Institutions on the lines of All India Institute of Medical Sciences 
and other such institutions to assist the working of Akademis and to provide ground reports to 
the Akademis. 
 (Para 19) 
Reply of the Ministry 
4.1 Akademis invite the nominations from States and Union Terr itories for its General 
Council. I t is purely a prerogative of Stat es and UTs to nominate legislature or Member of 
Parliament. The recommendation of the Committee will be placed for approval while 
formulating new constitutions and governing boards. 
 
Outreach and Inclusivity 
Recommendation/Observation 
5. The Akademis must work towards increasing cultural public infrastructure such as 
affordable workspaces and easy access to cultural centres and cultural hubs across the country. 
They should bring activities closer to people and increase outreach through different means such 
as the EAST (Easy, Attractive, Social and Timely) principle. 
 (Para 70) 
Reply of the Ministry 
5.1 Different Akademis have devised programs and events which are closer to the public 
viz., gramlok by Sahitya Akademi, theatre training workshops by NSD and SNA , outreach 
training programs by Kalakshetra and CCRT. The suggestion of the Committee would be taken 
seriously and all Akademis will be directed to enlarge the domain of their activities bringing the 
public closer and to build new audiences. 
Technological Advancements/Digital accessibility  

 
4 
  
Recommendation/Observation 
6. Akademis should develop online learning platforms or learning management systems that 
offer courses, workshops, and educational resources. These platforms can provide a range of 
content, including video lectures, interactive modules, downloadable materials, and assessments. 
 (Para 86) 
Reply of the Ministry 
6.1 The institutes employ online learning management systems to offer courses, workshops 
and educational resources. The Vedic Heritage Por tal of the Indira Gandhi National Centre for 
Arts (IGNCA) in an online portal that is serving as a  one-stop solution for the user, for any 
information regarding the Vedic heritage. 
6.2 The suggestion of the esteemed Committee has been informed to all Akademis and they 
are working on developing such modules. 
 
Protection of rural and tribal culture 
Recommendation/Observation 
7. The Committee also believes that it is important to prioritize the voices and perspectives 
of tribal communities, while also providing platforms for them to share their culture with a wider 
audience. Akademis should develop educational outreach programs that   promote tribal and 
rural culture in schools, colleges, and local communities. There is also a need for collaboration 
with tribal organizations, NGOs, and tribal development agencies to jointly support initiatives 
for the promotion of tribal culture. Further, Akademis must promote rural stays and tribal stays, 
especially among the younger generation to acquaint them with the cultural  heritage of the 
country. 
 (Para 118) 
Reply of the Ministry 
7.1 The Committee's recommendation is noted for compliance. 
 
Leveraging G20 
Recommendation/Observation 
8. The Committee recommends that Akademis should collaborate with tourism authorities 
and G-20 stakeholders to promote cultural tourism in India. Akademis should also encourage G -
20 delegates to explore Indian cultural treasures beyond the conference venues, thus promoting 
tourism and economic opportunities. Akademis can initiate collaborative pro jects between 
National Akademis and cultural institutions from G -20 member countries. This can involve joint 
exhibitions, performances, artist residencies, or cultural exchanges. Digital platforms like social 

 
5 
  
media handles, live streaming, and virtual exhi bitions can be utilised to extend the reach of 
National Akademis cultural initiatives during the G -20 summit and to engage a global audience 
and promote cultural exchange beyond physical boundaries. 
(Para 128) 
Reply of the Ministry 
8.1 The Committee's recommendation is noted for compliance. 
 
Need for international recognition of Kalaripayattu, Kathakali and other art forms  
Recommendation/Observation 
9. Ministry may take a look into the matter and take appropriate action in the matter. 
(Para 129{ix}) 
Reply of the Ministry 
9.1 Sangeet Natak Akademi being the nodal agency for Intangible Culture Heritage (ICH) 
has succeeded in inscribing the Kutiyattam and Mudiyettu art forms of Kerala in the 
Representative List of Intangible Culture Heritage of Humanity of UNE SCO in 2008 and 2010 
respectively. As regards the international recognition of Kalaripayattu and Kathakali, Akadem i 
will take up this matter at the appropriate level. 
 
Details of cultural activities organized in Kerala in Thrissur and Thiruvananthapuram  
Recommendation/Observation 
10. The details of the same may be provided to the Committee for information 
(Para 129{x}) 
Reply of the Ministry  
10.1 The details of cultural activities organized in Kerala in Thrissur and Thiruvananthapuram 
of various academies is enclosed at Annexure IV. 
 
 

 
6 
  
 
CHAPTER-II 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT 
DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE REPLIES OF THE MINISTRY 
 
Budgetary Allocation and Issues  
Recommendation/Observation 
1. The Committee notes that the overall budget allocation for the Ministry of Culture is only 
0.075% of the total budget, which is grossly inadequate. In particular, the combined budgetary 
allocation (2023 -24) for the National Akademis is just Rs. 401 crore. The Committee in this 
regard, recommends that the Ministry of Culture should increase the budgetary allocation to the 
National Akademis and other Cultural Institutions in order to increase their efficiency and 
outreach. 
 (Para 10) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1 The budget allocated to the Minis try is distributed among the stakeholders in accordance 
with the programmes/activities planned during the year. The total budget allocation to the 
Ministry for 2023-24 was Rs. 3399.65 crore. Out of which funds allocated to the Akademis was 
Rs. 401.27 crore  i.e. about 11.8% of the total allocation of the Ministry. Whenever, additional 
fund requirement is requested by the Akademis, during the year, the same is considered 
generously by the Ministry based on merits and required funds are made available through 
supplementary grants. 
  
Recommendation/Observation 
2. Committee observes that countries like China, the U.K., U.S., Singapore and Australia 
spend roughly 2%-5% of their budget on the promotion of art and culture and a majority of the 
amount spent by these countries on art and culture is sourced from non -Government sources 
which is not the case in India. 
 (Para 11) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1 Funds are allocated to various academies as per the budgetary alloca tion of Ministry of 
Finance. Ministry encourages th ese autonomous bodies to garner funds from other Non -
Government Sources as well, wherever feasible.   

 
7 
  
 
Recommendation/Observation 
3. Further, funds can also be raised as monetary benefits from YouTube channels and other 
OTT platforms. Akademis can organize  fundraising events such as galas, auctions, benefit 
concerts or cultural festivals. These events can attract donors, sponsors, and supporters who are 
interested in experiencing cultural performances and supporting the academy's mission. 
 (Para 14) 
Reply of the Ministry 
3.1 The Ministry of Culture advocates for improving source of revenue and encourages the 
institutions under the Ministry to explore all possible avenues for increasing their income, apart 
from grants received from the Government.  
 
Recommendation/Observation 
4. Akademis must augment resources to become sustainable and resilient. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that in order to develop a strong sustainable cultural environment, 
Akademis need to take significant steps to attract investment s from the Government and private 
sectors, to develop and maintain their cultural and social infrastructure. Akademis should start 
thinking outside the box with 'imagination and a vision' and draw up a plan to explore other 
suitable types of external finan cing. Investments should include audience engagement, 
supporting artists and subsidizing performance to optimize  public engagements. The Committee 
believes that along with tourists and visitors, citizens also constitute a major part of the 
consumers, who are willing to spend larger portions of their disposable income to seek 
entertainment. The Akademis should tap such potential of the citizens. 
(Para 15) 
Reply of the Ministry 
4.1 The Akademis generate revenue by way of sell ing tickets for their events, and  also 
renting out their performing spaces/ auditoriums at their campuses. These Akademis also engage 
and partner with other Ministries for various eve nts organized by the Government . Thus, the 
Ministry of Culture continuously encourages the Akademis to become self-dependent. 
 
Election and Tenure of Heads of the National Akademis and Cultural Institutions 
Recommendation/Observation 
5. The Committee also recommends that there is a need to increase the involvement of 
States in the overall functioning of the Na tional Akademis and other Cultural Institutions and 
this may be done by giving representation to all States in the administrative set -up and through 

 
8 
  
collaboration with cultural bodies at the state level. In this regard, proper consultations must be 
conducted with all States. 
 (Para 20) 
Reply of the Ministry 
5.1 Involvement of the States and UTs is already there in the administrative set up of the 
Akademis as their  General Council has representatives from all States and UTs. All the 
Akademis organize their festivals, events etc., in collaboration with State Governments and State 
Akademis.  
 
Regional Centres and Zonal Cultural Centre (ZCCs) 
Recommendation/Observation 
6. The Committee observes that at present, only a few National Akademis and Cultural 
Institutions have established regional centres across the country. States are not evenly covered 
in so far as the establishment of regional Centres in the country is concerned. The map given 
above shows that there is no representation of culturally rich regions lik e Mizoram, Nagaland, 
Himachal Pradesh,  Haryana, Punjab, Chhattisgarh, Bihar, Arunachal Pradesh and Madhya 
Pradesh. The Committee notes that a substantial chunk of the population is left out of the reach 
of the Cultural Institutions and Akademis. In Committee's view, this has greatly restricted the 
active local presence of these national cultural bodies. 
(Para 28) 
Reply of the Ministry 
6.1 Ministry would like to apprise the esteemed Committee that all the National Akademis 
have national presence through thei r regional centres (not state specific centres). Also some 
Akademis have project offices in different states for particular art form s. A list of all the 
Regional Centres and project offices of Akademis may be seen at Annexure I. Also, Ministry of 
Culture h as set up seven Zonal Cultural Centres (ZCCs) in the country with headquarters at 
Patiala (Punjab), Nagpur (Maharashtra), Udaipur (Rajasthan), Prayagraj (Uttar Pradesh), 
Kolkata (West Bengal), Dimapur (Nagaland) and Thanjavur (Tamil Nadu) to protect, promo te 
and preserve various forms of folk art & culture throughout the country and also to set up 
mechanism for development of the cultures of various regions. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
7. The Committee notes most of the cultural institutions are headquarter ed in Delhi. The 
Committee reminds that these cultural bodies can be relocated to various other parts of the 
country to ensure Pan India presence of the Institutions. 

 
9 
  
 (Para 29) 
Reply of the Ministry 
7.1 The Akademis have presence across the coun try through regional centres which help in 
organizing activities / programmes / events Pan India. The list of the Regional Centres may be 
found at Annexure II. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
8. The Committee, therefore, recommends that there is a need for establishing regional 
Centres in each State as well as in remote areas like tribal areas to promote tribal culture, and 
in rural areas to promote village culture. Further, Regional Centres must be set up in all 
culturally rich regions to promote art and culture at gras sroots level. The Committee also 
suggests that there is a need for cultural mapping of districts using the Standard Operating 
Procedure (SOP). Regional Centres must cater to all the aspects of art and culture of that 
region. 
(Para 30) 
Reply of the Ministry 
8.1 The Ministry is already working on setting up more regional hubs of all Akademis in 
regions where there are no presence as of now. The National Mission on Cultural Mapping 
(NMCM) is an initiative of the Ministry of C ulture, to develop a comprehensive database of art 
forms, artists, and other resources across the country. The consolidated detail of NMCM is 
attached at Annexure II. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
9. Zonal Cultural Centres (ZCCs) provide facilities for the promotion of arts and culture in 
their respective regions. The Committee, however, observes that the functioning of ZCCs is not 
always uniform across the States, thereby defeating the very purpose of fostering cultural 
activities equitably throughout the country. The Committee also recommends that the National 
Akademis and other Cultural Institutions must collaborate with ZCCs to remove this disparity 
across States. The Ministry of Culture needs to play a lead role in such coordination works. 
Ministry/ National Akademis must evolve a mechanism to ensure effective coordination of efforts 
between National Akademis/Cultural Institutions and ZCCs. 
(Para 31) 
Reply of the Ministry 
9.1 Ministry of Culture, through its Akademis and Zonal Cultural Centers has been 
executing the mandate of promotion and  preservation of tangible and intangible cultural 

 
10 
  
heritage.  State governments are involved in promotion of their re spective art forms through the 
state cultural academies. 
9.2 Further, Akademis alway ensure maximum participation of Zonal Centres in their 
activities and have already organized a number of festivals in different parts of the country in 
collaboration with the Zonal Centres. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
10. The Akademis, during the course of the discussion, agreed to the view that Members of 
Parliament and MLAs of the region can help the Akademis with outreach and accessibility to the 
interior parts as they are more aware of the cultural spread in their regions. The Committee 
appreciates that the views of the Committee in this regard are well tak en by the Akademis. 
Popular participation is essential to propagate and preserve various forms of our culture. The 
elected representatives of the area can contribute immensely to popularize the art and art forms. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that all MPs and MLAs of the region should be invited to 
the events organized by the respective organizations. Also, Ministry/ Akademis should actively 
involve Members of the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture. 
(Para 33) 
Reply of the Ministry 
10.1 The cultural activities and programmes are conducted by Akademis at the Headquarters 
and at various locations across the country. These academies are advised and persuaded to 
involve public  representatives including MLAs  and MPs, and civi l society and civic body 
workers/ members.  The suggestions of the august Committee have been well taken and will be 
kept in mind. Suitable instructions have been given to the Akademis in this regard. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
11. Committee recommends th e Ministry/ Akademis to attend the DISHA meetings. 
Representatives of the Ministry/Akademis should be encouraged to attend the DISHA meetings 
for consultation with Members of Parliament, State Legislatures and Local Governments 
(Panchayati Raj Institutions /Municipal Bodies). These Committees can monitor the 
implementation of the programmes and promote synergy and convergence for greater impact. 
They can also facilitate coordinated solutions to remove constraints, if any. 
(Para 34) 
Reply of the Ministry 
11.1 DISHA District Development Coordination and Monitoring Committees (DISHA), have 
been constituted by Ministry of Rural Development at district levels under the Chairpersonship 
of concerned Member of Parliament to monitor proper implementation of key Centra l Schemes/ 

 
11 
  
Programmes. The nature of activities carried out by the Akademis under the Ministry of Culture 
for promotion of culture, do not strictly conform to the object of the DISHA meetings. However, 
the suggestions of the august Committee have been well taken and will be kept in mind. 
 
Cultural knowledge and Expertise of Staff 
Recommendation/Observation 
12. The Committee notes that a majority of the administrative staff have little 
knowledge/expertise in arts and culture management. The Committee feels t hat extensive 
training programmes are required for better expertise of staff to enable proficiency and 
competency at scale, and across levels. The Committee, therefore, recommends that a 
comprehensive assessment of the training needs of the staff may be un dertaken to identify the 
areas where they require skill development or additional knowledge in art and culture and 
specific domains. The Ministry can also establish mentoring or coaching programmes where 
staff members are paired with experienced professionals in the field. 
(Para 44) 
Reply of the Ministry 
12.1 Training and skill upgradation of the staff and officers of the Akademis is an ongoing 
process, and Akademis will be advised to take the august Committee‟s suggestions into 
consideration. 
 
Governance and related issues 
Recommendation/Observation 
13. Committee feels that resolving governance issues in National Akademis requires a 
systematic and proactive approach. First of all, Committee suggests identifying the specific 
areas where governance problems exist, acknowledging the issues, and committing to addressing 
them. Further, there is a need to enhance transparency and accountability and promote a culture 
of ethical conduct and integrity within the Akademis. 
(Para 49) 
Recommendation/Observation 
14. Committee, further, flags that continuous monitoring and evaluation of the effectiveness 
of governance practices is also required at regular intervals. Akademis should seek feedback 
from stakeholders, conduct internal and external evaluations, and use the find ings to identify 
areas for improvement. 
(Para 50) 
 

 
12 
  
Reply of the Ministry 
14.1 It is submitted that the p ortals such as Public Grievance and  Right to Information are 
already in place to track the complaints, governance issues, and requests to enhance 
transparency and accountability and promotion of culture of ethical conduct and integri ty within 
the Akademis. The Akademis also regularly seek  feedback from Artists and general public 
through different platforms like social media etc. However, the august Committee's 
recommendation is noted for compliance. 
  
Recommendation/Observation 
15. In cases where governance issues persist or are complex, the Akademis should consider 
seeking external expertise or consulting services. Independent evaluations or audits can pr ovide 
valuable insights and recommendations for addressing governance challenges. 
(Para 51) 
Reply of the Ministry 
15.1 Regular audit of annual accounts  of the Akademis are already carried out by the CAG. 
Sufficient provisions for review of the functioning of autonomous organizations are already in 
place under Rule 229 (ix) of General Financial Rules, 2017. The suggestions of the august 
Committee are welcomed. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
16. Further, the Ministry/Akademis may also consider the possibility of  adopting new 
technological advancements in administration for improving the day -to-day functioning of the 
Akademis. 
(Para 52) 
Reply of the Ministry  
16.1 The Min istry of Culture persuades the Akademis to adopt the technological 
advancements in their day to day functioning. It is a continuous process. 
 
Segregation of Functions 
Recommendation/Observation 
17. The Committee feels that the function of the Akademis is to enable artists to create and 
express their creativity. The role of the Ministry should be to  help the organizations and their 
artists to realize the organizational vision and fulfil their mission. Its responsibility is to provide 
an atmosphere for artists to develop and realize their vision with resources that would otherwise 

 
13 
  
be unavailable or gr eatly diminished in the face of lack of opportunities. The Committee notes 
that the 2014 High Powered Committee also expressed that the Ministry has to work as a point 
of coordination for cultural expression and a catalyst for the dissemination of that exp ression 
through the encouragement and sponsorship of multifarious artistic activity. To this end, 
Committee feels that there should be proper and clear segregation of functions among the 
Akademis. 
(Para 54) 
Reply of the Ministry 
17.1 Ministry agrees with t he view point of Committee and would like to submit that each 
Akademi is established with a distinctive mandate.  The Sangeet Natak Akademi is responsible 
for promoting and preserving the performing arts, including music, dance, and theatre.  The Lalit 
Kala Akademi focuses on promoting and developing visual arts, including painting, sculpture,

establishing a uniform policy regarding appointment and governance structure across all
