vacancies within a fixed period. The Ministry may also apprise the Committee of the status of the 
matter. 
(Para 38) 
Reply of the Ministry 
5.1 As per Ministry of Finance guidelines dated 05.01.2024 regarding creation / revival / 
abolition of post s, all the p osts which are lying vacant for  more than five (05) years stand  
abolished, and to f ill these posts administrative M inistry needs to revive these posts by taking 
Ministry of Finance‟s approval. Ministry of Culture is making continuous efforts to revive these 
posts. Further, the posts which are lying vacant for less than 5 years, the recruitmen t process for 
these vacancies are undergoing expeditiously in all the academies. 
5.2 The current sanctioned / vacant strength of each Akademi is enclosed at Annexure III. 
 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
5.3 The Committee is concerned about the  huge difference between the sanctioned and 
in-position strength across all  seven Central Akademis. Specifically, three Akademis viz., 
Sangeet Natak Akademi, CCRT,  and Lalit Kala Akademi, are functioning with less than 
40% of the ir sanctioned strength. National Sc hool of Drama has approximately 48%, and 
IGNCA has around 36% vacancies against their sanctioned strengths.   
5.4 The Committee may be apprised of the reasons for such meager working strength in 
the Akademis and urges the Ministry to make concentrated effo rts to streamline the 
processes and initiate the recruitment process at the earliest.   
 
Segregation of Functions 
Recommendation/Observation 
6. The Committee observes that segregation of functions is also an important concept to 
internal control frameworks , financial reporting and regulatory compliance. The overall 

 
30 
  
effectiveness of the organization depends on an effective internal administration, adequate 
division of responsibilities, and the requirement of a sufficient number of staff who are 
adequately trained. Separation of functions is an important mechanism to help reduce the risk of 
fraud, error and other financial misconduct. In addition, it helps to promote accountability, 
transparency and ethical behaviour within the organization. The Committee, the refore, 
recommends segregation of the purchasing, provisioning, financing and policy -making functions 
within the Akademis. 
(Para 55) 
Reply of the Ministry 
6.1 There are various verticals  under each A kademi to handle internal frameworks. As per 
the Memorandum of Associations / Constitutions of th ese Academies, the Governing Board / 
Society is the supreme authority in each Akademi which formulates policies as per the mandate. 
Further, General Financial Rules (GFR) is applicable to all Autonomous Bodies of the  Ministry 
and hence follows all purchasing, financial policies as per GFR. Administration Unit of each 
Akademi is responsible for hiring manpower as per approved RRs. 
 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
6.2 The Committee is of the opinion that , given their distinct frameworks and mandate, 
each Akademi should have its own  dedicated functioning authority. The Committee notes 
the Ministry’s reply and reiterates that the administrative sections responsible  for tasks 
such as hiring manpower, purchasing, HR issues, and budget management  should be 
clearly defined in each Akademi and be empowered to ensure efficient functioning.  
 
Outreach and Inclusivity 
Recommendation/Observation 
7. The Committee feels that the National Akademis need to enhance its outreach, both  
within urban and rural areas, to make the arts more accessible and inclusive. Without effective 
outreach programmes, Akademis may struggle to reach a broader audience, beyond their 
immediate surroundings. A lack of outreach can reinforce existing cultural  hierarchies and 
exclude cultural practices that are not adequately represented or recognized. This exclusion can 
lead to marginalization of certain art forms, traditions or communities, thereby, limiting cultural 
diversity and stifling creativity. There i s also a risk of losing intangible cultural heritage, as 
there may be insufficient engagements with communities, artists and practitioners who are the 
custodians of these traditions. 
(Para 67) 
Reply of the Ministry 

 
31 
  
7.1 All the Akademi s through their  various regional centres try their  best to reach out to 
artists who are unaware of the functions and activities of t he Akademis. Also, some Akademis 
have project offices in different states for  particular art form. Further, Ministry of C ulture has 
set up seven Z onal Cultural Centres (ZCCs) in the country to protect, promote and preserve 
various forms of folk art & culture throughout the country and also to set up mechanism for 
development of the cultures of various regions. 
 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
7.2 The Committee feels that to enhance outreach and awareness, Ministry should issue 
directives to all the Akademis to implement specific measures.  Akademis could leverage  
social media platforms, radio stations, local newspapers , and other channels to enga ge 
communities, art practitioners and artists from across the country and tap into their full  
potential.  Additionally, t he Akademis should explore ways to publicize  their events, 
seminars and workshops through various platforms to reach a wider  audience a nd 
encourage greater participation.  
 
Infrastructure and Facilities  
Recommendation/Observation 
8. The Committee observes that investing in infrastructure for cultural Akademis is essential 
for supporting the growth, development, and sustainability of arti stic and cultural practices. 
Committee recommends that informal education may also be imparted through these Institutions. 
Ministry should provide the necessary funds and also promote synergy among the Institutions for 
sharing of infrastructural facilities. Committee also suggested Akademis to explore CSR funds to 
mobilise the resources for infrastructure developments including auditoriums, classrooms, 
studios, rehearsal halls and exhibition areas.  
(Para 82) 
Reply of the Ministry 
8.1 This Ministry envisage s to  strengthen regional presence to facilitate the people of 
different region s and promote synergy among the Akademis for sharing of infrastructural 
facilities. All Akademis are autonomous in nature and they are free to obtain CSR funds. 
 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
8.2 The Committee is of the opinion  that CSR funding could serve  as an additional 
budget source for the dev elopment and growth of Akademis.   The Committee may be 
apprised of the steps being taken by both the Ministry and the Akademis to secure and 

 
32 
  
utilize this funding.  The Committee also seeks information on the CSR funds received by 
each Akademi in the last three years and how these funds have been utilized.  
Returning of Awards  
Recommendation/Observation 
9. The Committee notes the i nstances of recipients of awards, given by Akademis (such as 
Sahitya Akademi Awards), returning their awards in protest of certain political issues which are 
outside the ambit of the cultural realms and the autonomous functioning of the concerned 
Akademi. Such inappropriate incidents involving the return of awards undermine the 
achievements of the other awardees and also impact the overall prestige and reputation of the 
awards. 
(Para 92) 
Recommendation/Observation 
10. A Member of the Committee opined agains t the view that artists, authors and other 
intellectuals and performers who have been recommended for awards must sign a commitment 
that they will not return the awards as a form of protest at any point in the future before they are 
able to receive it. He was of the view that India is a democratic country, and our Constitution 
has provided to every citizen the freedom of speech and expression and also the freedom to 
protest in any form. Returning of awards is only a form of protest. The Member added that th e 
Committee must strongly recommend to the Government to look into the actual issues in protest 
of which such awards have been returned and work towards resolving them. He was seconded by 
another Member. 
(Para 93) 
Recommendation/Observation 
11. The Committee questioned the re-engagement of such awardees who joined the Akademi 
after insulting it. Such inappropriate incidents involving the return of awards undermine the 
achievements of other awardees and also impact the overall prestige and reputation of the 
awards. The Member again submitted that the Akademis and the other Institutions should 
continue to work together with these artists and not shun them. 
(Para 94) 
Recommendation/Observation 
12. The Committee observes that the awards given by each Akademi con tinue to be top 
honors for an artist in India. The Committee emphasizes that Sahitya Akademi or other 
Akademis are apolitical organizations. There is no place for politics. The Committee, therefore, 
suggests that whenever an award is given, the consent of the recipient must be taken, so that 
he/she does not return it because of political reasons; as it is disgraceful to the country. The 
Committee recommends prior concurrence of short -listed candidates for awards before 

 
33 
  
finalization. A system may be put in p lace where an undertaking is taken from the proposed 
awardee citing acceptance of the award and that the awardees cannot dishonour the award at 
any point of time in future. Awards may not be given without such an undertaking. In the event 
that the awards a re returned, the awardee shall not be considered for such award in the award 
in the future. 
(Para 95) 
Reply of the Ministry 
12.1 The Ministry agrees with the Committee's perspective and would like to avoid 
controversies in all regards. However, obtaining a  signed commitment from the writer prior to 
the award announcement would unfortunately compromise the confidentiality surrounding the 
selection process. Additionally, the legal enforceability of such a pre -declaration commitment 
might be uncertain. 
 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
12.2 The Committee acknowl edges the  Ministry’s reply  and understands its concern 
about confidentiality and legal implications related to obtaining signed commitment s. The 
Committee suggests that the commitment document should  include a non-disclosure clause 
to protect against  breach of confidentiality. Alternatively, the Ministry should explore 
other measures to prevent similar issues i n the future. A dditionally, a policy should be 
established to monitor  artists who have return ed their award s but remain affiliated with 
the Akademi.  
 
Youth Engagement 
Recommendation/Observation 
13. The Committee notes that the efforts are largely targeted at getting children to learn art 
forms - namely dance and music. The Committee feels that intervention is required to make them 
aware of what these traditions are; at least to a point where they can identify some very basic 
ideas of the performing and visual arts. While the Ministry of Culture set up the CCRT with 
somewhat a similar idea of reach ing out and creating opportunities for young children, 
especially from smaller cities, and all regions including the North -East, the program needs to be 
seriously reviewed and updated. Further, it should be linked with other ongoing efforts of the 
Ministry. 
(Para 121) 
Reply of the Ministry 
13.1 The Sangeet Natak Akademi has two teaching institutions of dance and music , namely, 
Kathak Kendra in Delhi and Jawaharlal Nehru Manipur Dance Academy in Imphal. Akademi 

 
34 
  
through these institutions is imparting training of Kathak dance and Manipuri dance and music , 
respectively. These centres are also running Diploma Courses in their respective places. Sangeet 
Natak Akademi is also running various type of training programmes of local arts forms through 
its centres in Guwahati, Agartala, Chandankiyari and Thiruvananthapuram. 
13.2 In addition, internship programs are also provided by IGNCA to young artists and 
talented youth artists to provide them an opportunity for a direct learning in the field of art, 
dance, craft, music etc. 
 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
13.3 The Committee feels that  given the vast number of traditional dance and music 
forms in the country, it is crucial to support and nurture the talents of the youth. A handful 
of institutions and centres may n ot be adequate to address the diverge range of art forms. 
Therefore, it recommends that the Ministry and concerned Akademis make dedicated 
efforts to establish additional teaching institutions and centres, particularly in the North-
East Region, hilly areas, and islands, to create more opportunities for the young children.  
 
Representation and promotion of culture of North East States of India  
Recommendation/Observation 
14. North East India is known for its geographical location, ecology and diverse culture . It is 
the homeland of large number of ethnic groups. Each ethnic community has its own distinct 
culture including food, music, dance, dress, language, etc. However, despite this, the North East 
has not been represented to the degree it deserves to be rep resented. Ministry must take 
measures in this direction and implement more schemes to preserve and promote various forms 
of art and culture in the NER. Ministry must extend all kinds of assistance including financial 
support to the individual artists and organizations in this region. 
(Para 129{ii}) 
Reply of the Ministry 
14.1 Akademis through their region al centres established in North -East make  all possible 
efforts to preserve and promote various forms of art and culture in the NER. These centres also 
ensure the maximum participation of North-East in all their activities. 
 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
14.2 The Committee notes the reply and urges  the Ministry to allocate a specific portion 
of the budget for each Akademi to the development and promotion  of the rich  culture of 

 
35 
  
the North -East Region. It also reiterates the need for special emphasis on providing 
assistance to NER to ensure maximum support and cultural growth in the region.  
 
Handling, preservation and digitization of Manuscripts 
Recommendation/Observation 
15. Manuscripts are the primary source of historic information. Manuscripts are diminishing 
along with time. Despite their best efforts, it is difficult to save manuscripts in a physical form 
beyond a time frame. Digital preservation of man uscripts restores them from damage, larceny 
and decay. The Ministry should evolve a well -designed digitization program that includes not 
just digital capture, but also appropriate care and repair of original materials, and long -term 
management of the digital files it produces. 
(Para 129{iii}) 
Reply of the Ministry 
15.1 National Mission on Manuscripts (NMM) since its inception in 2003 till today has 
contributed immensely to the preservation, documentation and dissemination of Ind ia's rich 
manuscript heritage . As of now, NMM has documented 5.2 million number of manuscripts, 
conserved 90 Million folios, digitized 3.30 lakhs number of manuscripts, organized  228 
preventive and 33 curative conservation workshops, published 114 books, organized  78 Basic 
level and  26 Advance level workshops on Manuscript logy  and Paleography,  1.28 lakh  
digitized manuscripts have been uploaded in the cloud server, out of which 70 Thousand 
manuscripts are available online for research purpose without download/ print facility. 
 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
15.2 The Committee acknowledges the Ministry’s reply and applauds the Ministry for its 
efforts in preserving, documenting and disseminating the country’s rich  manuscript 
heritage. The Committee  seeks information on  the numbe r of manuscripts still pending 
digitization and Ministry’s roadmap to achieve 100% digitization.   
 
Non-availability of information in Hindi or any other local language 
Recommendation/Observation 
16. Culture is encased in our languages. Art, in the form of  literature, plays, music films etc. 
cannot be fully appreciated without language. In order to preserve and promote our diverse 
culture, we need to preserve and promote a culture’s languages. Further, information on the art  
and culture must also be made available in Hindi and the local languages. 
(Para 129{vi}) 

 
36 
  
Reply of the Ministry 
 
16.1 The Ministry is continuously striving to disseminate information regarding the art and 
culture, in various languages. 
 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
16.2 The Committ ee recommends the Ministry to take necessary steps to at least first 
make the various art forms available in Hindi and English languages in order to maximize 
reach and accessibility . Following this, t he Ministry, should work on making the 
information avail able in scheduled and other local languages, based on regional 
requirements, in a phased manner.

‘Construction Of Road -Over Bridges (ROBs), Road -Under Bridges (RUBs), Service Roads And

10th August, 2023.   
2.      The Action Taken Replies were received from the Ministry on 11th March, 2024 in respect 
of all the observations/ recommendations contained in the Report. The replies have been 
categorized as follows:- 
Chapter-I:

92, 96, 97, 110, 112, 114, 115, 119, 139, 140, 141, 149, 162, 163, 164, 172, 182, 187, 194, 
196.  
Total: 40 
Chapter-III: 
Recommendations/Observations in respect of which replies of the Ministry have not been 
accepted by the Committee: 
Paragraph Nos.: 16, 38, 43, 44, 69, 73, 79, 80, 82, 84, 85, 117, 132, 142, 143, 144, 166,

3. The Committee desires that final reply in respect of the recommendation/observation which 
has been categorized as interim reply by the Committee should be furnished at the earliest. 
 

2 
 
Chapter-I 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE 
MINISTRY 
Construction of ROBs and RUBs 
Recommendation/Observation 
1. The Committee apprecia tes the increase in annual average progress in the number of 
Level Crossings (LCs) replaced with Road -Over-Bridges and Road -Under-Bridges. However, 
it also notes that the target of replacement of 1100 LCs set for 2023 -24 is lower than the 
annual average of  1207 progress achieved during 2014 -2023. The Committee is of the view 
that the target should be increased and the pace of replacement of LCs with ROBs/ RUBs 
should be expedited in the interest of greater safety and seamless mobility of the commuting 
public. 
(Para 10) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1 As per the policy of the Ministry, all LCs on National Highways are to be replaced by 
ROB/RUB. Construction of ROBs/RUBs on NHs are taken up either on standalone basis or as part 
of improvement/ upgradation project of  a section of NH. The  recommendations of the Committee 
are noted and construction of ROBs/RUBs in replacement of existing LCs on NHs  will be 
expedited.  
Elimination of Level crossing 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
2. The Committee notes with satisfaction th at all unmanned level crossings on Broad 
Gauge have been eliminated by January 2019. However, existence of 559 Unmanned Level 
Crossings in both Metre Gauge and Narrow Gauge needs to be replaced with ROB/RUB 
expeditiously in a focused and time bound manner. 
(Para 19) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1 This matter comes under purview of the Ministry of Railways. Hence the recommendations 
have been forwarded to Ministry of Railways for necessary action. 

3 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
3. Incorporating the elements of community engagement into the guidelines would involve 
measures such as conducting public consultations, holding informational sessions, and actively 
seeking feedback from the affected community. By involving local residents, businesses, and 
other stakeholders in the decision-making process, road construction projects can better serve 
their specific needs and mitigate potential negative impacts. This may include implementing 
traffic management plans, providing alternative routes, adjusting construction schedules  to 
meet local requirement or minimising disruption. 
(Para 45) 
Reply of the Ministry 
3.1 The elements like traffic diversion plan, construction zone safety measures, construction 
scheduling are prepared based on existing standards and guidelines of Indian Roads Congress which 
are developed based indigenous research, international best practices and stakeholders feedbacks in 
different projects. Nevertheless further action will be taken for community engagement in these 
matters. 
Recommendation/Observation 
4. Ground Penetrating Radar (GPR) should be used to penetrate the ground or structure, 
allowing for subsurface inspection of ROBs/RUBs. It can identify hidden defects, such as 
voids, delamination, or corrosion in concrete or steel elements. GPR can provide va luable 
information on the internal condition of the structure without the need for invasive 
investigations. 
Structural Health Monitoring (SHM) Systems should be adopted to involve the installation of 
sensors and monitoring devices on ROBs/RUBs to continuou sly monitor their structural 
behaviour. These sensors can measure parameters like vibrations, strains, and deflections, 
providing real-time data on the performance and health of the structure. SHM systems enable 
early detection of structural abnormalities and help in proactive maintenance and 
intervention. 
(Para 49) 
Reply of the Ministry 
4.1 Ground Penetrating Radar is being widely used to assess underground utilities. Foundation 
of ROBs/RUBs are generally not distressed as they are not located on river bed . Ministry has 
recently used guidelines for structural health monitoring on real time basis of bridges and structures 

4 
 
including ROBs and RUBs based on span length, location such as in coastal/highly polluted areas, 
age and history of previous rehabilitation/retrofitting measures using various kinds of sensors. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
5. Non-Destructive Testing (NDT) Techniques, such as ultrasonic testing, magnetic 
particle testing, and radiographic testing, can be employed for ROB/RUBs inspection. These  
techniques assess the integrity of structural components, detect cracks, weld defects, or 
corrosion, and identify potential failure points. NDT methods are typically used in 
combination with visual inspections to provide a comprehensive assessment of the structure's 
condition. 
(Para 50) 
Reply of the Ministry 
5.1 Schmidt Hammer Test, Ultrasonic Pulse Velocity Test and other NDTs are carried out for 
condition assessment of different components of bridges and structures including ROBs/RUBs. 
 
Environment clearances and land acquisition 
Recommendation/Observation 
6. The Committee appreciates the initiatives of the Ministry of Road Transport and 
Highways in addressing the most important issue of land acquisition in fast tracking the 
ROB/RUB projects. The Bhoomira shi portal has undoubtedly expedited the process of land 
acquisition for National Highways. However, the Committee urges upon the Ministry and 
NHAI to accord continued priority to the land acquisition issue and fails to appreciate as to 
why huge Government  funds are parked with Competent Authority for Land Acquisition 
(CALAs). 
    (Para 55) 
Reply of the Ministry 
6.1  The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways has launched Bhoomi Rashi Portal as a 
single point platform for online processing of Land Acquisit ion notification and payment of 
compensation to accelerate Highways infrastructure in India. The portal is a new mile stone in the 
nation’s journey towards digitization and transparency. The objective of the portal is to fast track the 
process of Land Acquisition notifications and to obviate the necessity of parking of huge amount of 
government fund with Competent Authority for Land Acquisition. 
6.2  The Ministry has made it mandatory for payment of compensation of Land Acquisition 

5 
 
through Bhoomi Rashi Port al for the projects of the Ministry of Road Transport and Highway and 
National Highways Authority of India (NHAI). The Ministry is continuously impressing upon the 
NHAI to make payment only through Bhoomi Rashi portal. The efforts has also been made for on -
boarding of National Highways Infrastructure Development Corporation Limited (NHIDCL) for 
payment of compensation through Portal. 
 6.3  The Present system of payment of compensation in respect of Ministry of Road Transport 
and Highways does not allow park ing of any fund with CALA. In case of NHAI, limit is 
created/fund is deposited for particular projects in CALA account up to which CALA can make 
payment through PFMS directly into account of the beneficiary. Therefore, the present system in 
NHAI inherently does not allow parking of Government funds with CALA. However, in some cases 
CALA could not be able to release compensation due to litigations in Courts, non -acceptance of 
award by beneficiaries, mismatch of beneficiaries’ details, arbitration awards etc. and the funds/limit 
remain parked/unpaid in CALAs Accounts.  
6.4  NHIDCL deposits the LA compensation amount with the concern CALA after passing of 
award under section 3G of National Highways Act, 1956 so as to enable them to distribute the 
compensation amount to beneficiary. No payment is deposited to concerned CALA’s account prior 
to 3G Award. In addition, NHIDCL has opened Zero balance accounts for the CALAs with only 
drawing rights so that money gets placed with the CALA for disbursement only. However,  in some 
cases, the CALAs are in the process of shifting to Zero balance accounts system.  
6.5  It is anticipated that once all the Implementing Agencies are completely on - boarded on 
Bhoomi Rashi Portal, there would be no parking of government funds with CALAs in any manner. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
7. The Committee also recommends that Ministries should assign competent contract 
managers who have the necessary skills and expertise to effectively manage contracts. These 
managers should have a strong und erstanding of contract law, project management, and 
negotiation skills. Imparting them adequate skill training will enable them to fulfil their 
responsibilities.  
(Para 64) 
Reply of the Ministry 
7.1 Consultants (AE/IE /PMC) are engaged for project manageme nt of EPC /BOT projects. 
Further, the projects are monitored by field units of NHAI/NHIDCL/PWD. Projects are monitored 
/reviewed by Ministry, NHAI and NHIDCL headquarters at Delhi also. Therefore, there is already 

6 
 
established mechanism to manage the contra ct. Nevertheless, process is being strengthened to 
enhance competencies of the key personnel of AE/IE for more effective contract management. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
8. The Railways should look for a cost -effective and durable solution to the problem o f 
water-logging by modifying embankment height, providing suitable cross and longitudinal 
drains, cutting off the ingress of water from the catchment area into the subway, etc. 
(Para 72) 
Reply of the Ministry 
8.1 Following steps are being taken to prevent water logging at various underpasses: 
 
i. Rain Water Harvesting (RWH) wells are provided to collect & dispose off rain water 
at LHS. 
ii. Fixed Pumps, Mobile Pumps & Heavy -duty pumps are arranged & deployed to 
discharge rain water from LHS. 
iii. Covering sheds are prov ided at critical LHS to prevent entry of rain water into the 
LHS. 
iv. Flood gauges are provided at LHS to indicate depth of water logging (More than 3 feet 
depth), during heavy rain. 
v. Caution boards are provided at LHS Not to enter in LHS if depth of water is b eyond 
dangerous level (more than 3 feet in depth). 
vi. Protection walls & Humps at the approach roads are provided to prevent entry of 
outside water into the LHS. 
vii. Dedicated team of Officer's & Supervisor's has been deputed to regularly inspect and 
monitor the water logging status in LHS. 
 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
9. The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Railways should relook into ‘Gate 
Mitra’ scheme and ensure that these personnel are being provided with all basic amenities.  In 
the Committee’s view , proper implementation of the Gate Mitra scheme will promote the 
safety of road users, besides generating employment. 
(Para 87) 

7

deterioration, or structural weakness. Drones are particularly useful for accessing hard -to-
reach areas and can significantly reduce inspection time and costs.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH REPLIES OF THE 
MINISTRY HAVE NOT BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE COMMITTEE 
 
Construction of Service Roads 
The Committee, in this regard, would like to know the cu rrent status and the details of the 
steps that have been taken by the Ministry. 
                             (Para 1.2)  
Present Road Survey Guidelines 
The Committee would like to know the number of instances, when agencies/individuals have 
sought such information from the Ministry either through RTI or any other medium. 
                             (Para 2.2)  
Analysis of existing road survey guidelines 
The Committee would like to know whether any meetings with local community 
leaders/representatives are h eld before finalisation of DPR. The Committee also would like 
to know whether decisions/suggestions in the meetings are factored in the finalisation of 
DPR. 
                             (Para 3.4)  
Flooding/ water logging issues 
The Committee recommends th at the drainage pipes and outlets must be properly cleaned 
before the onset of the Monsoon. The survey must be conducted to identify such locations 
where water logging is a constant phenomenon. The Ministry must ensure that  these 
locations are free from water logging during Monsoon.  The Committee also recommends 
that the drainage design and construction needs to be further improved.  
                             (Para 4.2)  
 
  

57 
 
 
The Committee would like to know the measures taken by the Ministry, in this regard, during 
the last two years. 
                             (Para 5.2)  
Shortage of manpower 
The Committee recommends that the Ministry should expedite the recruitment process and 
fill up the vacancies for smooth working and expansion of road infrastructu re. Further, the 
cadre review with provision for capacity building should be taken undertaken as early as 
possible keeping in mind the five R’s recommended by the Committee. 
                             (Para 6.9)  
Budgetary Allocation 
The Committee recomm ends that a separate allocation must be provided to States for 
construction of RoBs/RuBs so that the process is expedited and there are no delays in the 
construction. 
                             (Para 7.2)  
(ii) Road Safety related issues 
The Committee re iterates that the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways should 
persuade State Governments to frame such rules under Section 210D of the MVAA Act to 
create adequate accountability framework to ensure that road -owning agencies, 
contractors and concessionai res are held accountable for faulty road design and 
construction. 
                             (Para 8.4)  
Absent Pedestrian and Cyclist Facilities 
The Committee notes that there are many roads where pedestrian and cycling facilities are 
not available. The  Ministry should identify such roads and provide pedestrian and cycling 
facilities at the earliest. 
                             (Para 9.2)  
The Committee would like to know how frequently the Group of Infrastructure Committee 
meets. The Committee also sug gests to include Public Representatives in this Group of 
Infrastructure Committee for better communication and functioning.  
                             (Para 10.2)  

58 
 
The Committee recommends that removal of encroachments must be a priority for improving 
the accessibility and safety of road users. The details of steps taken till now to remove 
encroachment must be shared with the Committee. 
                             (Para 11.5)  
 
Fund allocation and support to IRC 
The Committee feels that the Ministry sho uld evolve some alternative to provide a reasonable 
amount of corpus seed fund to the IRC to manage the function s of its Secretariat, the 
modalities of which may be worked out in consultation with the IRC. 
                             (Para 12.2)  
The Committee recommends that the Intelligent Transport System must also be launched in 
National and other State Highways to enhance road safety and better traffic management. 
                             (Para 13.2)  
 
The Committee is of the view that the Ministr y should identify the bridges showing signs of 
deterioration and thereafter structural health monitoring should be done of all those bridges 
on a regular basis. 
                             (Para 14.2)  
Private Sector Participation 
The Committee would like  to know about these stand alone projects which are being 
implemented on EPC mode and the present status thereof. 
                             (Para 15.3)  
 
The Committee would like to know how these modes are impartial enough to provide a fair 
and competitive bidding process. 
                             (Para 16.2)  
 
 
Sustainable and environment-friendly roads 
The Committee feels that there is an urgent need to explore more viable options other than 
Rain Water Harvesting Structures  alone. The Committee re iterated that the Ministries 

59 
 
should adopt features like rain gardens, bioswales, and permeable pavements to manage 
stormwater runoff and improve water quality. 
 
 (Para 17.2) 
The Committee enquires that even after adequate drainage measures are provided, there are 
problems of water logging at many places. The Committee recommends that the Ministry 
should focus on SuDS to manage surface water runoff from roads. 
                             (Para 18.2)  
 
The Committee recommends that the Ministry should make all efforts to utilise solar energy 
for lighting purposes all across NH stretches in the country.  
                             (Para 19.2)

Potential Tourist Spots  
Recommendation/Observation 
12.      In the meetings with the stakeholders, the    Committee was informed about various 
potential tourist spots in the country which have been placed at Annexure – IX. The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry may examine t he concept of Greenfield Tourism 
where new locations can be developed as potential tourism spots with the participation of 
Government of India and the concerned State Government with private investments for 
creation of modern tourist infrastructure, hotels  and all tourist            facilities          and 
connectivity by air, rail and road. The Statue of Unity near Kevadia in Gujarat is a classic 
example of Greenfield Tourism, being a man -made tourist destination which has earned a 
formidable reputation as a popular tourism spot. Another example is tourism on the sand 
dunes near the  Salasar Balaji Temple in the Churu District of Rajasthan where hotels and 
restaurants have come up to cater to the tourists who visit the temple and stay to enjoy the 
sand dunes in the desert. The Committee observes that development of such Greenfield tourist 
spots would take the pressure off the already established tourist spots which sometimes suffer 
from the adverse effects of over tourism..

Sustainable Tourism  
Recommendation/Observation 
1.       The Committee notes that India has been r anked at 139, 134, and 128 in the years 
2015, 2017 and2019, respectively under Environmental Sustainability in the World Travel  
and Tourism Competitiveness Ranking. While the new National Strategy and National Board 
for Sustainable Tourism have come into f orce in 2022, the Ministry had been  promoting 
Sustainable Tourism in India for nearly a decade after the launch of Sustainable Tourism 
Criteria for India in 2014. Not much progress has, however, been made in development of 
Sustainable Tourism in the last d ecade as substantiated by India’s low rankings in this 
category. The Committee emphasizes that economic development should not be at the cost of 
the environment and recommends that the Ministry may ensure that the revised Sustainable 
Tourism Criteria be sc rupulously implemented to minimize the adverse impact of tourism  on 
the environment. While a Certification programme  for tourism stakeholders, who have 
successfully implemented sustainable criteria ,has been inexistence for nearly a decade, only 
one Certification has been effected till date. The Committee desires to know the number of 
hotels surveyed for the Certification Programme and the strategy adopted for the survey. 
The Committee observes that while disbursement of monthly newsletters to stakeholders and 
workshops are useful for dissemination of information, the feedback from stakeholders like 
hoteliers and tour operators is equally important to comprehend the problems being faced 
while implementing policies on the ground level. The Committee feels tha t the pace of the 
Ministry in promotion of sustainability in tourism is sluggish and recommends that the 
Ministry may step up its coordination efforts with both the stakeholders and the other Central 
Ministries for effective promotional campaigns.. 
 (Para 19) 
Reply of the Ministry 

10 
 
1.1      In light of the global endorsement of the Travel for LiFE (TFL) program in the New 
Delhi Leader Declaration, the Sustainable Tourism Criteria for India (STCI) has been 
rebranded as “ TFL Certification powered by STCI” . The  certification has undergone 
modification as per necessary course corrections and industry feedback. The new version of 
TFL certification is now categorised as TFL certification for Classified Units and TFL 
certification for Unclassified Units. The TFL cer tification for Classified Units is applicable 
only for the accommodation units and tour operators with a valid classification certificate 
issued by the Ministry of Tourism, which will ease the application, desktop assessment and 
on-site assessment process. 
  
1.2 Once the application is submitted, it proceeds to the desktop assessment stage where 
the assessor examines the accuracy of the submitted documents. After the desktop assessment 
is concluded, the unit will undergo site inspection, which determines th e validity of issuing 
the certificate as per the scoring mechanism of the certification. At present, one unit has been 
awarded the certificate and four units are at the desktop assessment stage. 
  
1.3 To ease and assist the industry stakeholders, toolkits, user manuals and video 
tutorials are currently provided. Furthermore, the formulation of sustainability templates 
(Including, a sustainability management plan, details of initiative for social and community 
participation, details of initiative for preserv ation of flora and fauna and action plan for the 
preservation of flora and fauna) is being formulated. 
 
1.4 On the occasion of World Tourism Day 2023, TFL Signed Up was launched on the 
Nidhi Plus portal for accommodation units, tour operators, destinations  and other tourism 
eco-players. The TFL Signed Up is a voluntary commitment to sustainable practices and acts 
as a transitioning step of a tourism business which will demonstrate effective sustainable 
management, maximize socio - economic benefits to local communities and maximize 
cultural & historical heritage and environmental benefits. 
  
1.5 Sensitization and handholding session status for TFL Certification and signed up 
session with: 
  
a. States/UTs: Dedicated handholding sessions were organised for the Sta tes and UTs to 
assist in promoting TFL Certifications, including Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, 
Kerala, Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh. 
b. Associations: Awareness workshops were organised in collaboration with prominent 
tourism associations such as HAI, IATO, an d AMA stay to provide sensitise them on 
the certification process.

c. SD Destinations: Awareness workshops, conducted in collaboration with 
SwadeshDarshan destinations for the Travel for LiFE signed up and Certification,

operators, adventure guides and the tourists to provide support an d promotion of adventure

Ecotourism  
Recommendation/Observation 
8.      The Committee observes that guides and naturalists are one of the most important 
elements in imparting quality ecotourism experience by way of  providing valuable 
educational, interpretive and experiential services to the visitors. The Committee has been 
informed that a Certification Scheme for tour operators and other service providers for

Reply of the Ministry 
8.1    The Ministry of Tourism in collaboration with Ministry of Environment, Forest  and

17 
 
Ramsar Convention on Wetlands as part of the international network of wetlands important 
for the conservation of global biological diversity and for sustaining human life through the

tourism and Wet component of this initiative is being implemented jointly by MoT and

Meetings, Incentives, Conferences, and Exhibitions (Mice) & Wedding Tourism

.

.

Film Tourism 

22 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
17.      The Committee observes that films can h ave a massive impact on destination 
marketing as visitors are often inspired to visit filming locations featured in popular films. 
The impact is such that the annual tourist influx is said to have increased by 40% in New 
Zealand, the site of the movie tril ogy of “Lord of the Rings” after the release of the films. In 
India, the release of the film "3 Idiots" led to a significant increase in tourist arrivals in 
Ladakh to visit the Pangong Lake featured in the film. India produces the highest number of 
films in the world and film tourism has significant potential for growth in India. Many Indian 
films, especially those regarding period dramas, showcase historical places and characters 
and can be useful to highlight the history behind the tourist places. The Tam il movie 
“PonniyinSelvan” based on one of the greatest novels in Tamil literature, is a fictional 
account of the historical character of Raja RajaChola, the Chola king who built the 
Brihadeeswarar Temple in Thanjavur, one of the biggest temples of India. T he Chola dynasty 
was famous for building temples, many of which are now World Heritage Sites. The 
Committee notes that the Tamil Nadu Tourism Development Corporation has announced a 
“Chola Tourism Circuit” covering the Chola Temples and the Veeranam Lake, also built by 
the Cholas. Tourism potential of such historical and religious sites can be harnessed through 
the medium of films. The Committee feels that while India has the advantage of producing the 
highest number of films in the world which also in a wa y depict the innate historical 
significance of the places of tourism interests, the Ministry has not paid adequate attention to 
the great potential of films to showcase India. The Committee recommends that the Ministry 
should endeavour to devise the strategy to fully tap into the benefits of film tourism. 
(Para 77) 
Reply of the Ministry 
17.1    Under the Hospitality Scheme, Ministry of Tourism has a provision of supporting the 
visits of TV teams for undertaking shooting at tourism destinations of India, on the basis of 
proposals received from Indian Missions & Stakeholders. 
 17.2 In order to leverage the power of Film Tourism to promote destinations, an event on 
“Promoting Incredible India through Film Tourism” was organized on 22 ndMay 2023 on the 
side lines  of third Tourism Working Group meeting held at Srinagar. During the meeting 
draft National Strategy for Film Tourism was unveiled. 
  
Golf Tourism 
Recommendation/Observation 
18.      The Committee observes that Golf was introduced to India by the British a nd in 1829, 
the first golfing establishment, the Royal Calcutta Golf Club, was established. In contrast, 
Thailand’s first   professional golf was established only in 1924. Yet Thailand has emerged 
as the world’s top golfing destination while golf tourism i s yet to take shape in India. In fact, 
many Indians visit Thailand as golf tourists. The Committee observes that India has much of 

23 
 
the same landscapes and climatological conditions as Thailand, like a sunny climate all year 
around in most places which make s winter golf possible. Yet, India has not taken any special 
initiative to attract both domestic and international golf enthusiasts. Thailand has promoted 
a Thai Golf Pass which is a unique loyalty programme exclusive to Thailand providing a 
seamless golf experience. The Committee recommends that the Ministry should come up with 
initiatives such as developing world -class golf infrastructure, promoting tournaments, and 
providing holistic tourism experience to the visiting golfers in the country. 
 
(Para 80) 
Reply of the Ministry 
18.1    The development of tourism infrastructure is primarily undertaken by the State 
Governments. However, the Ministry of Tourism through its SwadeshDarshan scheme

Thenzawl, Mizoram for Rs.64.48 Cr. the responsibility of maintaining and operating the same

 Recommendation/Observation 
19.      The Committee observes that the Ministry is yet to take significant action on Golf 
Tourism, Eco-tourism, Film Tourism, and Wedding Tourism while taking some measures to 
promote Sustainable Tourism, Rural Tourism, MICE and Medical Tourism, and Cruise 
Tourism. A plethora of wildlife sanctuaries and tiger reserves exist in India yet not much 
attention seems  to have been paid to Wildlife Tourism. Kerala has shown the way for 
Caravan Tourism  with the establishment of one Caravan Park and proposal for 3 new 
Caravan Parks, 10 Caravans and subsidy of Rs. 7.5 lakhs for Caravan owners. Despite the 
successful effort s of Kerala towards promotion of Caravan Tourism, the Ministry has not 
endeavored to replicate the same in other states. The Committee also appreciates the efforts 
of Kerala Tourism to develop the “Muziris Heritage Circuit”, the largest Heritage 
Conservation Project in India which would reinstate the historical and cultural significance 
of the legendary port of Muziris and also the Alappuzha Heritage Circuit which includes the 
development of the defunct port of Alappuzha into a marina. The Committee recommends that 
the Ministry may explore the potential of Casino Tourism, Culinary Tourism, and Polo 
tourism, the last being believed to have originated in Manipur. The Committee also observes 
that in the aftermath of the pandemic “Remote Working” has gained trac tion. Due to the rise 
in online work, workers often move to locations even in other countries which offer a lower 
cost of living or scenic locations, etc. and continue to stay for a long period of time. India 
offers all modern facilities required for such remote working, like good internet facilities, a 
low cost of living compared to Western countries and many serene and beautiful places for 

24 
 
living. The Committee recommends that the Ministry may explore the possibilities of such 
niche tourism experience. 
 (Para 82)

25 
 
investment in tourism sector and public private partnerships has constituted a steering

 20.2 The PRASHAD Scheme is entirely funded by the central government (a central

connectivity, tapping the potential of medical tourism, pr omoting India as a hub for MICE

28 
 
(Para 89)

reports that the Government is planning to review the speed limits and recommends that the 
Tourist transport vehicles may not be treated in the same category as other commercial 
vehicles and the speed l imits may suitably be revised/  increased. Another minor but 
significant point raised by the stakeholders was that curtains should be allowed in tourist 
buses as tourists, especially the foreigners, are not used to tropical weather, especially the 
heat of I ndian summers. The Committee observes that tourism promotion is as much about 
the whole some journey experience as it is about  the destinations and recommends that the 
Ministry may consider the issue. 
(Para 90) 
Reply of the Ministry 
24.1    The matter in r egards to the same have already been taken up with Ministry of Road

comparison to neighbouring countries (Annexure – III) is affecting tourists‟ arrival in India.

29

destinations. Infrastructure development in the tourism sector can exist as a standalone 
activity and is not inherently confined to the concept of theme -based development. Thematic 
circuits, do not necessarily dictate t he nature of infrastructure projects. Independently 
developed destinations may naturally align with multiple themes, showcasing the versatility 
and adaptability of tourism infrastructure to diverse traveler preferences and interests. This 
flexibility allow s destinations to cater to a broad range of visitor experiences, enhancing

resources, support local communities, and minimize the ecological footprint, thereby 
creating destinations that not only attract visitors but also contribute positively to the well -
being of the environment and communities in the long run . The emphasis on sustainability 
reflects a holistic approach that aims to balance the economic benefits of tourism with the 
preservation of cultural and natural heritage for future generations.

effectively conveying the concept of destination management. They provide clear and 
comprehensive directives, aligning with the overarching goal of destination management in a

1.        The Committee observes that in  a predominantly agrarian and rural economy like 
India, rural tourism has immense potential for boosting employment a nd income for villagers 
while offering opportunities to the city dwellers to take a break from the hectic pace of urban 
life to experience nature and local culture at a much slower pace. India is home to a diverse 
range of unique villages, each with its own cultural, architectural and historical significance. 
Unique villages such as ‘Mattur’ in Karnataka where all the residents speak only Sanskrit 
and many others offer a glimpse into India’s rich traditions and culture. The Committee, 
however, observes that the Rural Tourism website does not provide details as to how to travel 
to the unique villages nor details regarding rural home  stays for most of the villages. Even 
the Khonoma village page does not provide any useful details for the tourists. The Committee 
recommends that the Ministry may ensure that the Rural Tourism website has all details of 
rural homestays, travel connectivity and tourist spots in respect of every village featured for 
the convenience of the tourists. 
. 
 (Para 26)

1.1      The Rural Tourism India website is integrated with the NIDHI+ portal and the content 
and the details related to the home stays are directly fetched from www.nidhi.tourism.gov.in 
Also the website is continuously upgrading the content on it. However, due to the excessive 
amount of data the time taken to upload the data varies. 
  
Further Recommendation/ Observation 


44 
 
1.2      The Committee appreciates the Ministry's ongoing efforts to integrate the Rural 
Tourism India website with the NIDHI+ portal and its commitment to upgrading the 
website's content.  
1.3 The Committee recommends for the implementation of regular content audits to 
ensure that the information on the Rural Tourism website is accurate, up -to-date, and 
user-friendly.  
1.4 The Ministry should create a schedule for these audits, prioritizing villages that 
are likely to attract a significant number of tourists. 
 
1.5 While recognizing the challenge s of handling large volumes of data, the 
Committee recommends the Ministry to explore more efficient methods for uploading 
and integrating data from the NIDHI+ Portal. This may include technological upgrades 
or the use of advanced data management tools to minimize delays and ensure that the 
latest information is easily accessible to tourists. 
 
1.6 The Committee recommends that the Ministry collaborate  and work  closely with 
local authorities and tourism boards in the featured villages  to ensure the accuracy and 
comprehensiveness of the information provided . T his collaboration will help capture 
and present all relevant details, including lesser -known travel routes and homestay 
options, accurately on the website. 
 
Adventure Tourism  
 Recommendation/Observation 
2.        The Committee notes that there have been a n increasing number of accidents in 
Adventure sports, especially in paragliding, which has claimed the lives of a number of 
tourists in the last few years. As per media reports, even “soft adventure” sports like trekking 
have led to casualties in certain situations. The Committee has been informed by stakeholders 
that 3 Gs - Guidelines, Guides and Gears – are critical in risk mitigation. The Committee has 
also been informed that the Ministry has released guidelines for safety and quality norms for 15 Land B ased, 07 
Air Based and 07 Water Based adventure tourism activities, which cover the entire range of thrilling activities. 
Besides, some States have also adopted various regulatory measures and safety protocols to address the 
inherent concerns of adventure tourism. ISO 21101:2014 and BIS have laid down safety management standards 
for compliance by adventure activities service providers that act as benchmarks for safe adventure activities. 
The Committee desires to know about the impact of such safety guidelin es    on    reduction    of accidents in 
adventure tourism. The Ministry may give data on the number of accidents as also the casualties which have 
taken place in adventure tourism in the country in the last five years. The Committee has also been informed  
that while testing and certification of PPE (Personal Protective Equipment) kits is necessary, it is difficult for 
small Indian manufacturing enterprises to obtain the universally accepted international certifications like UIAA 
(French) (International Cli mbing and Mountaineering Federation). The Committee recommends that testing 
labs where certification is done by the BIS may help small enterprises in this field.  
. 

45 
 
(Para 33) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1      The Ministry is committed to continuous improvement  and enhancement of safety standards in 
adventure tourism. In order to provide impetus to the development of adventure tourism in the country, the 
Ministry of Tourism has notified a National Strategy for adventure tourism. The Strategy focuses on 
developing adventure destinations, promoting safety in adventure tourism, skill development, capacity building 
and marketing.  
2.2 As part of implementation process of the aforesaid strategy document, Ministry of Tourism has 
drafted a “Model Adventure Tourism Safet y Law” after consultations with States, Line Ministries and various 
industry stakeholders. The final draft of the “Model Adventure Tourism Safety Law” has been circulated to 
Stakeholders and State/UT’s Governments for inputs.  
   
 Further Recommendation/ Observation 
2.3      The Committee acknowledges the reply of the Ministry but reiterates its request for detailed data 
on the number of accidents and casualties in adventure tourism over the last ﬁve years. This information 
is essential for evaluating the e ﬀectiveness of the safety guidelines and standards in mitigating risks 
associated with adventure sports. The Committee urges the Ministry to provide this data at the earliest, 
including a breakdown by speciﬁc activities (e.g., paragliding, trekking) and th e locations where these 
incidents occurred. The Ministry address the Committee's identified safety gaps.  
  
Recommendation/Observation 
3.        The Committee feels that strict adherence to safety guidelines and implementation of safety protocols can 
be possible only if responsible and licensed/ certified adventure tour operators handle the activities. Licensed 
tour operators play an important role in promotion of adventure tourism as they conduct thorough risk 
assessments, implement safety measures, and pro vide high quality safety gears, besides engaging experienced 
and professional guides to handle emergency situations. The Committee has been informed that presently, 
adventure tour operators‟ licenses are issued by either the Centre or the States and there are still a lot of 
unlicensed tour operators in the country’s adventure tourism sector who operate without requisite permits, 
certifications and regulatory approvals to meet the requirements of safety,quality and also the law in thefield. 
The Committee desires to know what action has been taken or is proposed to be taken by the Ministry on the 
unlicensed adventure tour operators. The Committee has also been informed that the Ministry has circulated a 
draft model adventure tourism law to all the States/UTs f or feedback. The Committee stresses that high risk 
adventure sports cannot be regulated only by guidelines and recommends that the Ministry may make all efforts 
to come out with laws soon so that only licensed and responsible operators who adhere to the la id down safety 
norms remain in business to provide adventure tourism services. 
. 
 (Para 34) 
Reply of the Ministry 
3.1      The Ministry of Tourism under its voluntary scheme only accords approval/recognition to Tour 
Operators, including Adventure Tour Oper ators, under the category of Tourism Service Providers, through 
NIDHI+ portal. It is not under the purview of the Ministry to issue licenses to Adventure Tour Operators or to 
maintain the list of license holders. However, during application, in order to ob tain recognition from the 
Ministry, Adventure tour operators are required to specify the specialization of activity like trekking, water 
sports, aero sports, scuba diving, safaris, etc. The field staff must obtain an Adventure Certificate from 
specialized organizations including State Govt. Institutes like NIM (Uttarkashi), JIM (J&K), AB Institute of 

46 
 
Mountaineering (Manali), HMI (Darjeeling), SonamGyasto Institute (Sikkim), NIMAS (Arunachal Pradesh) etc. 
for Mountaineering and NIWS (Goa) for Water/Aero Sports. 
  
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
3.2      The Committee observes that the Ministry's approval/recognition scheme is voluntary and does 
not enforce compliance with safety regulations or mandatory certification. This approach is inadequate 
for manag ing high -risk activities, as it does not ensure that all operators adhere to necessary safety 
protocols, thereby leaving tourists vulnerable. The Committee recommends that the Ministry implements 
centralized licensing framework for Adventure Tour Operators    at the national level. Despite the 
jurisdictional complexities, the Committee believes that a uniform licensing system is crucial for ensuring 
that all operators adhere to the required safety, quality and regulatory standards. The Ministry should 
collaborate with State/UT Governments to develop this framework, making licensing a mandatory 
requirement for operating in the adventure tourism sector. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
4.  Regarding the standardization of safety gears, the Committee ha sbeen    informed   that   presently, 
there is no single system of certification of adventure equipments in our country. The Bureau of Indian 
Standards (BIS) is working towards setting standards for adventure equipments that can demonstrate proven 
track record of reliab ility to help ensure a safe adventure experience. The Committee expresses its displeasure 
that India does not have standardized safety gears even for high risk adventure sports and recommends that the 
Ministry may expeditiously implement a uniform standard  across the country for all adventure tourism 
verticals, prepared by Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS).. 
(Para 36) 
 Reply of the Ministry 
4.1      Recognizing the importance of ensuring safety in high -risk adventure sports, particularly  through 
standardized equipment, the Ministry is actively working towards developing a framework.    
 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
4.2      The Committee seeks an update on  the progress made in develop ing a framework that emphasizes 
the importance of ensuring safety in h igh-risk adventure sports, particularly  through the use of 
standardized equipment.  
           
  
Golf Tourism  
Recommendation/Observation 
5.      During its Study Tour in Kerala, the Committee had been informed that an amount of Rs. 2464.99 lakh 
had been sanctioned to Sports Authority of India under the Scheme Assistance  to Central Agencies for Tourism 
Infrastructure Development” in Kerala for upgradation of the Golf Course at the 165  year old SAI Trivandrum 
Golf Club under the Sports Authority. The Committee observes that the project was sanctioned in 2016 - 17 but 
as per media reports, the upgradation seems to have been taken up only in 2020 -21. The Committee further 
observes that only half the sanctioned amount has been released and the status of the proje ct is stated to be 
“Project Closed”. The Committee desires to know the reasons behind this when in reality,  the project  is not 
completed. The Committee also desires to know whether other Golf clubs in the country have been given similar 
assistance under the Scheme. 

47 
 
(Para 81) 
Reply of the Ministry 
5.1  Due to huge delay and unsatisfactory progress the sanctioning Committee in the review meeting held 
under the chairmanship of Secretary(T) on 06.04.2023 took the decision to close the project and the same has 
been conveyed to the implementing agency vide letter dated 11.05.2023 with the direction to refund the parked 
funds. The unutilized amount is yet to be returned by Sports Authority of India (SAI) and the Ministry is 
regularly taking up the matter with SAI to return the unspent balance along with interest.  
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
5.2    The Committee desires that the Ministry provide the speciﬁc reasons for the delays and 
unsatisfactory progress in the Trivandrum Golf Club project. 
5.3    Further, it is recommended that the Ministry establish a more robust monitoring mechanism to 
oversee the implementation of projects funded under this scheme. The Ministry should ensure that future 
projects are completed on schedule, with regular progress reports and transparent communication 
among all stakeholders to prevent situations similar to those en countered with the Trivandrum Golf Club 
project.  The Committee also desires to  know  whether  other  Golf clubs in the country have been given 
similar  assistance  under  the Scheme.  
 
   
Recommendation/Observation 
6.      The Committee has been informed by the stakeholders that the present level of training and skilling is not 
adequate as niche tourism demands high level of training and skilling to meet the specific requirements and 
expectations of the tourists pertaining to that sector of niche tourism.  The Committee recommends that the 
tourism sector needs to undertake reskilling and upscaling of its manpower by way of imparting them skill 
upgradation capacity building training in different niche areas from time to time.  
(Para 87) 
Reply of the Ministry 
6.1    Ministry of Tourism conducts various short terms skilling and re -skilling training program under its 
scheme of Capacity Building for Service Providers (CBSP) in Tourism and Hospitality Sectors . 
  
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
6.2    The Committee observes that current initiatives may not fully address the increasing demand for 
specialized skills in niche tourism sectors, which often require advanced and continuous training. The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry may broaden its training pr ograms to include more specialized 
and advanced courses tailored to speciﬁc niche tourism sectors, such as adventure tourism, eco -tourism, 
wellness tourism, cultural tourism, and others. 
6.3 The Committee further recommends that the Ministry introduce cont inuous skill development 
programs, rather than focusing solely on short -term courses. This could include periodic refresher 
courses, advanced certiﬁcations, and  on -the- job training opportunities to ensure that the workforce 
stays current with the latest trends and best practices in their fields. 
  
Recommendation/Observation 
7.      The Committee observes that out of the 1,291 approved hotels in India only 565 hotels belong to Three 
Star and below categories and out of the 1,00,980 hotels rooms only 18,225  rooms belong to these categories 

48 
 
which is grossly inadequate to meet the tourism numbers targeted by the Ministry. The Committee also observes 
that tourists, especially in niche tourism, come from all strata of society and the hotel accommodation should 
cater to all categories of tourists. The Committee recommends that the Ministry should incentivise those in the 
hospitality business to make concerted efforts to ensure the availability of sufficient number of hotel rooms of all 
categories for the optimal growth of tourism sector. 
. 
(Para 88) 
 Reply of the Ministry 
7.1    Incentivising and providing benefits to the hospitality business is connected according to industry status to 
the tourism and hospitality sector, which is under the purview  of State Governm ents/UT Administrations. The 
Ministry has been following up on the position of all the States/UTs in according industry status to tourism and 
hospitality sector from time to time. 
.  
  
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
7.2    The Committee desires an upd ate on the progress in granting industry status to the tourism and 
hospitality sector under the jurisdiction of State Governments and UT administrations. The Committee 
recommends that the Ministry intensify its e ﬀorts to advocate this industry status to the tourism and 
hospitality sector across all States and UTs. Such status is essential for providing incentives such as tax 
beneﬁts, utility subsidies, and improved access to ﬁnancing, which can encourage the devel opment of 
more hotels in the Three Star and below categories. 
 
Swadesh Darshan 2.0  
Recommendation/Observation 
8.      The Committee observes the differences (Annexure – VIII) in funding pattern, disbursal of funds and 
receipt of Utilisation Certificates i n the Swadesh Darshan 2.0 Scheme, and appreciates the new features of 
Impact Assessment of the projects under the Scheme and monitoring     of     the     Scheme through a   
 Comprehensive Portal. The Committee, however, observes that all the themes of the S wadesh Darshan 1.0 
Scheme have been repeated in the 2.0 Scheme with no new additions. The claim of the Ministry to focus on 
fewer destinations in the second phase of the Scheme has also been diluted by the addition of 50 more 
destinations.. 
(Para 122) 
Reply of the Ministry 
8.1 While the SwadeshDarshan 1.0 was focused on development thematic circuits, the SwadeshDarshan2.0 
aims at development of sustainable and responsible tourism destinations. This involves adequate development of 
softer aspects as well at the identified destinations. Under SwadeshDarshan 2.0, a destination can be developed 
in one or more themes.  
 The Ministry of Tourism has now issued guidelines for ‘Challenge Based Destination Development’, a 
sub-scheme under SwadeshDarshan 2.0. The objec tive of the scheme is holistic development of the destination 
to enhance tourist experience across all points of the tourist value chain. The expenditure on the destinations 
proposed to be developed under this sub -scheme will be made from the budget alloca ted under the 
SwadeshDarshan scheme, by managing overall allocation on account of SD2.0 destinations and envisaged 
savings from SD1.0 scheme.. 

49 
 
  
 Further Recommendation/ Observation 
8.2    The Committee desires from the Ministry a detailed explanation on h ow the additional 50 
destinations align with the scheme’s objectives of promoting sustainable and responsible tourism. The 
Ministry should conduct and present an impact analysis to illustrate how this increase in the number of 
destinations will inﬂuence the overall  eﬀectiveness  and  success of the Swadesh Darshan 2.0 scheme. This 
analysis may include a comparative assessment with Swadesh Darshan 1.0 to evaluate any differences in 
outcomes. 
  
Promotion of Tourism Abroad By Indian Missions 
Recommendation/Observation 
9.        The Committee notes the events and programmes organised by the Indian Missions abroad to promote 
tourism and the budgets for the same. The Committee has been informed that the Tourism Officers posted in 
Indian Missions have tourism prom otion as additional charge. The Committee recommends that as 
responsibility for tourism promotion abroad now rests solely with the Indian Missions in all countries, the 
Tourism Officers may be given sole charge as far as possible as it is necessary for the  transitional change from 
the Overseas Tourist Offices to the Missions in many countries and to create confidence among the stakeholders 
that the Missions are attaching top priority to tourism promotion.    The Tourism Officers were designated by 
MEA in Oct ober, 2021. The Committee has been informed that since then the Tourism Officers have had only 
one meeting with  the Indian stakeholders a year back and desires to know how many meetings have been held 
with them as also the foreign tourism agents and B2B players since their appointment. 
(Para 149) 
 Reply of the Ministry 
9.1    5 meetings were held between Indian Missions and Ministry of Tourism officials for 
discussions relating to promotional activities for promotion of India as a preferred tourist 
destination and promotional activities including fairs and exhibitions. 
  
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
9.2    The Committee is concerned  about the limited number of meetings held by the 
Tourism Officers with Indian stakeholders and foreign tourism agents/B2 B players 
since their appointment. The Ministry should ensure that regular and frequent 
meetings are scheduled to foster better communication and collaboration.
