Chapter-I 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY 
THE MINISTRY 
  
Recommendation/Observation 
1.     The Committee notes the IWAI’s submission that the manpower sanction ed in 
IWAI is for 3 National Waterways only. During the discussions with the IWAI at the 
time of deliberations on the National Waterways Bill, 2015, (223 rd Report of the 
Committee) the Committee had been informed that the IWAI had a sanctioned strength 
of 419 with additional floating and contractual staff. Further, cadre reorganization in 
IWAI was underway.  
    The Committee desires to know the present sanctioned manpower in IWAI, the 
number of vacancies available and whether the sanctioned strength had be en increased, 
after the said reorganization, at the time of notification of the new 106 waterways or 
anytime thereafter. The Committee would like to know the reasons if such review was 
not carried out, as it reflects on poor management skills on the part o f the Ministry and 
IWAI. The Committee recommends that the Ministry and IWAI may take immediate 
steps to review the manpower requirement for the 23 Operational Waterways so that 
such constraints which are having a negative impact on the waterways developme nt 
could be removed. The Committee is of the opinion that manpower constraints cannot 
be allowed to be the limiting conditions for the implementation of the development 
projects that are crucial for ensuring the country’s economic prosperity. 
(Para 18) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1    The recommendations have been noted and the following process has been initiated: 
         Quotations from IPA/ NIC Empanelled Firms has been sought for a Comprehensive 
Review for the following: 
a. Organization Restructuring 
b. Cadre Review & Creation of Posts 
c. Comprehensive Revision of Recruitment Rules & HR Policy with DoP&T Guidelines 
 

3 
 
d. Framing of IWAI Employees Handbook and 
e. Preparation of Inspection Manual. 
      Based on the recommendation/ report of the Firm, proposal for creation of  posts/ Review 
of manpower is under formulation. 
Recommendation/Observation 
2.       Regarding the lack of cargo earmarked for IWT and insufficient facilities, the 
Committee observes that after decades of dependence on road and rail transport, 
shifting fro m road and rail to waterways would entail redesignating entire supply 
chains. The factors such as the slow pace of development of IWT, poor hinterland 
connectivity, high investment costs of vessels and equipments, etc. all discourage 
companies and shippers from shifting to the inland waterways mode. The Committee 
notes the Ministry’s submission that waterway usage charges have been kept at Nil 
and other charges kept at a low level to promote inland water transport. The 
Committee, however, feels that substan tial financial incentives rather than mere 
waiver of charges would be necessary to facilitate the modal shift to waterways. The 
Committee has been informed that no financial incentives are at present proposed by 
the IWAI. 
(Para 19) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1       The observation of the Committee for Financial Incentives to facilitate the modal shift 
to waterways is noted for compliance. 
 The logistics movement through inland waterways in the country has increasing 
trends after the initiative taken by the MoPSW, IWAI. 
 The Inland Water Transport sector of the country is at a very nascent stage and 
growth of IWT ecosystem would take time but the consistent efforts over decade 
make possible to reach expected outcome. However, as indicator, we are observing 
that after intervention and investment made in development of IWT infrastructure that 
bringing trends for positive growth in movement of cargo and passenger traffic along 
National Waterways is registered.  
 The initiative of Jal Marg Vikas Project is one of the r emarkable projects in this 
sector which envisages capacity augmentation of NW -1 (Ganga) from Varanasi to 
Haldia. 
 The multimodal terminal developed at Varanasi, Sahibganj and Haldia provides 
multimodal connectivity and the efforts are on to operationalize t hese terminals by 
engaging PPP concessionaire under suitable model of PPP projects. Haldia Terminals 
has already been awarded to Private Concessionaire. 

4 
 
 The tariffs for terminals along NW -1 were notified and stakeholders are being 
encouraged to shift their logistics movement along National Waterways. 
 IWAI has also initiated efforts for anchoring stakeholders by facilitating pilot 
movements, signing of long term transport agreements, providing green transportation 
solutions and storage facilities at terminal sites etc.   
         The development of freight village at Varanasi and Industrial Cluster cum Logistics 
Park (ICLP) at Sahibganj is under implementation by IWAI to facilitate modal shift of cargo 
from rail/ road to waterways. 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.    The Committee recommends that given the long term and slow nature of 
development of IWT, and the huge investments in the creation of requisite 
infrastructure and facilities and the fact that a large number of waterways are being 
developed in the coun try simultaneously, the Ministry and IWAI may consider giving 
certain financial incentives to shippers for the modal shift to waterways. The Committee 
is aware that Terminals for loading/unloading of cargo at various locations along the 
waterways are one o f the three essential requirements for successful navigation on 
Inland Waterways, apart from navigable fairways and aids to navigation. The 
Committee observes that while limited depths of rivers, erosion and meandering are 
determined by the forces of natur e and cannot be easily controlled, factors such as 
development of loading/unloading facilities at Terminals, increase of staff strength to 
deal with the expansion of operational waterways, connectivity to rail and road 
networks are not insurmountable obsta cles and should be taken up with priority in the 
usual course along with the development plans. The Committee observes that the CAG 
in its Performance Audit Report of Kerala Waterways (2015) had pointed out that 
several PSUs near the Kochi Port were transporting large volumes of cargo by road and 
were willing to shift to waterways mode if proper loading/unloading facilities were 
created. The Committee recommends that the Ministry and IWAI should focus on 
creating adequate terminal facilities at the loading and unloading points and ensure the 
availability of hinterland connectivity to encourage potential users, manufacturers and 
shippers to prefer waterways to rail and road. The Committee also observes that one of 
the proposed initiatives under the Blue Econo my Vision 2047 is mandating PSUs and 
Cooperative Companies to divert 10% of their cargo by coastal or inland waterways. 
The Committee desires to know as to whether at present, PSUs have been required to 
transport some percentage of their cargo by waterways. 
(Para 21) 
Reply of the Ministry 
3.1       Keeping in view the fact that incentives for modal shift to waterways can act as a 
driver for promoting the utilisation of these NWs by the cargo owners, a cargo promotion 
scheme is under active consideration. 

5 
 
3.2       Further, efforts are being made by IWAI for operationalization of terminals made 
under JMVP through hiring of PPP concessionaire and suitable PPP models are being 
developed to incentivize the users of IWT  
3.3   The river morphology and hydro -dynamics are very crucial for facilitating navigation 
therefore the expert’s team and help of IIT Madras (NTCPWC) are being taken in fairway 
development activities.  
3.4    The bottleneck for cargo handling infrastructures is resolved at identified O -D pairs, 
however, based upon requirement identified, the IWAI is taking speedy action to mitigate 
these issues. The authority is also encouraging private stakeholders to make investment in 
promotion of IWT business and developed several models, where private stakeho lders may 
invest in terminal operations and maintenance, vessel construction and operations and 
dredging activities etc.  
3.5       IWT sector is at nascent stage and this sector has shortage of skilled manpower to 
deal with daily affairs of IWT and expand  business. Therefore, IWAI has established new 
training institution and also strengthening NINI Patna for coping up with this issue. 
3.6   The infrastructure created under Jal Marg Vikas Project is planned to be operationalized 
by engaging PPP concessionai re which expect to provide end -end solution of logistics for 
stakeholders and also build market and eco -system with private parties for development of 
first mile and last mile connectivity solutions. IWAI has been making consistent efforts for 
development of road and railways connectivity along MMT Varanasi, MMT Sahibgnaj and 
MMT Haldia. The community jetties and Ro -Ro facilities that are being developed under 
JMVP-II initiatives, is also planned to be operated through respective agencies of State 
Government where O&M is expected to be done by the local Gram Sabhas. So, the JMVP 
project is an inclusive development initiative where every type of stakeholders are tried to be 
anchored in development of National Waterways.  
3.7       Under JMVP initiative the IWAI has made world record of piloting the journey of the 
World’s Longest River Cruise Journey from Varanasi to Dibrugarh of 3200 Kilometers and 
development initiatives of JMVP has led for promoting several river cruise vessels and they 
are presently operati onal to facilitate religious, cultural and heritage tourism activities along 
Ganga – Bhagirathi – Hooghly River system.  
3.8       There are 11 IWT Terminals on NW -3. All the terminals are provided with Cargo 
handling equipment (such as, Cranes & Fork lift s) and 24 Hours Navigation Aids are 
installed in entire route of NW -3. In addition, IWAI has taken up the modification of the 
navigational lock gate at Trikkunnapuzha on NW -3 (through Govt. of Kerala, on deposit 
basis), at a cost of Rs.38 Crore. The Cargo mobility by IWT mode is expected to increase 
once the lock gate is made operational. 
3.9       Efforts to increase cargo with other ministries & PSUs have been taken up as detailed 
– 

6 
 
3.9.1    IWAI approached more than 140 PSUs to consider using IWT mode fo r their freight 
operations. A significant number of PSUs have expressed interest and are willing to explore 
the possibility for transportation of their raw and finished goods via Inland Waterways 
Transport (IWT). 
3.9.2    Meetings have been organized with most of the potential PSUs like Food Corporation 
of India, IFFCO, CONCOR, Fertilizers and Chemicals Travancore (FACT) and Travancore 
Cochin Chemicals Ltd. (TCC), Indian Oil Corporation Limited (IOCL), Numaligarh Refinery 
Limited (NRL), SAIL, etc. in additi on to private companies like Tata Steel, Star Cement, 
Dalmia Cement, etc. 
3.9.3    Stakeholders Conference with cargo owners, shippers, vessel operators, ship builders 
were also organized at Kolkata, Kochi, Bhubaneshwar, Vijayawada and Goa in March/ April,  
2024 to discuss the challenges/ issues and their future plans for cargo enhancement on NWs. 
3.10     Parallel action has been taken to enhance the river cruise tourism by organizing the 
stake holders’ consultations with river cruise operators and State Tourism departments. 
Recommendation/Observation 
4.         The Committee further notes that while Inland Waterways is undeniably the 
most environment friendly mode of transport, development of waterways cannot be 
undertaken without its environmental costs as  development activities change a river’s 
hydrology and morphology. Indian rivers support much biodiversity and aquatic life, 
many of which are already endangered due to high levels of pollution. Dredging of the 
riverbed for providing requisite draft advers ely affects the ecology of the river 
systems and fish breeding activities. While river systems could play a crucial role in 
cargo transportation and reduction in logistics costs especially in landlocked States 
and thus, could be an economic gamechanger, th e concerns of environmental 
sustainability should also be given equal importance. A case in point is India’s 
national aquatic animal, the endangered Gangetic Dolphin. The NW -1 passes through 
the Vikramshila dolphin sanctuary, India’s only dedicated protect ed area for the 
Gangetic Dolphin, one of the only three surviving freshwater dolphin species in the 
world. The Gangetic Dolphins, essentially blind, rely heavily on echolocation, i.e., 
using sound to navigate and locate prey, and developmental activities s uch as capital 
dredging and construction interfere with their activities. The Committee observes that 
speed regulations, buffer zones and regulation of dredging were some of the measures 
proposed to be taken to minimize the deleterious impact on dolphins a nd other 
aquatic life and desires to know the status of implementation in this regard. 
(Para 23) 
Reply of the Ministry 
4.1       The inland transportation system of India aspires to become game changer for 
improving logistics performance for promoting trades to achieve five trillion economy. NW-1 

7 
 
(Ganga – Bhagirathi – Hooghly river system) from Varanasi to Haldia is prioritized for the 
development of river transportation with international benchmarking.  
4.2       The emphasis given on environment control m easures is highly monitored during 
development and operation phase of logistics movement along NW -1; the Environment 
Management Plan for NW -1 is already in place and its compliances are being regularly 
monitored.  
 State of the Art dredgers have been deploy ed for the dredging work. They are 
equipped with the noise reduction/ Masking equipment like AVP (Anti Vibration 
Pads) used in engine room foundation to reduce the noise generation inside water and 
outside, AVP is also bridged to reduce the high noise exposure to cabin crew.  
 Spill Kits are being placed on board containing Floating booms, socks, pads, pillows, 
Granular absorbent, PPEs and handling instruction. All necessary precautions are 
exercised to avoid oil spills of leakage. Daily weekly and monthly dredgers inspection 
checklist is maintained on board to ensure regular servicing and maintenance of 
dredgers to prevent any leakage of the equipment and machinery. Regular training is 
being imparted to the operation team and crew about the implementation of  
emergency response plan, handling of emergency response equipment. No spillage 
and accident to the dolphins recorded till date.  
 Dolphin deflector has been installed onboard dredgers to keep the dolphin away from 
the dredging areas. Dredging operation is halted in case of sighting of aquatic 
mammals.  
 Waste management plan is in place for the dredgers and vessels. Waste oil is stored & 
disposed as per the Hazardous and Other Waste Management Rules 2016. 
Authorization has also been obtained by contractor, a nd agreement with SPCB 
authorized vendor is also there.  
 STP/ Bio toilets are installed on board dredgers and no solid and liquid waste is being 
discharged in the river to follow the Zero discharge policy. Municipal waste is being 
segregated at the source and being stored in the color -coded bins and disposed as per 
the Solid Waste Management Rules 2016 through municipal corporation/local body 
along with river banks. Bilge water is being stored in closed containers and disposed -
off through authorized recycler regularly.  
 Apart from this, bandalling is being done to concentrate the flow of water towards the 
river channel as well as to prevent the deposition of silt from outside the channel to 
reduce the requirement of dredging.  
 Dredging is being avoided durin g the rainy season, while during the normal days 
dredged materials are discharged close to surface of the water body to minimize the 
dispersal of sediments. Disposal is being done at approx. 100 -150 m away from the 
channel.  

8 
 
 As part of the exercise dredged material is checked regularly for toxicity.  
 No contract for dredging operation is being done inside the Vikramshila Gangetic 
dolphin sanctuary area.  
 IWAI has obtained the Wildlife clearance for the vessel movements through Kashi 
Turtle Sanctuary.  
4.3       Vessel operators have been sensitized to maintain the buffer zone and speed limits 
upto 5 knots/ hr within sanctuary areas. 
  
Recommendation/Observation 
5.      Considering the constraints, the Committee recommends that the IWAI should 
concentrate its  efforts in developing the 23 Operational National Waterways. The 
Committee desires to know whether all requisite hydrographic and techno -economic 
feasibility studies and environmental and forest clearances have been obtained for these 
23 Operational NWs as no such studies had been carried out prior to the notification of 
the new waterways. The Committee exhorts the IWAI to give due importance to 
environmental studies along with techno -economic studies in the development projects 
on the 23 Operational NWs. The Committee has been informed that the Least Available 
Depth (LAD) for a waterway to be made operational in a profitable way must be two 
meters. The Committee recommends that those waterways which have a naturally 
available depth of two meters and above may be given top priority for development. 
The Committee also recommends that wherever Inland Water Authority of India 
proposes to conduct feasibility study, the State’s representation should be ensured in the 
proposed feasibility study and the State shoul d be given opportunity to be heard and its 
views on feasibility should be adequately taken into account.

accidents may also increase unless remedial measures are put in place to enhance boat 
safety and prevent accidents. The Committee observes that one of the main reasons for

Chapter-III 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH REPLIES OF 
THE MINISTRY HAVE NOT BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE COMMITTEE 
  
Recommendation/Observation 
1.    The Committee opines that while dev elopment of waterways is crucial for reduction of 
logistics costs and boosting economic growth, the environmental costs and the cost 
effectiveness of waterways on case to case basis have to be assessed in tandem with the 
overall economic goals. Moreover, a s stated by the Ministry, it takes close to a decade for 
the development and full utilization of a waterway. Out of the five NWs existing prior to 
2016, two NWs have still not been fully developed while development activities have only 
been started on 20 more waterways. In such a scenario, the Committee is in agreement with 
the IWAI that the 63 NWs which are not found to be viable, should at present not be taken 
up for development. The Committee also expresses its displeasure at the declaration of a 
huge number of NWs without making proper assessment about their viability. The 63 NWs, 
which have been found to be non -viable have created a peculiar situation whereby 
declaration of a NW through enactment has generated massive popular expectation about 
the devel opment of waterways by the Central Government thus absolving the State 
Government from its responsibility in the development and maintenance of the waterways 
in question, leaving the waterways in a state of perennial neglect and abandonment. 
(Para 24) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1       Declaration of all probable waterways as National Waterways has safeguarded their 
future navigational aspects in respect of structures like bridges to be constructed across such 
waterways with adequate vertical and horizontal na vigational clearance as per their 
classification of navigational capacities. Smaller waterways also help to promote inland water 

32 
 
transport as feeder routes with National Waterways creating fish -bone structure similar to 
State Highways connect with National Highways.  
Further, for better co -ordination with States for development of waterways sector in the 
country, Ministry of Ports, Shipping & Waterways constituted Inland Waterways 
Development Council (IWDC) in November 2023 which will be holding regular 
consultations with all concerned stakeholders including State Governments. First meeting of 
IWDC has been held on 08.01.2024 with stakeholders in this regard.   
Further Recommendation/Observation 
1.2       The Committee notes the Ministry's establishment of t he Inland Waterways 
Development Council (IWDC) in November 2023 to enhance coordination with State 
Governments for the development of waterways. While this is a positive step towards 
better stakeholder engagement, the Committee stresses the need for more r obust and 
transparent mechanisms to ensure effective participation of State Governments in the 
development and maintenance of NWs. 
1.3       The Committee suggests that the Ministry should work closely with State 
Governments to explore alternative uses and  development opportunities for the 
National Waterways currently deemed non -viable. This collaborative approach can 
help in optimizing the use of these resources for local economic development while 
ensuring environmental sustainability.

Recommendation/Observation 
 2.       The Committee observes that while the quantum of cargo moved on the National

5.3      Trial Run of Cargo Ship with 2500T of Rice from Sittwe, Myanmar to Chittagong, 
Bangladesh completed in Jan 2023. Inaugural run of cargo vessel with 1000T cement from 
Kolkata to Sittwe Port in Myanmar has successfully completed and the Sittwe port 
inaugurated on 09.05.2023. 
  
Further Recommendation/Observation 

36 
 
5.4       The IWAI and MEA should continue to strengthen bilateral cooperation with 
Myanmar to facilitate smooth implementation of the project. This includes resolving 
any logistical, regulatory, or operatio nal challenges that may arise during the execution 
of the second phase. 
5.5     Along with the completion of Phase -II, the Committee stresses the importance of 
regular maintenance of the infrastructure developed under the KMTTP. Ensuring the 
sustainability and functionality of the ports, terminals, and vessels will be crucial for the 
long-term success of the project. 
  
Recommendation/Observation 
6.         The Committee desires to know the number of voyages made in the IBP route in 2022-
23. The Committee notes that the Protocol provides for a 50:50 ratio for sharing on tonnage 
basis for inter -country and transit cargo by Indian and Bangladeshi vessels. The Committee 
desires to know the number of Indian vessels actually plying on the Indo - Bangladesh 
Protocol Route as compared to Bangladeshi vessels in 2022 -23. The Committee has been 
informed that in 2018-19, approximately 600 Bangladeshi vessels and 40 Indian vessels used 
the IBP route and in subsequent years also the number of Indian vessels has been much le ss 
than Bangladeshi vessels and desires to know the reasons for the same. The Committee 
further observes that the IWAI, as per its website, has 121 vessels (including 13 
accommodation boats, 07 cargo vessels, 03 classic watermaster, 01container crane, 09 crane 
pontoons, 12 cutter suction dredgers, 03 hydraulic surface dredger, 01 container crane, 07 
inspection boats, 01 Ro -Ro cargo, 18 survey vessels, 34 terminal barges and 12 work boats/ 
tugs) and desires to know whether the number is sufficient for full u tilization of the protocol 
route. 
(Para 70) 
Reply of the Ministry 
6.1       3,348 voyages were made during 2022 -23 on IBP route for transportation of cargo 
(mainly export of fly -ash) to Bangladesh. Out of these, 3,248 voyages were performed by 
Bangladeshi vessels and 100 voyages by Indian vessels. 
  
6.2        As per Protocol between India and Bangladesh on sharing of inter -country trade and 
transit cargo, it has been inter alia mentioned at Para 18 that “ the two Governments agree to 
sharing of the carriage  of inter country trade and transit cargo on an equal tonnage basis 
(i.e., 50:50) as far as practicable by the vessels of signatory countries”. 
  
6.3        The vessels owned by IWAI, as mentioned in the report, include dredgers, survey 
vessels, container crane, crane pontoons, etc., which includes only 11 no. of cargo vessels. 
The 11 nos. cargo vessels of IWAI are used for transportation of cargo only for 
demonstration of technical feasibility of the waterways on various stretches of National 
Waterways. Th e commercial operation on National Waterways as well as on IBP route is 
done by the private entities only. 

37 
 
  
6.4        The equal share of movement of cargo on IBP route could not be maintained due to 
following reasons. 
a. The number of Indian vessels is very less as compared to Bangladeshi vessels.  
b. Lower Capex and Opex of Bangladesh vessels as compared to Indian vessels.  
c. The trade is only for export cargo, i.e., India to Bangladesh and import cargo is almost 
nil through waterways. 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
6.5       The Committee recommends that efforts be made to increase the number of 
Indian vessels operating on the IBP route. This could involve incentivizing private 
entities to invest in and operate vessels on this route, potentially through s ubsidies, tax 
benefits, or low-interest financing options. 
6.6       To make Indian vessels more competitive, the Ministry should explore measures 
to reduce capital expenditure (Capex) and operational expenditure (Opex) for Indian 
vessel operators. This ma y include financial assistance, fuel subsidies, and streamlining 
regulatory processes to reduce administrative costs. 
6.7       The Committee suggests that the Ministry, in collaboration with relevant trade 
bodies, work on promoting and facilitating bilate ral trade via waterways. Identifying 
potential import cargo from Bangladesh to India and creating a balanced trade flow 
could significantly enhance the viability and utilization of Indian vessels on the IBP 
route. 
  
Recommendation/Observation

been allocated to develop Phase -I of the project in the last five years. (Details placed at 
Annexure-X). The Committee desires to be informed of the expenditure incurred i n this 
regard. 
(Para 78)

funds over the past five years. This underutilization of funds indicates potential 
inefficiencies in project execution and financial management. The Comm ittee 
emphasizes the need for better planning, monitoring, and utilization of allocated

8.         The Committee is of the view that Research and Developm ent activities is the key to 
success of any sector and recommends the Government to strengthen the Research & 
Development facilities for the desired development of Inland Water Transport sector in the 
country. The Committee also urges that Research and Dev elopment studies should be 
conducted for making assessment of the impact of the increased inland water transport 
activities on the aqua -marine life as development should invariably be in sustainable mode 
with due consideration to environment and ecology. 
(Para 101) 
Reply of the Ministry 
  
8.1     In line with the view of the Committee, Government has setup Research & 
Development cells in collaboration with IIT Madras, Chennai & IIT Kharagpur for 
development of IWT sector along with maritime sector in the country as detailed below: 
  
i.    National Technology Centre for Ports, Waterways & Coasts (NTCPWC), 
Department of Ocean Engineering, IIT Madras, Chennai has been envisioned as the Centre 
for technological innovations and evolution of new ideas and breakthr oughs for the port and 
maritime sector. It will work as the technology arm of Ministry of Ports, Shipping & 
Waterways providing the needful technological support to ports, IWAI and other institutions. 
  
ii.      Centre of Inland and Coastal Maritime Techno logy (CICMT) at IIT Kharagpur, to 
undertake R&D works and to provide a facility in Shallow Water Sea -keeping and 
Maneuvering Basin. This facility would be useful for model testing of any new designs being 
developed for inland vessels in future. Further, the Center will also study cargo movement for 
coastal and Inland Waterways and provide for intermodal (Coastal cum Inland) logistic 
solution for cost effective cargo movement. 
Further Recommendation/Observation 

39 
 
8.2     The Ministry should facilitate forums, workshops, and consultations to gather inputs from local 
communities, environmental groups, and industry stakeholders, ensuring that diverse perspectives are 
considered in the development process.  The findings from R&D activities, especially those related to 
environmental impacts and sustainable practices, should be documented and widely disseminated. This 
will help in the sharing of knowledge, best practices, and technological advancements with relevant 
stakeholders and the broader community. 
Public-Private Partnership 
Recommendation/Observation 
9.         The Committee strongly feels that active involvement of the private sector in the inland waterways sector 
is imperative to ensure greater efficiency and competitiveness and attract higher investment for i nfrastructure 
development. The Committee appreciates the efforts of the Ministry and IWAI taken so far to attract private 
investment in this critical infrastructure sector. 
(Para 106) 
Reply of the Committee 
9.1       For active involvement of the private sector in the inland waterways sector, steps have 
been taken up for O&M of terminals on NW -1 & 2 in respect of Multi -Modal terminals built 
under Jal Marg Vikas Project on the Ganga (NW -1) at Varanasi & Sahibganj. The tender 
process to award the work to PPP operator is at advanced stage. Haldia MMT, Pandu & 
Dhubri Terminal have already been awarded for O&M to PPP operators. 
  
9.2       Further, tendering process has been initiated for development of NWs in Odisha, 
Maharashtra & Gujarat on PPP mode by attracting Private Sector Participation. 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
9.3   The Committee recommends expanding the scope of private sector involvement in the inland water 
sector beyond terminal operations to include other critical areas such as vessel operat ions, maintenance 
services and infrastructure development. This broader engagement will enhance overall sector efficiency 
and innovation. 
Kochi Water Metro 
Recommendation/Observation 
10.       The Committee notes the introduction of the Kochi Water Metro a nd would like to 
know its performance assessment, both physical and financial, at periodic interval. The 
Committee would also like to know whether the Ministry has any plan to implement similar 
models in other States for the integration of waterways in the  public transport system or it 
would wait for an annual performance assessment of Kochi water metro for a better and 
meaningful plan for replication. 
(Para 131) 
Reply of the Ministry 

40 
 
10.1     Performance assessment, both physical and financial, at periodic  interval, is beyond the purview of 
Inland Waterways Authority of India (IWAI). IWAI is responsible for regulation and development of NWs for 
Shipping and Navigation in respect of infrastructure facilities primarily for cargo vessels. The facilities such 
created may also be utilised for the vessels and ferries operating on NWs under State Governments. Tourism 
and passenger movement operation is also mandated with State Governments and IWAI plays the role of 
technical facilitator in this regard. 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
10.2     The Committee understands that IWAI’s role is primarily technical. The Ministry should support 
State Governments in planning and implementing similar projects by providing technical guidance, 
funding assistance, and recommen dations on best practices. This support will help ensure that new 
projects are developed with a solid foundation based on the Kochi Water Metro’s experience.  
  
River Cruise-Ganga Vilas 
Recommendation/Observation 
11.       The Committee notes that following  the initiation of Ganga Vilas, the potential of river cruise tourism in 
the country has remained vast. It feels that river cruise will not only promote the tourism sector in the India by 
attracting foreign tourists, it will also aid in boosting the periph eral coastline economy of the country. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should take concerted efforts to increase the number of 
River Cruises plying in the country. It also recommends that the Ministry should launch programmes to 
incentivize river cruise operators so that the available potential can be fully realised.  
(Para 137) 
  
Reply of the Ministry 
  
11.1       State Governments of Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Assam and Odisha are being 
sensitized for increasing and developing tourist circuits in these states. 
  
11.2     60 Community Jetties have been planned in Arth Ganga Project in the Ganga (NW -1), out of which 37 
Jetties have been constructed and 23 are in progress. 
11.3     River cruise tourism is operational i n 09 National Waterways. Floating Terminal infrastructure for river 
cruise is completed at 04 locations on NW -2 (the Brahmaputra) during 2023 -24 in addition to existing terminal 
facilities. 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
11.4    The Committee recommend s launching incentive programs to encourage river cruise operators. 
These programs could include financial subsidies, tax incentives and streamlined regulatory processes to 
reduce operational costs and attract both domestic and international cruise operato rs. The Committee 
also recommends reducing charges for domestic tourists to ensure inclusivity.

FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE POLICY 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.         The Committe e observes that the earlier subsidy scheme of the Ministry of 5 
years offered shipbuilders 30% extra on building ocean -going merchant vessels that are 
more than 80 metres in length, if they are manufactured for the domestic market. For 
export orders, however, ships of all types and capacities were eligible for the subsidy. In 
the new ﬁnancial    assistance scheme, assistance will be given for all types of ships 
irrespective of size. In the new scheme, both state -owned and private yards will get the 
assistance only after they construct and hand over to the ship to the buyer to ensure 
timely delivery of ships. The new ﬁnancial assistance  scheme was therefore for double 
the period of the earlier subsidy scheme, the focus extended for all ships and ensured 
timely delivery which had been a constraint in the earlier scheme. The Committee also 
observes that when commercial orders dried up in the wake of the 2008 ﬁnancial crisis, 
Indian shipyards were focusing mainly on defence orders to stay aﬂoat. The 
Government’s ﬁnancial assistance policy was meant to help bring in more and major 
commercial ship building orders. 
(Para 13.5) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1       Comments of the Committee are agreed. Additionally, from the data available in the 
SBFAP scheme, about 88 vessel orders have been procured by 35 Shipyards during the last 5 
years from domestic as well as export orders and these orders are worth Rs. 8631 crore. 
Further, shipyards have delivered 128 vessels worth Rs. 1145 crore to domestic and 
international ship owners in last 5 years that have received assistance under SBFAP of about 
Rs. 327 Crore.   Also, with the latest Government of India initiative to provide higher SBFA 
funding to green fuelled ships and hybrid vessels, further shipbuilding orders are expected t o 
be received.

prerequisite in Ship Building industry. Ensuring proper education and training could 
bolster the effectiveness of the industry. The Committee observes that as per

the major shipbuilding nations. All these translate to about 20 -25 per cent cost 
advantage for major shipbuilding nations vis -à-vis India. The Committee 
recommends that investments in automat ion should be encouraged in order to 
improve labor productivity and reduce costs.

SHIP REPAIR 
Recommendation/Observation 
6.         The Committee notes that India is suitably located to offer repair services for the 
Indian Navy as well as the US Navy for its 5 th and 7 th Fleet deployed in the Indian 
Ocean and the Arabian Sea. It has also been seen that many contracts of the US Navy 
have been awarded to either private Indian Shipyards or to other foreign shipyards.   
Indian PSU Shipyards are not strong contenders for repair amidst global competition.   
The Committee has also learnt from media repo rts that the US Navy and L&T have 
signed a 5 year Master Ship Repair Agreement (MSRA) which shows that the US is 
committed to utilize ship repair facilities on a regular basis at the L&T shipyard in 
Katupalli in Tamil Nadu. The Committee understands that M azagon Docks 
Shipbuilders have also concluded an agreement with an entity of the US Navy. While 
appreciating the above -said achievements, the Committee feels that while other Asian 
countries, notably Singapore and Japan have bagged many foreign ship repair  orders, 
India has lagged behind due to inadequate infrastructural support services needed for 
ship repair. The Committee recommends that the Ministry may make efforts to 
improve the infrastructure to enable other shipyards to bag ship repair orders. 
(Para 53) 
Reply of the Ministry 
6.1       Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways has already joined hands with Siemens 
and Indian Register of Shipping (IRS) to build World Class Center of Excellence in Maritime 
and Ship Building (CEMS) in Mumbai and Vishakha patnam under the ministry’s flagship 
Sagarmala Programme.

Make in India and skill India efforts in the Maritime sector.

Recommendation/Observation 
7.         The Committee apprec iates the steps taken by all agencies involved to resolve 
the issues arising out of the Basel Ban Agreement and that EU ships may start to 
arrive in India from April, 2024 which would restore much of the problems affecting 
the recycling industry.    Regarding the issue of TMT bars, the Committee has learnt 
from media reports that the Committee set up by the Steel Ministry to look into the 
issue of the manufacturing TMT bars from ship steel has reportedly been unable to 
devise an SoP ( Standard Operating Proc edure) for usage of ship plates without 
testing of chemical composition. Non -standardised offerings and the absence of wider 
data are seen as major reasons for the rejection of using ship breaking steel plates for 
making TMT bars. The Committee studying th e issue has also suggested that ship 
breakers can sell the plates along with grade certiﬁcate and chemistry. The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry, GMB and Ship Recyclers may cooperate 
with the Committee and ensure that large size data is made availab le for long -term 
durability studies to settle the issue of use of TMT bars for structural purposes. The 
Committee also recommends that the industry may explore the possibility of making 
other forms of steel, apart from TMT bars, from ship scraps, like gril ls, strips and 
other bars which may not require the same standards as TMT bars. 
(Para 84) 
Reply of the Ministry 
7.1       Regarding exploring the feasibility of using ship breaking steel plates to produce 
TMT bars under the IS 1786,the Ministry of Steel, v ide letter dated 13.03.2024 has 
forwarded the final version of SoP (Standard Operating Procedure) to DG, BIS for 
consideration and further action. BIS have a working group especially for IS 1786, which 
gives the final recommendation to the main Committee b ased on the examination of reports 
and SoP.

3.         The Committee feels that a potential  Production Linked Incentive (PLI) 
scheme can go a long way to boost the shipbuilding industry. This multifaceted 
scheme could include output -based rewards, wherein shipbuilders stand to receive 
incentives commensurate with the quantity and type of ships t hey manufacture. 
Additionally, the PLI scheme might introduce investment incentives tailored to 
encourage shipbuilders to modernize their facilities and integrate advanced 
manufacturing technologies. Shipbuilding entities making investments in upgrading 
infrastructure and adopting state -of-the-art manufacturing processes could qualify 
for these investment incentives. This dual approach of incentivizing both production 
and investment could create a dynamic environment that propels the shipbuilding 
industry t owards technological advancement, increased efficiency and global 
competitiveness. 
(Para 35)

INTRODUCTION 
The Ministry of Civil Aviation plays a vital role in creating a safe, secure, 
affordable, and sustainable environment for air travel, catering to both passengers 
and cargo transportation. It establishes a comprehensive regulatory framework to 
ensure safety and security in air transport services while formulating policies to 
develop adequate infrastructure to accommodate the sector’s rapid growth. Given 
the global nature of civil aviation, the Ministry ensures adherence to international 
standards and norms. It supervises various attached offices and Public Sector 
Undertakings, ensuring effective governance. Additionally, it promotes ease of 
doing business and enhances passenger facilitation.  
2. The Ministry is responsible for implementing treaties and agreements related 
to civil aviation and administering the Aircraft Act, 1934, as well as the Airports 
Authority of India Act, 1994. Its remit includes the regulation of aircraft and air 
navigation, the provision and management of aerodromes, and the organisation of 
air traffic, excluding the sanitised control of air navigation. It also oversees the 
provision of navigational aids and other facilities related to air navigation. 
Furthermore, the Ministry is responsible for the carriage of passengers and goods 
by air, the development of commercial aero-related manufacturing and its 
ecosystem, and the issuance of technical licences, certificates, and approvals for 
civil aircraft operations. It also supports the growth of the private air transport 
industry, including cargo services, and handles matters related to Greenfield airport 
development by State Governments and private/joint-sector companies. 
GOALS AND OBJECTIVES 
3. The Outcome-Output Monitoring Framework (OOMF)/Outcome Budget for 
the Financial Year (FY) 2025-26 of the Ministry throws light on the Ministry’s 

2 
 
primary goalof bridging the regional connectivity gap, particularly in underserved 
and remote areas, while boosting economic growth through aviation sector 
development. Through itsRegional Connectivity Scheme (RCS-UDAN), it seeks to 
enhance regional air connectivity by focusing on infrastructure development, 
operational efficiency, and improved accessibility, particularly in underserved 
regions. The following key goals and objectives can be inferred: 
i. Expansion of Airport Infrastructure – The Ministry aims to upgrade and revive 
airport infrastructure in collaboration with the Airports Authority of India 
(AAI) and State Governments to support regional connectivity. This includes 
the development of new airports, heliports, and water aerodromes to improve 
accessibility. 
ii. Enhancing Regional Air Connectivity – A major objective is to operationalise 
new Regional Connectivity Scheme (RCS) routes and increase the number of 
flights under the scheme, thereby making air travel more accessible to the 
general public. 
iii. Improved Air Connectivity in the North Eastern Region (NER) – Recognising 
the strategic and economic significance of the North Eastern region, the 
Ministry seeks to operationalise additional airports, heliports, and water 
aerodromes, and introduce new RCS routes and flights in the region. 
iv. Increase in Passenger Traffic and Flight Operations – A clear objective is to 
facilitate higher passenger movement on RCS flights, targeting 20 lakh 
passengers and 40,000 RCS flights in FY 2025-26.  
v. Development of Specific Air Infrastructure Projects – The Ministry has outlined 
targeted infrastructure projects, such as: 
 Heliports: Tuting, Daparizo, Nagaon, and Bageshwar. 
 Water Aerodromes: Long Island, Shaheed Dweep, Swaraj Dweep, and 
Prakasam Barrage. 
 Airports: Fursatganj (Uttar Pradesh), Rangeilunda (Odisha), 
Rairangpur (Odisha), Shivpuri (Madhya Pradesh), and Ratnagiri.

AIR FARE REGULATION - THE NEED OF THE HOUR 
12.1 The Committee, while examining the Demand for Grants of the 
Ministry of Civil Aviation for 2025-26, recommends the establishment of a 
stringent airfare pricing regulation mechanism under the framework of an 
AI-powered predictive monitoring system, tentatively named “AirPrice 
Guardian.” This system should aim to address consumer grievances related to 
unpredictable and exorbitant airfare surges, particularly during peak travel 
periods and emergencies, while ensuring transparency and fairness in pricing 
practices. The Committee notes that the current regulatory framework under 
the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) lacks the capacity to 
proactively monitor and regulate airfare trends, necessitating a 
transformative approach leveraging advanced technology. 
12.2 The proposed “AirPrice Guardian” system will utilize machine learning 
algorithms and predictive analytics to forecast airfare trends based on 
historical data, demand patterns, fuel costs, seasonal fluctuations, and 
external factors such as festivals or emergencies. By establishing dynamic fare 
bands for each route, updated quarterly through predictive models, this 
system will empower regulators to monitor deviations in real-time and take 

10 
 
preemptive action against excessive pricing. The Committee recommends that 
DGCA be empowered with quasi-judicial authority to impose temporary price 
caps or penalties on airlines engaging in exploitative practices. Additionally, a 
Pricing Transparency Index should be developed to rate airlines on their 
adherence to fair pricing norms, with this information made publicly 
available through a consumer-facing portal. 
12.3 The Committee further recommends that the existing Tariff Monitoring 
Unit (TMU) within DGCA be revamped with AI-driven tools for real-time 
data analysis and anomaly detection.  
12.4 In alignment with the Ministry’s focus on regional connectivity under the 
RCS-UDAN scheme, the Committee underscores that airfare monitoring must 
extend to underserved routes to prevent excessive fares that undermine 
accessibility. A portion of the funds should be allocated for RCS and that 
should be utilized to integrate fare monitoring mechanisms into regional 
connectivity projects. This will ensure that affordable air travel remains a 
cornerstone of India’s aviation growth strategy. 
12.5 The Committee also highlights the need for public awareness campaigns 
to educate consumers about their rights under this new regulatory 
framework. The Committee recommends the development of a mobile 
application, “Airfare Vigil,” modeled on the Election Commission’s cVIGIL 
app, to empower citizens to report instances of arbitrary airfare pricing. This 
app will allow users to upload evidence such as screenshots of ticket prices 
and contextual details, with features like real-time geo-tagging, automated 
complaint tracking, and time-bound resolution mechanisms. Upon 
submission, users will receive a unique ID to track their complaint status, 
ensuring transparency and accountability. The app will also include 
safeguards against misuse, such as filtering duplicate or frivolous complaints, 
while allowing anonymous submissions to encourage wider participation. 

11 
 
12.6  “Airfare Vigil” will be integrated with the AI-powered “AirPrice 
Guardian” system, enabling citizen reports to complement predictive 
analytics in identifying exploitative pricing patterns. This initiative will foster 
participatory governance by involving citizens in airfare regulation while 
strengthening DGCA’s ability to address consumer grievances swiftly and 
effectively. 
12.7. Given the Ministry’s overall revenue expenditure allocation of ₹2,330.31 
crore and capital outlay of ₹70 crore for 2025-26, the Committee recommends 
reallocating from underutilized allocations (such as Air India liabilities) 
toward developing and implementing this airfare monitoring system. The 
timeline for implementation should span 18-24 months, with Phase I focusing 
on high-traffic routes within six months and nationwide rollout completed by 
2026. 
12.8 The Committee believes that implementing “Air Price Guardian” & 
“Airfare Vigil” will address long-standing consumer grievances regarding 
airfare volatility while fostering transparency and accountability in India’s 
aviation sector. By aligning this initiative with broader policy goals such as 
regional connectivity and sustainable aviation growth, it will not only protect 
consumer interests but also strengthen India’s position as a global leader in 
aviation innovation and regulation. 
REGULATORY OVERSIGHT AND SECURITY 
13. The Committee observes and appreciates the fact that the Directorate 
General of Civil Aviation (₹300 crore) and the Bureau of Civil Aviation 
Security (₹80 crore) have been accorded significant funding. However, the 
Commission of Railway Safety (₹22 crore) has received markedly lower 
funding, despite its critical role in ensuring passenger and freight safety in 
railway operations. The Committee advises a reassessment of this allocation, 
with a view to strengthening railway safety mechanisms. Simultaneously, it 

12 
 
urges regular performance evaluations of DGCA and BCAS funding to ensure 
that these resources translate into tangible improvements in aviation safety, 
regulatory efficiency, and security preparedness. The Committee also 
recommends that Ministry should establish an integrated safety oversight 
mechanism that promotes collaboration between transport safety regulators 
including DGCA, BCAS, and the Commission of Railway Safety, utilizing 
shared resources where appropriate and developing common standards for 
multi-modal transport safety. Further, Committee recommends for 
development of a sustainable funding mechanism for aviation oversight 
functions at both national and regional levels, potentially including air safety 
charges, to ensure regulatory bodies can fulfill their mandates effectively 
without complete dependence on general budgetary allocations. 
 
IMPROVING AIRCRAFT INTERIOR - ENSURING STANDARDS 
13.1 The Committee has taken cognizant of reports concerning premature 
deterioration of seating materials, ergonomic failures, and technological 
obsolescence plaguing multiple airlines. This urgent disparity demands 
ministerial intervention through a standardized regulatory framework to 
ensure Indian aviation maintains competitive parity with global leaders. The 
Committee proposes establishing the Aviation Interior Quality Commission 
with immediate effect to implement rigorous testing protocols, sustainability 
guidelines, and accessibility standards across all domestic carriers. The 
situation is particularly concerning given the considerable fleet expansion 
underway. With Air India alone having ordered 570 new aircraft—including 
the recent addition of 100 more Airbus aircraft comprising 10 wide-body 
A350s and 90 narrow-body A320 family planes—the potential scale of interior 
quality issues demands immediate ministerial attention. Sustainability must 
become a central consideration in interior design and material selection. The 
Commission would establish progressive environmental standards for cabin 

13 
 
interiors, including recyclability requirements, VOC emissions limits, and 
lifecycle assessment obligations. These standards would align with India’s 
broader environmental commitments while positioning Indian aviation as a 
leader in sustainable cabin design. 
REGIONAL CONNECTIVITY SCHEME  AND INFRASTRUCTURE 
EXPANSION 
14. The allocation of ₹540 crore to the Regional Connectivity Scheme, with 
₹240 crore earmarked for the North-Eastern Region, demonstrates the 
government's commitment to regional connectivity. However, the Committee 
notes that historical data shows significant variation in route sustainability 
and regional imbalances in performance. To enhance the effectiveness of this 
allocation, the Committee recommends:  
14.1 Institution of a tiered funding approach that prioritizes routes with 
proven passenger load factors exceeding 70% while providing targeted 
support for underperforming routes with high development potential, 
particularly in the Eastern, Northeastern, and Central regions where recent 
data shows promising growth trajectories. 
14.2 Development of comprehensive performance metrics beyond passenger 
numbers, including economic impact assessments, connectivity improvements 
for underserved communities, and operational sustainability of routes beyond 
the initial subsidy period. These metrics should inform quarterly reviews of 
fund disbursement. 
14.3 Creation of a dedicated infrastructure development component within 
the Regional Connectivity Scheme, targeting airports serving tourist and 
pilgrimage destinations which have demonstrated higher passenger traffic 
growth following route establishment. This approach would maximize 
economic returns on investment while enhancing sector sustainability. 

14 
 
 
INVESTMENT IN AVIATION EDUCATION AND TRAINING 
15. The Committee expresses serious concern regarding the inadequate 
allocations for the National Aviation University (₹10 crore) and Indira 
Gandhi Institute of Aeronautics (₹0.02 crore), which appear insufficient to 
meet the growing demand for aviation professionals. With pilot training costs 
ranging from ₹40 lakh to ₹1.5 crore per candidate, and the sector's projected 
expansion, the Committee recommends: 
15.1 Substantial enhancement of budgetary support for aviation education 
institutions with a minimum five-fold increase in allocation to the National 
Aviation University and a significant revision of IGRUA's funding to enable 
infrastructure modernization and curriculum enhancement aligned with 
international standards. 
15.2 Establishment of a National Aviation Scholarship Fund designed to 
support deserving candidates from economically weaker backgrounds and 
underrepresented regions to pursue aviation careers, addressing both talent 
gaps and regional imbalances in the aviation workforce. 
15.3 Development of a public-private partnership model for aviation training 
infrastructure, wherein government investments in educational institutions 
are complemented by industry contributions, creating centers of excellence 
that combine academic rigor with practical training facilities meeting current 
industry requirements.

tiered subsidy structure that progressively reduces support based on route 
maturity metrics, thereby encouraging operational sustainability while 
maintaining essential connectivity. Additionally, the Ministry should develop 
a comprehensive 'Last-Mile Air Connectivity Index' for evaluating and 
prioritizing route development decisions based on quantifiable social,

initiating pilot projects for small-scale, modular airport infrastructure 
development models specifically designed for low-traffic but strategically 
important destinations, with standardized designs that reduce construction 
timeframes and operational costs.

and higher education in aviation remain critically low. The National Aviation 
University received only ₹10 crore in 2025-26, while the Indira Gandhi 
Institute of Aeronautics (IGRUA) was allocated a mere ₹0.02 crore. The

comprehensive curriculum modernization, faculty development programs, 
and infrastructure upgradation at aviation institutions. Furthermore, the 
Committee recommends developing specialized 'Centers of Aviation 
Technology' at existing educational institutions, each focusing on emerging 
areas such as sustainable aviation fuels, unmanned aerial systems, and next-

outcomes. Additionally, the Ministry should implement an 'Aviation 
Scholarship Program' targeting students from underrepresented regions and 
economically disadvantaged backgrounds, with guaranteed industry 
placements upon graduation to address critical skill shortages in the sector.

Scheme for Drones and Drone Components received ₹57 crore in 2024-25, yet

incorporate an accelerated reimbursement pathway for qualifying 
manufacturers, with monthly rather than annual claim processing to address 
working capital constraints of smaller enterprises. The implementation should

manufacturers and an 'Innovation Track' with simplified compliance

'Drone Application Zones' in each state where regulatory exemptions and 
infrastructure support are provided for real-world testing and demonstration

allocation as per the requirement of the Aero Club of India may be enhanced

the oldest autonomous organization of the Ministry of Civil Aviation working 
to support development for flying training and has successfully established an 
ecosystem of flying training for last 50 years. The Aero Club of India 
headquartered at the Safdarjung Airport area, Sri Aurobindo Marg, New

aero sports and flying training by assets created by the budgetary funding of 

37 
 
the Government which intern created an ecosystem for pilots training in

FLYING TRAINING ORGANISATIONS 
41. The Committee notes that with the growth of the aviation sector, the 
airlines in India would require over 30,000 pilots in the next decade or so. 
Presently, in the country there is an acute shortage of Flying Training 
Organizations, with the limited infrastructure and resources. The Committee 
is of the opinion that the ecosystem for Flying Training Organizations is 
inadequate to meet the growing requirements which results in large numbers 
of Pilots going abroad for training. The requirement of commercial pilots in 
the country is roughly a thousand every year. However, with the existing 
FTOs, the country can barely produce 300 Commercial Pilots and another 
300 pilots train abroad, leaving a large gap of the requirement for commercial 
pilots. The training of pilots who go abroad, result in large foreign exchange 
drain. The present ecosystem of flying training has several shortcomings 
including long duration of training, high cost with constraints of shortage of 
trainer aircrafts, trainers / instructors, institutional funding, aircraft 
manufacturing, spares and training infrastructures. The Committee notes 
that there is an urgent need to proliferate flying training across the country to 

38 
 
meet the Pilot requirements of the future. The Committee recommends that 
the Ministry develop clear policy reforms to ensure strong partnerships with 
state governments, the Airports Authority of India (AAI), and other 
stakeholders. These reforms should also streamline the regulatory 
mechanisms of the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) for flight 
training. To further promote flight training and establish India as a global 
hub, the Committee advises making budgetary provisions for this sector. 
GREENFIELD INTERNATIONAL AIRPORT 
42. In the Budget, it was mentioned about Greenfield Airport project in 
particular reference to Bihar. The Committee is of the opinion that to cater 
the requirement of the state, which does not have a single International

MoPA (Goa) or for that matter Jewar (Uttar Pradesh), it would be essential to 
establish an International Greenfield Airport next to Patna for the futuristic 
requirement as desired by the state for next 50 to 70 years to meet the 
aspirational needs of 14 crore people of the State of Bihar. The Committee is 
of the opinion that an International Greenfield Airport like Jewar should be 
given a top priority for futuristic development and growth of aviation 
infrastructure along with other Greenfield projects across the country. The 
Committee also notes that, in order to match the anticipated growth in 
national and international air traffic across the country and to supplement 
RCS connectivity, greenfield infrastructure projects should be expedited to 
achieve overall greater connectivity and promote air travel.

2.  The Chairman, extended a warm welcome to the Secretary and other senior officials of 
the Ministry of Civil Aviation. 
3. The Chairman underlined the importance of the deliberations, particularly in the context 
of enhancing regional connectivity, ensuring efficient budget utilisation, strengthening civil 
aviation infrastructure, and addre ssing challenges related to airline regulation and pricing 
mechanisms. He emphasised that the aviation sector plays a crucial role in economic 
development and national connectivity , and therefore, its governance and financial planning 
warrant meticulous parliamentary scrutiny. 
4.  Commencing the presentation, Secretary, Ministry of Civil Aviation apprised the 
Committee about the total budgetary allocation of ₹2,400.31 crores  for the financial year 2025-
26 for the Ministry , outlining the key areas of expendi ture. He informed that a  substantial 
portion, ₹ 945.51 crores , has been earmarked for Air India Asset Holding Limited (AIAHL)  to 
service Non-Convertible Debentures (NCDs)  issued against Air India’s outstanding liabilities 
post-disinvestment. The Ministry a ssured the Committee that efforts were underway to develop a 
long-term strategy to phase out such financial obligations , ensuring that the government’s burden 
in this regard is progressively reduced . The Regional Connectivity Scheme (RCS -UDAN) has 
been allocated ₹540 crores , with ₹240 crores designated for the North -Eastern region , aimed at 
enhancing connectivity in underserved areas . The Ministry acknowledged, however, that only 
₹210 crores of the ₹502 crores allocated for the previous year had been utilis ed, citing delays in 
infrastructure readiness at smaller airports and operational challenges faced by airlines  as the 
primary reasons. 
5. Coming to the  regulatory and administrative expenditures, The Ministry informed that 
₹467 crores has been assigned for salaries and establishment costs  across various aviation bodies, 
including the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA), Bureau of Civil Aviation Security 
(BCAS), Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB), and other regulatory institutions . 
Moreover, ₹142.75 crores has been allocated to cover customs cost recovery charges at smaller 
international airports , where low customs revenue generation necessitates government support . 
The Ministry also highlighted the success of the Production -Linked Incenti ve (PLI) Scheme for 
Drones, with ₹120 crores in incentives disbursed to 23 companies , which has lead  to a tenfold 
increase in sector turnover to ₹1,300 crores . On the infrastructure front, the Ministry reported 
progress in greenfield airport projects , though land acquisition and regulatory approvals continue 

46 
to pose challenges. Efforts to revive seaplane operations  were also underway, with targeted 
regulatory clearances expected by mid-2025. The Ministry acknowledged concerns regarding 
high airfares , stating that DGCA was actively monitor ing airline pricing trends but d id not 
directly regulate fares. 
6. During the course of the deliberations, Members  raised several concerns and sought 
clarifications on the following issues:  
 Members questioned the government’s continued financial commitments towards Air 
India’s liabilities post-disinvestment. 
 Members sought explanations for the substantial underutilisation of allocated funds , 
particularly in the North -Eastern region, and demanded a clear roadmap for expe diting 
the operationalisation of awarded routes . 
 Serious concerns were raised over exorbitant airfares during peak seasons , with instances 
where domestic tickets cost more than international fares .  
 Members sought updates on the status of greenfield airpor t projects , particularly those 
facing delays due to land acquisition and regulatory hurdles . The issue of stalled projects 
in Haryana (Hisar and Ambala) was raised . 
 Concerns were raised over the high number of vacancies in DGCA, BCAS, and AAI , 
with members questioning how these shortages would impact aviation safety and 
regulatory efficiency. 
 Members noted the slow  progress in expanding seaplane operations  and urged  the 
Ministry to provide a clear timeline for revival efforts . 
 While appreciati ng the success of the PLI scheme for drones , M embers urged further 
efforts to promote domestic manufacturing of drone components to reduce reliance on 
imports. 
7. To address these concerns effectively, the Committee made the following actionable 
recommendations: 
 Formulating a definitive plan to phase out government -backed debt servicing  for Air 
India so that such financial burdens do not persist indefinitely . 
 Expediting of  infrastructure readiness at smaller airports  and implement ing a viability 
assessment for commercially unviable routes  to ensure efficient utilisation of allocated 
funds. 
 Strengthenening of DGCA’s  tariff monitoring framework  to prevent unjustified fare 
hikes, particularly during peak seasons and emergencies.  
 Fast-tracking of  greenfield airp ort projects , particularly in under-served regions , and 
implementation of a streamlined clearance mechanism to prevent unnecessary delays . 
 Urgently fill ing of  critical vacancies in regulatory bodies  so that  aviation safety and 
oversight are not compromised due to staffing shortages. 
 Submission of a  structured implementation plan which detailed  steps to address 
regulatory bottlenecks and timelines for the resumption of operations . 
 Introduction of dedicated policies to encourage domestic production of drone 
components, reducing dependency on imports and strengthening the country’s  aviation 
technology ecosystem.

revised to ₹ 3363.07 crore at the RE stage. The Ministry incurred an expenditure of ₹ 
3284.12 crore, which is approximately 97.65% of the revised allocation. 
6. For 2023-24, the budget was set at ₹ 3399.65 crore, later increased by ₹ 60.35 
crore to ₹ 3460 crore at the RE stage. The Ministry's expenditure for the year was ₹ 
3406.90 crore, representing 98.46% of the revised estimate. 
7. For 2024-25, the budgetary provision is ₹ 3260.93 crore, including ₹ 190.01 
crore under the Capital section. Although the Ministry proposed an RE allocation of ₹ 
3756.55 crore, reflecting an increase of ₹ 495.62 crore, the RE allocation remained the 
same as the BE allocation. The Committee acknowledges that the Ministry has 
undertaken additional activities such as the Kumbh at Prayag and the Republic Day 
tableau, which were not included in the RE stage. However, it is expected that the 

7 
 
allocated budget for 2024-25 will be utilized optimally as per the Ministry's planned 
activities. 
8. The Committee observes that there is a significant reduction in the 
Ministry's total budget from ₹ 3,406.90 crore (actual) in 2023-24 to ₹ 3,260.93 
crore (RE) in 2024-25 and an increase to ₹ 3,360.96 crore for 2025-26. The 
Committee further observes the reduction in the Ministry’s total budget from ₹ 
3,406.90 crore (actual) in 2023-24 to ₹ 3,260.93 crore (RE) in 2024-25 can be 
attributed primarily to the one-time expenditures related to the Azadi Ka Amrit 
Mahotsav (AKAM). The AKAM celebrations saw a substantial increase in 
expenditure, with a revision of the Budget Estimate (BE) from ₹ 185 crore to ₹ 
335 crore during 2023-24, resulting in an expenditure of ₹ 334.39 crore, which 
was more than 80% over and above the original BE allocation. 
9. The Committee acknowledges that the reduction in budget during the 
2024-25 fiscal year is a reflection of the conclusion of AKAM-related activities, 
which were exceptional in nature and not a recurring part of the Ministry's 
regular expenditure plans. However, the reduction in the budget allocation for 
2024-25 compared to 2023-24 highlights the need to ensure that the Ministry's 
cultural preservation and development initiatives are adequately funded, 
especially in light of long-term goals for heritage conservation.  
10. The Committee further notes that the budget formulation process for 
2024-25 did not adequately account for key national cultural commitments, 
including the Kumbh at Prayag and the Republic Day tableau, leading to an 
additional request for funds mid-year. The omission of such significant 
expenditures at the BE stage does seem to indicate deficiencies in financial 
forecasting and contingency planning. The Committee recommends the 
implementation of a comprehensive Multi-Year Budgetary Framework (MYBF) 
for the Ministry of Culture that extends beyond the annual budget cycle. This 
framework should incorporate: 

8 
 
a) A five-year rolling budget projection with annual revisions to accommodate 
changing priorities while maintaining long-term vision. 
b) Categorization of expenditures into core recurring activities, planned 
development initiatives, and special events/commemorations with separate 
budgetary provisions for each category. 
c) Establishment of a Budget Stabilization Reserve of approximately 5% of the 
total annual allocation to account for unforeseen cultural activities or 
emergencies, preventing mid-year fiscal disruptions. 
This approach would mitigate the abrupt budgetary fluctuations witnessed 
between 2023-24 and 2024-25, and provide greater stability for cultural 
institutions dependent on Government funding. 
11. The Committee further notes that although overall budget utilisation 
remains high, expenditure patterns across various cultural schemes have been 
inconsistent. Programmes such as museum development, cultural mapping, and 
global cultural engagement have experienced fluctuating levels of fund 
disbursement, with some initiatives facing under-utilisation in certain years and 
excessive allocations in other.  The Committee strongly recommends the 
development of a Cultural Calendar-Based Budgeting system that: 
a) Maintains a comprehensive five-year cultural events calendar that identifies 
recurring festivals, commemorations, and international engagements with 
historical budget requirements. 
b) Integrates cyclical cultural events (such as Kumbh Mela, which occurs every 
12 years) into long-term financial planning through a dedicated cultural events 
fund. 
c) Implements quarterly budget review mechanisms to assess expenditure 
against planned activities and make necessary adjustments before the Revised 
Estimates stage. 

9 
 
d) Develops an AI-assisted forecasting model that analyzes historical expenditure 
patterns and predicts resource requirements for upcoming cultural activities 
based on past event costs, inflation factors, and attendance projections. 
This systematic approach would ensure that cultural events of national 
importance receive appropriate financial provisions at the Budget Estimate stage 
rather than relying on mid-year adjustments 
 
12. The Committee observes a pattern wherein the Ministry relies heavily on 
mid-year budgetary adjustments, seeking substantial increases at the RE stage 
instead of ensuring that BE allocations accurately reflect financial needs. In the 
opinion of the Committee, this approach introduces uncertainty into long-term 
financial planning and may disrupt the timely execution of projects. A more 
accurate and predictive budget estimation process is required to minimise 
dependency on RE-stage adjustments. The Committee recommends that the 
Ministry strengthen its engagement with the Ministry of Finance to establish a 
more flexible, needs-based budget allocation framework, one that will ensure 
funding provisions are more effectively met with practical expenditure 
requirements. Also, the Ministry should establish a Corporate Social 
Responsibility (CSR) engagement cell within the Ministry to facilitate 
partnerships between businesses and cultural projects, capitalizing on the 100% 
tax exemption available under Section 80G(ii) of the Income Tax Act
