25 
 
 
CHAPTER-III 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH REPLIES OF 
THE MINISTRY HAVE NOT BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE COMMITTEE 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
1. The Ministry should conduct an urgent review of anticipated fund requirements for the 
remainder of FY 2025-26, identifying shipyards with confirmed orders that can demonstrate 
clear progress toward delivery milestones. Unutilized funds from the broader ₹4,000 crore 
allocation should be systematically redistributed to support these viable projects, ensuring 
maximum resource utilization before the current scheme expires in 2026. This reallocation 
should prioritize yards that have demonstrated consistent delivery performance and those 
engaged in constructing specialized or green vessels that align with future maritime needs. The 
experience gained from the previous shipbuilding financial assistance scheme, which has 
supported 135 delivered vessels, provides sufficient data to identify high-performing shipyards 
that can effectively utilize additional funding.   
 (Para 26.1)   
Reply of the Ministry     
1.1 Budget estimates for FY 2025-26 has accounted for all ships (green/others) for which an 
application is expected to be made (subsequent to the delivery of the vessel) in this financial 
year. Also, funds disbursed to green/hybrid/electric vessels under SBFAP would be separately 
accessible in the new portal. 
 
Further Recommendations/Observations 
1.2 The Committee further recommends that the Ministry should cross-verify the basis 
on which anticipated applications for FY 2025-26 have been estimated. Since actual 
applications are submitted only post-delivery, the Committee stresses the need for a robust 
verification mechanism to avoid over- or under-estimation of fund requirements, thereby 
ensuring realistic budgeting. 
 

26 
 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
2. Beyond simply allocating a portion of existing funds to green vessel construction, the 
Ministry should establish a dedicated Green Shipbuilding Innovation Fund within the SBFAP 
framework. This fund would finance not only vessel construction but also research and 
development activities focused on adapting international green shipping technologies to Indian 
conditions. The proposed SBFAP 2.0, with its enhanced subsidies for green vessels, creates an 
opportunity to institutionalize this approach. The fund should support collaborative projects 
between shipyards, research institutions, and technology providers to develop standardized 
designs for green vessels suited to Indian operational contexts. This would create a pipeline of 
technically validated vessel designs that Indian shipyards could offer to domestic and 
international clients at competitive prices.  
(Para 26.2)   
Reply of the Ministry     
2.1 In November 2021, the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways (MoPSW) released 
five variants of Approved Standardized Tug Designs (ASTDS) for use by major ports. These 
designs aim to streamline procurement processes and encourage construction within Indian 
shipyards. Further, Green Tug transition program(GTTP) and Green craft transition program 
(GCTP) have been implemented to ensure demand driven greener transition. 
 
 
Further Recommendations/Observations 
2.2 The Committee further recommends that the Green Tug Transition Programme 
(GTTP) and Green Craft Transition Programme (GCTP) be integrated with a long-term 
assured demand framework, whereby major ports, PSUs and inland waterway authorities 
commit to phased procurement targets for green vessels, thereby providing order visibility 
and reducing investment risks for Indian shipyards. 
 
 
 

27 
 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
3. The Committee observes that ₹ 475 crore revenue outlay is directed towards general 
administration of DGLL, operation and maintenance of maritime navigation aids, management 
of the Vessel Traffic Service at Gulf of Kachchh (VTSGOK), and upkeep of lighthouse tender 
vessels. It acknowledges that though these allocations support day-to-day functionality, there is a 
need for increased 30 investment in technological upgrades and human resource capacity-
building to bring the country’s marine navigation systems at par with international best 
practices. The Committee recommends that the Ministry allocate a greater proportion of revenue 
towards technological modernisation, particularly in automation of aids to navigation and 
regular training and capacity-building programmes for DGLL personnel to ensure efficient 
utilisation of advanced maritime technologies.   
(Para 31)   
Reply of the Ministry     
3.1 Revenue Expenditure is utilized for technological modernisation and capacity building at 
MNTI which conducts International and domestic trainings as detailed below: 
I. Enhancement of Navigational Services: A continuous improvement plan has been 
instituted that includes periodic audits, training programs to ensure that the DGLL remains 
aligned with international best practices in maritime navigation.  Additionally, funds under the 
Capital Head are strategically utilized for the technological modernization of Aids to Navigation 
(AtoN) infrastructure. 
II. MNTI, Kolkata has Scheduled international training on: 
 IWRAP Risk Assessment tool for international participants is scheduled on 07th July 2025 
to 11th July 2025  
 Level-1 AtoN manager training course from 27th Oct-2025 to 21st Nov-2025 
 Several training programs are planned during 2025–26 for domestic stakeholders and

Further Recommendations/Observations 
3.2 While taking note of the Ministry’s assurance regarding training initiatives at the

identifying skill gaps in emerging technologies such as e-Navigation, AI-based vessel traffic 
monitoring, remote AtoN management, and cyber security of navigation systems.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY 
THE MINISTRY 
  
DEMANDS FOR GRANTS (2025-26) 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
1. The Committee acknowledges the Ministry's commitment to infrastructure 
development but emphasizes the necessity for enhanced financial oversight, timely 
project execution, and rigorous quality control standards. It recommends establishing a 
comprehensive and independent monitoring framework, supported by advanced project 
management technologies and regular audits, to proactively address delays in land 
acquisition, regulatory approvals, and contractor inefficiencies. Additionally, the 
Committee advises careful and strategic management of asset monetization initiatives to 
safeguard long-term revenue sustainability without compromising future income 
streams.  
 (Para 7) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1 MoRTH has institutionalized independent online monitoring framework for addressing 
the delay in Land Acquisition, Environment & Forest Clearance and GAD for ROBs/RUBs 
approval.  
1.2 The complete Land acquisition process has been made online through Bhoomi Rashi 
Portal by leveraging the technology.3,200+ projects have been facilitated, covering over 
145,000 hectares of land and issuing 13,500+ gazette notifications. This has enabled direct 
transfer of Rs. 19,500 Cr to landowners, reducing leakages and also eliminating the need for 
Rs. 27,000 Cr. of float funds in CALA accounts. Overall, LA process has been shortened by 
~3 months, thus significantly improving efficiency and transparency. 
1.3 MoEF&CC has developed the Parivesh Portal 2.0 and customized for MoRT&H 
providing a single-window system for monitoring and managing environmental, forest, 
wildlife, and CRZ clearances. This enabled tracking the online status of clearances which 
helps in early Forest and Wildlife clearances. With real-time dashboards, color-coded alerts 
for delays, and a three-tier oversight structure, it ensures faster, transparent and accountable 
clearance processes while reducing bottlenecks. Analysis of delay shows that 75% of the 
delay is at State level and 25% is at central level. 
1.4 Similarly, MoRTH and the Ministry of Railways jointly launched RoB/RUB Portal, in 
July 2025, to centralize approvals for Road Over Bridges and Road Under Bridges. The 
portal sets fixed timelines for approvals, reducing the time for GADs from 70 to 50 days, 

- 3 - 
 
structural drawings to 11 days (plus 7 after compliance), and launching schemes and 
QAP/WPSS approvals within 30 days. With role-based access, dashboards, and auto-
notifications, the portal ensures predictable, time-bound approvals and closer coordination 
between highway and railway agencies. 
1.5 Data Lake MIS is MoRT&H’s in-house project and contract management system that 
enables continuous project monitoring, payment tracking and dispute resolution. Provides 
real-time project monitoring through GIS-enabled dashboards and customized reports for 
senior management. Accountability is ensured at all levels, from concessionaires and 
consultants to PIUs, regional offices, and headquarters, with automated alerts highlighting 
pending actions. Includes a dispute resolution module to ensure timely redressal of contractor 
and stakeholder issues.  
1.6 Together, these platforms form a cohesive digital stack that supports MoRTH’s vision 
for efficient National Highway development. By digitizing key processes across the lifecycle 
from land acquisition and clearances to implementation and monitoring, MoRTH has 
significantly improved project delivery and stakeholder coordination. 
1.7 Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs authorized MoRTH / NHAI to monetize 
public funded NH projects which are operational and are generating toll revenues for at least 
two years (which was later reduced to one year) after the Commercial Operations Date 
(COD) subject to approval of the Competent Authority in MoRTH/NHAI. Cabinet also 
approved the proposal to authorize MoRTH / NHAI to set up Infrastructure Investment Trust 
(InvIT) and monetize completed and operational NH projects. NHAI is also authorized to 
raise long term finance from banks by securitizing user fee receipts from toll plazas as an 
alternate mode of asset monetization.  
1.8 Accordingly, MoRTH through NHAI monetizes assets through three modes – Toll 
Operate & Transfer (ToT), InvIT, and Securitization [Project based Financing through 
Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV)]. Under ToT and InvIT, operational assets with stable cash 
flow are offered to investors, freeing them from pre-construction and construction risks. The 
concessionaires are exposed to revenue risk and operations and maintenance obligations. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
2. The relatively small reduction in maintenance funding (Rs.4,595 crore allocated 
against Rs.4,695 crore projected) may seem insignificant but requires deeper analysis. 
Research indicates that when agencies attend to routine maintenance (filling potholes, 
maintaining pavement edges) but neglect periodic maintenance and rehabilitation, they 
may save money in the short term but eventually face expensive reconstruction costs. 
(Para 16) 

- 4 - 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
3. The Ministry should transform its approach to maintenance by implementing a 
comprehensive 10-step maintenance planning process that includes facility audits, task 
definition, prioritization, scheduling, resource allocation, implementation, safety 
protocols, performance metrics, emergency preparedness, and documentation. This 
structured approach would ensure that maintenance budgets, though slightly reduced, 
deliver optimal outcomes through strategic targeting and efficient execution. 
(Para 16.1) 
Recommendation/Observation 
4. For effective implementation, the Ministry should develop a digitized asset 
management system that tracks the condition of all national highways and predicts 
maintenance needs based on traffic patterns, climate conditions, and construction 
materials. This system should prioritize maintenance based on safety concerns, 
economic importance, and cost-effectiveness rather than simply responding to visible 
deterioration. Furthermore, maintenance contracts should incorporate performance-
based incentives that reward contractors for maintaining high-quality road conditions 
rather than merely completing specified activities. 
(Para 16.2) 
Reply of the Ministry (2 to 4, above) 
4.1 Maintenance expenditure in the ongoing works which are ongoing and during Defect 
Libility Period / Concession period of Projects under EPC/HAM/BOT/TOT/INvIT are taken 
up the respective Contractor and Concessionaire. Such expenditure are not included in the 
MoRTH expenditure statement as these expenditure are not being done through Government 
Budget 
 
4.2 For all remaining sections of NHs stretches, where DLP has ended or is not under any 
concession period of BOT/HAM/TOT/InvIT project, Government has taken a policy decision 
to undertake maintenance works through Performance Based Maintenance Contract (PBMC) 
or Short Term Maintenance Contract (STMC). While STMC works are generally undertaken 
for a contract period of 1-2 year, PBMC works are undertaken for a contract period of about 
5-7 years. The maintenance work on PBMC mode is in line with the recommendation of the 
committee which ensures minimum performance standards in maintenance with time bound 
defect rectification. Any delay in account of defect rectification attracts automatic penal 
provisions.  
4.3 Year – wise details of expenditure incurred on M&R of such NHs stretches since 
2014-15 onwards is as under:-

4.5 As suggested by the committee for the 10 step maintenance planning process that

bituminous mixes, Fiber Reinforced Concrete, Cement Grouted Bituminous Mixes, etc. 
Automated and Intelligent Machine-Aided Construction has been adopted which ensures

4.8 Road condition assessment is carried out through Network Survey Vehicle (NSV) for 
the NHs stretches before start of work, before issue of completion certificate and thereafter at 
regular intervals of six months after completion of the work, thereby enabling quality 
assessment of NHs at regular intervals for (i) ensuring the maintenance during Concession

4.9 Further, app based monitoring through National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) 
One / Tatpar App facilitates highway project management by Field officers / Engineers /

Recommendation/Observation 
5. For effective implementation, the Ministry should develop a digital dashboard 
accessible to all stakeholders that provides real-time updates on project status, fund 
utilization, and achievement of milestones. Each project should have clearly defined 
quarterly targets with automatic escalation procedures if deviations exceed 
predetermined thresholds. This approach ensures early identification of implementation 
challenges and enables prompt corrective action before projects face serious delays. 
(Para 17.1) 
 
Reply of the Ministry 
5.1 MoRTH has developed online project monitoring portals (Data lake used by NHAI 
and Project Monitoring & Information System (PMIS) used by all other implementing 
agencies) in which access to dashboard is provided to all implementing agencies for getting 
real-time updates on achievements vis-à-vis targets, project progress, fund utilization, 
milestone achievement, etc. Development of additional features is underway and the plan is 
to have a single portal accessible to all implementing agencies. Data Lake portal enables 
access to all stakeholders that provides real-time updates on project status, fund utilization, 
and achievement of milestones. Each project should have clearly defined quarterly targets 
with automatic escalation procedures if deviations exceed predetermined thresholds. This 
ensures early identification of implementation challenges and enables prompt corrective 
action before projects face serious delays. 
 
 

- 7 - 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
6. The monitoring system should also incorporate emergency preparedness 
elements to address unexpected challenges such as natural disasters, material shortages, 
or contractor defaults. By establishing clear protocols for these contingencies, the 
Ministry can minimize disruption and maintain project momentum even when facing 
unforeseen obstacles. Additionally, comprehensive documentation and training 
procedures should be implemented to ensure institutional memory and consistent 
application of best practices across all projects regardless of individual staffing changes. 
(Para 17.2) 
Reply of the Ministry 
6.1 The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (MoRT&H) has recently notified 
Disaster Management Plan (DMP). The DMP provides comprehensive framework for 
managing disasters with a focus on maintaining and restoring traffic connectivity on roads 
and highways. The institutional framework of MoRT&H shall be laid down under two sub-
plans, one for all disaster events (eg. Landslide, Flood, Earthquake etc.) other than “Road 
Accident” (Volume-I: Overview and Disaster Management Sub-Plan for Highways) and 
"Road Accidents" as Nodal Ministry (Volume-II: Disaster Management Sub-Plan for Road 
Accidents). 
6.2 The document provides a comprehensive and integrated approach of managing 
disasters and reducing risk of disaster, with a clear-cut hierarchy and well assigned roles & 
responsibilities of officers of various agencies of MoRT&H. A Disaster Management 
Division (DM-Div.) headed by Chief Engineer/Joint Secretary level officer has been 
envisaged under this DMP, which shall act as Nodal Division of MoRT&H to coordinate 
with Ministries/Departments of the Central Government, State Government/ District 
Administration as well as executing agencies of MoRT&H. Further, a Standing Committee 
comprising of senior officials of the Ministry has been envisaged and has been assigned with 
the Role to approve policy / guidelines. 
6.3 Further, financial delegation have been assigned at various levels for sanctioning & 
execution of immediate restoration work in the wake of a Disaster event with bare minimum 
time ensuring uninterrupted traffic movement. 
6.4 Also all officers have been sensitized for effectively using the National Database 
for Emergency Management (NDEM) for study of flood pattern, hydrological study and 
Disaster Prone Zone to minimize the adverse impact of eco sensitive areas.

Recommendation/Observation 
7. Furthermore, the Ministry should commission independent third-party audits of 
selected projects to validate internal monitoring data and identify opportunities for 
systemic improvement. These audits should evaluate not just compliance with financial 
and technical specifications but also assess whether projects are delivering anticipated 
economic and social benefits. This external perspective would strengthen accountability 
while providing valuable insights for future planning and implementation. 
 
(Para 17.3) 
Reply of the Ministry 
7.1 As the NH network expanded in the last decade from ~91,000 km to 1.46 Lakh km, 
management and monitoring of NH quality is critical. To ensure standardized monitoring, 
equipment based condition monitoring system to monitor roughness, cracking, rutting, and 
potholes was designed by MoRT&H through Network Survey Vehicle (NSV). NSVs are 
mobile data collection and processing centres with sensors like laser profile meter, laser crack 
measurement system, GPS, 360 video imagery etc. To enable continuous pavement quality 
monitoring, MoRT&H has instituted periodic surveys (once in 6 months) of the NH network 
through Network Survey Vehicle.  A Centralized GIS platform developed for objective 
assessment of pavement condition based on inputs from NSV within 48 hrs. Process planned 
for report generation and responsibility fixing matrix within 10 days. For ensuring third party 
audit, Ministry has started the independent Network Survey Vehicle (NSV) survey for 
ensuring the pavement quality. This independent NSV survey is done apart from the regular 
NSV surveys through Supervision Consultant / Authority Engineer / Independent Engineer 
on the recently completed stretches which are within the defect liability period and also in 
PBMC contracts.  
7.2 MoRT&H has initiated NSV survey of the network, prioritizing the 38,000 km under 
O&M stage with NHAI currently - Phase 1 covering 21,000 km (about 1 Lakh lane km )has 
been completed for 1st round and initiated for 2nd round. Phase 2 covering remaining 17,000 
km of NHAI has been initiated in Oct’25.Government is planning to implement this survey 
PAN INDIA across all agencies.  
7.3 Additionally, Ministry also appoints Third Party Quality Auditors for systematic, 
independent and documented process of investigating the Quality Assurance/ Quality Control 
system of National Highway Projects as per the provisions of IRC: SP: 112-2017. Retired 
Officers from Central / State Government are empanelled as Team Leaders by NHAI and 
Special Project Monitors (SPMs) by NHIDCL for Quality Inspections of NHAI & NHIDCL

Recommendations/Observations 
8. The Committee is equally concerned by the lack of an effective emergency 
response system. While noting the pilot implementation of the cashless treatment 
scheme in six states, the Committee finds the pace of expansion inadequate. The 
Committee therefore directed the Ministry to ensure its nationwide rollout as a matter 
of priority, integrating it with a trauma care network along major highways and 
establishing clear coordination protocols between ambulance services, hospitals, and 
enforcement agencies. 
(Para 25) 
Recommendation/Observation 
9. Drawing from established emergency response frameworks, the Ministry should 
implement a four-phase emergency response strategy: detection, notification, response, 
and treatment. This requires developing an observability platform that integrates 
traffic monitoring systems, emergency call centres, ambulance services, and hospital 
trauma units into a unified response network. The cashless treatment scheme should be 
expanded nationwide within 12 months, accompanied by establishment of fully 
equipped trauma care centres at 100-kilometer intervals along all national highways. 
(Para 25.1) 
Reply of the Ministry (8 & 9, above) 
9.1 MoRTH has notified the cashless treatment of road accident victims scheme, 2025 on 
5th May, 2025 in consultation with Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW) to 
provide cashless treatment to victims of road accidents in the country. The detailed guidelines 
including process flow, stakeholder wise standard operating procedures and clearly 
delineated roles and responsibilities have also been notified on 4th June, 2025. 
9.2 Further, to motivate the citizens for helping victims of road crashes without fear, the 
Government has notified Rule 168 and Rule 169 under the Central Motor Vehicle Rules, 
1989 to protect the person, who in good faith, provide assistance to the victims of road 
crashes.  

- 11 - 
 
 9.3 The Good Samaritan Law allows a person, without expectation of payment or reward 
and without any duty of care or special relationship, voluntarily come forward to administer 
immediate assistance or emergency care to a person injured in an accident, or crash, or 
emergency medical condition. Good Samaritan Law protects Good Samaritans from 
harassment on the actions being taken by them to save the life of the road accident victims. 
9.4 MoRTH also administering a scheme for grant of Award to the Good Samaritan, who 
has saved life of a victim of an accident involving a motor vehicle by administering 
immediate assistance and rushing the victim to Hospital/Trauma Care Centre within the 
Golden Hour of the accident to provide medical treatment. The scheme provides each Good 
Samaritan with cash award of Rs. 25000/- and a certificate of appreciation per incident, 
subject to certain conditions including maximum 5 awards to an individual in a year.  
9.5 The response time for emergency services at accident sites depends on various factors 
including the traffic, weather, road condition, time, surroundings of the area etc. The 
Government has taken various initiatives for the emergency services at accident sites which 
inter-alia include: 
(i) Integrated Emergency Response Support System (ERSS) is designed with a single 
emergency number 112, to address different emergencies of citizens. 
(ii) Provision for free passage to emergency vehicles, such as an ambulance or fire service 
vehicle, etc. (Section 194E of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988). 
(iii) Protection of Good Samaritans who provide emergency medical or non-medical 
assistance to victims of motor vehicle accidents (Section 134A of the Motor Vehicles Act, 
1988). 
(iv) Provision for First-aid kit in all vehicles. (Rule 138(4) of the Central Motor Vehicles 
Rules, 1989) 
(v) Sanction of 196 Trauma Care Facilities in Government Hospitals/Medical Colleges 
across the Country under "National programme for Prevention & Management of Trauma 
and Burn injuries" by Ministry of Health & Family Welfare. 
(vi) Emergency helpline number 1033 by National Highways Authority of India (NHAI). 
(vii) Provision for Patrolling Vehicles, Ambulances, Tow-away cranes etc. in the model 
concessionaire agreement. 
(viii) Advanced Traffic Management System (ATMS) is installed in high traffic density 
National Highways by NHAI. ATMS has provisions for various electronic enforcement 
devices which help in speedy identification of incidents on the highway stretches and

effectively monitor the highways, thereby improving the response time of the on-site 
assistance.

formulated:- 
(i). Regular Inspections of the vulnerable spots for preventive action and installation of 
warning signs. 
(ii). Keeping in stock/ on-offer excavators / backhoe loaders / dozers, saw cutters for tree 
cutting, sand bags, traffic cones & Signages, etc., in required quantities at required locations. 
(iii). Alerting and instructing the concerned contractors for the works like bridge closing, 
tree removal, landslide clearance, diversion of roads, etc.  
Recommendation/Observation 
20. The Committee notes that the Ministry has set an ambitious asset monetization 
target of ₹39,000 crore fo r2024-25 and ₹30,000crorefor2025-26. The reduction in target

Moreover, the use of funds from Toll Operate Transfer (TOT) for NH development and 
Infrastructure Investment Trusts (InvIT) solely for debt repayment seems to indicate a 
structured, but limited, reinvestment strategy. The Committee recommends that the 
Ministry may consider expanding the pipeline of assets available for monetization to 
maintain fiscal momentum. Further, it would be prudent to assess whether an optimal 
balance is being achieved between debt reduction and reinvestment in infrastructure 
projects.

(Para 43) 
Reply of the Ministry 
20.1 MoRTH through NHAI has mobilized Rs. 28,724 Crore in FY 2024-25 through the

account of less raising of resources through Special purpose vehicle as Delhi Mumbai 
Corridor is coming to an end. Keeping in view the actual fund raised in FY 2024-25, the 
target for FY 2025-26 has been kept as Rs. 30,000 Crore. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
21. The Committee also notes with satisfaction that the signing of TOT Bundle-16 
(₹6,661 crore) and the launch of bids for four additional TOT Bundles (₹18,000 crore) 
points towards progress. However, with InvIT Bundle-4 expected to realise ₹20,000 
crore only by March 2025, any procedural or market-related delays may impact 
financial flows and project timelines. It therefore recommends that the Ministry ensures 
that all regulatory approvals and preparatory work are completed in advance to 
prevent any unforeseen delays. 
(Para 44) 
Reply of the Ministry 
21.1 There were no procedural or market-related delays and all regulatory approvals and 
preparatory work were completed in timely manner by NHAI InvIT thereby successfully 
raising Rs. 17,738 Crore (including premium) in March, 2025. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
22. The Committee observes that the Ministry currently faces 366 vacancies out of 
1,118 sanctioned posts, with Group A (114 vacancies), Group B (127 vacancies), and 
Group C (125 vacancies) experiencing notable shortages. It further notes that though 
regular recruitment is conducted via UPSC (for Group A) and SSC (for Groups B & C), 
the unfilled positions may impact administrative efficiency and project execution. The 
Committee therefore recommends that the Ministry may consider expediting 
recruitment processes to ensure adequate staffing, particularly in technical roles. 
Information under compilation. 
(Para 46) 
Recommendation/Observation 
23. The Committee notes that the Group B and Group C positions, particularly in 
regional offices and headquarters, continue to witness vacancies despite regular 
notifications to SSC. At the headquarters level, only 78 out of 136 sanctioned Group C 

- 43 - 
 
(MTS) posts are filled, which may impact routine administrative functions. The 
Committee therefore suggests that the Ministry may wish to enhance coordination with 
SSC for timely recruitment while exploring alternative mechanisms such as direct 
recruitment drives or contractual hiring for urgent requirements.

Transport & Highways has been approved by the Cabinet on 09.10.2024. Consequent upon

increased by 97 posts i.e. from 328 posts to 425 posts. Presently, there are 316 CES (Roads) 
officers against the sanctioned strength of 425 posts. 
23.3 A five year recruitment plan has been prepared in consultation with Department of 
Personnel & Training for filling up these increased 97 posts at the entry level of Assistant 
Executive Engineer (Civil). Accordingly, 25 vacancies have been intimated to UPSC for 
filling up through Engineering Service Examinations, 2025.

‘B’ and ‘C’) posted in its Regional offices. The details of posts and their incumbency position 
is as under:-

recruitment through SSC. The vacancies in these grades have been intimated to SSC for

Project Reports (DPRs) and the functioning of project consultants involved in the 
Bharatmala Pariyojana and other expressway and national highway projects. The 
Committee expresses dissatisfaction with how the project consultants have been 
preparing DPRs without adequate consultation with local stakeholders, including 
practical experts and local representatives, particularly Members of Parliament. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry reviews the current process of 
engaging project consultants and consider conducting an audit of past awarded work of 
Project Consultants by the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) in advance, to 
ensure greater accountability and efficiency in the project implementation process. 
(Para 48) 
Reply of the Ministry 
24.1 Preparation of Detailed Project Report (DPR) is an extensive process and is generally 
carried out through Consultants procured through open competitive bidding. However, 
Government has witnessed the poor quality of DPRs resulting in quality issues, change of 
scope and time overrun etc. 
24.2 Accordingly, in line with the Committee’s recommendation, Government has initiated 
the process of completely revamping the DPR process. Major changes being considered are 
(i) Fixed cost RFP, (ii) Rating of DPR Consultants, (iii) Performance Security and rating

documents have been prepared and public comments have also been received. Government 
will shortly come out with the revamped DPR RFP document and rating of consultants.

CHAPTER-III 
  
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH REPLIES OF 
THE MINISTRY HAVE NOT BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE COMMITTEE 
 
BUDGETARY SUPPORT FOR TRANSPORT, RESEARCH AND SAFETY 
Recommendation/Observation 
1. The Committee's directive for a time-bound action plan for black spot rectification 
requires a more systematic approach than previously implemented. The persistent existence 
of identified black spots represents a significant governance failure that directly translates to 
preventable deaths. The Ministry should implement a three-tier prioritization framework 
categorizing black spots based on severity (frequency and impact of accidents), complexity of 
intervention required, and population exposure. 
(Para 23) 
Recommendation/Observation 
2. For immediate action, the Ministry should adopt a rapid-response protocol for 
Category A (highest risk) black spots, with mandatory intervention within 30 days of 
identification. This should include deployment of temporary safety measures while 
permanent solutions are designed. For Category B and C black spots, the Ministry should 
establish 90-day and 180- day rectification deadlines respectively, with penalties for non-
compliance by implementing agencies. 
(Para 23.1) 
Recommendation/Observation 
3. Each rectified black spot should undergo mandatory post- implementation  safety 
audits at 3-month and 12-month intervals to ensure the effectiveness of interventions. 
Additionally, the Ministry should develop a public dashboard displaying the status of all 
identified black spots, rectification progress, and responsible authorities, enhancing 
transparency and accountability in the process. 
(Para 23.2) 
Reply of the Ministry (1 to 3, above) 
3.1 Earlier Accident Data was collected manually through all police department and than 
across all states and there was a delay of 3 to 4years. Now Electronic-Detailed Accident 
Report (E-DAR) is a central accident database management system designed to analyse the 
causes of crashes and devise safety interventions to reduce such accidents developed by 
Ministry through National Informatics Centre (NIC).E-DAR has been successfully rolled out 
in 36 states and union territories across the country. The project enables real-time collection 

- 46 - 
 
of accident data through an integrated digital platform for all stakeholder departments. It is 
available as both a web-based module and a mobile app.  
3.2 Government has launched a central repository for reporting, management and analysis 
of road accidents data to enhance road safety, rolled out in all States/UTs named e-DAR 
(Electronic Detailed Accident report). Its complete integration with VAHAN, SARATHI, PM 
GATI Shakti, TMS, Data Lake has already been done. Also, further integration is ongoing 
with CCTNS (26 States completed) and e-Courts (Pilot testing ongoing in Delhi). Now all 
accident locations identified through e-DAR are being attended on priority and short term 
measures are ensured quickly. 
3.3 Based on the E-DAR data, All accident spots are inspected by the concerned field 
officers and short-term measures are taken immediately. Requirement of permanent spot 
rectification measures are analysed and if required, DPR is initiated and projects are 
undertaken. 
3.4 So far Ministry has identified 32,183 from 2023-2025 (till 30thJune, 2025) via eDAR. 
Among these, remedial measures are required on 14,090 after analysis of the locations.  Short 
terms measures have been completed on 6,009 and ongoing on 284 spots. Long terms 
measures have been completed on 700 and ongoing on 559 spots. 
3.5 Also, Ministry has identified 12,462 black spots from 2016 to 2022. Out of which, 
short term measures have been taken in 11,703 locations and long term measures are 
completed for 5,197 location.  
3.6 IIT Kanpur has also been engaged for AI based analysis of E-DAR data for the 
frequent accident spots and its rectification measures 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
3.7 The Committee expressed its expectation that the concerned authorities should 
take prompt and decisive action to expedite the resolution of the following pending 
issues. It emphasize that timely progress on these matters is essential to ensure effective 
implementation and improved outcomes. 
3.8 The Committee recommends that the Ministry complete the pending integrations 
by expediting full linkage of e-DAR with CCTNS in the remaining States and with e-
Courts nationwide following the pilot phase and ensure time-bound rectification 
through uniform procedures for immediate short-term measures at all accident spots 
identified via e-DAR.  
3.9 It further urges the Ministry to facilitate faster long-term solutions by 
prioritising the quick preparation and sanctioning of DPRs to accelerate engineering 
interventions, while instituting regular quarterly monitoring of progress on both short-

- 47 - 
 
term and long-term rectification. The Committee also emphasises the need to leverage 
AI-based insights from the analysis conducted by IIT Kanpur for planning, design 
improvements and preventive safety measures; strengthen capacity building through 
standardised training for all stakeholder departments to ensure accurate e-DAR data 
capture and effective field response; enhance transparency by developing a public 
dashboard displaying State-wise accident spots and the status of remedial actions and 
share best practices by documenting and disseminating successful State models to 
promote their adoption nationwide. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
4. The Committee's finding that only 28 Driving Training Centres exist for 650 districts 
reveals a critical infrastructure gap in driver education. Research consistently demonstrates 
that proper driver training significantly reduces accident risks, particularly for new drivers 
and commercial vehicle operators. The inadequacy of current training infrastructure 
fundamentally undermines road safety objectives regardless of other interventions. 
(Para 24) 
Reply of the Ministry: 
4.1 MoRTH has reviewed the guidelines for financial assistance for setting up of Driving 
Training Institutions [Institute of Driving Training & Research (IDTRs), Regional Driving 
Training Centres (RDTCs) and Driving Training Centres(DTCs)] in States / UTs for the 15th 
Finance Commission Period. The revised guidelines with relaxed eligibility criteria, 
Automation of Test tracks at DTC, increased financial assistance for DTCs and Training 
Testing Cluster approach for setting up Automated Testing Stations (ATSs) with Driving 
Training Institutions has been approved and circulated to States/UTs on 15.01.2025 with the 
request to send suitable proposals to MoRTH.  
4.2 Under the Scheme, MoRTH has sanctioned total 100 DTIs (31 IDTRs, 14 RDTCs and 
55 DTCs) till date. 
4.3 In addition, private developers are also eligible to establish Driving Training Schools 
or establishments using their own resources, as per the provisions of Section 24 of the Motor 
Vehicles Act, 1988. To make these Driving Training Schools commercially viable, the 
provision for Accredited Driving Training Centres has been introduced under Section 31B of 
the Motor Vehicles Act, through the Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Act, 2019. 
 
 
 
 

- 48 - 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
4.4 In view of the Ministry’s submission, the Committee notes that the revised 
guidelines issued on 15 January 2025—which include relaxed eligibility norms, 
enhanced financial assistance, automation of test tracks, and the integrated Training-
Testing Cluster model—be operationalise in a time-bound manner across all States and 
UTs. The Committee emphasizes that sanctioning 100 DTIs so far is a welcome step, but 
immediate action is required to ensure that State Governments proactively submit 
proposals to bridge the substantial gap between current capacity and nationwide 
demand for driver training. The Ministry shall prepare a district-level rollout plan, 
prioritising high-fatality and underserved regions, and establish periodic monitoring to 
track progress of IDTRs, RDTCs, and DTCs under the 15th Finance Commission 
period. Further, the Committee instructs the Ministry to develop a facilitation 
framework for private participation under Sections 24 and 31B of the Motor Vehicles 
Act, 1988, ensuring that Accredited Driver Training Centres become commercially 
viable, standardized, and closely integrated with Automated Testing Stations. A 
consolidated implementation roadmap, including timelines, State-wise status and 
utilisation of central assistance, should be submitted to the Committee within three 
months.

training programs covering not just mechanical operation of vehicles but traffic laws,

qualified and experienced instructors using modern teaching methodologies tailored to 
different learning styles.

incentives and operational subsidies while maintaining strict quality control through regular 
certification audits.

Institutes to be set up under this Scheme need to be authorized by the State Government as 
Accredited Driving Training Centres. A Driving License aspirant on successful completion of 
training at such centre shall be issued certificate in Form 5B of the CMV Rules, 1989. The 
holder of course completion certificate (Form5B) will be exempted from requirement of 
driving test.  
6.2 The Government aims to establish Driving Training Centres (DTCs) in every district 
and setting up of additional DTC in districts with a population exceeding 10 lakh increasing 
the ceiling for financial assistance to DTCs to ensure their financial viability and to 
encourage more such proposals.  Scheme also aims to establish one Institute of Driving 
Training and Research (IDTR) for every 2.5 crore Population, one Regional Driving Training 
Centre (RDTC) for every 1 crore population (with at least one RDTC in each state, regardless 
of population). 
6.3 As on date, the Ministry has sanctioned 67 Driving Training Centres (DTCs), 21 
RDTCs and 31 IDTRs in various States across the nation. 
6.4 T he implementation of the scheme depends on the States/UTs, as proposals require 
specific recommendations of the concerned District Magistrate/Collector and the respective 
State Transport Authorities, as applicable. DO letters are issued on 27 May,2025 to the Chief 
Secretaries of all States/UTs, urging them to submit suitable proposals under the scheme. 
6.5 Also, presently the impact assessment study of the scheme is in progress. Based on 
the outcome of the study, the scheme shall be re-designed and submitted for kind approval 
during 16th FC.  
 
Further Recommendation/Observation

Training Institutes (DTIs) established under the 15th Finance Commission Cycle should 
comply with the criteria for Accredited Driving Training Centres under the CMV 
Rules, 1989 and that successful trainees from such Centres shall be exempted from the 
driving test upon issuance of Form 5B certificates. The Committee also takes note of the 
Ministry’s plan to expand the network of Driving Training Centres (DTCs), Regional 
Driving Training Centres (RDTCs) and Institutes of Driving Training and Research 

- 50 - 
 
(IDTRs) based on district and population criteria, as well as the current sanction of 67 
DTCs, 21 RDTCs and 31 IDTRs across the country.

assessment study, it observes that progress under the scheme remains dependent on

significant gap persists between the sanctioned Centres and their operationalization and

Ministry to complete the proposed restructuring of the scheme under the 16th Finance 
Commission Cycle.

procedural delays in coordination with States and complete the impact assessment study

emphasize fatigue management, defensive driving in adverse conditions, and updates on

enforceability and tracking of compliance. These measures were intended to strengthen 

- 51 -

under adverse conditions and regular updates on evolving traffic regulations.

licence renewal or the creation of a digital training database. The reply remains

recurring refresher training framework envisioned by the Committee. 
7.4 The Committee, therefore, reiterates the need for the Ministry to formulate a 
concrete implementation plan for periodic refresher courses and a unified digital 
monitoring mechanism, which are essential for enhancing the competency and safety 
standards of commercial drivers nationwide.

Utilisation of Budgetary Allocations 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
4 The Committee notes with serious concern the chronic pattern of fund 
underutilization by the Ministry of Tourism, which represents not merely an administrative 
challenge but a fundamental impediment to the growth of India's tourism potential. The 
alarming statistics of only 33.4% utilization of allocated funds in 2023-24 (₹801.81 crore out 
of ₹2400 crore) and the continuation of this trend in 2024-25 (only ₹396.82 crore utilized 
thus far out of ₹2479.62 crore) indicates deep-rooted systemic inefficiencies that require 
comprehensive structural reforms. While the Ministry has attributed this underperformance 
to administrative bottlenecks, procedural delays, and coordination challenges with 
implementing agencies, the Committee finds these explanations inadequate and reflective of 
entrenched operational weaknesses that demand immediate redressal. 
(Para 19) 
Reply of the Ministry 
4.1 The observation of the Committee is noted.  In this regard, it is to mention that the 
Ministry of Tourism under Swadesh Darshan scheme sanctioned projects till 2018-19, after 
which the scheme was reviewed. Thereafter, the scheme of Swadesh Darshan was revamped 
as Swadesh Darshan 2.0 with the focus on Destination Centric Approach.  Accordingly, the 
Ministry of Tourism till now has sanctioned 48 projects under SD 2.0 for Rs. 1930.31 Crore.  
Further, 36 projects have been sanctioned under Challenge Based Destination Development 
(CBDD), a sub-scheme of Swadesh Darshan for Rs. 623.13 Crore.  Since a robust pipeline of 
sanctioned projects has now been recreated under SD 2.0, Ministry of Tourism is hopeful of 
achievingits financial targets from FY 2025-26 onwards.   
  

5 
 
4.2 It is submitted that for financial year 2024-25 under DPPH scheme, in Revised 
Estimate Rs. 92.95 Crores was allocated out of which 89.69 Crores were utilized. 
  
4.3  It is also submitted that for the FY 2024-25, an amount of Rs. 30 crore was allocated 
under Overseas Promotion and Publicity (OPP) Scheme. Out of this, Rs. 29.26 crore was 
utilized during the last FY which is more than 97% of the total Budget Estimate allocated 
under the Scheme. It is further submitted that the existing Scheme is being revamped to 
tackle deficiencies in the existing scheme and to make it more relevant due to the changing 
times. 
  
4.4 The Ministry of Tourism does regular monitoring of funds through the CNA model, 
as the information is updated in the CNA modules on day to day basis. Under the scheme of 
Assistance to IHMs/FCI/IITTM/NCHMCT, budget provision of Rs.37.50 Crore was kept at 
RE for FY 2023-24, of which an amount of Rs.31.71 Cr was utilized during the financial 
year. Whereas, budget provision of Rs.32.00 Crore was kept at RE stage for FY 2024-25, of 
which an amount of Rs.24.40 Cr was utilized during the financial year. The reason for 
underutilization of funds is lack of timely receipt of Utilization Certificate and pegging of 
funds to a particular project. The concern of pegging of funds to a particular project has now 
been addressed and optimum utilization of funds is expected to be achieved. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
5 The Committee recommends establishing Regional Tourism Coordination Councils 
(RTCCs) that bring together clusters of states with similar tourism characteristics for 
quarterly coordination meetings to address regional implementation challenges. These 
councils would facilitate peer learning, regional tourism circuit development, and coordinated 
infrastructure planning while creating a forum for regular interaction between the Ministry 
and state implementation agencies. Additionally, the Ministry should develop Standard 
Operating Procedures (SOPs) for all critical processes including fund requests, utilization 
certificate submission, and project closure documentation, eliminating ambiguities that 
frequently cause delays. Further, the Committee recommends creating a Tourism 
Implementation Support Cell (TISC) in each state tourism department with dedicated 
officials trained specifically in Ministry of Tourism scheme implementation protocols. These 
structural enhancements to state coordination would address the root causes of 
implementation delays while creating sustainable mechanisms for ongoing collaboration. 
(Para 21)

5.1 The observation of the Committee regarding Regional Tourism Coordination 
Councils (RTCCs) is noted.

Transforming the Chalo India Initiative into a Strategic Diaspora Engagement 
Program 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
8 The Committee recommends a significant enhancement of the Chalo India Global 
Diaspora Campaign, transforming it from primarily an incentive program into a strategic 
diaspora engagement framework that systematically cultivates the Indian diaspora as tourism 
ambassadors. The Ministry should implement a tiered Diaspora Tourism Ambassador 
certification program, providing specialized training, promotional materials, and digital 
tools to formally recognized diaspora members who actively promote Indian tourism. 
Furthermore, a sophisticated tracking and attribution system should be developed to measure 
the direct impact of diaspora-generated tourism, enabling performance-based incentives and 
recognition for top-performing ambassadors. The initiative should incorporate regular 
virtual forums connecting diaspora communities with tourism stakeholders in India, creating 
channels for continuous feedback on international visitor experiences and emerging 
preferences. Additionally, the Committee recommends establishing Diaspora Tourism 
Innovation Grants to support creative diaspora-led projects that enhance India's tourism 
appeal in their respective countries. This strategic approach would transform the diaspora 
from passive supporters to active, measurable contributors to India's tourism growth, with 
clearly defined performance indicators ensuring accountability and effectiveness.  
(Para 36.3)

8.1 The recommendations of the Committee are duly noted.

Developing Destination-Specific Transformation Initiatives 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
9 The Committee recommends that beyond the general development of 50 tourist 
destinations announced in the 2025-26 budget, the Ministry should implement a Strategic 
Destination Transformation Program that selects 10 high-potential destinations annually for 
comprehensive development as global tourism excellence centers. Each selected destination 
would receive integrated support including infrastructure enhancement, digital 
transformation, capacity building, and targeted international promotion, creating showcase 
models of world-class tourism management. The program should incorporate Destination 
Experience Laboratories where innovative tourism concepts, technologies, and service 
models can be tested and refined before broader implementation. Furthermore, the 
Committee recommends establishing Destination Management Organizations (DMOs) with 
public-private governance structures for each selected destination, ensuring professional 
management and sustainable growth through dedicated expert oversight. These initiatives 
would transform India's approach to destination development from incremental improvement 
to comprehensive excellence, creating globally competitive tourism products that 
significantly enhance India's tourism appeal and international rankings. 
(Para 38) 
Reply of the Ministry 
9.1 The recommendation of the Committee is noted.

Transforming Hospitality Education through Industry-Integrated Learning 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
13 The Committee emphasizes that traditional curriculum development processes in 
hospitality education have become inadequate for preparing professionals in the rapidly 
evolving tourism landscape where technological proficiency, sustainability expertise, and 
experiential delivery capabilities are increasingly essential. The Committee recommends 
establishing a National Tourism Education Innovation Council comprising industry leaders, 
academic experts, digital technology specialists, and international hospitality education 
partners to fundamentally reimagine hospitality curriculum beyond incremental updates. This 
collaborative body would develop core curriculum frameworks incorporating emerging 
competencies including digital guest experience management, sustainable tourism 
operations, cultural interpretation techniques, and tourism entrepreneurship. Furthermore, 
the Committee recommends implementing a Mandatory Industry Immersion Program 
requiring all hospitality faculty to complete annual industry placements of at least four 
weeks, ensuring instructors maintain current practical knowledge alongside theoretical 
expertise. Additionally, the Ministry should establish a Hospitality Education Digital 
Transformation Initiativethat provides all IHMs and FCIs with integrated learning 
management systems, virtual reality training environments for practical skills development, 
and AI-powered personalized learning pathways that adapt to individual student learning 
patterns. These innovations would transform hospitality education from institution-centered 
to learner-centered while ensuring graduates possess the precise competencies required for 
India's tourism growth. 
(Para 49)

National Council for Hotel Management& Catering Technology (NCHMCT) is to co-
ordinate the growth and general advancement in the development of hospitality management

chairmanship of Senior Economic Advisor (Tourism) to review the curriculum, courses and

pedagogy of tourism and hospitality institutes under the purview of Ministry of Tourism. On

Pioneering Sustainable Funding Models for Tourism Education 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
14 The Committee recognizes that the current allocation of ₹35 crore for FY 2025-26 
represents a significant constraint on the necessary expansion and modernization of 
hospitality education infrastructure. Beyond conventional funding approaches, the 
Committee recommends establishing a Tourism Education Investment Fund through strategic 
partnerships with major tourism industry stakeholders, international development agencies, 
and corporate CSR initiatives. This dedicated fund would provide sustainable financing for 
infrastructure development, technology acquisition, and faculty excellence programs across 
hospitality education institutions. The Committee also recommends developing a Tourism 
Education Revenue Diversification Framework that enables institutes to generate 
supplementary income through establishing commercial training restaurants, student-
operated boutique hotels, specialized consulting services, and executive education programs 
for industry professionals. Furthermore, the Ministry should implement the Destination 
Adoption Program wherein tourism-intensive destinations contribute to hospitality education 
infrastructure in exchange for dedicated workforce development programs tailored to their 
specific requirements. These innovative funding mechanisms would transform hospitality 
education financing from government-dependent to multi-stakeholder supported, 
substantially expanding available resources while creating greater alignment between 
educational institutions and industry needs. 
(Para 50) 
14.1 The recommendations of the Committee are duly noted.

Recommendation/Observation 
1. While the allocation for domestic tourism promotion remains relatively consistent at 
₹136.90 crore for 2025-26, the Committee recommends a more balanced approach that 
strengthens both domestic and international tourism sectors. The Ministry should develop a 
Dual Growth Strategy that identifies complementary objectives for both sectors, with 
domestic tourism focusing on developing emerging destinations and international tourism 
emphasizing unique cultural and experiential offerings. To stimulate domestic tourism 
innovation, the committee recommends allocating ₹50 crore specifically for developing and 
promoting new tourism concepts such as Caravan Tourism across states with appropriate 
infrastructure and regulatory frameworks. This initiative would diversify tourism offerings 
while creating new entrepreneurial opportunities in emerging tourism segments.  
(Para 13) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1 The Ministry of Tourism promotes India in a holistic manner, through various 
initiatives. As part of on-going activities; promotion of various tourism destinations and 
products of India including Caravan Tourism are taken up. 
  
1.2 Development of Tourism is primarily done by the respective State Governments/ UT 
administrations. However, the Ministry of Tourism under its Swadesh Darshan scheme 
complements these efforts by sanctioning projects for development of tourism 
infrastructure.  Based on the recommendation of the State Governments, submission of 
project proposals and adherence of the scheme guidelines etc., the Ministry of Tourism may 
consider sanctioning projects under various themes including Caravan Tourism.  A separate 
allocation for the same may not be required.  
  
1.3 Ministry of Tourism had earlier formulated a policy for development and promotion 
of caravan and caravan camping parks. The States of Maharashtra, Kerala, Goa and UT of 
Andaman & Nicobar Islands have caravan tourism policies. The State of Chhattisgarh has 
included caravan tourism in their tourism policy. 
  

13 
 
1.4 The Ministry is also envisaging the development of curated residences centered 
around thematic products such as wellness, cuisine, wildlife, culture etc. to enhance global 
tourism. 
 
 Recommendation/Observation 
2 The Committee views with grave concern the reduction in allocations and negative 
recoveries recorded under the 'Safe Tourist Destinations for Women' initiative. This 
regression contradicts the fundamental principle of inclusive tourism development and may 
significantly impact women travelers' confidence in Indian destinations. The Committee 
recommends establishing an Inter-Ministerial Women's Tourism Safety Task Force 
comprising representatives from the Ministries of Tourism, Women & Child Development, 
Home Affairs, and state tourism departments to develop comprehensive safety protocols, 
monitoring mechanisms, and emergency response systems specifically designed for women 
tourists. Additionally, the Ministry should allocate funds for implementing technology-driven 
safety measures, including GPS-enabled transportation monitoring, CCTV surveillance at 
tourist hotspots, and a centralized tourism safety application with real-time assistance 
features and emergency response capabilities. 
(Para 14) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1 Security of tourists is essentially a State Government subject. However, the Ministry 
of Tourism has been periodically requesting all State Governments and Union Territories for 
availing the benefits of the ‘Safe Tourism Destinations for Women’ under Nirbhaya fund 
which can be utilized for projects specifically designed to improve the safety and security of 
women tourists. In regards to the proposal submitted by Madhya Pradesh Tourism Board, 
Government of India sanctioned Rs. 16.79 crore (approx.) under the “Safe Tourism 
Destination for Women” Scheme. The final and 3rd installment of Central share of Rs. 5.27 
crore was released by Ministry of Tourism in the financial year 2024-2025.

Introduction 
 I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee  on
 Transport,  Tourism and Culture, having been authorised by the 
 Committee, to present on its behalf this Three Hundred  and  Eighty-Sixth 
 Report on the subject “Holistic Development  of India’s Tourism Sector 
 through  Formal  Skill  Development  University- Level Courses 
 and Professional  Training  for Guides, Hospitality and Eco-Tourism.” 
 
2. The Committee selected this subject in view of the growing strategic importance of 
tourism as a pillar of economic growth, employment generation, cultural preservation, 
and India’s global engagement. Tourism is uniquely positioned as a sector that 
integrates infrastructure, services, heritage, livelihoods, and soft power. The 
Committee notes that while physical infrastructure and destination promotion have 
received sustained policy attention in recent years, the human dimension of tourism 
has not evolved at a commensurate pace. 
 
3. The Committee is of the considered view that the future trajectory of India’s tourism 
sector will be determined not merely by the creation of assets, but by the quality, 
integrity, and professionalism of the human interfaces through which tourists 
experience the country. Guides, hospitality professionals, destination managers, 
cultural interpreters, and facilitators collectively shape visitor perception. Deficiencies 
in training, ethical conduct, and career structures in these roles directly erode trust and 
suppress tourism’s economic potential. 
 
4. Recent policy initiatives announced by the Government, including the creation of a 
National Destination Digital Knowledge Grid and the institutional upgradation of the 
National Council for Hotel Management and Catering Technology into a National 
Institute of Hospitality, represent significant structural interventions. The Committee, 
however, observes that such initiatives can yield sustained outcomes only when 
anchored in a comprehensive framework for formal education, professional 
certification, continuous skill upgradation, and institutional accountability. 
 
5. In the course of examination of the subject, the Committee held multiple oral 
evidence sessions with the Secretary and senior officials from the Ministry of 
Tourism. The Committee also received detailed presentations from academic and 
training institutions, including the National Council for Hotel Management and 
Catering Technology, Indian Institute of Tourism and Travel Management, Indian 
Culinary Institute, Jamia Millia Islamia, State Institute of Hotel Management 
Faridabad, Banarsidas Chandiwala Institute of Hotel Management, Madurai Kamaraj 
University, the Central University of Tamil Nadu, FHRAI,IATO, Hotel Association 
of India (HAI), and ATOAI. The Committee places on record its sincere appreciation 
for the comprehensive presentations and inputs received during the examination of 
this subject. During its sitting on 4 February 2026 with the Secretary, Ministry of 
Tourism, the Committee examined in detail the Ministry’s three‑pillar skill 
development framework, institutional presentations from NCHMCT, IITTM, ICI, 
universities and industry associations, and the alignment of tourism skilling with the 
Union Budget 2026‑27 priorities of employment generation and local economic 
development. 
 

iii 
 
 
6. To examine implementation at the regional and institutional level, the Committee 
undertook a study visit to Chennai on 21 January 2026. During this visit, the 
Committee interacted with officials of the Ministry of Tourism, representatives of the 
Government of Tamil Nadu, and faculty members of Central and State universities. 
These interactions provided valuable insights into decentralised models of tourism 
education, university-community partnerships, and the integration of heritage, 
research, and livelihood development. An oral evidence was again held in New Delhi 
on 4th February, 2026 with the Ministry of Tourism and other industry stakeholders. 
 
7. This Report synthesises evidence received from the ministry of Tourism, institutions, 
industry stakeholders, and academic experts. It places human capital at the centre of 
tourism policy and emphasises the need for standardisation, ethical conduct, digital 
capability, and coordination between the Ministry and other industry stakeholders. 
The Committee expects that the recommendations contained in this Report will 
contribute to professionalising the tourism sector, restoring visitor trust, and 
positioning India as a globally competitive tourism destination. 
 
8. The Committee places on record its appreciation of the assistance rendered by the 
officers of the Rajya Sabha Secretariat and the cooperation extended by the Ministry 
of Tourism, institutions, and stakeholders who contributed to this examination. 
9. The Committee considered and adopted the Report in its meeting held on the 11th 
February, 2026.

iv 
 
Executive Summary 
1. This Report presents a comprehensive assessment of the present state of tourism in 
India, with particular reference to formal skill development, university‑level education 
and professional training frameworks. The Committee notes that the Union Budget 
2026‑27 explicitly identifies tourism as a significant employer and a key driver of 
local economic development, which in turn underscores the need for a structured 
human capital framework rather than a series of project‑centric interventions. 
 
2. The Committee observes that tourism has emerged as one of the most 
employment‑intensive sectors of the Indian economy, with strong multiplier effects 
across agriculture, handicrafts, transport, construction and allied services. The sector 
currently contributes approximately five to six and a half per cent of national GDP 
and sustains nearly twelve to thirteen per cent of total employment. 
 
3. The Committee notes that India’s distinctive cultural, historical, spiritual and natural 
endowments provide a robust foundation for expanding India’s share of global 
tourism. Comparative analysis placed before the Committee, however, shows that 
countries with far fewer attractions record higher international tourist arrivals and 
tourism receipts, indicating that India’s under‑performance is not primarily on account 
of infrastructure gaps or under‑promotion. 
 
4. The Committee’s review points instead to systemic weaknesses in service delivery 
and human engagement as key constraints. Evidence received highlights a persistent 
trust deficit at several tourist destinations, arising from untrained or inadequately 
trained human interfaces, inconsistent service standards and unethical practices such 
as touting, harassment and extortion, which not only deter repeat visits but also create 
negative digital narratives that undermine national tourism branding. 
 
5. The Committee also notes a structural paradox. While tourism is projected to generate 
employment at scale, there is declining student interest in traditional hospitality and 
tourism courses, high vacancy levels in training institutions and significant attrition at 
entry level. Stakeholders attributed this trend to low starting wages, unclear career 
progression, limited professional recognition and the perception of tourism as an 
informal vocation rather than a structured profession. 
 
6. Oral evidence indicated that current formal tourism and hospitality training pipelines 
together reach only tens of thousands of learners annually, whereas the projected 
workforce requirement for a target of 100 million foreign tourists by 2047, along with 
associated domestic growth, is in the range of many millions. The Committee notes 
with concern that only about one per cent of the current tourism workforce is 
estimated to be formally skilled. 
 
7. The Committee therefore regards human capital not as an ancillary input but as the 
defining asset of the tourism economy. The Report accordingly advocates a shift from 
fragmented skilling schemes to a nationally coherent professional framework, centred 
on structured career pathways supported by formal education, mandatory institutional 
attachments, continuous professional development, and periodic certification and 
re‑certification. 
 
8. The Committee places particular emphasis on alignment of tourism education with the 
National Education Policy 2020. Flexibility through multiple entry and exit options, 
credit linkage via the Academic Bank of Credits, and a strong focus on experiential 
learning are viewed as essential to attract diverse learners and reduce drop‑outs, with 

v 
 
Central Universities envisaged as hubs for research and specialised training and State 
Universities and affiliated colleges as spokes for mass skilling and regional delivery. 
 
9. Ethical conduct and trust restoration form a core pillar of the Report. The Committee 
recommends embedding ethical training across all tourism education programmes, 
instituting enforceable licensure regimes, strengthening grievance redress mechanisms 
and linking professional certification to digital reputation and feedback systems, so 
that visitors can rely on transparent, accountable and respectful engagement at 
destinations. 
 
10. Recognising the rapid transformation of global tourism through technology, the 
Committee underlines the need to build digital and creative capabilities within the 
tourism workforce, including competencies in artificial intelligence, immersive 
technologies and digital storytelling, so that India develops the capacity to design, and 
not merely consume, tourism technology and content. The Report also flags emerging 
and under‑served segments such as border tourism, spiritual tourism, medical tourism, 
ecological circuits, cruise tourism and sites of historical trauma, each of which 
requires specialised skills, regulatory oversight and ethical sensitivity; without 
targeted human capital development, infrastructure‑led efforts in these segments risk 
significant under‑performance. The Committee is of the view that the 
outcome‑oriented and implementation‑focused recommendations contained in this 
Report, taken together, can professionalise tourism, strengthen visitor trust, generate 
dignified employment and position India as a global hub for tourism education and 
expertise in alignment with the national vision of Viksit Bharat 2047.

REPORT 
1 Context and Rationale 
1.1 Tourism as an Economic System 
1.1.1 The Committee observes that tourism is not a standalone sector but a complex economic system 
that integrates multiple industries, services, and livelihoods. The tourism economy encompasses direct 
expenditure by visitors on accommodation, food, transport, attractions, and shopping; indirect economic 
activity generated through supply chains serving tourism establishments; induced effects arising from 
expenditure by tourism workers in local economies; and catalytic impacts on infrastructure development, 
entrepreneurship, and regional investment. 
1.1.2 Unlike manufacturing or extractive industries, tourism distributes economic benefits across a 
wide geographic and social spectrum. Expenditure by tourists flows directly into local communities, 
including artisans, farmers, transport operators, guides, and small entrepreneurs. The Committee notes 
that this decentralised multiplier effect makes tourism uniquely suited for inclusive growth, particularly in 
regions with limited industrial alternatives, and aligns with recommendations for high-value spiritual and 
cultural tourism pathways (Recommendation 21) and targeted skilling for underrepresented groups 
(Recommendation 28). 
1.1.3 The Committee further notes that tourism has one of the lowest capital-to-labour ratios among 
major economic sectors. This characteristic enables large-scale employment generation with relatively 
modest capital investment, making tourism particularly relevant for absorbing India’s young workforce 
and addressing regional employment imbalances through knowledge-based roles for humanities graduates 
(Recommendation 23) and national apprenticeship programmes (Recommendation 20). 
1.2 Employment and Demographic Relevance 
1.2.1 Evidence placed before the Committee indicates that the tourism sector currently supports 
approximately twelve to thirteen per cent of total employment in the country. Employment opportunities 
span the full skill spectrum, from entry-level service roles to highly specialised positions in heritage 
interpretation, destination management, digital content creation, and tourism technology, supported by a 
dedicated Knowledge and Interpretation Stream within a National Tourism Professional Cadre 
(Recommendation 5). 
1.2.2 The Committee notes that tourism offers significant opportunities for women, youth, and rural 
populations. Many roles in tourism leverage local knowledge, cultural familiarity, and interpersonal skills 
rather than formal technical training alone. This makes tourism an important pathway for integrating 
traditionally underrepresented groups into the formal economy, as emphasized in recommendations for 
women and inclusion (Recommendation 28) and local community capacity building (Recommendation 
26). 
1.2.3 The Committee also observes that tourism employment has strong linkages with informal and 
micro-enterprise activity. While this flexibility provides livelihood opportunities, it has also resulted in 
fragmented skill development, inconsistent service quality, and limited professional recognition. 
Addressing this imbalance between accessibility and professionalism is central to the Committee’s 
examination, through Recognition of Prior Learning (Recommendation 15) and continuous upskilling 
(Recommendation 29). 

2 
 
1.3 Global Tourism Context and India’s Position 
1.3.1 The Committee notes that global tourism contributes approximately ten per cent of world GDP 
and supports one in ten jobs worldwide. International tourist arrivals have rebounded strongly following 
the pandemic, demonstrating the sector’s resilience and adaptability. 
1.3.2 Despite possessing a civilisational heritage, cultural diversity, and natural endowments 
unmatched by most destinations, India’s share of global tourism remains comparatively modest. 
Countries with far fewer historical and cultural assets attract substantially higher numbers of international 
visitors and generate greater tourism receipts. 
1.3.3 The Committee examined multiple explanations for this gap, including infrastructure, 
connectivity, marketing, and visa facilitation. While acknowledging that challenges remain in these areas, 
the Committee is of the view that the most persistent constraint lies in the quality of on-ground experience 
delivery, which is fundamentally a function of human capability, addressed through redesigning tourism 
curricula (Recommendation 7) and international collaboration (Recommendation 31). 
1.4 The Centrality of Human Interfaces 
1.4.1 The Committee observes that tourism is experienced through people. Guides, hotel staff, transport 
providers, site managers, and facilitators constitute the human interface between the visitor and the 
destination. Even the most iconic monument or pristine landscape can fail to deliver value if mediated 
through untrained, indifferent, or unethical human engagement. 
1.4.2 Evidence presented to the Committee highlighted recurring issues at tourist destinations, 
including misinformation, lack of interpretative depth, inconsistent service standards, and unethical 
practices such as touting and coercive selling. These experiences erode visitor trust and generate 
reputational damage that far exceeds the immediate transaction, mitigated by ethical guardrails 
(Recommendation 13) and linking ethical evaluation to certification (Recommendation 14). 
1.4.3 The Committee notes that digital platforms amplify both positive and negative visitor 
experiences. A single adverse interaction can influence thousands of potential visitors through online 
reviews and social media. Human capital deficiencies therefore have systemic consequences for national 
tourism performance, supported by national digital platforms for guide matching (Recommendation 17). 
1.5 Trust Deficit as a Structural Constraint 
1.5.1 The Committee identifies the trust deficit as one of the most damaging structural constraints 
facing India’s tourism sector. Trust encompasses safety, transparency, professionalism, and respect. 
Tourists gravitate towards destinations where they feel protected and valued, regardless of price or 
distance. 
1.5.2 The Committee observes that trust deficits arise not only from criminal or unethical behaviour but 
also from inadequate training, poor communication skills, and lack of accountability. In many cases, 
individuals operating at tourist sites are neither formally trained nor institutionally supported, leading to 
inconsistent behaviour and outcomes, addressed via destination-level narrative teams (Recommendation 
3). 
1.5.3 The Committee is of the view that restoring trust requires systemic intervention rather than 
isolated enforcement measures. Professionalisation through education, certification, ethical training, and 
institutional oversight is essential for sustainable trust restoration, including a national tourism 
professionals database (Recommendation 16). 

3 
 
1.6 Tourism Education: From Vocation to Profession 
1.6.1 The Committee notes that tourism in India has historically been treated as a vocational activity 
learned informally or on the job. While this approach enabled rapid workforce expansion, it has not kept 
pace with the increasing complexity of tourism as an experience-driven and technology-enabled sector. 
1.6.2 Contemporary tourism requires competencies in history, culture, communication, digital tools, 
sustainability, crisis management, and ethics. These competencies cannot be reliably developed through 
ad-hoc training alone. The Committee therefore emphasises the need to reposition tourism as a formal 
profession grounded in structured education, continuous learning, and research, through curriculum 
redesign (Recommendation 7) and long-duration field residencies (Recommendation 8). 
1.6.3 The Committee also observes that the absence of clear career pathways and professional 
recognition has contributed to declining student interest in tourism and hospitality courses. Elevating 
tourism education within the higher education ecosystem is essential to attract talent and retain skilled 
professionals, via clear career pathways (Recommendation 6) and early education integration 
(Recommendation 33). 
1.7 Rationale for Parliamentary Intervention 
1.7.1 The Committee considers that tourism’s multi-sectoral nature necessitates parliamentary 
oversight and coordinated policy direction. Human capital development in tourism intersects with 
education, culture, skill development, technology, internal security, and external engagement. 
1.7.2 Individual institutional or ministerial measures can deliver local gains, but a joined-up approach 
is required to tackle systemic challenges at scale. A coherent national framework, guided by 
parliamentary recommendations, is required to align institutional roles, standardise outcomes, and ensure 
accountability, through inter-ministerial coordination (Recommendation 10). 
1.7.3 This Report is therefore anchored in the Committee’s mandate to examine policy coherence, 
institutional effectiveness, and long-term national interest. The recommendations that follow seek to 
establish a sustainable human capital architecture for tourism that supports economic growth, social 
inclusion, cultural preservation, and global engagement, avoiding new apex bodies (Recommendation 9) 
and declaring narrative leadership as India’s advantage (Recommendation 25). 
2 The Tourism Workforce Landscape 
2.1 Overview of the Tourism Workforce 
2.1.1 The Committee observes that the tourism workforce in India is diverse, decentralised, and 
heterogeneous in nature. It spans multiple sub-sectors, including hospitality, travel and transport services, 
heritage and cultural interpretation, destination management, adventure and eco-tourism, spiritual 
tourism, medical tourism, and emerging digital tourism services. This diversity reflects the breadth of 
India’s tourism assets but also poses challenges for standardisation, quality assurance, and professional 
recognition. 
2.1.2 The tourism workforce comprises both organised and unorganised segments. While a portion of
