1.4 Growth of the Civil Aviation Sector 
1.4.1 The Ministry submitted that India's civil aviation sector has been on a robust growth trajectory. 
The cumulative airport capacity has risen from 525 MPPA in 2023 -24 to 534 MPPA in 2024 -25 and 
574 MPPA in the first three quarters of 2025 -26. The  scheduled airline fleet has grown from 716 
aircraft to approximately 860 aircraft over the past five years, with an average fleet age of 7.3 years 
compared to the global average of 14.8 years. Indian airlines have placed orders for over 1,600 new 
aircraft to cater to projected demand growth. The number of operational airports has expanded from 
74 in 2014 to approximately 163 by 2025-26, with a long-term target of 350-400 airports by 2047. 
1.4.2 The Committee noted the sectoral growth trajectory and observed that the expansion of the fleet 
and the order book of over 1,600 new aircraft will place substantial additional demands on the 
regulatory, safety and infrastructure capacity of the sector. The Committee observed that the 
alignment between the pace of fle et growth and the pace of regulatory capacity -building merits 
careful monitoring, particularly given the safety events documented during 2025-26. 
1.5 AAI Revenue Buoyancy and Budgetary Paradox 
1.5.1 The Committee observed a striking paradox in the Ministry 's financial architecture. While AAI 
reported revenue of Rs. 20,648.25 crore and profit of Rs. 7,233.28 crore in FY 2024 -25, and Airport 
Lease Revenue surged thirty -six-fold from Rs. 87.25 crore (FY 2020 -21) to Rs. 3,192.75 crore (FY

2024-25), the Ministry's own Demand (No. 8) declined from Rs. 3,113.36 crore (BE 2023 -24) to Rs. 
2,102.87 crore (BE 2026-27), a reduction of 32.5 per cent over three years. The Committee notes that 
this creates a structural disconnect: the entity generating the bulk of sectoral  revenue (AAI) operates 
outside parliamentary budgetary oversight, while the entity exercising budgetary authority (the 
Ministry) administers an increasingly constrained and legacy -dominated Demand. The Committee is 
of the view that this disconnect warrant s institutional correction through enhanced parliamentary 
visibility of AAI's capital investment programme.

3.1.5 The Committee noted with concern that the absence of a structured exit strategy is compounded

Committee noted that UDAN airports face challeng es with capacity utilisation and questioned the

exceeding Rs. 9,200 crore, requires a formal independent impact asses sment covering cost per 
passenger, route -wise viability metrics, and the proportion of routes that have achieved self -
sustainability upon VGF completion.

FY 2024 -25. However, Alliance Air Aviation Limited (AAL) reported a loss of Rs. 682.94 crore, 
Hotel Corporation of India Limited (HCL) a loss of Rs. 80.40 crore, and AI Airport Services Limited 
(AIASL) saw its profit collapse from Rs. 40.42 crore in FY 2023 -24 to Rs. 2.94 crore in FY 2024 -25. 
The total outstanding Non -Convertible Debentures stood at Rs. 14,985 crore with annual interest 
obligations of approximately Rs. 1,107 crore. 
3.2.3 The Committee noted with interest that the allocation for AIAHL has been progressively 
declining from BE Rs. 1,144.49 crore in 2023 -24 to BE Rs . 757.39 crore in 2026 -27. The Ministry 
informed that this reduction is attributable to receipts from monetisation and rental proceeds and 
interest income earned from fixed deposits. The Committee observed that the disinvestment of the 
three subsidiaries r emains at a preliminary stage, with Inter -Ministerial Group and Core Group of 
Secretaries meetings still being held. The continuing management of these subsidiaries under AIAHL 
entails ongoing fiscal obligations on the Consolidated Fund of India. 

8 
 
3.3 Maintenance, Repair and Overhaul (MRO) 
3.3.1 The Ministry informed that the MRO sector in India has grown to 166 facilities. India's share of 
the global MRO market is estimated at approximately 1.5 per cent against a domestic fleet share 
exceeding 3 per cent. O nly approximately 14 per cent of total MRO expenditure by Indian carriers 
was handled domestically in the most recent reporting period, with the remaining 86 per cent flowing 
to overseas facilities, primarily in Singapore, Dubai, Sri Lanka and the EU. The MoCA MRO 
Committee found that 'prevailing royalty rates of 14-20 per cent have no basis' and recommended that 
AERA study and recommend a rationalised mechanism. DGCA -EASA engagement on a bilateral 
aviation safety agreement (BASA) has included two technical  meetings in 2025 with a phased 
roadmap. 
3.3.2 The Committee noted that the Union Budget 2026 -27 has extended customs duty exemption on 
aircraft components and MRO tools, and that a uniform 5 per cent IGST now applies to imports of 
parts, components, testing equipment, tools, and toolkits for aircraft. Crisil Ratings projects domestic 
MRO revenue to exceed Rs. 4,500 crore in FY 2026, a 50 per cent growth over FY 2024, driven by 
rising fleet size and the GST rationalisation. However, the Committee observed t hat the 86 per cent 
outflow of MRO work to overseas facilities represents an annual foreign exchange drain of several 
thousand crore that could be progressively retained domestically through the completion of BASA 
negotiations and the operationalisation of new heavy-maintenance facilities. 
3.3.3 The Committee noted with satisfaction that the DGCA signed a new Working Arrangement with 
the FAA on 5 March 2026 under the India -US Bilateral Aviation Safety Agreement framework, 
establishing a structured mechanism for coordination on aircraft and engine certification activities and 
introducing greater clarity in validation procedures. The arrangement brings Boeing, GE Aerospace, 
and Pratt & Whitney into a coordinated regulatory framework. The Committee observed tha t while 
this is a significant step, a comprehensive BASA with the European Union, particularly covering 
mutual recognition of MRO certifications, remains the missing link that may be filled in the sector's 
regulatory architecture. 
3.3.4 The Committee furth er notes that the Civil Aviation Minister has articulated an ambition of 
capturing 50 per cent of the domestic MRO market by 2030. This is at variance with the current 
domestic retention of only 14 per cent. The Committee observed that bridging this gap re quires not 
merely tax incentives but concurrent action on hangar infrastructure, skilled workforce development, 
engine overhaul capabilities, and the completion of the EU BASA. 
3.4 Drone Sector and PLI Scheme 
3.4.1 The Ministry submitted that the drone eco system has grown to 38,039 registered drones, 234 
Remote Pilot Training Organisations, and 146 type -certified models. The PLI scheme for drones 
showed actual disbursement of Rs. 37.10 crore against BE of Rs. 57.00 crore in FY 2024 -25, with no 
explicit allocation visible in the BE 2026-27 documentation. 
3.4.2 The Committee noted from the Ministry's response to its Questionnaire that the UTM 
(Unmanned Traffic Management) roadmap envisages Phase 1 (segregation) continuing until 2030. 
The Committee further note d that GST on unmanned aircraft was reduced from 18 -28 per cent to 5 
per cent under GST 2.0 reforms effective September 2025, which is a welcome policy development. 
However, the Committee observed that the extended UTM Phase 1 timeline may constrain the 
commercial scaling that the PLI scheme was designed to catalyse. 

9 
 
3.5 DGCA and Aviation Safety 
3.5.1 The Ministry submitted that DGCA's revenue allocation has been increased from Rs. 300.00 
crore (BE 2025-26) to Rs. 325.00 crore (BE 2026-27), while capital allocation has been reduced from 
Rs. 30.00 crore to Rs. 17.00 crore. DGCA issued 1,652 Commercial Pilot Licences in calendar year 
2025, the highest in the preceding decade. India's ICAO USOAP Effective Implementation score was 
raised to 85.65 per cent from 69.95 per cent. 
3.5.2 The Committee noted that the reduction in DGCA capital allocation from Rs. 30.00 crore to Rs. 
17.00 crore needs to be reconciled with the Ministry's stated focus on strengthening regulatory 
capacity. The Committee observed that DGCA, a s the primary safety regulator with expanding 
oversight responsibilities, requires sustained capital investment for technological upgradation and 
modernisation of its surveillance equipment. 
3.5.3 The Committee noted from the Ministry's response to its Que stionnaire that DGCA has 843 
incumbents against a sanctioned strength of 1,630, a vacancy rate of 48.3 per cent, with 787 posts 
lying vacant. The Ministry stated that this 'shortfall has not impacted surveillance plans.' The 
Committee observed that this cl aim is difficult to reconcile with the expanding regulated entity 
universe. 
3.5.4 The Committee noted with concern that a DGCA audit of 754 commercial aircraft conducted 
between January 2025 and February 2026 revealed that 377 aircraft, nearly half the fle et reviewed, 
showed recurring technical defects. Out of 166 Air India aircraft inspected, 137 showed repeated 
defects. Air India Express reported 54 of 101 aircraft with persistent technical problems. A 
comprehensive DGCA audit of Air India conducted from 1-4 July 2025, following the Ahmedabad 
crash, flagged approximately 100 safety lapses including seven Level 1 violations requiring urgent 
remediation, recurrent training gaps for Boeing 787 and 777 pilots, insufficient cabin crew on at least 
four internati onal flights, and flight duty time limitation breaches including one Milan -New Delhi 
flight that exceeded the limit by 2 hours and 18 minutes. The Committee observed that these findings, 
combined with the 48.3 per cent vacancy rate, raise fundamental quest ions about whether the 
regulator has the capacity to ensure adequate surveillance of a fleet that is growing faster than 
regulatory resources.

3.6.3 RGNAU: The Rajiv Gandhi National Aviation University's allocation stands at Rs. 30.00 crore.

3.6.4 IGRUA:  The Indira Gandhi Rashtriya Uran Akademi's allocation has been substantially

CHAPTER 4 
Past Demands and Fulfilment 
4.1 Trend in Budget Estimates, Revised Estimates and Actuals 
4.1.1 The Committee examined the three -year financial performance of the Ministry to assess the 
degree of alignment between initial budgetary projections and actual expenditure outcomes. The 
analysis reveals a persistent pattern of significant deviation between  Budget Estimates and Actuals 
across multiple major heads. 
4.2 Revenue Section: Head-wise Analysis 
4.2.1 AIAHL SPV:  In 2023-24, the BE of Rs. 1,144.49 crore was revised sharply downward to Rs.

January 2026 was Rs. 280.00 crore against RE of Rs. 945.51 crore. The Committee observed that the

4.2.2 Customs Cost Recovery Charges:  In 2024-25, the BE was nil but Actuals were Rs. 124.17 
crore. In 2025 -26, the BE of Rs. 142.75 crore was drastically reduced to Rs. 1.17 crore at RE stage, 
with nil actual expenditure up to January 2026. For 2026-27, the BE is Rs. 47.39 crore. This extreme

4.2.3 Regional Connectivity Scheme:  In 2023-24, the BE was Rs. 1,244.07 crore, RE Rs. 850.00 
crore and Actuals Rs. 822.22 crore. In 2024 -25, the BE was Rs. 502.00 crore, RE was Rs. 800.00 
crore and Actuals were Rs. 789.32 crore. In 2025 -26, expenditure up to January 2026 was only Rs.

4.2.4 Tax Matters of Erstwhile AI:  In 2024-25, the BE was nil but expenditure of R s. 159.00 crore 
was incurred at Actuals stage, primarily on account of Vivad se Vishwas scheme settlements. In 2025-
26, BE of Rs. 80.00 crore was reduced to nil at RE stage. For 2026 -27, a token provision of Rs. 1.00

4.3 Capital Section: Head-wise Analysis 
4.3.1 The Capital Section performance reveals persistent under -utilisation at the organisational level. 
BCAS capital expenditure in 2025 -26 was Rs. 2.68 crore against BE of Rs. 15.00 crore (17.9 per 
cent). The combined capital allocat ion for the Ministry (Secretariat + AAIB) was reduced from Rs. 
25.00 crore (BE) to Rs. 3.00 crore (RE), with actuals of only Rs. 2.04 crore. For 2026 -27, the 
combined allocation has been further reduced to Rs. 5.00 crore. The Committee noted that the reasons 
cited, including non-finalisation of building proposals, pending ICT procurement orders, and delayed 
receipt of construction bills from AAI, are recurrent across multiple financial years and organisations. 
4.3.2 Despite this empirical evidence of persistent and material variances, the Committee noted that in 
response to its Questionnaire, the Ministry stated categorically that 'there is no underutilization or 
overspending noticed in the previous budgets.' The Com mittee find this self -assessment to be at 
variance with the financial data placed before them and the Committee urge the Ministry to strengthen 
its internal expenditure monitoring framework.

CHAPTER 5 
Cross-cutting Thematic Scrutiny 
5.1 Test I: Budget Realism 
5.1.1 The Committee applied a test of budget realism by examining the ratio of Actuals to Budget 
Estimates across major heads. The AIAHL SPV head showed Actuals at 56.8 per cent of BE in 2023 -
24 and 70.6 per cent in 2024 -25. The Customs head swung fr om nil (BE) to Rs. 124.17 crore 
(Actuals) within 2024-25. The Committee observed that such divergent patterns indicate that Budget 
Estimates for several heads are not being formulated on the basis of realistic assessments of 
implementation capacity and likely expenditure trajectories. 
5.2 Test II: Regional Equity 
5.2.1 The Committee examined the regional distribution of budgetary allocations and noted that Rs. 
130.00 crore  of the RCS allocation is specifically earmarked for the North Eastern Region. The 
OOMF targets 16 routes to be operationalised in NER with a target of 1 lakh passengers and 4 new 
airports/heliports to be connected. 
5.2.2 The Committee scrutinized the regi onal distribution of AAI's major infrastructure works and 
observed a significant regional imbalance. Of 23 major ongoing projects with a combined award cost 
exceeding Rs. 10,932 crore, only 1 project is in the North Eastern Region, the Imphal International  
Airport terminal (Rs. 421.57 crore), representing 3.9 per cent. The Northern Region accounts for 7 
ongoing projects, the Southern Region 7, the Western Region 5, and the Eastern Region 3. No 
ongoing project exists in Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Manipur ( beyond Imphal), Mizoram, 
Meghalaya, Sikkim or Tripura. 
5.2.3 The Committee further notes that the NER, comprising eight states with a combined population 
exceeding 46 million, has only one major ongoing AAI project. This 3.9 per cent share is grossly 
disproportionate to the region's needs. Proposals for advanced landing grounds in Arunachal Pradesh 
(Dharam, Daporjah, Anini, Kalinka) have been submitted but not approved, Gulbarga Airport in 
Karnataka ceased operations despite significant potential, and Bihar 's first greenfield airport took 16 
years to receive site clearance in principle. The Committee observed that the absence of any ongoing 
project in seven of the eight NER states represents significant scope for enhancement of regional 
equity, warranting urgent and focused attention. 
5.2.4 The bulk of AAI's ongoing capital investment continues to flow to airports in the Northern, 
Southern and Western regions. Completed projects also reflected concentration in states with 
established aviation demand, such as Tamil Nadu (5 projects, Rs. 3,352 crore) and Gujarat (4 projects, 
Rs. 1,657 crore), while the completed NER projects totalled 3 (Rs. 1,372 crore). 
5.3 Test III: Efficiency-Outcome Linkage 
5.3.1 The Committee examined the OOMF for 2026 -27 and noted that the  targets are stated to be 
provisional and subject to change upon approval of the Modified scheme. The Committee further 
notes that the OOMF does not include specific outcome indicators for several of the Ministry's stated 
policy priorities, including DigiY atra adoption targets, drone sector scaling metrics, MRO domestic 
value retention, or BASA negotiation milestones. The absence of quantifiable outcome indicators for 
these areas limits the scope for systematic performance evaluation. 

12 
 
5.4 Test IV: Institutional Governance 
5.4.1 The Committee examined the institutional governance framework and noted that the AAI, as the 
principal infrastructure agency, operates through I&EBR of Rs. 4,699.92 crore which is more than 
double the size of Demand No. 8. AA I reported revenue of Rs. 20,648.25 crore and profit of Rs. 
7,233.28 crore in FY 2024 -25. Airport Lease Revenue grew from Rs. 87.25 crore in FY 2020 -21 to 
Rs. 3,192.75 crore in FY 2024 -25. The Committee observed that AAI's I&EBR does not receive the 
same l evel of parliamentary scrutiny as the Demands for Grants, creating a visibility gap in the 
oversight of public aviation infrastructure investment. 
5.5 Test V: Market Concentration and Airline Sustainability 
5.5.1 The Committee notes that the domestic aviat ion market is characterised by significant 
concentration, with the largest carrier commanding over 54 per cent of scheduled seats. India's 
aviation history includes a troubling pattern of airline failures, raising questions about systemic 
factors that prev ent airline sustainability. The Committee raised this concern during oral evidence, 
emphasising that the Ministry should act as a facilitator rather than a barrier to aviation growth. 
5.5.2 The Committee further noted that dynamic pricing of air tickets wa s a specific concern raised 
during oral evidence, with instances of fares fluctuating dramatically for the same flight, route and 
timing. The Ministry informed that while fares are deregulated, caps were imposed following 
operational disruptions. The Committee observed that AERA's Tariff Monitoring Unit covers only 27 
per cent of domestic traffic, and that the ad-hoc imposition of fare caps during crises is not a substitute 
for a systematic tariff monitoring and consumer protection framework. 
 
  

13 
 
CHAPTER 5A 
Aviation Safety — A Systemic Assessment 
5A.1 The Committee has examined the state of aviation safety with particular attention in this Report, 
given the gravity of events during the period under review. The Ahmedabad crash of 12 June 2025, in 
which Air In dia Flight AI171, a Boeing 787 -8 Dreamliner, crashed shortly after take -off killing 260 
persons and leaving one survivor, represents the deadliest aviation disaster in India in recent decades. 
The preliminary investigation by AAIB revealed that both engine s abruptly stopped receiving fuel 
within seconds of each other shortly after take-off, with cockpit recordings indicating pilot confusion. 
On 12 February 2026, AAIB stated that media reports suggesting the crash probe had been concluded 
were "incorrect and speculative" and that the investigation remains in progress. 
5A.2 The Committee noted that in the six months preceding July 2025, Air India received nine show -
cause notices for safety violations from DGCA. By late 2025, DGCA had issued 19 safety violation  
notices across operators, citing breaches of Flight Duty Time Limitations, lapses in quality assurance, 
unauthorised cockpit access, and aircraft operated with expired emergency equipment. In February 
2026, DGCA imposed a penalty of approximately Rs. 1 cr ore on Air India for operating an Airbus 
A320 on eight commercial flights without a valid Airworthiness Review Certificate on 24 -25 
November 2025. 
5A.3 The Committee further note that DGCA issued a sweeping safety warning to Non -Scheduled 
Operator Permit holders following the Jharkhand air ambulance crash of February 2026, announcing 
measures including mandatory public disclosure of aircraft age and maintenance history, a safety 
ranking system for NSOPs, licence suspensions of up to five years for FDTL viol ations, and personal 
accountability for senior leadership of operators for systemic non -compliance. DGCA also grounded 
four aircraft operated by one NSOP after discovering multiple violations during a special safety audit. 
5A.4 The Committee observed that while these enforcement actions are welcome, they are reactive in 
character. The pattern of repeated safety violations, recurring technical defects in nearly half the 
audited fleet, and multiple crashes within a single year poi nts to structural inadequacies in the 
preventive safety architecture. The Committee are of the considered view that India's aviation safety 
framework requires a fundamental reset that addresses root causes: regulatory staffing, surveillance 
depth, maintenance oversight, pilot training quality, and crew fatigue management. 
5A.5 Pilot-to-Aircraft Ratio and Crew Buffer Capacity.  The Committee notes that India's pilot-to-
aircraft ratio of approximately 14 is below the global benchmark of 18 -20. Globally, airlines maintain 
20-25 per cent spare crew capacity to absorb operational shocks; Indian carriers operate at near -total 
utilisation, allowing minor disruptions to cascade across networks. Between 2020 and 2024, 
approximately 5,700 Commercial Pilot Licences were issued, against a projected requirement of 7,000 
pilots between 2024 and 2026 and 25,000 -30,000 over the next decade. Air lines have resorted to 
hiring foreign pilots, with 236 temporary licences issued in 2025, a costly and unsustainable approach. 
The Committee observed that the pilot shortage is not merely a quantity problem but a systemic 
structural deficit that constrains operational resilience. 
5A.6 Passenger Rights and Complaint Redressal.  The Committee noted that during oral evidence, 
significant concerns were raised about passenger service quality, particularly on Air India 
international flights. The Ministry informed that a 24/7 Air Service helpline (2463 2987) was 
established. The Committee observed that the establishment of a helpline is necessary but not 
sufficient. India lacks a comprehensive statutory passenger rights framework comparable to those in 

14 
 
other major aviation markets. The Committee are of the view that a formal Passenger Rights Charter, 
backed by an enforceable compensation framework, is overdue for a market carrying over 350 million 
passengers annually.

CHAPTER 6 
Observations and Recommendations (Observations 1–53) 
The Committee, having scrutinized the Demands for Grants (2026 -27), the Annual Report (2025-26), 
the Output-Outcome Monitoring Framework, and the Ministry's written replies to its Questionnaire, 
and having taken oral evidence of the representatives of the Ministry of Civil Aviation on 25 February 
2026, place on record the following observations and recommendations. 
6.1 Financial Management and Budgetary Discipline 
6.1.1 Observation 1 — Overall Budgetary Allocation and Structural Fiscal Com position: The 
Committee scrutinized the Detailed Demands for Grants (Demand No. 8) for 2026 -27 and note that 
the total allocation of Rs. 2,102.87 crore is overwhelmingly Revenue in character, with the Capital 
Section constituting a mere Rs. 45.00 crore (approximately 2.1 per cent). Over 62 per cent of the total 
Demand is directed towards AIAHL SPV debt servicing (Rs. 757.39 crore) and the Regional 
Connectivity Scheme (Rs. 550.00 crore), leaving limited fiscal space for capital investment and new 
developmental initiatives from budgetary support. The bulk of airport infrastructure investment is 
financed through AAI's Internal and Extra Budgetary Resources of Rs. 4,699.92 crore, which do not 
form part of this demand, creating a widening gap between the Ministry 's policy ambitions and its 
direct fiscal instruments. The Committee sought clarification during oral evidence as to why large 
National Infrastructure Pipeline figures are not reflected in the Ministry's own budget. 
6.1.2 Recommendation: The Committee reco mmends that the Ministry undertake a comprehensive 
review of the composition of Demand No. 8 with a view to progressively enhancing the share of 
developmental and capital expenditure as the legacy AIAHL liabilities are wound down. The Ministry 
should prepare a medium-term expenditure framework projecting the anticipated trajectory of AIAHL 
obligations over the next five years and the consequent fiscal space that may become available for 
reallocation towards capacity-building and infrastructure. 
6.1.3 Observ ation 2 — Realism of Budget Estimates and Internal Self -Assessment: The 
Committee observes a consistent pattern of significant deviation between Budget Estimates and 
Actuals in several major heads. The AIAHL SPV allocation exhibited BE -to-Actuals gaps of R s. 
494.49 crore in 2023 -24 and Rs. 340.61 crore in 2024 -25. Despite this evidence, the Ministry stated 
categorically that 'there is no underutilization or overspending noticed in the previous budgets.' The 
Committee find this self-assessment to be at varia nce with the financial data and the Committee urge 
the Ministry to strengthen its internal expenditure monitoring framework. 
6.1.4 Recommendation: The Committee recommends that the Ministry revisit its internal assessment 
framework for budget utilisation and institutionalise a structured feedback loop between the outturn of 
the preceding two financial years and the formulation of the succeeding year's Budget Estimates, 
incorporating monetisation receipt projections, pipeline analysis and actual claim -settlement rates 
rather than top-down normative allocations. 
6.1.5 Observation 3 — Temporal Distribution of Expenditure and End -Year Concentration:  
The Committee scrutinized the expenditure data for 2025-26 (up to 31 January 2026) and note that the 
AIAHL SPV head showed expenditure of Rs. 280.00 crore against RE of Rs. 945.51 crore (29.6 per 
cent utilisation) and the RCS showed Rs. 118.60 crore against RE of Rs. 434.50 crore (27.3 per cent). 
Such concentration of expenditure in the closing months may reflect a st ructural inability to plan and 
execute disbursements on a steady-state basis. 

16 
 
6.1.6 Recommendation: The Committee recommends that the Ministry institute a structured monthly 
expenditure plan for each major head aligned with the Modified Cash Management System and 
negotiate quarterly disbursement milestones linked to verifiable output targets, with any s hortfall 
triggering a mandatory internal review by the Financial Adviser. 
6.1.7 Observation 4 — Capital Expenditure Utilisation Patterns:  The Committee scrutinized the 
Capital Section performance and noted that BCAS capital expenditure in 2025 -26 was merely Rs. 
2.68 crore against a BE of Rs. 15.00 crore (17.9 per cent utilisation). The reasons cited, including non-
finalisation of building p roposals and delayed procurement, are recurrent across multiple financial 
years and organisations. 
6.1.8 Recommendation: The Committee recommends that the Ministry institute a centralised capital 
procurement tracking system with defined milestones for each  stage, from administrative approval 
through tendering, award, execution and bill submission, with root -cause analysis of recurring delays 
in specific organisations. 
6.1.9 Observation 5 — AIAHL SPV: Debt Servicing and Subsidiary Financial Performance:  
While AIAHL standalone reported a profit of Rs. 257 crore in FY 2024 -25, the subsidiary picture is 
concerning: AAL reported a loss of Rs. 682.94 crore, HCL a loss of Rs. 80.40 crore, and AIASL saw 
its profit collapse from Rs. 40.42 crore to Rs. 2.94 crore. Outstanding NCDs stood at Rs. 14,985 crore 
with annual interest of approximately Rs. 1,107 crore. 
6.1.10 Recommendation:  The Committee recommends that the Ministry prepare a formal exit 
strategy for AIAHL incorporating year -wise debt servicing projections, pr epayment and restructuring 
options, and a consolidated financial picture encompassing all subsidiaries. The continuing losses of 
AAL and HCL and the collapsing profitability of AIASL warrant accelerated disinvestment or 
alternative strategic restructuring. 
6.1.11 Observation 6 — Customs Cost Recovery Charges: Allocation Volatility:  The Committee 
note the extreme volatility in this head: nil (BE 2024 -25) to Rs. 124.17 crore (Actuals 2024 -25), 
followed by Rs. 142.75 crore (BE 2025-26) to Rs. 1.17 crore (RE) to nil (Actuals up to January 2026), 
and Rs. 47.39 crore (BE 2026-27). A budgetary head that swings between nil and Rs. 142 crore within 
successive years cannot be considered to be budgeted on any rational basis. 
6.1.12 Recommendation: The Committee recommends that the Ministry undertake a comprehensive 
review of the Customs Cost Recovery Charges scheme, including establishment of a formal MoU 
with CBIC clearly delineating cost -sharing, escalation norms and billing procedures, and assess 
whether an alternative funding mechanism would provide greater stability. 
6.1.13 Observation 7 — Medical Benefits to Retired Air India Employees:  Expenditure was Rs. 
103.00 crore in 2024 -25 against RE of Rs. 85.00 crore, indicating a 21 per cent overrun. 
Approximately 45,000 active CGHS cards are maintained. The budgetary projections do not appear to 
be informed by an actuarial assessment. 
6.1.14 Recommendation:  The Committee recommends that the Ministry commission an actuarial 
assessment of the long -term medical benefit oblig ations and explore whether a transition to an 
insurance-linked arrangement or a defined -contribution healthcare trust, funded from AIAHL 
monetisation proceeds, would provide more sustainable financing. 
6.1.15 Observation 8 — Disinvestment of AIAHL Subsidia ries: The disinvestment of AIASL, 
AIESL and AAAL remains at a preliminary stage. Meanwhile, AIASL's profit declined precipitously 
from Rs. 40.42 crore to Rs. 2.94 crore, raising questions about the trajectory of the asset's value. 

17 
 
6.1.16 Recommendation: The Committee recommends that the Ministry accelerate the disinvestment 
process with a firm roadmap with defined milestones, engage proactively with DIPAM, and assess 
whether the declining financial trajectory of AIASL warrants consideration of asset -level 
monetisation as an alternative. The fiscal impact of continued holding should be explicitly quantified 
in future Demand documentation. 
6.2 Project Implementation and Connectivity 
6.2.1 Observation 9 — RCS-UDAN: Absence of Structured Exit Framework:  The Mini stry 
acknowledged 'no structured exit strategy' for VGF -completed routes. The Committee observed that 
this is inadequate for a scheme that has operationalised 657 routes with cumulative expenditure 
exceeding Rs. 9,200 crore since inception. 
6.2.2 Recommend ation: The Committee recommends that the Ministry develop a formal exit 
framework including route -wise viability assessments, a graduated VGF taper mechanism, and 
categorisation of all 657 routes into self -sustaining, VGF -dependent, and candidates for 
discontinuation. 
6.2.3 Observation 10 — UDAN 5 Series: Cumulative Implementation Backlog:  The cumulative 
uncommenced backlog exceeds 150 routes across UDAN 5 series rounds, suggesting systemic 
constraints in infrastructure readiness, operator capacity, or route-level viability. 
6.2.4 Recommendation:  The Committee recommends that the Ministry undertake a systematic 
review of the uncommenced route backlog, introduce a sunset clause on uncommenced route awards, 
and calibrate Modified UDAN targets to demonstrate ab sorption capacity rather than aspirational 
benchmarks. 
6.2.5 Observation 11 — Modified UDAN Scheme: Approval Status: The Modified UDAN scheme 
is 'presently under approval stage, yet to be implemented,' and the OOMF targets are accordingly 
provisional. The financial year 2026-27 is already underway. 
6.2.6 Recommendation: The Committee recommends that the Ministry expedite the approval of the 
Modified UDAN scheme and develop an interim implementation framework for preparatory activities 
that can proceed in advance of formal scheme approval. 
6.2.7 Observation 12 — Airport Infrastructure: Project Timelines:  Several projects have 
experienced significant timeline extensions, including Patna (commenced October 2018, PDC May 
2026) and Dholera (commenced July 2022, PDC June 2026). The Committee raised specific concerns 
during oral evidence about delays at Noida (Jewar) Airport. 
6.2.8 Recommendation: The Committee recommends that the Ministry institute a formalised project 
monitoring dashboard modelled on the PRAGATI p latform, incorporating timeline reconciliation 
showing original, revised and current expected completion dates, with clear escalation protocols for 
overruns exceeding 10 per cent. 
6.2.9 Observation 13 — AAI Capital Investment: Parliamentary Visibility:  AAI's I&EBR of Rs. 
4,699.92 crore is more than double the entire Demand No. 8. AAI reported revenue of Rs. 20,648.25 
crore and profit of Rs. 7,233.28 crore. The I&EBR does not receive the same level of detailed 
parliamentary scrutiny. 
6.2.10 Recommendation:  The Committee recommends that the Ministry include a comprehensive 
annexure on AAI's I&EBR in future DfG documentation, including project -wise allocations, 

18 
 
expenditure, and outcome indicators, and prepare a consolidated public investment statement covering 
budgetary support, AAI I&EBR, and PPP investment. 
6.2.11 Observation 14 — Fire Safety at RCS Airports:  Fire safety at UDAN airports is 'provided 
by concerned State Government,' creating a safety dependency on resource -constrained State 
Governments. 
6.2.12 Recommendation: The Committee recommends that the Ministry review the fire safety 
framework for RCS airports, consider establishing a co -financing mechanism for ARFF upgradation, 
and direct DGCA to conduct a comprehensive safety audit of all operational RCS airports. 
6.2.13 Observation 15 — Pawan Hans Limited:  Pawan Hans reported a loss of Rs. 16.01 crore in 
FY 2024-25 following a loss of Rs. 16.15 crore in the preceding year. Revenue declined from Rs. 
443.25 crore to Rs. 381.55 crore. The attempted disinvestment was abandoned. 
6.2.14 Recommendation: The Committee recommends that the Ministry articulate a clear strategic 
direction for Pawan Hans, whether restructuring, re -attempting disinvestment, or repositioning as a 
strategic helicopter operator for NER and island connectivity. 
6.3 Aviation Safety and Regulatory Capacity 
6.3.1 Observation 16 — DGCA Staffing: DGCA has 843 incumbents against 1,630 sanctioned, a 
vacancy rate of 48.3 per cent. The Ministry's claim that this 'shortfall has not impacted surveill ance 
plans' is contradicted by the DGCA audit of 754 aircraft finding recurring defects in 377 (50 per cent), 
the issuance of 19 safety violation notices by late 2025, and the pattern of safety events documented 
in Chapter 5A. The Committee are of the cons idered view that the 48.3 per cent vacancy rate 
constitutes a clear and present risk to aviation safety and not merely an administrative shortfall. 
6.3.2 Recommendation: The Committee recommends that the Ministry treat DGCA vacancies as an 
urgent priority, fast-track the 165 UPSC-recommended candidates, explore lateral hiring for emerging 
domains, commission a staffing adequacy study benchmarked against FAA, EASA and CASA 
inspector-to-regulated-entity ratios, and ensure that the capital reduction from Rs. 3 0.00 crore to Rs. 
17.00 crore does not compound the staffing deficit by constraining technological modernisation. 
6.3.3 Observation 17 — BCAS Staffing and NCASA:  BCAS has 417 incumbents against 598 
sanctioned (30.3 per cent vacancy), while simultaneously p roposing a National Civil Aviation 
Security Academy. The Committee observed this is incongruous. 
6.3.4 Recommendation: The Committee recommends that the Ministry prioritise filling 181 vacant 
BCAS posts before or concurrently with pursuing the NCASA propos al, and develop a phased 
roadmap contingent on staffing milestones. 
6.3.5 Observation 18 — ICAO Safety Scores:  India's overall score is 85.65 per cent, but 
Aerodromes (AGA) is 62.16 per cent and Accident Investigation (AIG) is 49.02 per cent, both below 
the ICAO GASP target of 75 per cent. The AIG score of 49.02 per cent is particularly concerning in 
light of the Ahmedabad crash, the investigation into which remains pending. 
6.3.6 Recommendation: The Committee recommends that the Ministry develop targeted c orrective 
action plans for AGA and AIG areas with dedicated budgetary resources, set a national target of 90 
per cent overall EI score with area -wise sub -targets, and ensure that AAIB is provided with ring -
fenced capital funding independent of the Ministry's main capital head. 

19 
 
6.3.7 Observation 19 — AAIB Budget:  The combined Ministry (Secretariat + AAIB) capital 
allocation was slashed from Rs. 25.00 crore to Rs. 5.00 crore while the AIG score is 49.02 per cent. 
This constitutes a policy contradiction. 
6.3.8 Recommendation: The Committee recommends that the Ministry reconcile this reduction with 
the imperative of improving the AIG score, develop a cost infrastructure and capability roadmap for 
AAIB, and assess whether the Bureau's institutional structure and independence are adequate for the 
third-largest domestic aviation market. 
6.3.9 Observation 20 — Safety Oversight: Regulatory Depth:  The Committee raised concerns 
during oral evidence about the depth of DGCA's oversight. With 787 of 1,630 posts vacant, the 
capacity to execute the Annual Surveillance Plan at the designed frequency is a legitimate concern. 
6.3.10 Recommendation: The Committee recommends that the Ministry commission an independent 
benchmarking study of DGCA's surveillance capacity against FAA, EASA and CASA, and 
institutionalise annual publication of surveillance outcomes, including inspections conducted, findings 
issued, enforcement actions taken, and operator compliance trends. 
6.3.11 Observation 21 — Pilot Training:  Record issuance of 1,652 CPLs in 2025, but the order 
book of 1,600 new aircraft implies a requirement of 30,000 to 40,000 additional flight crew over the 
next decade. India's pilot -to-aircraft ratio of approximately 14 is below the global benchmark of 18 -
20. The cost of pilot training at Rs. 35 -50 lakh makes the profession inaccessible to most Indian 
families. 
6.3.12 Recommendation:  The Committee recommends th at the Ministry prepare a comprehensive 
demand-supply projection for commercial pilots over the next ten years, address the affordability 
dimension through interest -subvention schemes and public -sector FTO expansion, and evaluate the 
quality dimension including pass rates, employability profiles and the FTO ranking framework. 
6.3.13 Observation 22 — Commission of Railway Safety Workload:  The CRS allocation is Rs. 
25.00 crore. The metro rail pipeline will place substantially greater demands on inspection and  
certification capacity. 
6.3.14 Recommendation: The Committee recommends an independent assessment of CRS staffing, 
technical capabilities and budgetary allocation relative to its expanding metro inspection workload, 
and assessment of whether its administr ative placement under MoCA continues to serve optimal 
governance. 
6.4 Sector Reforms, Regulatory Matters and Institutional Strengthening 
6.4.1 Observation 23 — MRO: Royalty and BASA:  The Committee noted with satisfaction the 
DGCA-FAA Working Arrangement si gned on 5 March 2026 and observed that a similar structured 
engagement should be pursued with EASA on a priority basis. Only 14 per cent of Indian carriers' 
MRO expenditure is handled domestically. 
6.4.2 Recommendation:  The Committee recommends that AERA c omplete the royalty 
rationalisation exercise expeditiously, the Ministry accord highest priority to the EU BASA 
negotiation, and the Ministry set a measurable target of raising domestic MRO value retention from 
14 per cent to at least 25 per cent by 2028 a nd 50 per cent by 2031, with annual progress reporting to 
Parliament. 
6.4.3 Observation 24 — GIFT-IFSC Aircraft Leasing: 38 entities registered, 370 assets leased. The 
PIAO Act 2025 improved the CTC Compliance Index. However, structural challenges remain 

20 
 
including tax litigation uncertainty, underdeveloped treaty network, BEPS Pillar 2 complications for 
large lessors, and unresolved dividend tax. 
6.4.4 Recommendation: The Committee recommends a comprehensive competitive benchmarking of 
GIFT-IFSC against Dublin and Singapore across tax efficiency, legal certainty, turnaround time, and 
financing ecosystem depth, with identific ation of remaining friction points and quantification of 
incremental impact. 
6.4.5 Observation 25 — Drone PLI: PLI disbursement was Rs. 37.10 crore against BE Rs. 57.00 
crore in FY 2024 -25, with no explicit 2026 -27 allocation visible. GST reduction to 5 pe r cent is 
welcome. UTM Phase 1 timeline extends to 2030. 
6.4.6 Recommendation:  The Committee recommends that the Ministry clarify the PLI status and 
budgetary provision for 2026 -27, conduct a comprehensive impact assessment, and articulate a 
successor incentive framework. 
6.4.7 Observation 26 — Aviation Manufacturing: The Embraer-Adani MoU, HAL-UAC MoU, and 
H-125 assembly have been announced. The Committee questioned during oral evidence whether these 
represent genuine manufacturing or merely assembly. 
6.4.8 Recommendation:  The Committee recommends a consolidated monitoring framework 
distinguishing between announcement, MoU, regulatory approvals, construction, production 
commencement and delivery stages, with explicit differentiation of assembly from integra ted 
manufacturing and measurable targets for domestic value addition. 
6.4.9 Observation 27 — ATF Tax:  ATF constitutes 35 -40 per cent of airline operating costs and 
remains excluded from GST, resulting in cascading tax incidence that inflates airfares and c onstrains 
route viability. 
6.4.10 Recommendation: The Committee recommends that the Ministry intensify engagement with 
remaining States that have not reduced VAT on ATF and advocate before the GST Council for 
inclusion of ATF under GST with full input tax credit, supported by a comprehensive impact analysis. 
6.4.11 Observation 28 — AERA TMU Coverage:  The Tariff Monitoring Unit monitors only 78 
routes covering approximately 27 per cent of domestic traffic. 
6.4.12 Recommendation:  The Committee recommends urge nt expansion of TMU coverage to a 
substantially higher proportion of domestic traffic, with exploration of whether AERA's mandate 
requires updating to encompass service quality monitoring, ground handling standards, and airfare 
trend analysis. 
6.4.13 Observation 29 — IGRUA, RGNAU and Human Capital:  The combined allocation is Rs. 
34.92 crore. No comprehensive integrated human capital strategy exists mapping demand across all 
aviation disciplines. 
6.4.14 Recommendation:  The Committee recommends a comprehensiv e integrated human capital 
strategy for the aviation sector mapping projected demand across all disciplines over the next decade 
and aligning training institution output against this projection. 
6.5 Technology, Digital Governance and Cross-cutting Concerns 
6.5.1 Observation 30 — DigiYatra: Implemented at 30 airports with over 8.6 crore uses. However, 
outcome metrics on average processing time reduction have not been placed before the Committee. 

21 
 
6.5.2 Recommendation:  The Committee recommends a robust outcome  measurement framework 
tracking average reduction in passenger processing time, an independent data privacy and security 
assessment, and a phased rollout plan for all airports handling more than 5 lakh passengers annually. 
6.5.3 Observation 31 — eGCA Platform: 298 DGCA services digitized. The O&M phase extends 
until August 2026, creating a continuity risk. 
6.5.4 Recommendation: The Committee recommends that the Ministry ensure long -term continuity 
of the eGCA platform beyond August 2026, covering maintenanc e, security upgradation, AI -assisted 
compliance monitoring, and integration with the Digital Sky platform. 
6.5.5 Observation 32 — Advanced Air Mobility and SAF: DGCA has released eVTOL regulations. 
SAF blending targets are 1 per cent by 2027, 2 per cent by  2028, and 5 per cent by 2030. IOCL has 
obtained ISCC CORSIA certification. 
6.5.6 Recommendation:  The Committee recommends a comprehensive AAM Roadmap with 
identification of 2-3 pilot cities, and a detailed SAF production and pricing roadmap with engagement 
with the Ministry of Petroleum to align production targets with refinery upgradation plans. 
6.5.7 Observation 33 — Air Cargo: Volume grew from 2.53 MMT (FY 2014-15) to 3.72 MMT (FY 
2024-25) with operations at 74 airports. The Customs Cost Recovery scheme volatility documented in 
Observation 6 undermines cargo facilitation. 
6.5.8 Recommendation: The Committee recommends an updated Air Cargo Development Strategy 
integrating Greenfield airport cargo potential, fast -track clearance benchmarked against interna tional 
standards, and assessment of dedicated air freight corridors as PPP initiatives. 
6.5.9 Observation 34 — Cybersecurity: The ongoing digital transformation creates an expanded 
attack surface. No comprehensive sectoral cybersecurity framework has been placed before the 
Committee. 
6.5.10 Recommendation:  The Committee recommends a comprehensive sectoral cybersecurity  
framework covering audit frequency, CERT -In and NCIIPC coordination, incident response 
procedures, and assessment of whether a dedicated aviation cybersecurity cell within DGCA is 
warranted. 
6.5.11 Observation 35 — ATM Modernisation and ATCO Staffing: ATM modernisation roadmap 
for systems replacement during 2026 -2029. 1,636 ATCO posts created between 2022 and 2024. 
Fatigue Management Policy operationalised. 
6.5.12 Recommendation: The Committee recommends a staffing adequacy assessment for ATCOs 
benchmarked against projected air traffic growth, assessment of whether the current Watch Duty 
Time Limitation -based approach is sufficient or whether a scientifically designed Fatigue Risk 
Management System is warranted, and adequate funding and sequencing for ATM modernisation. 
6.6 Comprehensive Safety Reform, Crew Capacity and Passenger Protection 
6.6.1 Observation 36 — Comprehensive Aviation Safety Reset 
The Committee observes that the pattern of the Ahmedabad  crash (260 fatalities), the Jharkhand air 
ambulance crash (7 fatalities), the Baramati chartered plane crash, the DGCA audit finding recurring 
defects in 377 of 754 aircraft, approximately 100 safety lapses flagged in a single Air India audit, 19 
safety violation notices by late 2025, and a penalty for operating flights without a valid Airworthiness 

22 
 
Review Certificate, taken together, indicate systemic rather than episodic failures in the aviation 
safety architecture. 
6.6.2 Recommendation:  The Committee re commends that the Ministry constitute an independent 
High-Level Committee on Aviation Safety, comprising domain experts from DGCA, AAIB, airline 
operators, international safety bodies, and independent technical experts, to conduct a root -cause 
analysis of the systemic safety failures observed during 2025 -26. The Committee should submit its 
findings within 90 days, with particular attention to maintenance oversight, pilot training quality, crew 
fatigue management, and the regulatory capacity of DGCA to perfo rm surveillance at the frequency 
and depth required by the current size of the regulated entity universe. 
6.6.2.1 The Committee further recommends that the Ministry institute a real -time, integrated safety 
monitoring system across DGCA, airlines and mainte nance agencies, with regular public disclosures 
of key safety indicators to prevent risks arising from delayed and fragmented oversight. 
6.6.3 Observation 37 — Pilot-to-Aircraft Ratio and Crew Buffer Norms 
The Committee observed that India's pilot -to-aircraft ratio of approximately 14 is below the global 
benchmark of 18 -20, and that Indian carriers operate at near -total crew utilisation without the 20 -25 
per cent spare capacity maintained globally, allowing minor disruptions to cascade across networks. 
6.6.4 Recommendation: The Committee recommends that the Ministry, in consultation with DGCA, 
establish mandatory minimum pilot-to-aircraft ratios and crew buffer capacity norms for all scheduled 
operators, benchmarked against international standards, with quar terly compliance reporting and 
enforcement action for persistent non -compliance. The unsustainable practice of hiring foreign pilots 
on temporary licences should be progressively phased out as domestic pilot output is scaled up. 
6.6.4.1 The Committee furth er recommends that the Ministry link approvals pertaining to fleet 
expansion to demonstrated availability of adequate pilots, including buffer pilots, as unrestrained fleet 
growth without matching human resources could manifest as periodic difficulty in airline operations. 
6.6.5 Observation 38 — Statutory Passenger Rights Framework 
The Committee observed that India lacks a comprehensive statutory passenger rights framework. The 
current framework of CAR-based guidelines, supplemented by an ad -hoc helpline, is inadequate for a 
market carrying over 350 million passengers annually. 
6.6.6 Recommendation:  The Committee recommends that the Ministry prepare a comprehensive 
Passenger Rights Charter, enforceable through statutory provisions under the Bharatiya Vayuyan  
Adhiniyam 2024, covering compensation for flight cancellations and delays beyond specified 
thresholds, mandatory refunds for defective in -flight services, standardised baggage loss and damage 
compensation, transparent complaint redressal timelines, and penalties for non-compliance. 
6.6.6.1 The Committee further recommends the setting up of an independent aviation ombudsman for 
both the domestic and international sector in India, with time -bound grievance redressal authority 
backed by a statute. 
6.7 Scheme Assessment and Regulatory Readiness 
6.7.1 Observation 39 — UDAN Impact Assessment 
The Committee observed that the cumulative public expenditure on RCS -UDAN exceeding Rs. 9,200 
crore over eight years has not been subjected to a formal independent impact assessment. 

23 
 
6.7.2 Recommendation: The Committee recommends that the Ministry commission a comprehensive 
independent impact assessment of RCS-UDAN covering cost per passenger on each route, route -wise 
viability metrics, the proportion of routes achieving self -sustainability upon VGF completion, 
comparison of cost -effectiveness between different aircraft types deployed, passenger demographic 
and connectivity outcomes, and employment generated. The Modified UDAN scheme design should 
incorporate lessons from this assessment. 
6.7.2.1 The Committee further recommends that each UDAN route be periodically reviewed with 
clearly defined entry and exit criteria so that routes with less than threshold performance could be 
restructured, as continued support without review could reduce the efficiency of the scheme. 
6.7.3 Observation 40 — Seaplane Certification and Regulatory Framework 
The Committee observed that as of the date of examination, zero seaplanes are certified to operate in 
India despite VGF announcements in the 2 026-27 Budget. The Twin Otter aircraft has been 
attempting to enter the Indian market for 22 years. The Committee raised concerns during oral 
evidence about the announcement of VGF before completing due diligence on aircraft certification. 
6.7.4 Recommenda tion: The Committee recommends that the Ministry expedite the certification 
framework for seaplane operations and ensure that the regulatory framework for water aerodrome 
operations, aircraft certification, and operator licensing is in place before further  fiscal commitments 
are made. Policy credibility requires that announcements of financial support follow rather than 
precede regulatory readiness. 
6.7.4.1 The Committee further recommends that new aviation segments be taken up only after 
ensuring that basi c regulatory approvals are in place and that a fast -track approval mechanism be 
instituted to avoid delays that undermine policy credibility. 
6.8 Fiscal Policy, International Strategy and Sector Development 
6.8.1 Observation 41 — ATF Inclusion under GST: Quantified Advocacy 
The Committee observed that the Ministry's advocacy for inclusion of ATF under GST has been 
insufficient. ATF constitutes 30 -40 per cent of airline operating costs in India, compared to 
significantly lower proportions in competing jurisd ictions, directly inflating airfares and constraining 
route viability on short-haul and regional routes. 
6.8.2 Recommendation:  The Committee recommends that the Ministry prepare and present to the 
GST Council a comprehensive quantified impact analysis demo nstrating the effect of ATF inclusion 
under GST on airline operating costs, ticket prices, route viability, and traffic growth, drawing on the 
experience of the 21 States that have already reduced VAT. 
6.8.2.1 The Committee further recommends that the Mini stry consider instituting a structured and 
transparent ATF pricing framework, including publishing a comparative Fuel Price Index and a 
regular comparison of fuel prices across States, along with incentives for States to support lower ATF 
costs. 
6.8.3 Observation 42 — International Hub Strategy 
The Committee observed that despite India's strategic geographic location and population of 1.4 
billion, the country lacks a major international aviation hub. During oral evidence, the Committee 
drew comparisons with Dubai and Sharjah, which handle 30 -40 million international passengers with 
minimal local populations. 

24 
 
6.8.4 Recommendation:  The Committee recommends that the Ministry prepare a formal 
International Hub Development Strategy, requiring coordinated action o n airport infrastructure, slot 
allocation, bilateral air service agreements, transit visa policy, ground handling standards, and airline 
scheduling. The Ministry should identify two to three candidate airports and prepare an integrated 
action plan. 
6.8.4.1 The Committee further recommends that the Ministry explore building partnerships with 
established international hubs through coordinated flight schedules and smoother transit facilities to 
ensure seamless coordination between Indian carriers and global ne tworks, while Indian airports 
gradually develop as transit hubs. Further, identification of select airports as national hubs with 
focused policy support, including tax measures and multiple bilateral alignments, would strengthen 
India’s position in international aviation. 
6.8.5 Observation 43 — General Aviation Development Policy 
The Committee observed that general aviation has never developed in India despite 80 years of 
independence. This concern was raised during oral evidence, comparing India with the U nited States, 
which has approximately 40,000 airports including 20,000 private airports. 
6.8.6 Recommendation: The Committee recommends that the Ministry formulate a comprehensive 
General Aviation Development Policy addressing regulatory simplification, sm all airport 
development, airspace access, and creation of an enabling environment for private aviation. The 
absence of general aviation infrastructure constrains not only recreational and business flying but also 
pilot training capacity and the aviation ecosystem more broadly. 
6.8.6.1 The Committee further recommends the introduction of a National Open Skies  for General 
Aviation framework to provide a single -window, pan -India clearance across airstrips, along with 
mandatory baseline safety standards, periodic audits, and pilot training norms to complement ease of 
operations with robust safety oversight. 
6.9 Cybersecurity, Data Governance and Pilot Training Access 
6.9.1 Observation 44 — Cybersecurity Maturity Assessment 
The Committee observed that the expanding digital attack surface created by eGCA, DigiYatra, 
Digital Sky, EPL, ATM infrastructure, and airline systems has not been subjected to a systematic 
maturity assessment. 
6.9.2 Recommendation: The Committee recommends that the Ministry direct DGCA to commission 
a comprehensive Cybersecurity Maturity Assessment of all constituent organisations and major 
regulated entities. The assessment should establish baseline maturity scores with improvement targets 
and be completed within one year. 
6.9.2.1 The Committee further recommends that the Ministry consider instituting a dedicated Aviation 
Cyber Security Operatio ns Centre (A -CSOC) with sector -wide coverage, integrating threat 
intelligence sharing, real-time network monitoring, supported by periodic red-teaming exercises. 
6.9.3 Observation 45 — FTO Geographic Distribution and Affordability 
The Committee observed severe geographic concentration in pilot training infrastructure: Bihar (130 
million population) has only one flying club, Uttar Pradesh (240 million population) has five, and 
entire states in the North East have zero FTOs. The cost of pilot training at Rs. 35 -50 lakh makes the 
profession inaccessible to the vast majority. 

25 
 
6.9.4 Recommendation: The Committee recommends that the Ministry develop a plan for equitable 
geographic distribution of FTOs, explore interest subvention schemes, scholarship programmes 
funded through a civil aviation development cess, expansion of public -sector FTO capacity through 
IGRUA, and partnerships with international training providers to bring down costs and improve 
access. 
6.9.4.1 The Committee further rec ommends that the Ministry explore the feasibility of establishing 
Flight Training Organisations in underserved regions, drawing on the United States’ widely 
distributed and airport-linked pilot training ecosystem, to further democratise access to pilot tra ining. 
Additionally, the Committee recommends that the Ministry institute a periodic audit of pilot training 
programmes across countrywide FTOs covering parameters such as training quality, cost of training, 
and instructor quality, among other critical parameters. 
6.10 Infrastructure Quality, Privacy and Safety Accountability 
6.10.1 Observation 46 — Noida International Airport: Timeline Accountability 
The Committee observed that security clearance issues including BCAS compliance requirements and 
an incompl ete perimeter wall (7 of 14.5 km) have delayed the Noida International Airport. The 
opacity of communication on the status of this nationally significant project was a specific concern 
during oral evidence. 
6.10.2 Recommendation:  The Committee recommends t hat the Ministry provide a detailed status 
report on the Noida International Airport to the Committee within 90 days, including current BCAS 
compliance status, perimeter wall completion, revised timeline, and measures to prevent recurrence of 
such delays. 
6.10.3 Observation 47 — Airport Quality Assurance and Defect Liability 
The Committee observed with concern the reports of damaged fixtures within three months of the 
inauguration of the Patna airport terminal despite an investment of Rs. 1,400 crore over e ight years. 
The degradation of publicly funded infrastructure within weeks of commissioning is unacceptable. 
6.10.4 Recommendation:  The Committee recommends that the Ministry institute a formal defect 
liability and quality assurance framework for newly con structed airport terminals, review the defect 
liability period, retention money provisions, and third -party quality audit mechanisms in AAI's 
standard contract conditions. 
6.10.5 Observation 48 — DigiYatra Data Privacy and Biometric Governance 
The Committee observed that over 2 crore citizens have enrolled in DigiYatra and that the system 
processes sensitive biometric data at 30 airports. No independent audit report on data privacy and 
security has been placed before the Committee. 
6.10.6 Recommendation: The Committee recommends that the Ministry commission an independent 
data privacy and security assessment of the DigiYatra system, covering consent architecture, 
biometric data storage and retention policies, data breach vulnerability, compliance with applic able 
data protection legislation, and governance of the DigiYatra Foundation. 
6.10.7 Observation 49 — Consolidated Annual Aviation Safety Report 

26 
 
The Committee observed that the current fragmented reporting across DGCA, AAIB, and BCAS does 
not provide Parli ament or the public with a single authoritative assessment of the state of aviation 
safety in India. 
6.10.8 Recommendation: The Committee recommends that the Ministry direct DGCA to publish an 
annual Consolidated Aviation Safety Report, on the lines of the EASA Annual Safety Review, 
providing a comprehensive picture including accident and incident statistics, enforcement actio ns, 
surveillance outcomes, fleet airworthiness data, pilot licensing statistics, and safety improvement 
recommendations. 
6.10.9 Observation 50 — Performance Audit of Air India Post-Privatisation Safety Compliance 
The Committee observe that Air India received nine show-cause notices in six months preceding July 
2025, approximately 100 safety lapses were flagged in a single DGCA audit, 137 of 166 inspected 
aircraft showed recurring technical defects, and a penalty was imposed for operating flights without a 
valid Airworthiness Review Certificate. These findings occurred in the context of India's deadliest 
aviation disaster in recent decades. 
6.10.10 Recommendation:  The Committee recommends that the Ministry request the Comptroller 
and Auditor General to conduc t a performance audit of Air India's post -privatisation safety 
compliance and regulatory adherence, covering the period from the Tata Group's acquisition in 
January 2022 to the present. The severity and recurrence of safety findings warrant independent 
examination by the supreme audit institution. 
6.11 Geopolitical Resilience and Inter-ministerial Coordination 
6.11.1 Observation 51 — Impact of War in Gulf on India’s Civil Aviation 
The Committee noted with concern the closure and restriction of airspace across several countries in 
West Asia, beginning 28 February 2026, arising from the escalating Iran –Israel–United States 
conflict, which has posed significant and multi-dimensional challenges to India’s civil aviation sector. 
As roughly half of India’s int ernational passenger traffic transits through Gulf hubs such as Dubai, 
Doha and Abu Dhabi, the disruption led to cancellation of over 2,600 flights by Indian carriers within 
the first week, with 410 flights cancelled on 28 February and 444 on 1 March alone , stranding an 
estimated 60,000 passengers on the first day. Airspace closures by Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain, 
the UAE and Israel effectively shut down the primary air corridor linking Asia, Europe and Africa. 
Airlines were forced to reroute westbou nd flights via the Indian Ocean and Mediterranean airspace, 
adding 2 to 4 hours of flight time and substantially increasing fuel consumption. Block times on the 
Dubai–Delhi sector rose from 3 hours 30 minutes to nearly 6 hours. The Committee appreciated th e 
Government’s swift and decisive evacuation response: over 2,20,000 Indian nationals were facilitated 
to return from Gulf countries between 1 and 16 March 2026, including 32,107 on Indian carriers in 
the first week alone, with the Ministry of External Aff airs establishing a dedicated Special Control 
Room, 24/7 Embassy helplines, and coordinating land border crossings from Iran into Armenia and 
Azerbaijan. The Committee further observed that the disruption has had cascading consequences 
across three critical dimensions. First, on international route viability: carriers have been compelled to 
suspend, curtail or reroute services, with Air India alone suspending 50 westbound flights on 1 March, 
and Emirates, Qatar Airways and Etihad temporarily halting all ope rations. Second, on Air Turbine 
Fuel supply and pricing: global jet fuel prices surged by 58.4 per cent to USD 157.41 per barrel in the 
week ending 6 March 2026 (IATA/S&P Global Platts), crude oil briefly touched USD 119.50 per 
barrel on 9 March, and ATF i n India was revised upward by Rs. 5,215 per kilolitre effective 1 March 
2026 to Rs. 96,638 per kilolitre, prompting Air India, IndiGo and Akasa Air to impose fuel surcharges 
ranging from Rs. 199 to Rs. 2,300 per sector. Third, on domestic flight frequency:  the redeployment 

27 
 
of aircraft and crew for longer international routings, combined with elevated fuel costs, has reduced 
the fleet and crew available for domestic operations, with the Civil Aviation Minister acknowledging 
that the ATF price impact would be  felt from April 2026 and that the matter requires a multi -
departmental exercise involving the Ministry of Civil Aviation, the Ministry of External Affairs, and 
the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas. 
6.11.2 The Committee observed with particular concer n that the rapid escalation in international 
crude oil prices arising from the West Asia crisis has placed the Indian airline industry under acute 
financial stress. With ATF priced on the basis of international crude benchmarks and constituting 35 
to 40 per cent of airline operating costs, the burden on domestic carriers has become severe. Airlines 
face a stark choice between incurring unsustainable losses or grounding capacity, both of which 
outcomes are against the larger public interest of maintaining ai r connectivity across the country. The 
Committee noted that between 2022 and 2024, the Government had instituted a mechanism capping 
the floor and ceiling of ATF pricing for domestic airlines, which provided a measure of stability 
during a period of global  price volatility. The Committee is of the considered view that the present 
crisis, which is more severe in its scale and duration than earlier episodes, warrants the revival of a 
similar ATF pricing stabilisation arrangement in the public interest. The Co mmittee accordingly 
recommends that the Ministry of Civil Aviation and the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas jointly 
and urgently examine the feasibility of reinstating a structured ATF pricing band for domestic airline 
operations for the duration of t he crisis, calibrated to protect both airline viability and passenger 
affordability, while ensuring that Oil Marketing Companies are not subjected to uncompensated 
under-recoveries. 
6.11.3 Recommendation: The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Civil Aviation, building on 
the Government’s demonstrated and commendable crisis response capability including the evacuation 
of over 2,20,000 nationals, develop a comprehensive inter -ministerial Aviation Resilience and 
Diversification Framework (ARDF) in coord ination with the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, 
the Ministry of External Affairs, the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Airports Authority of India, and 
the Directorate General of Civil Aviation, structured on three time-bound pillars: 
(a) Accelerate p oint-to-point long -haul services: Incentivise Indian carriers to launch and expand 
direct wide -body services from emerging and secondary hubs (Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Chennai, 
Kolkata, Pune) to Europe and North America within 12 months, progressively reducin g dependence 
on Gulf transit. Fast-track slot allocation, wet-lease approvals, and bilateral air service agreements on 
under-used routes, in close coordination with the Ministry of External Affairs. The Committee notes 
that Turkish Airlines continued operations via Istanbul and European carriers (Air France, Lufthansa, 
British Airways) maintained US–India connectivity by avoiding Gulf airspace entirely, demonstrating 
the viability of non-Gulf routing. 
(b) Identify and secure alternative transit hubs: Conclu de overflight and traffic -right arrangements 
with non -Gulf nodes (Istanbul, Athens, Frankfurt in Europe; Nairobi in Africa; and Singapore in 
South-East Asia) to provide contingency connectivity when Gulf hubs are compromised. Leverage 
existing air -service agreements and, where needed, negotiate temporary contingency clauses under 
ICAO Annex 9. The Committee notes that the Government has already identified ‘safe airports’ 
including Muscat, Fujairah, Ras al Khaimah, Jeddah, Riyadh and Abu Dhabi for consolidat ion and 
evacuation, a model that should be institutionalised. 
(c) Deploy pre-defined contingency routing protocols and inter-ministerial coordination: Mandate that 
every scheduled international operator file three alternate routings (northern corridor via Central Asia, 
southern corridor via the Indian Ocean, and Pacific-side corridor via South-East Asia) with associated 
fuel-stop plans. Establish a permanent 24/7 Aviation Crisis Cell under DGCA, modelled on the 
successful coordination demonstrated during th e current crisis, to issue real -time NOTAM synthesis, 
coordinate evacuations, and activate pre -approved reroutes within two hours of airspace closure. In 

28 
 
parallel, the Ministry should coordinate with the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas to ensure 
contingency ATF supply arrangements at alternate refuelling points, institute a crisis -period ATF 
pricing stabilisation mechanism, drawing on the floor -ceiling pricing band that operated successfully 
between 2022 and 2024, to moderate the impact of global crud e price surges on domestic airline 
operations (noting that ATF prices surged 58.4 per cent in a single week in March 2026 and carriers 
were compelled to impose fuel surcharges), monitor the cascading effect on domestic flight frequency 
arising from fleet a nd crew redeployment on longer international routings, and engage with the 
Ministry of Finance to explore temporary tax relief on ATF during periods of sustained geopolitical 
disruption. 
6.11.4 Expected outcome: Building on the Government’s decisive and co mmendable evacuation 
response and the demonstrated inter -ministerial coordination between the Ministry of Civil Aviation, 
the Ministry of External Affairs, and the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, the ARDF would 
ensure improved continuity of essentia l air connectivity during geopolitical disruptions, a calibrated 
and progressive reduction in excessive dependence on Gulf transit hubs over the medium term, stable 
ATF supply and pricing during disruption periods through institutional coordination with th e 
petroleum sector, minimised impact on domestic flight availability and airfares, and progressive 
strengthening of Indian carriers as independent long -haul operators capable of connecting India 
directly to major global destinations. 
6.12 Helicopter Safety Policy  
6.12.1 Observations 52 - Institutionalizing Helicopter Safety 
The Committee observes a systemic gap in safety oversight within the charter sector of the aviation 
industry, transitioning from a "lightly regulated adjunct" to a high -risk sector. Fat al incidents —
specifically the June 15, 2025, Aryan Aviation crash (Bell 407) and the non -fatal February 24, 2026, 
Pawan Hans sea crash -landing—expose a "pressure culture" where the consideration for commercial 
revenue and VIP schedules tends to override "N o-Go" weather decisions during the high -density 
pilgrim rush. Technical evidence points to recurring mechanical instability, including stuck collective 
controls and tail rotor malfunctions, which are lethal in high -altitude or maritime corridors when 
flying single-engine helicopters that lack power redundancy. Furthermore, the absence of localized 
Air Traffic Control (ATC) and 24 -hour weather stations, coupled with chronic Flight Duty Time 
Limitation (FDTL) violations, indicates that the current regulatory framework is inadequate in 
protecting the lives of the crews and passengers operating the 250+ registered units. 
6.12.2 Recommendation: The Ministry of Civil Aviation (MoCA) may consider incorporating a 
dedicated Helicopter Wing within the DGCA, led by tec hnical aviation professionals, to 
institutionalize specialized maintenance audits and ex -military pilot "familiarization" training, since 
the drive to reach a destination or complete a task overrides prudent safety decisions, such as delaying 
or cancelling a flight due to adverse weather, when ex -military pilots fly civilian aircraft. A statutory 
mandate could be considered under the aegis of a high -powered committee to transition all high -risk 
pilgrimage and inter -island routes to twin -engine helicopters o nly, providing a vital safety buffer 
against mid -air technical snags. To manage operational saturation, the DGCA must fast -track the 
deployment of localized ATC systems and automated weather interlocks that prohibit takeoffs during 
"poor visibility" windows. Finally, the regulator must enforce transparency by ranking the 133 Non -
Scheduled Operators (NSOs) on safety performance, auditing ADS -B (Automatic Dependent 
Surveillance Broadcast) and CVR (Cockpit Voice Recorder) data to ensure the 12 -hour rest mandate 
is met, and fixing accountability for any flight launched with known mechanical deficiencies or under 
commercial duress. 
6.13 Aviation Safety Pertaining to VIP and Charter Flights 

29 
 
6.13.1 Observation 53 
The Committee notes with concern that incidents invo lving chartered jets ferrying VIPs point to a 
recurring pattern of operational vulnerabilities. Evidence suggests that adverse weather conditions, 
including poor visibility, have frequently been a contributing factor. The Committee is particularly 
concerned that pilots may, at times, face implicit or explicit pressure to adhere to demanding 
schedules, even when prevailing conditions fall below safe operational thresholds. 
6.13.2 The Committee further observes that the sterile cockpit rule, which prohibits non-essential 
communication during critical phases of flight, is not consistently respected during VIP charter 
operations. This introduces avoidable distraction at moments demanding absolute crew attention. 
6.13.3 The Committee also notes that frequent las t-minute schedule changes impose considerable 
strain on flight crew, compelling already fatigued personnel to extend duty hours beyond safe limits. 
This raises concerns regarding crew alertness and sound decision-making. 
6.13.4 The Committee places on reco rd its appreciation for the DGCA's firm position that no 
commercial or logistical consideration may override any safety parameter. 
6.14 Recommendations 
(a) When visibility falls below prescribed safety minima, diversion to a better -equipped airport 
must be the only acceptable course of action. The sterile cockpit rule must be strictly enforced across 
all charter and VIP operations. 
(b) Flight Duty Time Limitations must be enforced uniformly, without exception, across all 
categories of flights. Pilot trainin g must mandatorily cover weather awareness and sound decision -
making in uncontrolled environments. 
(c) The Committee further emphasises that ex -military pilots transitioning to civilian aviation 
must undergo structured familiarisation training. In civil av iation, delaying or cancelling a flight on 
safety grounds is not a failure of resolve. It is an affirmation of professional responsibility.

Introduction 
1. I, the Chairman, Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture, 
having been authorised by the Committee, have the honour  to present on its behalf this Report on the Demands 
for Grants (2026 -27) of the Ministry of Culture (Demand No. 18). The Committee was constituted in 
accordance with the Rules and Procedures governing Parliamentary Standing Committees and authorised by th e 
Hon’ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha, to examine the said Demands for Grants and to present its Report to the 
House. 
2. The Committee has examined the Demands for Grants of the Ministry in view of the central importance that 
the preservation, promotion, and dis semination of India’s tangible and intangible cultural heritage occupies in 
the nation’s civilizational identity and global standing. With a Budget Estimate of Rs. 3,416.63 crore for 2026 -
27 and a Ministry -projected requirement of Rs. 5,219.97 crore, the M inistry of Culture administers a wide -
ranging portfolio encompassing the Archaeological Survey of India, national museums, libraries, akademies, 
zonal cultural centres, Buddhist and Tibetan institutions, and flagship missions including the Gyan Bharatam 
Mission and the National Mission on Cultural Mapping. 
3. The Committee undertook a structured examination of the Demands in accordance with established 
parliamentary practice. The Ministry furnished its Detailed Demands for Grants (Demand No. 18, 2026 -27), and 
budgetary documentations comprising covering the Expenditure Statement, the Output Outcome Monitoring 
Framework (OOMF) for 2026 -27, head -wise financial summaries, and scheme -wise physical and financial 
targets. In addition, the Ministry submitted Writte n Replies to questions put by the Committee. The 
representatives of the Ministry were also heard in oral evidence on 24 February 2026. The Annual Report of the 
Ministry of Culture for the year 2025 -26 was also placed before the Committee and served as an i mportant 
corroborating source of performance information. 
4. The Committee’s examination encompassed five principal thematic areas: the Financial Architecture and 
Budgetary Discipline; Scheme -Wise Performance and Physical Outcomes covering the ASI, Centena ries and 
Anniversaries, Kala Sanskriti Vikas Yojana, Development of Museums, Development of Libraries, Gyan 
Bharatam Mission, Global Engagement, and the National Mission on Cultural Mapping; Historical Expenditure 
Trends and Savings Analysis; Cross -Cutting Governance and Equity; and Audit Compliance and 
Accountability.  
5. This Report synthesises evidence received from the Ministry, the detailed budgetary documentation, oral 
evidence tendered on 24 February 2026, and the Committee’s own analysis of multi -year financial trends. It 
places fiscal prudence, outcome accountability, and equitable regional development at the centre of its 
assessment. The Committee’s recommendations are framed in a spirit of constructive engagement and are 
intended to support the Mi nistry in strengthening the planning, execution, and monitoring of its programmes. 
The Committee expects that the Ministry will give careful and sympathetic consideration to these 
recommendations and that appropriate action taken notes will be communicated  to the Committee in a timely 
manner. 
6. The Committee places on record its sincere appreciation of the assistance rendered by the officers of the 
Rajya Sabha Secretariat in facilitating the examination of the Demands for Grants, and of the cooperation 
extended by the Ministry of Culture in providing detailed documentation, responses to the Committee’s 
questionnaire, and written submissions.
