REPORT 
CHAPTER I: BUDGETARY ANALYSIS 
A. Overview of Demands for Grants (2026-27) 
1.1 The Ministry of Culture is the nodal agency for formulation of national policies and programmes for 
the preservation and promotion of India’s cultural heritage. The Ministry oversees the Archaeological 
Survey of India (ASI), National Archives of India, national museums, national academies (Sahitya 
Akademi, Sangeet Natak Akademi, Lalit Kala Akademi), the National School of Drama, Zonal Cultural 
Centres, and 34 Autonomous Bodies, among other institutions and organisations. 
1.2 The Ministry informed the Committee that for the financial year 2026 -27, it has been allocated Rs. 
3,416.63 crore (Demand No.  18) against its projected demand of Rs. 5,219.97 crore, a shortfall of Rs. 
1,803.34 crore (approximately 34.55 per cent). The approved allocation represents an increase of only Rs. 
55.67 crore (1.66 per cent) over the Budget Estimate of 2025 -26. The allocation comprises Revenue 
expenditure of Rs. 3,216.63 crore and Capital expenditure of Rs. 200 crore. 
1.3 The Committee notes that the Ministry’s budgetary structure is institution-centric, with approximately 
87 per cent of the allocation directed towards institutions and only 13 per cent available for central sector 
schemes. The ASI accounts for Rs. 1,235.78 crore (36.17 per cent of the total allocation). 
1.4 The Committee observes that the gap of Rs. 1,803.34 crore between the Ministry’s projected 
demand and the allocation constitutes a constraint on the Ministry’s capacity to fulfil its mandate. 
Given that the Ministry has reported near 100 per  cent expenditure rates and has received 
additional funds in Revised Estimates in the current year, the Committee is of the view that the 
budgetary allocation is not commensurate with the projected demand and the expenditure 
performance demonstrated by the Ministry. The Committee recommends that the Ministry engage 
with the Ministry of Finance to secure enhanced allocations, including through Supplementary 
Demands, and present a detailed justification note linking the additional demand to specific 
programme outcomes and deliverables. 
B. Budgetary Trends and Fund Utilisation 
1.5 The Committee notes that the Ministry has reported near 100 per cent expenditure rates in the current 
financial year and has received additional funds at the Revised Estimate stage. 
1.6 The Committee notes from the Detailed Demands for Grants that the Capital expenditure head has a 
Budget Estimate of Rs. 200 crore for 2026 -27. The actual Capital expenditure in 2025 -26 stood at Rs. 
66.84 crore (up to 19 January 2026), representing a ut ilisation rate of approximately 33.4 per cent. The 
Committee observes that this level of Capital expenditure is a matter of concern. 
1.7 The Committee recommends that the Ministry prepare a detailed Capital expenditure plan for 
2026-27 with quarterly milestones and furnish quarterly progress reports to the Committee. 

2 
 
C. Ticketing Revenue 
1.8 The Committee further notes that the Ministry stated that ticketing revenue from centrally protected 
monuments amounts to approximately Rs. 365 crore annually. This rev enue goes to the Government 
exchequer and is not available to the Ministry or the ASI as departmental revenue for reinvestment in 
conservation and maintenance activities. 
1.9 The Committee recommends that the Ministry, in consultation with the Ministry of Finance, 
earmark a portion of the ticketing revenue of Rs. 365 crore annually for reinvestment in the 
conservation, maintenance, and visitor infrastructure of centrally protected monuments. The 
Ministry may present a detailed proposal for such a ring -fenced revenue mechanism to the 
Committee within six months. 
D. Shortfall in Projected Demand 
1.10 The Committee repeatedly emphasised during the evidence that the budget is insufficient given the 
scope of the Ministry’s work. The Museums Development scheme and  the proposed new infrastructure 
scheme under the 16th Finance Commission cycle require substantially higher allocations. NITI Aayog 
has set annual targets of 8 new museums and 15 new public libraries. The Committee observed that these 
targets cannot be achieved with current funding levels. 
1.11 The Committee recommends that the Ministry prepare a demand note for the 16th Finance 
Commission cycle, clearly linking budgetary requirements to the NITI Aayog targets for museums 
and libraries (as noted in Para 1. 10), the proposed infrastructure scheme, and the institutional 
capacity requirements of autonomous bodies and subordinate organisations. The demand note 
should include a phased expenditure plan, institutional capacity assessments, and a strategy for 
leveraging additional resources including CSR funds, the National Culture Fund, and PPP models. 
E. Alternative Revenue and Funding Sources 
1.12 The Committee observed during the evidence that Rs. 35,000 crore in CSR funds are available 
nationally, while the Mini stry’s budget is approximately Rs. 3,416.63 crore. The Committee suggested 
that the Ministry should actively tap CSR funds for museums and libraries in each district. The 
Committee notes that under Schedule VII of the Companies Act, 2013, protection of national heritage, art 
and culture, including restoration of buildings and sites of historical importance, is already an eligible 
category for CSR expenditure. In FY 2022 -23, corporate spending on heritage, art and culture stood at 
approximately Rs. 441 crore  nationally, indicating significant headroom for enhanced engagement 
between the Ministry and the corporate sector. 
1.13 The Committee further suggested that cultural heritage should be included as an eligible category for 
Members of Parliament Local Area Development (MPLAD) fund expenditure. The Committee cited the 
example of earning Rs. 18 crore from a planetarium developed under the Smart City project. 
1.14 The Committee recommends that the Ministry develop a strategy for leveraging alternative 
funding s ources, including: (a) a dedicated CSR engagement plan for museums, libraries, and 
heritage conservation, with clear guidelines for corporate participation and model project 
frameworks to facilitate adoption by eligible companies; (b) a proposal to the Min istry of Finance 

3 
 
and Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation for inclusion of cultural heritage as an 
eligible expenditure category under the MPLAD scheme; and (c) expansion of the restructured 
National Culture Fund model to attract private don ations for conservation. The Ministry may 
furnish this strategy to the Committee within six months. 
F. Grant-in-Aid Salary Reduction 
1.15 The Committee notes that the GIA Salary head has been reduced from Rs. 429 crore (BE 2025-26) to 
Rs. 352 crore (BE 202 6-27), a reduction of Rs. 77 crore (17.95 per cent). All 34 Autonomous Bodies 
under the Ministry remain entirely dependent on Government grants-in-aid for salary expenditure. 
1.16 The Committee is concerned at the reduction of Rs. 77 crore in the GIA Salar y head for 
Autonomous Bodies at a time when these bodies already face significant vacancy levels. The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry furnish to the Committee: (a) a body -wise break-up of 
the GIA Salary allocation for 2026-27, with the rationale for the reduction; (b) the current vacancy 
position in each Autonomous Body; and (c) an assessment of the impact of the reduction on the 
functioning of these bodies. The Committee would like to be apprised of the action taken in this 
regard. 
G. Mandatory Sub-Allocations: SCSP, TSP, and NER 
1.17 The Committee notes that the mandatory sub -allocations for 2026-27 include Rs. 49.50 crore under 
the Scheduled Caste Sub-Plan (8.3 per cent of schemeable BE), Rs. 25.65 crore under the Tribal Sub-Plan 
(4.3 per cent), an d Rs. 59.64 crore for the North -East Region (10.0 per cent), totalling Rs. 134.79 crore 
(22.6 per cent of schemeable BE). 
1.18 The Committee recommends that the Ministry furnish a scheme -wise and State-wise break-up 
of expenditure incurred under the SCSP, TSP, and NER mandatory sub -allocations for 2024 -25 
and 2025 -26 (up to date), along with the physical outcomes achieved under each allocation. The 
Committee further recommends that the Ministry ensure that these earmarked funds are utilised 
for the intended beneficiary categories and not diverted to general expenditure. The Ministry may 
furnish utilisation reports within three months. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

4 
 
CHAPTER II: SCHEME-WISE ANALYSIS 
A. Restructured Schemes for the 16th Finance Commission Cycle 
2.1 The Ministry informed the Committee that it is restructuring from 7 existing programmes to 6 new 
schemes for the 16th Finance Commission period (2026-31): 
(a) Centenaries and Anniversaries (with infrastructure component removed). 
(b) Kala Sanskriti Vikas Yojana (expanded scope). 
(c) Gyan Bharatam Mission (continuation with existing 5-year allocation). 
(d) Expanded Global Engagement Scheme, now incorporating Project Mausam (for multinational 
UNESCO nominations) and Project Bharat Bharat (focus on multinational heritage inscriptions). 
(e) New Infrastructure Scheme: Development and Enhancement of Sanskrit Sampada and Heritage, 
comprising seven elements: (i) 15 excavation and heritage site development; (ii) new science 
cities and centres; (iii) new public libraries; (iv) new museu ms and enhancement of existing 
facilities; (v) protection of architectural heritage (100 -200 year old facades); (vi) creative 
economy component for artisan and artist market opportunities; and (vii) YugeYugeen Bharat 
Museum. 
(f) YugeYugeen Bharat Museum as a standalone project. 
2.2 The Ministry informed the Committee that the proposed infrastructure scheme involves a proposed 
investment of Rs. 12,000 crore and above over five years. The Centre -State cost-sharing formula was not 
specified in the documents examin ed by the Committee. If Expenditure Finance Committee (EFC) 
approvals are obtained, scheme funding would increase from the current Rs. 569 crore to approximately 
Rs. 2,000 crore. 
2.3 The Committee notes that the proposed infrastructure scheme uses a centra lly-sponsored format 
requiring State participation and ownership for sustainability. The Ministry stated that it has written to all 
State Governments seeking support. 
2.4 The Committee recommends that all EFC notes for new schemes under the 16th Finance 
Commission cycle be accompanied by: (a) detailed implementation roadmaps with year -wise 
milestones; (b) institutional capacity assessments, given the current staffing shortages across the 
Ministry and its subordinate organisations; (c) State -wise absorption plans; (d) a phased scaling 
mechanism linked to demonstrated expenditure performance; and (e) a clear framework for 
recurring operational costs, specifying the Centre -State cost -sharing formula and sustainability 
provisions beyond the scheme period. The Co mmittee further recommends that the Ministry 
present the draft EFC notes to the Committee before final submission. 
2.5 The Committee further recommends that the Ministry notify a performance -linked Centre -
State cost-sharing framework for the proposed herit age infrastructure scheme at the outset, with 
funding tranches to States tied to measurable outcomes such as conservation quality indices, visitor 
footfall growth, local artisan and craftsperson employment generation, and annual site 
maintenance compliance . The experience of outcome -based funding models in comparable 
centrally-sponsored schemes suggests that tying financial flows to demonstrated results promotes 

5 
 
both accountability and long -term sustainability. The Ministry may apprise the Committee of the 
framework so devised. 
B. Centenaries and Anniversaries 
2.6 The Ministry informed the Committee of the current commemoration programmes: (a) 150 years of 
Vande Mataram (continuing till November); (b) Lokmanya Ahilyabai (concluded); (c) Dr. Shyama Prasad 
Mukherjee 125th birthday; (d) Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji 350 years of martyrdom (ongoing); and (e) Acharya 
Vidyanand (Jain Muni, concluded). 
2.7 The Committee notes from the financial data that the Centenaries and Anniversaries scheme has 
exhibited pronounced inter-year volatility: Rs. 106.13 crore (actual 2024 -25), Rs. 35 crore (BE 2025 -26), 
and Rs. 98 crore (BE 2026 -27). The OOMF targets for 2026 -27 include 200 organisations, 230 events, 
and 5,00,000 footfall. 
2.8 The Committee recommends that the Ministry deve lop a standardised impact assessment 
framework for all national commemoration programmes, quantifying outcomes in terms of public 
participation levels, geographical spread of engagement, educational outreach conducted, digital

programme effectiveness and to inform the planning of future com memorations. The Committee 
expects to be apprised of the framework so developed.

indicates a structural problem in liability management under the scheme.

recommends that the Ministry examine the feasibility of dedicating a small percentage of proceeds 
from all Akademi-facilitated art exhibitions and cultural sales to a Heritage Conservation Corpus,

India’s cultural patrimony. The Committee further recommends th at the Ministry furnish a note 
on the pending liabilities under the KSVY, the measures taken to prevent their recurrence, and the  

6 
 
adequacy of the Rs. 150 crore allocation for 2026 -27. The Committee would like to be apprised of 
the action taken in this regard.

27; and (c) a quarterly expenditure plan with milestones linked to the OOMF targets. The

release mechanism for the Mission, whereby subsequent quarterly tranches are released upon 
demonstrated achievement of the preceding quarter’s physical and financial targets , as reported 
through the Public Financial Management System (PFMS). This approach would incentivise timely 
execution and strengthen expenditure accountability. The Committee would like to be apprised of 
the action taken in this regard.

2026-27 is Rs. 50 crore. 

7 
 
2.17 The Committee is concerned at the chronic underutilisation under the Development of 
Libraries scheme. The Committee recommends that the Ministry furnish: (a) an explanation for the

CHAPTER III: ARCHAEOLOGICAL HERITAGE AND MONUMENT 
CONSERVATION 
A. Archaeological Survey of India: Overview 
3.1 The Committee notes that the ASI maintains 3,685 centrally protected monuments through 38 Circles. 
The ASI has been allocated Rs. 1,235.78 crore for 2026 -27, constituting 36.17 per cent of the Ministry’s 
total allocation. During 2025 -26, ‘Maratha Military  Landscapes of India’ was inscribed as a World 
Heritage Site, and 14 sites were added to India’s UNESCO Tentative List, bringing the total to 69. India 
now ranks 6th globally for World Heritage Sites. 
3.2 The Committee notes from the financial data that AS I conservation expenditure has maintained 
utilisation rates above 99 per cent over the period 2021 -22 to 2024 -25. In 2025 -26, the utilisation rate 
stood at 67.17 per cent (Rs. 232.52 crore against Rs. 346.15 crore, up to 21 November 2025). 
3.3 The Committee notes the sustained high utilisation rates in ASI conservation expenditure over 
2021-22 to 2024-25 and recommends that the Ministry ensure that the utilisation rate for 2025 -26 is 
brought to the level of previous years by the close of the financial year.  The Ministry may furnish 
the final utilisation figures for 2025-26 within 90 days of the close of the financial year. 
3.4 The Committee further notes that India’s growing portfolio of World Heritage Sites, now 
ranking sixth globally with 44 inscribed properties, carries with it a corresponding obligation under 
the UNESCO Operational Guidelines to maintain standards of conservation, interpretation, and 
visitor management commensurate with the Outstanding Universal Value of these sites. With the 
inscription of the Maratha Military Landscapes in 2025, India’s international visibility in the 
heritage domain has been further enhanced. The Committee recommends that the Ministry, in 
coordination with the ASI, undertake a comprehensive review of maintenance standards and visitor 
facilities at all World Heritage Sites and prepare a time -bound upgradation plan to ensure that the 
condition, interpretation infrastructure, and management of these sites are aligned with their 
global recognition. The Committee expects to be apprised of the action taken in this regard. 
B. Sites and Excavations 
3.5 The Ministry informed the Committee that the development of 15 significant archaeological sites has 
been announced, including Rakhigarhi, Dholavira, Hastinapura, Adichanallur, and Shivsagar, with visitor 
infrastructure and interpretation centres. 
3.6 The Ministry stated that the excavation process is archaeologist-driven. Under the new initiative, sites 
will be developed for visitor access, a departure from the traditional practice of closing excavated sites. 
3.7 The Committee recommends that the Ministry furnish a detailed project -wise status report for 
all 15 archaeological site development projects, including physical and financial progress, timelines 
for completion, and provisions for ongoing conservation and visitor management, within 90 days. 
C. Underwater Archaeology 
3.8 The Ministry stated that underwater archaeology offers significant scope for expansion. The Ministry 
informed the Committee that it has planned 8 -10 expedition s in the coming financial year through 

9 
 
collaborations with the National Institute of Oceanography, the Indian Navy, the Indian Coast Guard, and 
international groups, including a Danish collaboration for a 17th century shipwreck off the Tamil Nadu 
coast. The Ministry stated that the division is being strengthened. 
3.9 The Committee recommends that the Ministry present an action plan for underwater 
archaeology to the Committee within 90 days, including: (a) the proposed expeditions with 
timelines and budgetar y provisions; (b) the institutional strengthening plan for the underwater 
archaeology division; (c) international collaboration agreements; and (d) a strategy for display of 
findings. The Committee further recommends that all findings from underwater archa eological 
expeditions be systematically documented and made accessible through a dedicated digital 
repository, thereby preserving and disseminating the knowledge generated from these explorations 
for research and public awareness. The Committee also recomm ends that the Ministry explore 
structured collaboration with the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways for logistical and 
maritime support in underwater heritage survey and recovery operations. 
D. Monument Protection and Maintenance 
3.10 The Committee raised concerns during the evidence about ASI -protected sites lacking protectors. 
The Committee noted that monuments are being used as relieving spots due to the absence of staff 
presence. The staffing implications are discussed in detail in Chapter VII. 
3.11 The Ministry informed the Committee that it denotified 18 sites during the current year after careful 
survey, while notifying 15 -16 new sites. The Ministry stated that the denotification  process is conducted 
carefully to prevent manipulation by real estate developers. 
3.12 The Committee raised the specific issue of British -era horse monuments in various parts of the 
country where the ASI’s restrictions prevent repair of a school located w ithin 100 metres of the protected 
site. 
3.13 The Ministry informed the Committee that the AMASR Act amendment has been prepared for 
Parliament. The Ministry stated that the new rules will make the 100 -metre and 200 -metre buffer zone 
limits flexible. 
3.14 The Committee recommends that: (a) the Ministry ensure expeditious passage of the AMASR 
Act amendment, with particular attention to the flexible buffer zone provisions; (b) the ASI 
formulate clear Standard Operating Procedures for denotification decisions, with a defined 
timeline not exceeding 90 days from receipt of application to final decision; (c) the Ministry 
establish a time -bound mechanism for responding to denotification requests, particularly where 
essential public infrastructure such as schools and  hospitals is affected; and (d) the staffing 
measures recommended in Chapter VII be implemented on priority for ticketed monuments. The 
Committee further recommends that the Ministry actively explore models of structured community 
participation in the cons ervation and upkeep of protected monuments, particularly in areas where 
ASI staffing levels remain below sanctioned strength. Drawing upon the experience of the ‘Adopt a 
Heritage’ initiative and community -based conservation models, the Ministry may develop  
guidelines for engaging local communities, heritage volunteers, and self-help groups in the custodial 
care and routine maintenance of monuments, with appropriate training and supervision 
frameworks. The Ministry may report on each of these measures within 90 days. 

10

3.15 The Ministry informed the Committee that 55 centrally protected monuments now have PPP 
souvenir shops. The Ministry stated that it plans to expand to 200 ticketed monuments from the current 
143. 
3.16 The Committee recommends that the Ministry furnish a progress report on the expansion of 
the souvenir shop programme, including revenues generated, artisan participation, and a timeline 
for reaching the target of 200 ticketed monuments.

3.17 The Ministry informed the Committee that the National Culture Fund has been restructured to a

3.18 The Committee recommends that the Ministry set measurable annual targets for the 
restructured National Culture Fund, including: (a) the number of monuments covered; (b) the total 
investment mobilised from corporate and private donors; and (c) a quality assurance framework to 
ensure conservation standards are maintained. The Ministry may report progress annually.

and galleries. The Ministry stated that all barracks are now curated and the complex functions as a

that the Ministry document this model and examine the feasibility of replicating it at other major 
heritage sites.

DIGITAL INITIATIVES AND AI INTEGRATION 
A. AI-Enabled Unified Search Tool

capability. The Ministry stated that it is engaging an agency to build an AI tool connecting all portals for

6.3 The Ministry informed the Committee that the MGMD portal has received inputs from villages across

INSTITUTIONAL AND GOVERNANCE ISSUES

driven repairs that alter the original character of structures. The Committee called for SOPs for

Railways, Ports, Shipping and Waterways, and Civil Aviation for preservation of he ritage assets;

9.11 The Committee raised the issue of Vedic heritage centres in villages named Riga, Athari, Yajur, and 
Samar in Bihar. 
9.12 The Committee also highlighted the existing state of infrastructural facilities, its poor conditions and 
expensive costumes at the National School of Drama. 
9.13 In view of the observations regarding the villages of Riga, Athari, Yajur and Samar in Bihar,  
which are believed to have possible associations with the Vedic tradition, the Committee 
recommends that the Ministry examine the matter and explore the feasibility of undertaking 
appropriate studies, in consultation with the Archaeological Survey of Indi a and other concerned 
institutions, to ascertain the historical and cultural significance of these sites. The Committee also 
recommends that the Ministry take appropriate steps to address issues relating to infrastructural 
facilities and the cost of costumes at the National School of Drama. The Committee would like to be 
apprised of the action taken in this regard.

CHAPTER X:  
SUMMARY OF RECOMMENDATIONS 
The following is a consolidated summary of the thirty two recommendations made by the Committee. For 
full context, the relevant paragraph references are indicated. 
I. Financial Management and Budgetary Discipline

of Finance to secure enhanced allocations, inc luding through Supplementary Demands, and present a

INTRODUCTION 
1. I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, 
Tourism and Culture, having been authorised by the Committee, present this Report on the 
Demands for Grants (2026-27) of the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways (Demand 
No. 78). 
2. The Committee examined the Demands for Grants in the context of the strategic centrality 
of the maritime sector to India’s economic architecture, trade competitiveness, and logistical 
efficiency. India possesses a coastline of 11,098 km, 12 Major Ports, approximately 217 
other-than-major ports, and 111 declared National Waterways. The maritime sector transports 
approximately 95 per cent of India’s trade by volume and 68 per cent by value. The Ministry 
of Ports, Shipping and Waterways exercises policy and regulatory oversight across this 
sector, encompassing port development, shipping regulation, shipbuilding promotion, ship 
repair and recycling, dredging, lighthouse administration, and inland water transport. The 
pace and quality of infrastructure modernisation, regulatory reform, and capacity creation 
within this sector have a direct bearing on the nation’s logistics costs, trade facilitation, and 
the objective of establishing India as a global maritime leader under the Maritime Amrit Kaal 
Vision 2047. 
3. The Committee’s scrutiny was directed not merely at the adequacy of financial allocations 
but at the structural coherence between budgetary intent and ground-level outcomes. 
Particular attention was devoted to: the absorptive capacity of the Ministry for an 
unprecedented 78 per cent increase in net GBS; the operationalisation of three new schemes 
(SBFAS, SbDS, and MDF) approved barely three months before the commencement of the 
financial year; the persistent concentration of IWT cargo on five waterways out of thirty-two 
operational; the disparity between created port capacity and actual throughput; the rate of 
Sagarmala project completion after a decade of implementation; the adequacy of last-mile rail 
and road connectivity to ports; the implementation architecture for five landmark maritime 
Acts enacted in 2025; and the readiness of the maritime workforce for a projected forty-five-
fold expansion in shipbuilding capacity by 2047. 
4. In the course of its examination, the Committee issued a detailed questionnaire to the 
Ministry and scrutinized the following documents: 
(i) Detailed Demands for Grants (Demand No. 78), financial year 2026-27; 
(ii) Ministry’s Written Submission to the Committee’s Questionnaire; 
(iii) Ministry’s Depositional Notes (scheme-wise Reply/Status); 
(iv) Annual Report of the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways (2025-26); 
(v) Output-Outcome Monitoring Framework (OOMF), financial year 2026-27; 
(vi) Annual Action Plan 2026-27 and Sector-wise Budgetary Outlays; 

 
iii 
(vii) Statement indicating Budget Estimates, Revised Estimates and Actuals for 2023-
24, 2024-25, 2025-26 (expenditure incurred up to January 2026) and Budget 
Estimates of 2026-27; 
(viii) Focus Areas of the Ministry for 2026-27; 
(ix) Outstanding Audit Paras contained in the CAG Report and the action taken or 
proposed to be taken thereon; 
(x) NITI Aayog policy documents pertaining to the Ministry. 
5. The Committee’s examination encompassed six principal thematic dimensions: the overall 
financial architecture and its consonance with stated policy objectives; scheme-wise scrutiny 
of major programmes; a structured review of past demand versus fulfilment over three 
financial years; cross-cutting tests of budget realism, regional equity, port capacity utilisation, 
last-mile connectivity, efficiency-outcome linkage, and institutional governance; the green 
shipping transition and digital transformation; and a focused assessment of workforce 
development and legislative implementation readiness. The Committee further took oral 
evidence of the Secretary and senior officials of the Ministry on 25th February 2026. 
6. The Ministry, in its written submission to the Committee’s questionnaire, covered twenty-
two questions, spanning port modernisation, shipbuilding competitiveness, inland waterways, 
logistics cost reduction, digital initiatives, workforce development, environmental clearances, 
and the Maritime Development Fund. The reply disclosed, inter alia, that 145 out of 283 
berths at major ports are fully mechanised, handling 78 per cent of total cargo, with a target 
of 93 per cent by 2030; that cargo handling capacity has risen from 800.52 MTPA in 2013-14 
to 1,681 MTPA in 2024-25 (an increase of 110 per cent); that average turnaround time has 
improved from 93.6 hours to 49.5 hours (47 per cent reduction); that Indian shipyards face a 
25–30 per cent cost disadvantage relative to China, Korea, and Japan; and that 32 National 
Waterways are now operational, carrying 160.86 million tonnes up to December 2025. The 
Ministry’s depositional notes further recorded [Depositional Notes, Reply/Status] that only 5 
per cent of India’s EXIM cargo is carried by Indian-owned or Indian-flagged ships; that 
Indian-built ships account for merely 7.63 per cent of Indian-owned vessels; and that 
commercial shipbuilding capacity requires a forty-five-fold expansion from 0.1 million GT to 
4.5 million GT by 2047. These submissions have been examined in detail across Chapters 1 
through 5 and inform the Committee’s thirty-three observations and recommendations in 
Chapter 6. 
7. The OOMF for 2026-27 was examined with particular attention to the measurability of 
output and outcome indicators. The Committee note that both SbDS and SBFAS carry the 
designation ‘Target not amenable’ for all quantitative indicators in 2026-27, on the ground 
that the schemes are in their inaugural year and project identification is at an initial stage. The 
Jalvahak scheme targets 3,12,000 tonnes of modal-shift cargo and 16,800 tonnes through 20 
ICSL scheduled voyages. The IWT in NER programme targets 8 DPR/feasibility studies, 10 
vessels, and 2 terminals. These targets have been evaluated in the context of their adequacy 
relative to the allocations sought. 

 
iv 
8. The Annual Report (2025-26) provided the Committee with a comprehensive factual 
foundation, including port-wise performance indicators, turnaround times, cargo traffic 
disaggregation, the status of PPP projects, the operational details of digital platforms, the 
green transition initiatives, the progress of Sagarmala projects, and the institutional 
developments at Cochin Shipyard Limited, Garden Reach Shipbuilders and Engineers 
Limited, Hooghly Cochin Shipyard Limited, the Shipping Corporation of India, the Dredging 
Corporation of India, the Sagarmala Maritime Finance Corporation Limited, and the Indian 
Port Rail and Ropeway Corporation Limited. The Committee have drawn upon this material 
extensively. 
9. This Report synthesises the Committee’s analysis of the budgetary documentation, the 
Ministry’s written submission to the Committee’s questionnaire, the Ministry’s depositional 
notes, the Annual Report, the Annual Action Plan, and the OOMF. It places fiscal discipline, 
outcome accountability, maritime safety, equitable regional development, and workforce 
readiness at the centre of its assessment. The Committee’s thirty-three recommendations are 
framed in a spirit of constructive engagement and are intended to strengthen the planning, 
execution, and monitoring of the Ministry’s programmes. 
10. The Committee place on record their appreciation of the assistance rendered by the Rajya 
Sabha Secretariat, and of the cooperation extended by the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and 
Waterways and all organisations under its administrative purview in furnishing 
documentation and oral submissions. 
11. The Committee considered and adopted this Report at its meeting held on 23rd March 
2026.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY 
0.1.1 The total budgetary allocation under Demand No. 78 for 2026-27 is Rs. 5,764.80 crore 
(gross), comprising Rs. 4,464.88 crore under Revenue and Rs. 1,299.92 crore under Capital (net: 
Rs. 5,164.80 crore). The Internal and Extra Budgetary Resources (IEBR) of Rs. 12,702.94 crore 
bring the combined outlay to Rs. 17,867.74 crore. Three newly-approved schemes, SBFAS, 
SbDS, and MDF, command Rs. 1,765 crore (34 per cent of net GBS), notwithstanding their 
operational guidelines having been released only on 26th December 2025. 
0.1.2 The Ministry's depositional notes record that India ranks 17th in global shipbuilding, 
contributing less than 1 per cent to global capacity. Only 5 per cent of India's EXIM cargo is 
carried by Indian-owned or Indian-flagged ships. Indian-built ships constitute merely 7.63 per 
cent of Indian-owned ships. The sector carries an employment multiplier of 6.4 and an investment 
multiplier of 1.82. The Ministry's written submission to the Committee's questionnaire further 
disclosed that Indian shipyards face a 25-30 per cent cost disadvantage compared to major 
shipbuilding nations such as China, Korea, and Japan, attributable to higher financing costs, 
limited economies of scale, and gaps in advanced technology. The depositional notes further 
record that India's commercial shipbuilding capacity requires expansion from 0.1 million GT to 
approximately 4.5 million GT per annum by 2047, constituting a forty-five-fold increase. 
0.1.3 Against a BE of Rs. 3,470.58 crore for 2025-26, the RE was reduced to Rs. 2,899.11 crore 
(a contraction of 16.5 per cent), and actual expenditure as on 31st January 2026 stood at Rs. 
2,329.86 crore (80.4 per cent of RE). The OOMF lists 'Target not amenable' for virtually all 
quantitative indicators under SbDS and SBFAS, limiting outcome accountability in the inaugural 
year. Major Ports handled 854.86 MMT of cargo in 2024-25, with 8.22 per cent year-on-year 
growth. IWT cargo expanded from 18 MMT in 2013-14 to 146 MMT in 2024-25. Sagarmala has 
completed 277 of 839 projects (33 per cent) after approximately a decade. The SMFCL, now 
functioning as an NBFC (RBI licence dated 19th June 2025), has sanctioned Rs. 4,198.10 crore in 
lending. 
0.1.4 The Global Maritime India Summit 2025, held in October 2025 in Mumbai, was attended 
by 93 countries, and resulted in over 600 MoUs valued at approximately Rs. 12 lakh crore, 
signalling growing international engagement with India's maritime sector. 
0.1.5 This Report details thirty-seven observations and recommendations across seven thematic 
groups: financial management and budgetary discipline; port infrastructure, connectivity and 
capacity utilisation; shipbuilding, ship repair, recycling and dredging; inland waterways, cruise 
tourism and NW development; sector reforms and regulatory architecture; technology, digital 
governance and green transition; and workforce development, international connectivity and 
heritage. 
 
 
 

 
1 
 
REPORT 
 
CHAPTER 1 
Overall Assessment of the Ministry's Demands 
1.1 Role and Mandate 
1.1.1 The Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways administers policy, regulation, and 
developmental oversight across India's maritime sector. The Ministry's jurisdiction 
encompasses 12 Major Ports, approximately 217 other-than-major ports, 111 declared 
National Waterways (of which 32 are operational across 20,187 km in 23 States and 4 Union 
Territories), the regulatory apparatus governing shipping, and the promotion of 
shipbuilding, ship repair, ship recycling, and dredging. The Ministry submitted in its Annual 
Report that it was reconstituted from the erstwhile Ministry of Shipping on 9th November 
2020, reflecting the policy emphasis on waterways development. 
1.2 Key Policy Priorities for 2026-27 
1.2.1 The Ministry's depositional notes set out its focus areas for 2026-27, which the 
Committee have examined. The Ministry submitted that its priorities include: development 
and operationalisation of 20 new National Waterways beginning with NW-5 (588 km); 
operationalisation of SBFAS and SbDS for shipbuilding expansion; establishment of the 
MDF; advancement of Sagarmala including the NMHC at Lothal; implementation of ONOP 
and Maritime Single Window 2.0 (MSW-Sagar Setu); development of river cruise tourism 
across 17 circuits; green shipping transition through hydrogen fuel-cell and electric vessels; 
procurement of 11 dredgers by DCI; establishment of ship repair ecosystems at Varanasi and 
Patna; setting up of Regional Centres of Excellence at Varanasi and Dibrugarh; and 
implementation of the five maritime Acts of 2025. 
1.2.2 The Ministry further submitted during oral evidence that three Budget 
announcements for 2026-27 pertain to the Ministry: a Rs. 10,000 crore Container 
Manufacturing Scheme over five years to scale domestic container production capacity from 
70,000 to approximately 7 lakh containers annually; the operationalisation of 20 new 
National Waterways with Regional Centres of Excellence and ship repair facilities at 
Varanasi and Patna; and a Coastal Cargo Promotion Scheme to raise the modal share of IWT 
and coastal shipping from 6 per cent to 12 per cent by 2047.

from 2 hours to 23 minutes. The modernisation of the older lock is targeted for completion

2025 in Mumbai with the participation of 93 countries, resulted in over 600 MoUs valued at 
approximately Rs. 12 lakh crore. The Special Secretary submitted during oral evidence that 
the National Monetisation Pipeline 2.0, launched in February 2026, assigns a monetisation 
target of Rs. 2,63,700 crore for the maritime sector for the period 2025-26 to 2029-30. The 
Committee note that under NMP 1.0, the Ministry achieved monetisation of Rs. 21,699 crore 
against a target of Rs. 12,828 crore. The Committee observes that NMP 2.0 represents a

CHAPTER 3 
Scheme-wise Scrutiny of Major Programmes 
3.1 Sagarmala Programme 
3.1.1 The Ministry's depositional notes record that the Sagarmala Programme provides 
financial assistance across five pillars: port modernisation, port connectivity, port-led 
industrialisation, coastal community development, and coastal shipping and IWT. The 
Ministry, in its written submission to the Committee's questionnaire, further states that 
Sagarmala 2.0 is under formulation with six pillars, adding ship repair and recycling, and 
island development to the original framework. The Annual Report records that 277 of 839 
projects have been completed (33 per cent), 209 are under implementation, and 353 remain 
at the planning stage. The allocation for 2026-27 is Rs. 616.88 crore. Under Sagarmala, 128 
projects costing Rs. 8,912 crore have been sanctioned, with GBS support. Thirty-seven 
fishing harbour projects worth Rs. 6,583 crore are underway, of which 12 (Rs. 1,078 crore) 
are complete. The Special Secretary submitted during oral evidence that 78 Sagarmala 
scheme-funded projects valued at Rs. 5,355 crore have been completed, and 50 projects 
worth approximately Rs. 3,500 crore are under implementation. The Committee note the 
distinction between the broader Sagarmala programme (839 projects across multiple 
ministries and funding sources) and the projects directly funded through the Ministry's 
Sagarmala scheme allocation, and recommend that future documentation clarify this 
distinction to facilitate accurate monitoring. 
3.1.2 RoPax and passenger ferry services developed under Sagarmala have demonstrated 
measurable impact. The Annual Report records that the Mumbai-Mandwa route reduced 
travel time from 3 hours to 45 minutes, the Ghogha-Hazira route from 9 hours to 
approximately 4 hours, and the Raigad-Ratnagiri distance was shortened by 60 km. These 
services have enabled the movement of over 1 lakh cargo trucks, saving more than 2 crore 
litres of fuel. 
3.1.3 The NMHC at Lothal, approved by the Cabinet on 9th October 2024, has been 
earmarked Rs. 100.88 crore for 2026-27. Five fishing harbours adjacent to Major Ports, 
Kochi, Chennai, Visakhapatnam, Paradip, and Mallet Bunder, have been sanctioned for 
modernisation. 
3.2 Shipbuilding: SBFAS, SbDS, and MDF 
3.2.1 The Ministry, in its written submission to the Committee's questionnaire, provides a 
detailed exposition of the four-pillar strategy approved by Cabinet on 24th September 2025 
to enhance shipbuilding competitiveness. The written submission states that under SBFAS, 
for normal vessels, assistance is 15 per cent up to Rs. 100 crore and 20 per cent on the 
portion above Rs. 100 crore; for specialised, hybrid, and green vessels, the incentive is 15 per 

 
7 
 
cent on the first Rs. 100 crore and 25 per cent on the remaining value. The Maritime 
Development Fund provides Rs. 25,000 crore through a blended-finance structure 
comprising the Maritime Investment Fund (Rs. 20,000 crore for equity support) and the 
Interest Incentivization Fund (Rs. 5,000 crore for reducing borrowing costs). The India Ship 
Technology Centre, with a proposed outlay of Rs. 305 crore under the Indian Maritime 
University, is to serve as the apex body for indigenous design and technological capability. 
The Ministry's depositional notes further record that the total SBFAS corpus up to 2036 is 
Rs. 24,736 crore; that the shipbreaking credit note provides 40 per cent of fair scrap value; 
and that the National Shipbuilding Mission is the designated institutional body to 
coordinate implementation. 
3.2.2 SbDS, with Rs. 19,989 crore, comprises: greenfield cluster development (Rs. 9,930 
crore through 50:50 Centre-State SPVs with 100 per cent capital support for common 
maritime infrastructure); brownfield expansion (Rs. 8,261 crore at 25 per cent capital 
assistance); and shipbuilding risk coverage (Rs. 1,443 crore for pre-shipment, post-
shipment, and vendor default insurance). The Ministry submitted that the scheme intends to 
promote shipbuilding clusters as part of the long-term vision and that government 
assistance is critical given the scale of the required capacity expansion. 
3.2.3 MDF, with Rs. 25,000 crore, provides blended finance through the Maritime 
Investment Fund (Rs. 20,000 crore for equity support at 49 per cent Government equity) 
and the Interest Incentivisation Fund (Rs. 5,000 crore for up to 3 per cent interest subsidy 
through SMFCL). The Committee note that SMFCL has been registered as an NBFC (RBI 
licence 19th June 2025) with an approved borrowing limit of Rs. 25,000 crore and has 
sanctioned Rs. 4,198.10 crore. 
3.2.4 The Annual Report records that Kolkata-based shipyards, GRSE and Hooghly-CSL, 
are integral to the national ecosystem. GRSE has established a training programme covering 
marine welding, structural fitting, electrical work, and pipe fitting, with 25 candidates 
trained per role. Hooghly-CSL, a wholly-owned subsidiary of CSL, operates a state-of-the-art 
facility at Nazirgunge. The Safety Training and Labour Welfare Institute at Alang-Sosiya has 
trained over 1.5 lakh workers in occupational safety and hazardous material handling. 
3.2.5 The Special Secretary submitted during oral evidence that the Ministry has 
undertaken demand aggregation to provide market visibility for shipbuilding. The 
aggregated pipeline encompasses 437 vessels worth over Rs. 2.2 lakh crore, covering PSU 
requirements (including SCI, oil sector PSUs, and DCI), a new container shipping line, and 
dredging orders. The Committee note that demand aggregation addresses a longstanding 
market coordination failure and provides a basis for private investment in shipyard capacity. 
However, the documentation does not specify the region-wise or shipyard-wise distribution 
of anticipated orders, including the share of eastern India's shipyards (GRSE, Hooghly-CSL) 
in the pipeline. 
3.2.6 The Special Secretary further submitted that several States, including Tamil Nadu, 
Andhra Pradesh, and Odisha, are at an advanced stage in identifying greenfield shipbuilding 
cluster sites, with Gujarat and Maharashtra having completed Techno-Feasibility Reports. 

 
8 
 
Tamil Nadu is expected to have a Detailed Project Report ready within two to three months. 
Multiple foreign shipyards, including from South Korea, the Netherlands, and the UAE, are 
in discussions or have signed MoUs with Indian counterparts, both government and private. 
3.3 Inland Water Transport 
3.3.1 The Ministry, in its written submission to the Committee's questionnaire, furnished a 
comprehensive account of IWT progress. On NW-1, the entire 1,390 km stretch from 
Varanasi to Haldia is being developed under JMVP with a Least Available Depth of 2.2/3 
metres and 45-metre bottom width through contract dredging. Sixty community jetties have 
been installed and commissioned on NW-1 for facilitating the general public, farmers, and 
fishermen. The written submission further records that fairway development works are 
under way on NW-2 and NW-16 (32-metre width, 2.0/2.5-metre depth) through DCI, and 
on NW-3 in Kerala (2-metre depth, 32-metre width year-round). The Annual Report records 
that the JMVP has a revised cost of Rs. 4,600.58 crore with World Bank support and targets 
completion by 30th June 2026. The Ministry's depositional notes further record that two 
QPOMs in Uttar Pradesh and Bihar are operational, with 8 more planned by 2027. 
3.3.2 The Committee note with concern the status of the Kalughat Intermodal Terminal on 
NW-1. During oral evidence, a Member raised the issue that the terminal, despite an 
investment of over Rs. 125 crore and approximately five years since the foundation stone was 
laid, has not received a single vessel. Questions were raised regarding the availability of 
navigable water depth at the terminal site, the adequacy of the initial site assessment, the 
role and accountability of the concessionaire (Summit Alliance Port East Gateway (India) 
Private Limited), and whether dredging operations now being undertaken represent an 
additional and avoidable expenditure. The IWAI Chairman acknowledged the issues and 
submitted that dredging has been undertaken through challenge mode, that a customs 
notification under Sections 7 and 8 is awaited to handle Nepal-bound transit cargo, and that 
the Authority would furnish details in writing. The Committee observes that the Kalughat 
case raises systemic questions about the adequacy of hydrological and navigational 
assessment prior to terminal construction on river systems with high sedimentation loads 
and significant seasonal water-level variation. He Committee recommends that the Ministry 
furnish a detailed status report on the Kalughat Intermodal Terminal, including the total 
expenditure incurred, the current navigational status of the approach channel, the terms of 
the concession agreement, and the timeline for operationalisation. 
3.3.3 NW-5 developments in Odisha is planned at Rs. 13,865 crore over 588 km, connecting 
Talcher, Angul, and Kalinga Nagar to Paradip and Dhamra ports. Infrastructure includes 
three terminals (Kakudi, Kurunti, Pankapal), nine weirs with navigation locks, two check 
dams, and two rubber dams, designed for 2,000 DWT vessels with 3.0 m depth and 50 m 
bottom width. Modal shift targets are 11 MT by 2032-33 and 19 MT by 2052-53. During oral 
evidence, a Member raised the possibility of integrating the historic East Coast Canal system 
with NW-5 to reduce capital costs. The IWAI Chairman submitted that a feasibility study 
had identified cross-structures and encroachments on the canal, and that the river-based 

 
9 
 
alignment (Brahmani and Kharsua) was being prioritised in the first phase, with the canal 
option to be examined subsequently. 
3.3.4 The Ministry's depositional notes record plans for Regional Centres of Excellence at 
Varanasi and Dibrugarh, each on 12 acres, training 5,400 personnel annually across vessel 
operations, terminal management, dredging, hydrography, river engineering, and navigation 
systems. The Ship Repair Ecosystem at Varanasi and Patna is to include transfer bays, hoist 
cranes, workshops, and fabrication units. The IWAI Chairman clarified during oral evidence 
that these facilities are intended for inland vessel repair rather than ocean-going ship repair, 
and that the nomenclature 'ship repair' is a misnomer. The facilities are necessitated by the

3.3.5 The Jalvahak Cargo Promotion Scheme, launched December 2024, offers incentives of

movements with 17.29 million TKM of cargo. The Ministry's depositional notes record that 
an MoU with Rhenus Logistics envisages deployment of 100 vessels and pusher tugs across 
NW-1, NW-2, NW-16 and IBP routes, with 20 barges and 6 pusher tugs in the first phase. 
3.3.6 The Ministry's depositional notes record that river cruise tourism reached 443 voyages 
in 2024-25 across 17 circuits spanning 9 States. The Ministry's written submission to the 
Committee's questionnaire records that 17 circuits are operational across 15 National 
Waterways. Cruise terminals are proposed at Varanasi, Bishwanath Ghat, Patna, and 
Neamati Ghat. The Annual Report records that Hooghly-CSL has signed contracts for 
construction of luxury cruise vessels for Heritage River Journeys, and that Viking Cruises is 
preparing to launch luxury services on the Brahmaputra. NW operations extend to the Indo-
Bangladesh Protocol route. NW-73 (Narmada River) is operational with two concrete jetties 
sanctioned. The IWAI Chairman submitted during oral evidence that cruise services on the 
Narmada between the Statue of Oneness (Madhya Pradesh) and Statue of Unity (Gujarat) 
are planned, with IWAI's jetties ready and State Government terminal construction 
underway. 
3.3.7 On the issue of North-Eastern waterways, a Member submitted during oral evidence 
that the major tributaries of the Brahmaputra originating in Arunachal Pradesh, including 
the Kameng, Subansiri, Siang, Dibang, Lohit, and Tirap, should be considered for waterway 
development. The Member highlighted that large hydropower projects under construction in 
Arunachal Pradesh (including a 2,800 MW dam on the Dibang and over 16,000 MW 
planned on the Siang) would require waterway transport for over-dimensional cargo 
equipment that cannot be moved by road or rail. The Member also raised the potential of the

Pasighat. The IWAI Chairman submitted that a navigability feasibility study would need to 
be conducted before tributaries can be added as National Waterways, and that the Authority 
would examine the proposals. The Committee observes that these submissions merit serious 

 
10 
 
attention, given the scale of hydropower investment in the North-Eastern region and the
