FRISKING
The Committee was informed that at the Indian airports, manual frisking is carried out for each and every passenger,
 instead of using sophisticated modern equipments.  Consequently, the passengers at the airports have to wait for a long
 time in a queue for their security check.  The Committee recommends that the security arrangements for frisking should
 be thoroughly modernised so that dependence on manual checking is reduced to the minimum.  Placing more reliance
 on modern security equipments would expedite security checks and reduce long waiting time and congestion outside
 the security hold areas.  Security personnel carrying out physical search should be friendly and courteous.
HAJ TERMINAL
During its visit to the Indira Gandhi International Airport at Delhi, the Committee visited the newly constructed Haj
 Terminal.  The Committee was informed that the Terminal would serve as a single point area for the departure and
 arrival of Haj Pilgrims.  The Committee noted that outside the terminal, there were no sheds/tents for taking rest by the
 relatives who had come to receive and see off the Haj pilgrims.  The Committee also noted that there was lack of basic
 facilities like drinking water, toilets, canteen etc. outside the Terminal.
The Committee appreciates the construction of a new Haj Terminal at Delhi by the Airports Authority of India for the
 benefit of Haj pilgrims.  The Committee feels that the new Haj Terminal would help in smooth and expeditious
 clearance of Haj pilgrims.  The Government may explore the possibility of having such Haj Terminals catering to Haj
 flights at other airports also.  However, the Committee recommends that some shed etc. may be constructed outside the

ETIQUETTES, BEHAVIOUR AND TRAINING OF THE STAFF
It has come to the notice of the Committee that the officials deputed at immigration & customs counter generally behave
 rudely with the passengers.  This type of behavior does not go well with the tourists and creates an unpleasant
 atmosphere.  Today national/international airports are gateways of any country.  The passenger/tourist gets first
 impression of a particular country at the airport itself, which represents the culture and society of any country, as the
 immigration counter is the first point of contact for any traveller.    A pleasant smile and courteous behavior of the
 airport officials can give a sense of relief to a person tired from the journeys.  The Committee, therefore, recommends
 that officials deputed at the airports, especially at the immigration/custom counters should be strictly asked to be
 courteous and behave good mannerly with the passengers.  The Committee is of the view that this could be done only
 by constant training and strict supervision.  A regular training, based on latest managerial and behaviour modules
 developed by consultants of national repute, should be imparted to the officials in dealing with the passengers/tourists
 to make them more tourists friendly.  The officials so trained would be better equipped to welcome the tourists with a

 smile on their faces.  This would go a long way in creating a courteous atmosphere at the Airports.
 
TRANSPORT SYSTEM AT THE AIRPORT
During its interaction with the tours and travel operators, the Committee was apprised that when a passenger lands at the
 Airport he has to face a lot of problem in hiring Transport.  It was noticed by the Committee that pre-paid taxi counters
 had not been opened at some of the Airports.  If a counter is there, adequate number of taxis are not available to the
 passengers.  Taxis that are available at the airport are of 20-35 years old and are in bad condition.  Old people, ladies
 with children always face problem in getting taxis as they are not in a position to run with their baggage.  There is no
 display board mentioning the rates to be charged for various destinations, which always leaves the possibility of
 cheating, specially with the foreigners.  Taxi drivers are generally without uniform and identity badges. 
 Passengers/tourists are some times forcefully stopped and looted by the private taxi owners.  Sometimes passengers are
 not allowed to reach pre-paid taxi counters.  The Committee also noted that most of the Airports do not have their own
 carrier facilities for the passengers to reach their destination/airport.  The Committee was informed that AAI are
 running free buses for inter-terminals movements for passengers.  However, for their journeys outside the airports, it is
 done by other public transports or taxi services.
The Committee, therefore, recommends that pre-paid taxi counters at the airports should be increased and opened at all
 the airports in the country where this facility is not available.  The Government should make it compulsory that all the
 taxis, which operate at the airports, should be neat, clean and in good condition.  There should also be facility of air-
conditioned taxis for those passengers who prefer this mode of transport.  It should also be made compulsory for the taxi
 drivers to wear uniform and show their identity badges/names on the dress.  More counters of pre-paid taxis should be
 opened to avoid rush at one place and a queue system should be introduced and preference should be given to old
 people/ladies with children. Some police personnel should also be deputed at the prepaid taxi stands to ensure that the
 queue system functions properly.  A rate-list showing charges for various destinations within the city should be
 prominently displayed at the prepaid taxi counters.  A mechanism should be developed whereby the private taxis
 operating at the airports are not able to overcharge/cheat the passengers.  Private taxi owners should not be allowed
 inside the airport.  The Committee also suggests that AAI itself should make some arrangement for providing bus
 services at the minimum charges from the airport to the city.
The Committee has also been informed that parking area is not well connected with the arrival/departure halls at the
 airports.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that these areas should be well connected.
 
DUTY FREE SHOPS
The Committee noted that most of our airports are very congested and duty free shops at our international airports are
 limited in number with limited stock of items and there is also not enough space for the shopkeepers to demonstrate
 their wares. The Committee is of the view that since the shopping areas are earning a lot of money for the AAI, they
 should be given enough space to display their items.  The Committee desires that number of duty free shops should be
 increased and these shops should also have items of Indian handicrafts.  The Committee feels that at Indian airports
 there is a lot of potential to generate revenue from non-aeronautical sources and that a conscious effort should be made
 towards increasing the share of commercial revenue by fully exploiting the commercial potential of the airports.
 
CIVIC AMENITIES AT THE AIRPORTS
It has come to the notice of the Committee that there is utter lack of civic amenities like toilets, drinking water etc. at the
 airports.  The cleanliness and hygienic conditions of these places are not up to the mark and these are not being
 maintained properly.  It is noted that the officials working at the airports also use the same toilets, which are meant for
 the passengers/tourist.  The Committee was also informed that the toilet facilities are not available outside the
 arrival/departure halls of the airports.  Persons who come to receive/see off their clients/guests experience difficulty due
 to the absence of toilets outside the arrival/departure lounge.  Lack of toilet facility at car/taxi parking area outside the
 Airports also creates inconvenience.  Drivers are using the open space for toilet purpose as a result of which the whole
 parking area stinks. The Committee, therefore, recommends that there should be separate toilets for the officials
 working at the airports.  The Committee also recommends that toilet facilities are also to be provided outside the
 arrival/departure lounge and parking areas in order to avoid inconvenience to the persons who visit the airports to
 receive/see off their near and dear ones.  There should always be one or two persons on duty for proper cleaning of
 these places and regular inspection of these areas should be carried out for their proper maintenance.
 
TOUT PROBLEM

Tout menace at the airports is one of the major problems.  At almost all the airports, they are exploiting the people.  As
 soon as the passengers/tourists arrive at the airport, the touts surround and misguide them by giving all sort of wrong
 information.  Sometimes they even take them to far away places and grab all their valuable belongings and leave them
 to their fate.  This creates a bad image of the country.  The issue of tout menace is of prime concern and is reported
 from time to time on the city side area under the jurisdiction of Airport Police Station.  AAI has no direct control to
 prevent the touting on the city side.  The matter is discussed regularly in the Airport Security Committee Meetings of
 which Dy. Commissioner of Police (Airport Security) is the convenor.  AAI has taken various steps to educate/caution
 the passengers by displaying notice boards and informing various facilities available over CCTV monitors.  Free inter-
terminal shuttle coach facility has also been provided to passengers for their inter-connecting flights.  Further, the
 airlines are also operating similar services between terminals, besides pre-paid taxi services and car rental services, to
 prevent the passengers from touts.  AAI will also be interacting with the State Governments to tackle this menace.
The Committee recommends that to overcome the problem of touts, special teams should be constituted which may
 conduct surprise checks on a daily basis.  The Committee further recommends that like Railways, which have their own
 Railways Protection Force, AAI can also have their own airport protection force to look into this problem.
 
VISA ON ARRIVAL
The Committee understands that in many countries facility for stamping the visa are made available to foreign tourists at
 the respective airports on arrival.  Since the Indian Embassy offices are situated at far away places in many countries,
 the foreign tourists have to travel very long distances to obtain visas to visit India.  Distance has acted as a disincentive
 to visit India.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should explore the possibility of
 introducing the facility of granting visa to visiting foreign tourists on arrival at the International Airports.
 
MEETING AND GREETING AREA
Many relatives/friends come to the airports to see off/receive their near and dear one, which creates congestion at the
 airport.  It has come to the notice of the Committee that most of the airports lack facility relating to the meeting and
 greeting place where people could meet a person to whom they have come to receive and see off.  It has also come to
 the notice of the Committee that passengers remain unaware of the friends/relatives who have come to the airport to
 meet and receive them.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that Airports Authority of India should create meeting
 and greeting area facility at all the airports where people can receive and see off their friends/relatives.  In addition to a
 computerised information centre, facility for a message desk should also be provided at the airports so that the
 incoming passengers get the information that somebody is waiting for them.
 
‘MAY I HELP YOU’ COUNTER
A passenger can have some problems at the airport regarding visa, custom or requires some information related to delay
 flights etc., for which they look here and there. The Committee noted during discussion that such counters are not
 available at the airport.  The Committee, therefore, suggests that all the international airports in the country should open
 ‘May I Help You’ counters round the clock and an official should be present at these counters.  It would certainly give
 the impression that this country is welcoming the passengers/tourists.
 
AEROBRIDGES
Today, aerobridges at the airports are needed not only from the security point of view but also for the convenience of
 the passengers.  It was noticed by the Committee that even some of the major airports in the country are not equipped
 with the aerobridges.  In Delhi, at the Domestic Airport, there are no aerobridges and the passengers have to walk
 through or travel in bus after the flight lands.  It was also noted that aerobridges were not being fully utilised at the
 airports or remain inoperational over a considerable period due to lack of adequate maintenance facilities.   Therefore,
 the Committee, keeping in view the security reasons and the convenience of the passengers, recommends that Airports
 Authority of India should give preference to build aerobridges at all the major airports in the country.  Wherever the
 aerobridges are lying dysfunctional, they should be made operational and put to use.
 
MEDICAL FACILITIES
Medical facilities at the airports are primary requirement now a day.  Most of the airports in the country do not have first
 aid facility to be used in case of need.  The Committee understands that there have been cases of death at the airports
 due to the absence of medical facilities.  Therefore, the Committee recommends that medical aid counters/chemists
 shops should be made available at all the airports where passengers can be treated in case of emergency and buy

During its interaction with the Tour & Travel operators, the Committee was informed that no separate counter is
 available to the tour operators at the airport so as to provide detailed information about the availability of the hotels and
 tourist spots in a particular city.  The Committee is of the view that a separate counter should be made available at the
 airports to all the three prominent operators i.e. (i) Hotel and Restaurant Federation of India (ii) Tour Operators
 Association of India and (iii) Indian Association of Tour Operators where all sorts of information regarding hotels,
 tariff, reservation of rooms and other facilities could be provided to the needy passengers/tourists.  However, during its
 visit to the Indira Gandhi International Airport, the Committee found that although tourist information assistance
 counters had already been made available, no officials were present there.  The Committee took it very seriously and
 observed that once the Airports Authority of India provides the space for some useful purpose, that purpose should be
 achieved.  The Committee is of the view that some officials should always be present at these counters so that
 necessary information is provided to the tourists and that they are not harassed/misled by selfish minds.
 
TRANSIT PASSENGERS
Today transit passengers are major sufferer of delay or cancellation of flights.  To catch the connecting flight a
 passenger has to wait from half an hour to forty-eight hours.  A passenger who lands at the airport after one journey and
 has to catch another flight needs facilities like lockers, rest-room, bathroom, restaurant etc. It has been noticed by the
 Committee that no locker facility is provided at the airports for these passengers in the name of security.  At some of
 the airports no rest room and bathroom is available to these transit passengers.  The Committee recommends that
 restrooms, along with bathrooms, should be provided to the transit passengers at all the airports.  As regards the locker
 facility the Committee suggests that such a facility could be provided outside the Main Terminal Building at the airport
 to overcome the problem of security.
 
PROPER SIGNBOARDS
Proper signboards, guiding the passengers as to how to go and where to go after check in, are not available at most of
 the airports.  The Committee is of the view that there should be proper signboards inside the airport, beautifully
 decorated to attract the passenger and to show them the right way.  One person from each organisation like custom,
 immigration, security etc. should always be available at the halls in the airport so that in case of any difficulty the
 passenger could contact him.
 
LUGGAGE TROLLEYS
The Committee understands that sufficient numbers of trolleys are not available at most of the airports.  Passengers face
 a lot of difficulties in transporting their luggage, as they have to wait for these trolleys.  It has also been brought to the
 notice of the Committee that the trolleys available at the airports have also not been designed keeping in mind the
 requirement of the passengers.  It is very difficult for passengers to keep their luggage in the presently available
 trolleys.  Therefore, the Committee recommends that AAI should look into the matter of providing sufficient number of
 spacious luggage trolleys.

        Tourism is not only a major social  phenomenon of the modern society with enormous economic
 consequences but also  the world’s largest export industry, which accounts for about 8% of the total
 world’s exports, more than 30% of international trade in services, 10.7% of the  global work force and
 about 12% of world GDP.   It is also dubbed as the ‘Largest Smokeless Industry’ and contributes
 towards preservation of clean environment.
 2.Tourism is presently India’s second  largest net foreign exchange earning export industry after
 textiles/garments.  The estimated foreign exchange earning during January to December 99 were
 $2916.01 millions as compared to $2819.62 millions during the same period of  1998 showing an
 increase of 3.4%. Foreign tourist arrival has gone upto 2471848  during 1999 registering a growth of
 4.8% as compared to 1998.
 3.Tourism is of a particular significance  so far as India is concerned since it contributes to the
 environment and to the  national integration as it helps in the interaction amongst social and cultural
 lives of the people.   Over 160 million domestic  tourists visiting different parts of the country every
 year return with a  better understanding of the people living in the other regions of the country  and the
 cultural diversity of India.
 4.Tourism not only has the capacity to  generate large-scale employment opportunities in remote and
 backward areas but  also provides employment to a large number of women, both educated and
 uneducated.   In fact women are employed  in a large number in hotels, airlines services, travel agencies,
 handicrafts making, cultural and other tourism-related activities.
 5.The Ministry of Tourism functions as the  nodal agency for development of tourism in the country by
 coordinating and  supplementing the efforts of the State/Union Territory Governments, catalysing
 private investment, strengthening promotional and market efforts and in  providing trained manpower
 resources.
 6.The Ministry of Tourism has under its administrative control the following public sector
 undertaking/autonomous bodies:-
a)  India Tourism Development Corporation Limited;
b) National Council for Hotel Management and Catering  Technology;
 c) Indian Institute of Tourism & Travel Management;
d) Institutes of Hotel Management, Catering Technology and  Applied Nutrition at different locations in
 the country;
e)  Food Craft Institutes at different locations;
f)   Indian Institute of Skiing & Mountaineering;
g) National Institute of Water Sports.
 7.In  addition to the Head-quarters Organisation at New Delhi, the Directorate  General of Tourism has
 21 tourism offices in India and 18 tourist offices overseas.
 8. Demand No.82, containing the details of  budget allocations of Ministry of Tourism for the financial
 year 2000-2001, was considered by the Department-Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on
 Transport & Tourism at its meeting held on the 23rd March 2000.
 9. The details of the plan allocations approved for the Ministry of Tourism for the last four years of the
 plan period  are as under:-

10.     From a perusal of the Demands for Grants of  the Ministry of Tourism for 2000-2001, the
 Committee found that plan outlay of  the Ministry for the year 1999-2000 had been reduced from
 Rs.160.50 crores to  Rs.110 crores at RE stage.   Also the  plan outlay for the year 2000-2001 has been
 kept at Rs.135.00 crores which is less by Rs.24.50 crores as compared to BE for the year 1999-2000.
 11.     On being asked about the reasons for  reduction of plan outlay for 1999-2000 at RE stage and
 lower BE for the year  2000-2001, the Ministry of Tourism have stated that due to resource  constraints,
 not only BE 1999-2000 has been reduced but also proposed budget  allocation for the year 2000-2001
 has been subjected to drastic cut and the  Planning Commission has approved allocation of Rs.135.00
 crores only. The  Government    has neither been able to  enhance its own investment in the tourism
 sector nor mobilise private  investment to the desired extent due to the capital structure of industry,
 longer gestation period, low rates of return and certain infrastructural and  procedural problems.
 12.    The Committee has been  consistently recommending not to reduce the plan outlay of the Ministry
 at RE  stage. Moreover, while examining the Demands for Grants 1999-2000, the Committee  in its 37th
 Report had specially recommended a proportionate or at  least 20% increase over the previous year’s
 budget allocations.   However, to the surprise of the Committee,  plan outlay of Rs.135 crores has been
 approved for the year 2000-2001 against  the BE of Rs.160.5 crores for the last year.
 13.    The  Committee further observed that out of Rs.135.00 crores for the year 2000-2001,  Rs.49.75
 crores have been allocated for overseas campaign, thereby leaving only  Rs.85.25 crores for Human
 Resource Development, Tourist Infrastructure and  Domestic Campaign etc. in the country.
 14.         Tourism has a huge potential of employment opportunity in  rural and backward areas without
 causing migration to distant places, foreign  exchange earning industry, a tool for sustainable human
 development including  poverty alleviation, environmental conservation and regeneration, job creation
 and advancement of women and other disadvantaged groups.
 15.    The  Committee, therefore, again recommends that adequate funds be made available to  the
 Ministry of Tourism and there should be no reduction in the plan outlay at  RE stage.   The
 Committee is of the view that an amount Rs.85.25 crores is not sufficient to meet the requirement
 for  Domestic Campaign, Tourist Infrastructure, Training (Human Resource  Development) and
 other Expenditure and recommends that it should be increased at RE stage.
16.    The Committee is also concerned to note  that the Government policy has so far not been able to
 attract the private  investment in tourism sector to the desired extent.   The Committee is of the view that
 the Government alone, through  its limited resources, will not be able to meet the requirements of funds
 for  proper development of tourism sector.   The Committee, therefore, further  recommends that the
 Government, while acting as a facilitator and coordinator  and encouraging involvement of private
 sector in the development of tourism,  should take steps to remove the infrastructural and
 procedural hurdles which the private sector has to face and ensure the availability of land,
 electricity, water supply, sewerage system and do away with the multiplicity of  permits and
 approvals.
17.    The Committee notes that as against the  proposed outlay of Rs.5370 for the 9th Plan Period, only a
 minuscule  amount of Rs.485.75 crores was approved.   The Committee also notes that the Ministry of
 Tourism has so far been  allocated Rs.455.46 crores out of the total plan outlay of Rs.485.75 for the
 entire 9th Five Year Plan period. Now about Rs.30.29 crores remain  for the last financial year of the
 9th Plan Period i.e.  2001-2002.   The Committee feels that  this amount of Rs.30.29 crores would not be
 sufficient for the implementation  of various schemes already under consideration of the Ministry of
 Tourism.   The  Committee, therefore, recommends for substantial enhancement of the Plan Outlay
 of the Ministry of Tourism for the year 2001-2002 and that Planning Commission and Ministry of
 Finance should intimate the Ministry of Tourism about the  quantum of plan outlay well in
 advance, so that Ministry of Tourism may be able  to project its demands properly for the year
 2001-2002.  
CENTRAL ASSISTANCE FOR  TOURISM INFRASTRUCTURE & PRODUCT DEVELOPMENT  
18.     Since most of the tourist attractions and delivery systems are  within the purview of State/UT
 Governments, a large part of the Central  Government investment for the improvement and creation of
 tourist facilities is channelised through the State Governments on a cost-sharing basis.   In order to
 ensure integrated development of  tourism infrastructure including basic amenities and other facilities,
 the  Ministry of Tourism provides assistance to State/Union Territory Governments for the
 implementation of composite projects.   A total amount of Rs.29.10 crores has been allocated under this
 Head which  includes Rs.18 crores for integrated development of Tourist/Pilgrim Centres,  Special

 Tourism Areas, Major Tourism Projects, setting up of Paryatan Bhawan  etc., Rs.6.75 crores for
 development of facilities for domestic tourists such  as Budget Accommodation, Wayside Facilities etc.,
 Rs.4.10 crores for Product  Development such as refurbishment of monuments, Sound and Light
 Shows/Flood  Lighting, Adventure Tourism etc. and Rs.25 lakh for Externally Aided Projects.
 19.Central assistance for infrastructure development is provided  to the States based on two types of
 funding patterns – (1) Normal Funding and  (2) Equity Scheme.   The most popular  pattern of funding,
 which has been continuing over successive plan periods, is the normal funding. The Ministry of
 Tourism almost meets the entire expenditure  except the cost of land and interior decoration in the
 construction  projects.   A new method of funding,  namely ‘Equity Scheme’, had been introduced during
 1992-93 in which the  assistance from the Ministry of Tourism is limited to 28% of the project  cost.  
 12% of the project cost is to be  provided by the State Government/Union Territory and the balance 60%
 has to be  raised as loan from financial institutions/banks.   This method of funding is applicable to
 bankable projects requiring large investments.

 22.     The Committee had, in its 37th report on the Demands for Grants (1999-2000) of the Ministry of
 Tourism, identified the condition of  transferring the title of the land from State Government to the
 Government of  India as one of the major bottlenecks resulting in delay in the completion of  projects
 and had recommended the waiving off of this condition for development  of tourism in the country.   The
 Ministry  has informed that the Ministry of Urban Affairs & Employment, and also  Planning
 Commission, have supported the waiving of the condition of  transferring the title of land to
 Government of India.   The Ministry of Finance, however, has agreed  to substitute the condition of
 transfer of land by long-term lease.   However, many States have expressed their  reservation even on
 this requirement.   The Committee, therefore, recommends that  the matter may be taken up with
 the concerned State Government and the Ministry  of Finance to sort it out expeditiously so as to
 arrive at an amicable solution and the funds earmarked for implementation of various projects
 under this scheme are fully utilised without any further delay.  
23.      The Committee was also  informed that the State Governments are reluctant to approach Ministry
 of  Tourism for funds under the Equity Scheme since they have to share 12% of the  project cost and
 have also to obtain funds from financial institutions on loan  basis.   The Committee feels that the
 scheme is not bearing the desired fruits since it has not been able to encourage the participation
 of the States.   The Committee, therefore, recommends that in view of the indifferent attitude of
 the States, the viability of the scheme may  be reassessed since it is leading to non-utilisation of
 funds every year.   The Government should also try to modify the  scheme, in consultation with the
 State Governments, so that it becomes more  acceptable to the States and encourage their
 participation in this centrally  assisted financial scheme.  
SETTING UP OF PARYATAN BHAWAN
24.     The Committee has been informed that the Government proposes to  construct Bharat Paryatan
 Bhawan in Delhi for which 10870 sq. meters of land  has been allotted by the Ministry of Urban
 Development in Connaught Place area.  A token provision of Rs.1 crore has been made for this purpose

REPORT
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/41streport.htm[28-08-2018 12:45:04]
 in the BE  2000-2001. This Bhawan will house tourist information and booking offices of  all the State
 Governments, Airlines, Railways, Travel Agents, tour Operators,  Foreign Exchange Dealer(s), Bank(s),
 Post Office, Restaurant etc.   The proposed Bhawan will also house the  offices of the Ministry of
 Tourism, Government of India.   Besides facilitating tourists, such a  facility will also be useful for
 business promotion as prospective investors and businessmen visiting the country can obtain all the
 details at a single  place.   The Government of India, it is envisaged, would only be required to pay the
 cost of Land (Rs.22.44 crores) to  Ministry Urban Development as per their demand letter.   Remaining
 part of the project would be  set-up on a self-financing basis. The  Committee appreciates the plan for

 and integrate the services in the tourism sector.   The Committee  feels that the plan will help in
 improvement of facilitation and information services to tourists who have to visit a number of
 offices located in different  parts of the city to gather information and for booking air and rail
 tickets,  package tours, accommodation etc.   Bringing all these facilities under one roof will be of
 immense use to  the tourists.   The Committee, therefore,  recommends that the detailed project
 report for Bharat Paryatan Bhawan may be  completed soon so that the work for the actual
 construction may begin at the  earliest.

25.     The Ministry of Tourism allocates funds every year to the State  Governments for creating wayside
 amenities for tourists.   These include tourist reception centres,  restaurants/cafeterias, drinking water
 facilities, public conveniences, kiosks,  general store and parking area etc. The Ministry of Tourism
 prioritises projects in consultation with the State Governments and release funds on  receipt of the
 specific proposals prioritised during the financial year.   An amount of Rs.4.00 crores has been
 allocated for the purpose during the year 2000-2001.
 26.    The  Committee feels that to keep pace with the fast developing highway tourism in the
 country, a well-knit network of wayside facilities on the roads connecting  important tourist
 centres is a must.   The Committee also feels that the allocation of Rs. 4 crores for wayside
 amenities in the BE 2000-2001 is simply not enough and recommends that the  allocation under
 this head must be increased.   The Government should also explore the possibility of involving the
 participation of private parties/voluntary agencies for the maintenance of  toilet/drinking water
 facilities and other civic amenities created under this scheme.  
PILGRIM TOURISM
27.     The Committee has been informed that for the development of  infrastructure facilities including
 basic amenities in the identified  tourist/pilgrim centres, the Ministry of Tourism has decided to provide
 financial assistance to the State/Union Territory Governments for the  implementation of composite
 projects in 50 selected centres.   The maximum assistance will be Rupees one  cores, subject to matching
 contribution by the State Governments, and it will  be provided at the rate of Rs.50 lakh for a period of
 two years.   The Ministry of Tourism has decided to set  up a ‘Pilgrim Tourism Development Board’ to
 advise the Ministry in all matters relating to Pilgrim Tourism.
28.    The  Committee is of the view that in India, there are a large number of pilgrim centres and if
 basic amenities/facilities are provided to the tourists/pilgrims, it  will encourage the arrival of the
 tourists at these places.   The Committee recommends that the ‘Pilgrim  Tourism Development
 Board’ may be set up immediately and the State Governments may be requested to provide the
 matching financial contributions so that  development work may take place at the selected tourist
 centres in their States on priority basis.        
MEGA-TOURISM PROJECTS/SPECIAL TOURISM AREAS 
29.     Mega Tourism  projects have brought revolution in tourism sector in Maxico and Indonesia and
 tourist arrivals have gone up substantially there.   In India an ambitious scheme for identification and
 development  of ‘Special Tourism Areas’, also known as “Mega Tourism Projects”, was taken up  during
 Eighth Plan period.   The State  Governments of Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Orissa and Maharashtra and Union
 Territory  Administration of Daman and Diu declared Bekal Beach (Kerala), Puri-Konark Area  (Orissa),
 Sindhudurg (Maharashtra), Muttukadu-Mamallapuram (Tamil Nadu) and Diu  as Special Tourism Area
 for integrated development.   The intensive development of these areas was envisaged in  coordination
 with the concerned State Governments and private sector.   The Ministry of Tourism has proposed an

 Resorts Corporation.   A Master  Plan for the development of the area has been prepared and land

 Special Tourism  Area.   The Central Ministry of Tourism  has prioritised a project for the preparation of
 the Master Plan of Puri as a  Special Tourism Area.   The State  Government of Tamil Nadu constituted a
 State Level Authority for setting up a  Special Tourism Area in the Muttukadu-Mamallapuram Beach.  
 The State Government is yet to prepare the  Master Plan for which the Central Ministry of Tourism has
 agreed to provide  financial assistance.
31.    The Committee is disappointed with the slow pace of work being done in respect of Special
 Tourism Areas. Most of the  projects are still in the planning stage.   The Committee finds that
 most of the State Governments have not even completed the necessary formalities.   The concept of
 a Mega Tourism project was coined in the 8th Plan Period.   Now three years of the 9th Plan are
 already over.   Only the  Government of Kerala has done something appreciable in the direct
 implementation of the project.    The  performance of the other State Governments has not been
 satisfactory.  
32.    The Committee, therefore, recommends that the  Ministry of Tourism may take up the matter
 with the concerned State Governments extensively as well as intensively underlining the
 importance of Mega Tourism  Projects and request them to priorities the action with regard to
 these  projects.   The Committee also recommends that the States whose performance has been

HERITAGE HOTELS
33.     An amount of Rs.2 crores has been allocated for Heritage  Hotels/refurbishment of
 monuments/Heritage sites.   The concept of Heritage Hotels was introduced with a view to  convert the
 old palaces, havelies, castles, forts and residences built prior to  1950 into accommodation units as
 these traditional structures reflect the  ambience and life-style of the bygone era and are immensely
 popular with the  tourists.   The Committee was informed  that till the end of September 99, as many as
 62 properties have been classified  as Heritage Hotels providing a room capacity of 1816 rooms.   At
 present, 53 heritage properties are  approved as projects, which on completion would add 1188 rooms in
 the heritage  category.   The Heritage Hotels outside  the metropolitan areas are eligible for interest
 subsidy @ 5% in respect of  loans from Central and State financial institutions.  
34.    The  Committee appreciates the concept of Heritage Hotels introduced by the Ministry  of
 Tourism and feels that these hotels can serve as a good instrument for  promoting tourism.   The
 Committee,  therefore, recommends that the concept of Heritage Hotels should be promoted more
 intensively so as to ensure that old properties, which are landmarks of  our heritage, are not lost
 due to decay but become financially viable  properties providing additional room capacity for the
 tourists.  
HUMAN RESOURCE  DEVELOPMENT
35.     A major responsibility of the Central Government is Human  Resource Development to meet the
 needs of tourism industry.   It can be achieved by creating the necessary  institutional infrastructure for

 Head “Training (Manpower and Catering  Institutional Development)”.   This includes an allocation of
 Rs.9.10 crores for Hotel Management and Catering  Institutes and Food Crafts Institute, Rs.2 crores for
 Indian Institute of  Tourism & Travel Management, Rs.5 crores for Tourism Education Grid, Rs.50  lakh
 for National Institute of Water Sports and Rs.5 lakh for other programmes.   The existing facilities
 include the following:-

36.         Trained/skilled manpower is essential  for attaining quality and efficiency in service.   Ministry
 of Tourism has set up 21 institutes of Hotel Management  and 13 Food Craft Institutes in different part

 objective of providing the  trained manpower towards meeting the requirements of the accommodation
 and  catering industry to produce a professional work force.   The total turn out of all the hotel and
 catering technology schools in India is about 7,000 students per year as against the actual requirement
 of 20,000 persons per year.   Thus, a huge gap is anticipated between the  supply and demand of the
 trained manpower in this sector.   The Committee was informed that the Ministry  has commissioned a
 manpower survey through National Council for Hotel  Management and Catering Technology to
 determine the qualitative and  quantitative requirement of the trained manpower in the country.   The
 Council will also assess the capacity of  the private institutes for providing the trained manpower.
37.     The Committee was informed that in order to  strengthen the existing training infrastructure, the

 and Headquarters of National Council for Hotel  Management and Catering Technology at NOIDA.   An
 allocation of Rs.5 crores has been made in BE 2000-2001 for the proposed  Grid.   The entire complex
 will be designed  in such a manner that certain common facilities such as the library, computer  centre
 and other amenities will be utilised by the faculty and students of  different disciplines.   The National
 Culinary Institute will provide training to chefs, with special emphasis on  research and documentation
 of variety of Indian cuisine and food production  whereas the Advance Hotel Management Institute will
 focus on advanced  management training for the hotel and hospitality industry.  
38.      The Committee feels that the  availability of trained manpower is an essential pre-requisite
 for promoting  any tourist destination.   The Committee  hopes that the Grid will produce highly
 skilled manpower for hospitality and travel industry for specialised functions and upgrade the
 qualities of the  tourism product in order to make India a competitive tourist destination in all
 respects and thus help in promoting tourism to the country.   The Committee recommends that all
 necessary  steps should be taken to complete the project as per schedule and it should not  be
 allowed to suffer due to non-availability of funds.  
39.    The  Committee takes note of the various steps being taken by the Government to  increase the
 availability of trained manpower by expanding the infrastructure  of Institutes of Hotel
 Management and setting up of new Food Craft  Institutes.   However, the Committee is of the view
 that due to the paucity of funds, the efforts made by the  Government will not be sufficient to
 bridge the gap between the demand and supply of trained manpower and therefore, the private
 sector has to play an important role in this regard.   The  Committee takes exception to the fact
 that the Government is not aware of the  capacity of the private institutes to provide the trained
 manpower in this sector.     The Committee feels that in the absence of such data, the  Government
 will not be able to devise proper strategy to meet the requirement  of trained manpower.  
 Recognising the role  of private sector in providing the trained manpower, the Committee
 recommends that the assessment regarding capacity of private institutes to provide trained
 manpower should be made at the earliest.   The Committee also recommends that the Government
 should evolve  attractive packages for ensuring greater involvement of private sector in this field.  
40.     The Committee has been informed that the  various Institutes of Hotel Management and Food Craft

 create an institutional development fund from the additional resources generated by them so that they

 depend on budgetary resources. Efforts are being made to increase the intake of the Institutes upto an

A perusal of the above data indicates that on the one hand there has been  under utilisation of funds in

45.    The attention of Ministry of Tourism was drawn to the fact that the share of India in world
 tourism arrivals and world  tourism receipts was only 0.38% & 0.39% and 0.68% and 0.71% during
 1996 and  1997 respectively, which does not commensurate with the amount and efforts spent on tourist
 offices abroad and overseas campaign.   Ministry of Tourism informed that Tourist  Offices overseas
 basically do promotional activities and that the expenditure  incurred on these offices does not
 necessarily reflect corresponding  increase/fall in tourist arrival.   The  Committee was also informed that
 the Ministry had also commissioned a study  through the World Tourism Organisation (WTO) to
 evaluate the Marketing  strategies of the overseas offices.   Two  of the main recommendations of the
 WTO Report were:-  
(i)          Review location of offices keeping in mind marketing potential.
(ii)        Management of overseas offices.  
46.    The  Committee is of the view that substantial portions of the total budgetary  allocations of
 the Ministry of Tourism are being provided for overseas campaign since the last few years.  
 However, the  net increase in number of foreign tourists does not justify the high amount of
 allocations in this sector.   The  contention of the Ministry of Tourism delinking the performance of
 tourist offices abroad from  the increase/fall in foreign tourist arrival in India does not hold good.  
 Without any correlation between the two, it  would be very difficult to assess the performance of
 the tourist offices abroad and review their location keeping in mind marketing potential, as
 recommended by  the WTO report.   In view of the huge allocations made in this area, the
 Committee recommends that cost benefit ratio in respect  of each overseas office should be worked
 out and these offices should be made  accountable for the foreign tourist arrival in India.   The
 Government should also explore the possibility of utilising  the services of professional agencies
 abroad to boost the image of India as tourist destination instead of having separate tourist offices
 overseas.   The Committee recommends that immediate  necessary action may be taken upon all the
 recommendations of the World Tourism  Organisations and the action taken upon them may be
 brought to the notice of  the Committee.
ECO-TOURISM 
47.         Today eco-tourism is being promoted as a  means of ‘giving nature value’ and hence of
 achieving ‘sustainable  development’.   Tourism has contributed  to the protection of natural environment
 and cultural heritage.   The Ministry of Tourism has informed that  they have formulated a
 comprehensive Eco-tourism Policy and guidelines in  consultation with all the concerned agencies.   The
 Committee feels that there are numerous places scattered  throughout the country, such as mountains,
 wildlife and beach resorts, which  hold unlimited varieties of flora and fauna to entertain eco-friendly
 tourists.   The Committee, therefore, recommends that special attention should be  given on the
 development of eco-tourism, which will not only boost tourism but  also help protect landscape,
 fauna and flora from destruction by modern development.   India offers a huge  potential for
 adventure tourism like trekking, mountaineering, river rafting,  winter sports, water sports etc.
 and efforts should also be made to attract  tourists to these places.

48.         Despite abundance of natural beauty,  snow peaked mountains and white water rivers, the flow

50.    The Committee observes that inspite of its geographical location and tremendous potential for

58.    The Committee has failed to understand as to why the Government  has been ignoring such an
 important sector and not providing sufficient funds,  which are required by the Ministry for the
 development of tourism in the  country.   The Committee expresses its anguish over the treatment being

OBSERVATIONS/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS AT  A GLANCE  
The Committee has been consistently recommending  not to reduce the plan outlay of the Ministry at RE
 stage. Moreover, while  examining the Demands for Grants 1999-2000, the Committee in its 37th  Report
 had specially recommended a proportionate or at least 20% increase over  the previous year’s budget
 allocations.   However, to the surprise of the Committee, plan outlay of Rs.135 crores has been
 approved for the year 2000-2001 against the BE of Rs.160.5 crores for  the last year.                         
                                
 (Para 12)  
The Committee further observed  that out of Rs.135.00 crores for the year 2000-2001, Rs.49.75 crores
 have been  allocated for overseas campaign, thereby leaving only Rs.85.25 crores for Human  Resource
 Development, Tourist Infrastructure and Domestic Campaign etc. in the  country.   
         (Para 13)  
The Committee, therefore, again recommends that adequate funds be made available to the Ministry of
 Tourism and  there should be no reduction in the plan outlay at RE stage.   The Committee is of the view
 that an amount  Rs.85.25 crores is not sufficient to meet the requirement for Domestic  Campaign,
 Tourist Infrastructure, Training (Human Resource Development) and  other Expenditure and
 recommends that it should be increased at RE stage.   (Para 15)
 The Committee is also concerned  to note that the Government policy has so far not been able to attract
 the  private investment in tourism sector to the desired extent.   The Committee is of the view that the
 Government alone, through its limited resources, will not be able to meet the  requirements of funds for
 proper development of tourism sector.   The Committee, therefore, further recommends that the
 Government, while acting as a facilitator and coordinator and  encouraging involvement of private
 sector in the development of tourism, should  take steps to remove the infrastructural and procedural
 hurdles which the  private sector has to face and ensure the availability of land, electricity,  water
 supply, sewerage system and do away with the multiplicity of permits and  approvals.  (Para 16)

 utilised without any further delay.The  Committee feels that the scheme is not bearing the desired fruits
 since it has not been able to encourage the participation of the States.   The Committee, therefore,
 recommends that in  view of the indifferent attitude of the States, the viability of the scheme may  be
 reassessed since it is leading to non-utilisation of funds every year.   The Government should also try to
 modify the  scheme, in consultation with the State Governments, so that it becomes more  acceptable to
 the States and encourage their participation in this centrally  assisted financial scheme.
(Paras 22 and 23)
Setting up of Paryatan Bhawan
The Committee appreciates the  plan for the construction of a Paryatan Bhawan and hopes that it would
 promote  uniformity and cohesion and integrate the services in the tourism sector.   The Committee feels
 that the plan will help  in improvement of facilitation and information services to tourists who have to
 visit a number of offices located in different parts of the city to gather  information and for booking air
 and rail tickets, package tours, accommodation  etc.   Bringing all these facilities under  one roof will be
 of immense use to the tourists.   The Committee, therefore, recommends that the detailed project  report
 for Bharat Paryatan Bhawan may be completed soon so that the work for  the actual construction may
 begin at the earliest.              (Para 24)  
Wayside Amenities
The Committee feels that to  keep pace with the fast developing highway tourism in the country, a well-
knit  network of wayside facilities on the roads connecting important tourist centres is a must.   The
 Committee also feels that the allocation of Rs. 4 crores for wayside amenities in the BE 2000-2001  is
 simply not enough and recommends that the allocation under this head must be  increased.   The
 Government should also  explore the possibility of involving the participation of private
 parties/voluntary agencies for the maintenance of toilet/drinking water  facilities and other civic
 amenities created under this scheme.                   
 (Para 26)
Pilgrim Tourism
The Committee is of the view that in India, there are a large number of pilgrim centres and if basic
 amenities/facilities are provided to the tourists/pilgrims, it will encourage  the arrival of the tourists at
 these places.   The Committee recommends that the ‘Pilgrim Tourism Development Board’  may be set

REPORT
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/41streport.htm[28-08-2018 12:45:04]
 up immediately and the State Governments may be requested to provide  the matching financial
 contributions so that development work may take place at  the selected tourist centres in their States on
 priority basis.                        
 (Para 28)
 Mega-Tourism Projects/Special Tourism Areas 
The Committee is disappointed with the slow pace of work being done in  respect of Special Tourism
 Areas. Most of the projects are still in the  planning stage.  The Committee finds that most of the State
 Governments have not even completed the necessary  formalities.   The concept of a Mega  Tourism
 project was coined in the 8th Plan Period.   Now three years of the 9th Plan  are already over.   Only the
 Government  of Kerala has done something appreciable in the direct implementation of the  project.   
 The performance of the other  State Governments has not been satisfactory.  
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Tourism may  take up the matter with the
 concerned State Governments extensively as well as intensively underlining the importance of Mega
 Tourism Projects and request  them to priorities the action with regard to these projects.   The
 Committee also recommends that the  States whose performance has been satisfactory in comparison to
 other States must be provided with higher allocation of funds.              (Paras 31 and 32)   
Heritage Hotels
The Committee appreciates the  concept of Heritage Hotels introduced by the Ministry of Tourism and
 feels that  these hotels can serve as a good instrument for promoting tourism.   The Committee,
 therefore, recommends that  the concept of Heritage Hotels should be promoted more intensively so as
 to  ensure that old properties, which are landmarks of our heritage, are not lost  due to decay but become
 financially viable properties providing additional room  capacity for the tourists.                             
                                       
   (Para 34)
Human Resource Development
The Committee feels that the availability of trained manpower is an essential pre-requisite for
 promoting any tourist destination.   The Committee hopes that the Grid will produce highly skilled
 manpower for hospitality and travel industry for specialised functions and upgrade the qualities of the
 tourism product in order to make India a competitive tourist destination in all respects and thus help in
 promoting tourism to the country.   The Committee  recommends that all necessary steps should be taken
 to complete the project as per schedule and it should not be allowed to suffer due to non-availability of
 funds.  
The  Committee takes note of the various steps being taken by the Government to  increase the
 availability of trained manpower by expanding the infrastructure  of Institutes of Hotel Management and
 setting up of new Food Craft  Institutes.   However, the Committee is of the view that due to the paucity
 of funds, the efforts made by the  Government will not be sufficient to bridge the gap between the
 demand and  supply of trained manpower and therefore, the private sector has to play an  important role
 in this regard.   The  Committee takes exception to the fact that the Government is not aware of the
 capacity of the private institutes to provide the trained manpower in this sector.     The Committee feels
 that in  the absence of such data, the Government will not be able to devise proper  strategy to meet the
 requirement of trained manpower.   Recognising the role of private sector in providing the trained
 manpower, the Committee recommends that the assessment regarding capacity of  private institutes to
 provide trained manpower should be made at the  earliest.   The Committee also recommends that the
 Government should evolve attractive packages for ensuring greater involvement of private sector in
 this field.                                                

REPORT
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/41streport.htm[28-08-2018 12:45:04]
The  Committee appreciates that these training institutes are trying to generate  their own resources but
 feels that pace of work in this field is rather  slow.   The Committee observes that the  Ministry of
 Tourism has not been able to allocate sufficient funds to these  training institutes due to the financial
 constraints.   The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should  make all these
 institutes self-sufficient so that the desired objective of  reducing the dependence of these institutes the
 Central Budget is achieved in a  time bound manner.        
(Paras 38, 39 and 41)  
Marketing & Publicity  
The  Committee feels that the potential of the information technology in marketing  and promotion of
 tourism in India has not been exploited to the desired  extent.   The Committee find that most of  the
 projects in this field such as installation of Touch screen based  information Kiosks at Delhi, Mumbai,
 Calcutta and Chennai, developing thematic  CD-ROMs on Wild Life, Railways, North-Eastern States,
 providing IVRS at Mumbai  and Calcutta etc. are still underway and hopes that the completion of these
 projects will spread awareness among domestic and foreign tourists and help in  promoting tourism in
 India.  
A perusal of the above data indicates that on the one hand there has been under  utilisation of funds in
 the plan side and on the other hand, there has been excess expenditure of funds on the non-plan side. 
The  Committee is of the view that substantial portions of the total budgetary  allocations of the Ministry
 of Tourism are being provided for overseas campaign  since the last few years.   However, the  net
 increase in number of foreign tourists does not justify the high amount of  allocations in this sector.  
 The  contention of the Ministry of Tourism delinking the  performance of tourist offices abroad from the
 increase/fall in foreign tourist  arrival in India does not hold good.   Without any correlation between the
 two, it would be very difficult to  assess the performance of the tourist offices abroad and review their
 location  keeping in mind marketing potential, as recommended by the WTO report.   In view of the huge
 allocations made in this area, the Committee recommends that cost benefit ratio in respect of each
 overseas office should be worked out and these offices should be made  accountable for the foreign
 tourist arrival in India.   The Government should also explore the possibility of utilising  the services of
 professional agencies abroad to boost the image of India as tourist destination instead of having
 separate tourist offices overseas.   The Committee recommends that immediate  necessary action may be
 taken upon all the recommendations of the World Tourism  Organisations and the action taken upon
 them may be brought to the notice of  the Committee.  
(Paras 43, 44 and 46)  
Eco-Tourism  
The Committee feels that there  are numerous places scattered throughout the country, such as
 mountains,  wildlife and beach resorts, which hold unlimited varieties of flora and fauna  to entertain
 eco-friendly tourists.   The  Committee, therefore, recommends that special attention should be given on
 the  development of eco-tourism, which will not only boost tourism but also help  protect landscape,
 fauna and flora from destruction by modern development.   India offers a huge potential for adventure
 tourism like trekking, mountaineering, river rafting, winter sports, water  sports etc. and efforts should
 also be made to attract tourists to these  places.
(Para  47)
North-Eastern States &  Sikkim
The Committee observes that  inspite of the enormous tourism potential of the area, the Government has

REPORT
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/41streport.htm[28-08-2018 12:45:04]
 so  far neglected the North-Eastern region.  
The Committee welcomes decision  to earmark 10% of the total budget allocation for the North-Eastern
 States & Sikkim.   The Committee feel that  since the total budgetary allocation of the Ministry of
 Tourism is only  Rs.135.00 crores, the allocation for North-Eastern State & Sikkim is very  meagre.   The
 Committee, therefore,  recommends that in order to fully exploit the tourism potential of the region,  the
 Ministry should chalk out schemes/projects pertaining to Tourist  Infrastructure, Training and
 Promotion & Publicity etc. for development and  promotion of tourism in the region so that the funds
 provided for the purpose  are fully utilised.   Efforts should be  made for speedy implementation of the
 various projects, in co-ordination with  the State Governments, so that the North-Eastern regions of the
 country could  become the leading tourist destinations of the country in the near future.                         
  (Paras 48 and 49)
Andaman & Nikobar and  Lakshadweep Islands
The Committee observes that  inspite of its geographical location and tremendous potential for attracting
 a  large number of Tourists both Indian and foreign, no consideration has been  given to the Andaman &
 Nicobar and Lakshadweep Islands.   These island offer tourist attraction in a  big way and there is
 immense potential for development of tourism.   However, very little appears to have been  done for the
 promotion of tourism in these islands.   The Committee, therefore, recommends that these islands
 should be  developed at a faster pace from the tourism point of view.   The Committee also recommends
 that Andaman  & Nicobar and Lakshadweep Islands should also be considered within the  ambit of the
 Government policy for development of tourism in the N.E. region.                                             
         (Para 50)
National Tourism Development Fund  The Committee appreciates the setting up of National Tourism
 Development  Fund.   The Committee recommends that the  fund be made functional and necessary
 formalities therefor be obtained on  priority basis.   Given the financial  constraints the Ministry of
 Tourism is facing at present, the Committee hopes the fund would meet the demands of the
 entrepreneurs for assistance required  for executing tourism projects in the country, which will bring
 improvement in  education and standardise the tourism product to meet international  levels.    The
 Committee further hopes that the Planning Commission and the Ministry of Finance would release the
 remaining amount of Rs.9.00 crores in the coming year to the corpus of Rs.10.00  crores, as proposed by
 the Ministry of Tourism.   (Para 52)  
India Tourism  Development Corporation
The  Committee observes that there has been under-utilisation of funds to the extent  of 30% in 1998-99.  
 Also plan outlay for  the year 1999-2000 was reduced from Rs.70.00 crores at BE stage to Rs.35.00
 crores at RE stage. Now for the year 2000-2001, the proposed outlay is Rs.60.00 crores.   The
 Committee feels that in  view of the financial performance during the last few years, the proposed
 outlay for 2000-2001 is on the higher side.        
The Committee also observes that the profits earned by ITDC are going  down since the last few years.  
 An  increase of 15% in net profit in 2000-2001 as compared to 1999-2000 is expected, but these are
 only projected and not actual figures.   The Committee notes with concern that no  regular Chairman has
 been appointed for the last two years, which has also  adversely affected the performance of ITDC.   The
 Committee recommends that a full time Chairman of ITDC may be  appointed at the earliest so that
 declining trend in overall performance of  ITDC may be arrested.Paras 55 and 56)
Coordination between  Ministry of Tourism and Ministry of Civil Aviation
Tourism is closely interlinked  with Civil Aviation Sector.   The  Committee feels that air linking of the

REPORT
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/41streport.htm[28-08-2018 12:45:04]
 various tourist places in the country  as well as places abroad from where tourist arrival is expected is
 essential  for development of tourism in India.   The Committee, therefore, recommends that Ministry of
 Tourism and  Ministry of Civil Aviation should make coordinated efforts in this direction. (Para 57)  
General Observation
The Committee has failed to understand as to why the  Government has been ignoring such an important
 sector and not providing  sufficient funds, which are required by the Ministry for the development of
 tourism  in the country.   The Committee expresses its anguish over the treatment being meted out to the
 tourism industry for  which a meagre allocation is being approved and that too is being subjected to
 drastic cuts every year at RE stage. Although during April 99 to December 99,  the estimated foreign
 exchange earning was Rs.8817.91 crores, for the last  three financial years, the plan outlay for the
 tourism, the second highest  foreign exchange earning sector, has been more or less equal to the cost of
 one  fighter plane. The Committee, therefore, recommends that keeping in view the  role of tourism in
 the future of Indian economy, Ministry of Finance and  Planning Commission should make available
 sufficient funds to the Ministry of  Tourism so that it could take adequate steps for the promotion and
 development  of tourism in the country.
(Para 58)

REPORT
 
 The Civil Aviation Sector provides services, which can be categorised as operational, infrastructural and
 regulatory-cum-developmental. The task of framing of national policies and programmes for development
 and regulation of Civil Aviation Sector in the country has been entrusted to the Ministry of Civil Aviation.
 The Ministry of Civil Aviation is also responsible for planning or executing the schemes for qualitative
 growth and expansion of civil air transport. The Ministry oversees the establishment of new aerodromes,
 maintenance and upgradation of the existing aerodromes, regulation of carriage of traffic by air and
 ensuring civil aviation security. Railway Safety, including enquiries into serious railway accidents, also
 constitutes one of the allied functions of the Ministry.
2. The civil aviation sector is monitored and regulated by two separate organisations under the Ministry of
 Civil Aviation i.e. Directorate General of Civil Aviation and Bureau of Civil Aviation Security. The
 functions pertaining to Railway Safety are entrusted to a Commission. The Ministry of Civil Aviation has
 the following Public Sector Undertakings/Companies/Autonomous Bodies under its administrative
 control:-
i. Air India Limited and its wholly owned subsidiaries viz. Hotel Corporation of India Limited and Air
 India Charters Limited.
ii. Indian Airlines Limited and its wholly owned subsidiary viz. Airlines Allied Services Limited.
iii. Airports Authority of India.
iv. Pawan Hans Helicopters Limited.
v. Indira Gandhi Rashtriya Uran Academy.
 
3. Demand No.7 pertains to the Ministry of Civil Aviation. The Committee considered the Demands for
th

 Grants of the Ministry for the year 2000-2001 at its meeting held on 24  March 2000. The Secretary and
 other official were also present in the meeting and clarified the points raised by the Members on the
 subject.
4. For the year 2000-2001, the total outlay for the Ministry is Rs.2229.52 crores out of which the gross
 budgetary support is Rs.55.00 crores. The remaining amount i.e. Rs.2174.52 crores includes the internal
 and extra budgetary resources.
5. Out of the total budgetary support of Rs.55.00 crores Rs.37.53 have been allotted to Airports Authority
 of India, Rs.6.75 to Indira Gandhi Rashtriya Uran Academy, Rs.5.00 crores to Director General of Civil
 Aviation and Rs.5.72 have been earmarked for Bureau of Civil Aviation Security. No Budgetary support
 has been extended to Air India Ltd., Indian Airlines Ltd., Pawan Hans Helicopters Ltd. and Hotel
 Corporation of India, pending decision on proposal of restructuring thereof.
6. The Committee is of the view that Civil Aviation sector is closely linked to the tourism and trade
 sectors. Therefor, it is important that airport infrastructure and air service should not be allowed to
 suffer for want of budgetary support since degradation of Civil Aviation sector would also affect the
 trade and tourism. The Committee, therefore, recommends that Ministry of Civil Aviation should
 make a realistic assessment of requirements of various organisations and if necessary, increase the
 budgetary support to maintain the existing Civil Aviation infrastructure properly till a final
 decision is taken about restructuring thereof.
7. The Committee took up provisions of plan outlays of some of the undertakings within the purview of the
 Ministry of Civil Aviation for extensive examinations as per details given in the succeeding paragraphs.
BUREAU OF CIVIL AVIATION SECURITY
8. Bureau of Civil Aviation Security (BCAS) is responsible for laying down the standards of pre-
embarkation security and anti-sabotage measures in respect of civil flights in India. Actual enforcement on
 the ground is entrusted to the respective State/UT Police and Central Industrial Security Force (CISF).
 The Bureau keeps a constant vigil and monitors the enforcement of the security measures.
9. The approved plan outlay of BCAS for the year 2000-2001 is Rs.5.72 crores which includes Rs.90.00
 lakhs for setting up of Civil Aviation Security Academy for imparting training to the security personnel
 deployed at the various airports. The project is in the formulation stage and a token provision has been
 made for this scheme. The Committee was informed that since the land for the proposed Academy could
 not be identified, the work could not commence and the provision made for this scheme had to be
 dropped. The Committee feels that security, an important element of civil aviation operations, is
 being ignored by the Government, as is evident from the way the project of setting up of Civil
 Aviation Security Academy is being handled. The Committee is disappointed to note that amounts
 are being earmarked for setting up the Civil Aviation Security Academy since 1998-99, however, till
 now even the land where the Academy is proposed to be set up has not been identified. During 1998-
99 and 1999-2000, amounts to the tune of Rs.10.00 lakhs and Rs.50.00 lakhs respectively, allocated
 for the purpose, lapsed. Now for the year 2000-2001, Rs.90.00 lakhs have been earmarked. The
 Committee is of the view keeping Rs.90.00 lakhs as token provision is on the high side. The
 Committee, therefore, recommends that necessary formalities may be completed expeditiously so

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/42rep.htm[28-08-2018 12:46:05]
 that the training services of the Academy are available to the nation.
ANTI HIJACKING MEASURES
10. The Bureau of Civil Aviation Security has a Contingency Plan to deal with emergencies arising out of
 hijacking and other threats to civil aviation. Among other things, it provides for the establishment of a
 Control Room at each airport. The Control Room comes into action immediately on the occurrence of any
 emergency, like unlawful seizure of aircraft etc. Keeping in view the operational requirements, the
 Contingency Plan is being suitably amended and is under review.
11. The Committee was apprised that subsequent to the incident of hijacking of Indian Airlines flight IC-
814 at Kathmandu, the following special steps have been taken to prevent hijacking and other terrorist
 activities:
(i) Deployment of Central Industrial Security Force (CISF) personnel in place of State Police
 for security duties at the domestic operational airports in a phased manner. The CISF has
 already taken over the security duties at some of the airports.
(ii) Frisking of passengers and hand baggage at the time of entry into sterile area has been
 tightened. Ladder point secondary frisking has been introduced.
(iii) Strict control on access to the airports is being ensured by comprehensive review of Photo
 Identity Cards to restrict the number of pass-holders and banning of entry of the visitors upto
 31.3.2000.
(iv) Deployment of Sky Marshals on flights at random basis as an added safety precaution.
(v) Replacement of old X-ray machines and installation of new colour X-ray machines
 wherever necessary so as to ensure that at least two X-ray machines are available at every
 point.
(vi) Modernisation and upgradation of security related technological set up of the airports is
 being done in a phased manner.
12. The Committee expresses its concern on the hijacking of the flight IC-814 at Kathmandu. The
 Committee also notes the security measures taken for further beefing up security at airports and
 safety of air passengers after the hijacking incident. The Committee feels that the contingency plan
 devised by BCAS has not proved effective while handling the plane-hijacking incident. The
 Committee is of the view that any contingency plan should ensure avoiding delay in decision-
making process and recommends that the latest technological equipments available in the field of
 airport security may be procured at the earliest to prevent recurrence of any such incident. The
 Committee feels that the lesson drawn from the handling of the hijacked flight No.IC-814 should
 help the concerned Departments in drawing future plans to handle such situations. While
 strengthening the airport security, due care should be taken that the passengers are not
 unnecessarily harassed.

 inconvenience to the Haj pilgrims as well as the visitors/relatives waiting at the airport.

11.     In the Ninth Plan, the objective of National Highway development is to lay stress on increased mobility of road
 transport system.  It is proposed to follow a methodology by which the traffic would be provided with “high level of
 service” corridors along selected routes running across the country and then distributed to spurs of lower level of
 service.  This would be achieved by developing National Highways falling in the alignment of NHDP (spine and grid
 system) comprising of the Golden Quadrilateral connecting the four metropolitan cities of Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and
 Calcutta, North-South (Kashmir to Kanyakumari) and East-West (Silchar to Saurashtra) corridors and NH-47
 connecting Salem to Cochin.  The total length that will be upgraded under NHDP is 12000 kms. (Approx.)  This project
 has been entrusted to National Highways Authority of India (NHAI).  The total fund requirement for this project has
 been worked out at Rs.54,000 crores and this project is targeted to be completed by March 2009.  Four laning of
 Golden Quadrilateral is targeted for completion by March 2004.  Also expressways would be considered along the
 existing alignments based on the projected traffic.  With this spine and grid system, it would be possible to optimise the
 utilisation of resources and, at the same time, ensure increased mobility.  This will also provide a basis for achieving
 uniform economic development over all the regions of the country.
 12.     The Committee appreciates this ambitious National Highway Development Programme which comprises 4/6
 laning of Highways from Srinagar to Kanyakumari and Silchar to Saurashtra of North-South and East-West Corridor
 respectively and Golden Quadrilateral connecting Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and Calcutta. 
13.     The Committee, however, is disappointed to find that the coastal area from Mumbai towards south upto
 Kanyakumari that includes major ports viz Mumbai, JNPT, Mangalore, Goa, Cochin and other  important centres like
 Karvar have been ignored.  This coastal area has been completely left out which is of great importance from the point
 of view of commercial and industrial production.
14.     The Committee, therefore, recommends that road connectivity of the Golden Quadrilateral and Corridors with the
 Major Ports of the country should also be taken into consideration while implementing the National Highway
 Development Programme. 
15.     It has also come to the notice of the Committee that several State Governments are interested in participating in
 this ambitious National Highway Development Project Programme.  State Governments have developed and spent huge
 money on stretches of roads, which are situated within their States, but those stretches have been neglected by the
 National Highway Authority of India and have not been included in the Golden Quadrilateral and Corridors. 
16.     The Committee is of the view that the initiative taken by the State Governments should be taken into account
 while implementing the NHD Programme and stretches of roads developed by State Governments should also be
 included in the NHD Programme, as State Governments have spent money on them.  This will definitely ensure faster
 execution of NHD Programme and avoid duplication of work. The Committee also feels that it would reduce the
 financial burden of the Govt. of India to some extent.

39. The Committee was informed that in view of the accumulating huge losses, the Government of India has decided in
 February 2000 to wind up the Indian Road Construction Corporation Ltd. (IRCC).  The existing employees of the
 Corporation numbering 151 will be forced to opt for voluntary retirement as per the present scheme, failing which they
 will be entitled to compensation payable on closure as per the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947.
40.  The Committee also came to know that the reasons for the accumulation of huge losses was due to the ban imposed
 by the Central Government prohibiting the corporation from undertaking any further work.  The said ban was imposed
 in February, 1986 and inspite of repeated requests of the Corporation, the Central Government did not allow the
 Corporation to undertake any new work.  The Corporation thus was made non-functional by the Central
 Government.
         
41.     The Committee fails to understand as to why the Government have imposed the ban on IRCC prohibiting it from
 undertaking further work especially so when it had been a profit making undertaking and for not taking any steps for its
 revival.  The Committee is aware of the fact that in the past, as and when any undertaking/establishment was closed, the
 Central Government consistently followed the policy of absorbing the employees in its other Public Sector
 Undertakings/establishments rather than terminating their services viz Vayudoot Airlines, Akbar Hotel, Lakshmi
 Commercial Bank and New Bank etc.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that consistent with the national
 approach and in view of the increasing manpower requirements of NHAI, the possibility of accommodating the
 employees of IRCC in PSUs of the Ministry may be explored.
       
 ROAD TRANSPORT SECTOR
42.       The Committee was apprised that to keep pace with the economic development in the country and consequent
 surge in demand for transport services, passenger and freight, various modes of transport experienced substantial
 growth over the years.  Road transport, however, is the most dominant mode of transport both for movement of
 passengers and goods and is likely to continue to enjoy this status increasingly in the coming years.  The users
 preference towards road transport is on account of its inherent advantages viz. easy availability, adaptability to
 individual needs, door-to-door service, and reliability.  At present 80% of passengers and over 60% of freight is
 estimated to move by roads.  It also acts as a feeder service to Railways, Ports and Air Traffic.
 
43.     The Ministry further apprised the Committee about the various schemes pertaining to Road Transport Sector.

 Safety; Grants-in-aid to agencies administering Road Safety; Training Programme; Study on Transport Industry; other

 disinvestment of Air India and decided to discuss the matter with the representatives of Ministry of Civil Aviation and

 restructuring/disinvestment in Air India.  The main recommendations of the Commission are as under :-
(i)   Infusion of Government equity of Rs.1000 crores and finally bringing down the Government share holding in Air India
